children.text: asmai evaṃvide evaṃvidarthaṃ bhavati //1//
children.translated_text: For this one who knows thus — it becomes so for the sake of such a knower. // 1 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.2.1: 'There was nothing whatsoever here in the beginning.' 'Here' — in the sphere of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), nothing whatsoever — no particular differentiated entity in the form of name and form — existed, i.e., was present, 'in the beginning' — before the creation of the beginningless [universe]. [Objection:] Would it then be mere void, since the <s>śruti</s> says 'there was nothing whatsoever here'? [Reply:] Neither the effect nor the cause existed. And because of origination — for a pot originates, hence before its origination the pot is non-existent. [Objection:] But the cause is not non-existent, since a lump of clay and the like are seen. [Reply:] Only that which is not perceived is non-existent. Let the effect be non-existent, but not the cause, since it is perceived. [Reply:] No, because before origination nothing at all is perceived. [Objection:] If non-perception is the ground of non-existence, then before the origination of the entire world, neither cause nor effect is perceived; therefore let everything be non-existent. [Reply:] No, because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'It was covered by Death.' For if nothing at all existed — neither that which covers nor that which is covered — then it would not say 'this was covered by Death.' For one does not say 'the son of a barren woman is covered by a sky-flower.' But the <s>śruti</s> does say 'this was covered by Death'; therefore both existed before origination — the cause by which it was covered and the effect that was covered — since the <s>śruti</s> is authoritative and this can also be inferred. And the existence of cause and effect before origination is inferred: for the origination of an existent effect is seen when the cause is present, and is not seen when it is absent. Therefore, the existence of the cause of the world too before its origination is inferred, just as the existence of the cause of a pot and the like. [Objection:] The cause of pots and the like is also non-existent, since without destroying the lump of clay and so forth, the pot and the like do not originate. [Reply:] No, because clay and the like are the cause. For clay, gold, and the like are the cause of pots, bangles, and the like — not the particular shape of the lump — since [pots and the like] come into being even in its absence. Even when the particular lump-shape is absent, the origination of effects such as pots and bangles is seen from the mere causal substance of clay, gold, and the like alone. Therefore the particular lump-shape is not the cause of pots, bangles, and the like. But when the substance of clay, gold, and the like is absent, pots, bangles, and the like do not arise — hence the substance of clay, gold, and the like alone is the cause, not the particular lump-shape. For every cause, in producing an effect, brings about the disappearance of its own previously manifested effect and produces another effect, since multiple effects cannot co-exist simultaneously in a single cause. And the destruction of a prior effect does not entail the destruction of the cause itself. Therefore, the observation that an effect arises upon the destruction of a lump and the like is not a valid reason for the non-existence of the cause before origination. [Objection:] Since clay and the like do not exist apart from the lump and the like, this is improper. [Reply:] When the prior effect in the form of lump and the like is destroyed, the cause in the form of clay and the like is not destroyed — it continues in other effects like pots — this is what you say is improper. [Objection:] Because the cause is not perceived apart from its effects such as lump and pot? [Reply:] No, because the causal substances clay and the like are seen to persist when the lump and the like cease and pots and the like arise. [Objection:] The observation of continuity is merely due to similarity, not the actual continuity of the cause. [Reply:] No, because when the very particles of clay and the like that were in the lump are directly perceived in the pot, it is improper to construct [explanations based on] similarity and the like, since there is no scope for such pseudo-inference. For there is no contradiction between perception and inference in their unerring nature — since inference is always based on prior perception, and if [inference were unreliable] there would be universal distrust. Moreover, if everything is momentary, then the cognition 'this is the same' would require another cognition of identity, and that another, leading to infinite regress; and since even the cognition 'this is similar to that' would be false, there would be universal distrust everywhere. And if neither the cognition 'that' nor the cognition 'this' has an agent, the relation [between them] is impossible. [Objection:] The relation is through similarity. [Reply:] No, because it is impossible for the cognitions 'that' and 'this' to have each other as their objects. And without having each other as objects, the apprehension of similarity is impossible. [Objection:] The cognition of identity arises even without [actual] similarity. [Reply:] No, because then even the cognitions 'that' and 'this' would, like the cognition of similarity, have non-existent objects. [Objection:] Let all cognitions have non-existent objects. [Reply:] No, because then even the cognition of cognition would have a non-existent object. [Objection:] Let that be so too. [Reply:] No, because if all cognitions are false, even the cognition of their falsity is impossible. Therefore, the claim that the cognition of identity arises from similarity when things are [really] non-existent is false. Hence, the existence of the cause before the origination of the effect is established. And because the effect has the characteristic of manifestation. The existence of the effect too before its origination is established. How? Because it has the characteristic of manifestation — that which has manifestation as its defining mark. Manifestation is the attainment of being directly an object of cognition. Just as an object such as a pot that is covered by darkness and the like in the world, upon the removal of the covering by light and the like, attains the status of being an object of cognition — it does not deviate from its prior existence. Similarly, we understand that this world too [existed] before its origination. For a non-existent pot is not perceived even when the sun has risen. [Objection:] It is not perceived because of the absence of non-existence — it would indeed be perceived [if it existed]. [Reply:] For you, the effect such as a pot is never non-existent, so it would always be perceived when the sun has risen and the lump of clay is present and there is no covering of darkness and the like, since it [always] exists. [Reply:] No, because the covering is of two kinds. For the effect such as a pot has two kinds of covering: for [the pot] that is not yet differentiated from the clay and other [components], [the covering is] darkness, wall, and the like; and prior to its manifestation from clay and the like, [the covering is] the configuration of the particles of clay and the like in the form of other effects such as lumps. Therefore, even though the effect such as a pot exists before origination, it is not perceived because it is covered. But the difference in words, concepts, and cognitions of 'destroyed' and 'originated,' 'existence' and 'non-existence,' is relative to the two kinds of manifestation and concealment. [Objection:] This is improper because the covering by lump and potsherd is different [in nature from covering by darkness and wall]. For darkness, wall, and the like, which are the covering of pots and the like, are seen to be in a different location from the pot, but a lump or potsherd, which are seen in the same location, are not like that. Therefore, the claim that because the pot, though existing, is covered by the configuration of lump and potsherd, it is not perceived — is improper, due to the difference in the nature of the covering. [Reply:] No, because milk in water is seen to be in the same location as its covering, the milk and the like. [Objection:] Since the particles such as potsherd-fragments are included within the effect such as a pot, they are not a covering. [Reply:] No, because when differentiated [from the pot], they constitute different effects, and hence can serve as a covering. [Objection:] If one should make effort only for the removal of the covering — if the effect such as a pot exists even in the states of lump and potsherd but is not perceived because it is covered, then should not one who desires the effect such as a pot make effort only for the destruction of that covering, rather than for the production of the pot? And this is not the case. Therefore the claim that it is not perceived because, though existing, it is covered, is improper. [Reply:] No, because there is no fixed rule. For the manifestation of a pot and the like is not invariably [achieved] through the mere effort of destruction alone. In the case of pots and the like covered by darkness, effort is seen [to be directed] toward the production of a lamp and the like. [Objection:] That too is only for the destruction of darkness. [Reply:] Whatever effort is made for the production of a lamp and the like, that too is for the removal of darkness; when that [darkness] is destroyed, the pot is perceived by itself — nothing [new] is added. [Objection:] [This is wrong] because the pot is perceived as having light. [Reply:] Just as the pot is perceived as possessing light, it was not so perceived before the making of the lamp. Therefore, the making of the lamp is not merely for the removal of darkness; rather, it is for the [pot's] possession of light, since what is perceived is perceived precisely as possessing light. In some cases, effort may also be directed toward the destruction of the covering, as in the destruction of a wall and the like. Therefore, there is no fixed rule that one who desires manifestation must make effort only for the destruction of the covering. And because of the fixed purposefulness [of specific causal operations]: We said that the effect existing in the cause is the covering of other effects. If, in that case, effort were made only for the destruction of the previously manifested effect — the lump — or of the potsherd which is in the way, then other effects such as halves and powder would also arise, and the pot, being covered by those too, would not be perceived — thus yet another effort would be required. Therefore, for one desiring the manifestation of a pot and the like, the specific operation of the causal factors is necessarily purposeful. Therefore, the very same effect [exists] even before origination. And because of the difference in cognitions of past and future: The cognitions 'a past pot' and 'a future pot' — like the cognition of a present pot — cannot reasonably be without an object. And because there is activity motivated by a future object of desire. For activity motivated by a non-existent desired object is never seen in the world. And because the knowledge of <s>yogins</s> concerning past and future is valid. If the future pot were non-existent, then the omniscient direct perception of the future pot would be false — but direct perception is not to be explained away figuratively. We have already stated the inference for the existence of the pot. And because of contradiction: If, while potters and others are engaged in activity for the purpose of a pot, it is ascertained by a valid means that the pot will come into being in a certain future time, and yet it is said that at that very time the pot is non-existent — this is contradictory. If it is said that the future non-pot is non-existent, then it means it will not come into being — as when one says 'this pot does not exist [now].' But if it is said that the pot is non-existent before its origination, then, while potters and others are engaged in activity for the purpose of a pot, just as the potters and others are present in the form of their activity, the pot is not present in that same way — this is the meaning of the word 'non-existent,' and it is not contradictory. Why? Because the pot exists in its own future form. For the present existence of the lump or of the potsherd is not the existence of the pot. Nor is their future state the [future state of] the pot. Therefore, the statement 'the pot is non-existent before origination' — relative to the present existence of the potter's activity — is not contradictory. If the pot's own future nature, its effect-form, were negated, that negation would be contradictory. But you do not negate that. And not all active causal factors have the same mode of present existence or future existence. Moreover, among the four kinds of non-existence: the mutual non-existence (<s>itaretarābhāva</s>) of the pot is seen as something other than the pot — just as the non-existence of a pot is merely cloth and the like, not the pot's own nature itself. And the cloth, which is the non-existence of the pot, is not of the nature of non-existence while being existent; rather, it is of the nature of existence alone. Similarly, the prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>), the absolute destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>), and the absolute non-existence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>) of the pot would also be other than the pot — since they are designated by [reference to] the pot, just as mutual non-existence. And similarly, they would be of the nature of existence, [just as mutual non-existence]. This being so, the prior non-existence of the pot does not mean that the pot's own nature itself does not exist before origination. But if by 'prior non-existence of the pot' the very nature of the pot itself were meant, then the designation 'of the pot' would be impossible. And if one were to designate [it] by a fiction, as [one speaks of] 'the body of the son of a stone' — even so, 'the prior non-existence of the pot' would be a designation of a fictitious non-existence by [reference to] the pot, not of the pot's own nature itself. [Objection:] But if the non-existence of the pot is something other than the pot — this has already been answered. Furthermore, before origination, for the pot which is non-existent like a hare's horn, the relation with the existence of its own cause is impossible, since a relation requires two real terms. [Objection:] There is no fault for things that are inseparably connected (<s>ayutasiddha</s>). [Reply:] No, because inseparable connection between existence and non-existence is impossible. For between an existent and a non-existent, there could be either separable or inseparable connection — but not between existence and non-existence, nor between two non-existences. Therefore, it is established that the effect exists even before origination. What is the nature of that Death by which [the world] was covered? To this he says: '<s>Aśanāyā</s>' — the desire to eat is <s>aśanāyā</s> (hunger); that itself — it is the mark of Death, by Death marked by that hunger. How is hunger Death? This is explained: 'For hunger is Death.' The word 'hi' illuminates a well-known reason. For one who desires to eat, immediately after hunger, kills creatures; therefore he is marked by hunger as Death — hence he says 'for hunger [is Death].' Hunger is the attribute of the intellect-self (<s>buddhyātman</s>); this <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>, who abides in the intellect, is called Death. By that Death, this effect [the world] was covered — just as pots and bells are covered by clay in its lump-state. 'That [Death] created mind.' 'That' refers to mind. That Death under discussion, desiring to create the forthcoming effects, created the internal organ called 'mind,' characterized by volition (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) and the like, capable of contemplating those effects. With what intention did he create mind? This is explained: '<s>Ātmanvī</s>' — 'May I become endowed with a self.' 'May I become possessed of mind through this self, i.e., mind' — this is the intention. That <s>Prajāpati</s>, having become possessed of mind through the manifested mind, worshipping, honoring, [thinking] 'I am fulfilled' — he moved about. As that <s>Prajāpati</s> worshipped and honored, the Waters, of the nature of essence (<s>rasa</s>), being accessories of worship, were born. Here it should be stated that the origination of the three [elements] beginning with space occurred prior [to this], based on the authority of other <s>śruti</s> passages and the impossibility of an alternative in the order of creation. 'While worshipping, there was joy (<s>ka</s>) for me — this is water (<s>udaka</s>)' — thus he thought. Because he is Death, from that very reason, fire used in the <s>Aśvamedha</s> sacrifice has the name '<s>Arka</s>' — its being called <s>Arka</s> has this etymological basis. From worshipping (<s>arcana</s>) — performing worship that causes happiness — and from its connection with water, fire has this secondary name '<s>Arka</s>.'

children.text: kaḥ punarasāvarkaḥ? ityucyate-
children.translated_text: Now, what is that <s>arka</s>? It is said:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,2.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.2.2]

children.text:
āpo vā arkaḥ |
tad yad apāṃ śara āsīt tat samahanyata |
sā pṛthivy abhavat |
tasyām aśrāmyat |
tasya śrāntasya taptasya tejoraso niravartatāgniḥ || BrhUp_1,2.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'Water indeed is the <s>arka</s>. That which was the froth of the waters — that solidified. That became the earth. On it he exerted himself. From him, wearied and heated, his essence of splendor came forth — fire.' // BṛhUp 1.2.2 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,2.2 āpo vai yā arcanāṅgabhūtāstā evārko 'gnerarkasya hetutvāt /
apsu cāgniḥ pratiṣiṭhita iti /
na punaḥ sākṣādevārkastāḥ, tāsāmaprakaraṇāt, agneśca prakaraṇam /
vakṣyati ca'ayamagnirarkaḥ'(bṛha.u.1 / 2 / 7) iti /
tattatra yadapāṃ śara iva śaro dadhna iva maṇḍabhūtamāsīttatsamahanyata saṅgātamāpadyata tejasā bāhyāntaḥpacyamānam /
liṅgavyatyayena vā yo 'ṣāṃ śaraḥ samahanyateti /
sā pṛthivyabhavatsa saṃghāto yeyaṃ pṛthivī sābhavat /
tābhyo 'dbhayo aṇḍamabhinirvṛttamityarthaḥ /
tasyāṃ pṛthivyāmutpāditāyāṃ sa mṛtyu prajāpatiraśrāmyacchramayukto babhūva /
sarvo hi lokaḥ kārya kṛtvā śrāmyati /
prajāpataścatanmahatkāryaṃ yatpṛthivīsargaḥ /
kiṃ tasya śrāntasya? ityucyate tasya śrāntasya taptasya khinnasya tejorasasteja eva rasastejoraso rasaḥ sāro niravartata prajāpatiśarīrānniṣkrānta ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: What happened to him when wearied? It is said: from him, wearied and heated, i.e., exhausted — his essence of splendor, that is, the quintessence of his radiance, came forth, issued from <s>Prajāpati</s>'s body — this is the meaning.

children.text: ko 'sau niṣkrānta? agniḥ /
children.translated_text: What was it that came forth? <s>Agni</s> (fire).

children.text: so 'ṇḍasyāntarvirāṭ prajāpatiḥ prathamajaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātavān jātaḥ /
children.translated_text: He, inside the cosmic egg, became <s>Virāj</s> <s>Prajāpati</s>, the first-born, endowed with the aggregate of body and organs.

children.text: sa vai śarīri prathamaḥ iti smaraṇāt //2//
children.translated_text: Because of the <s>smṛti</s> text: 'He indeed was the first embodied one.' // 2 //

[Commentary:] The waters that served as components of the act of worship (<s>arcana</s>) — they indeed are the <s>arka</s>, because water is the cause of <s>Agni</s>, the <s>arka</s>. And [it is said] '<s>Agni</s> is established in the waters.' But they are not directly the <s>arka</s> themselves, because they are not the topic [under discussion], while <s>Agni</s> is the topic. And [the text] will say: 'This fire is the <s>arka</s>' (BṛhUp 1.2.7). There, that which was the froth of the waters — like the froth, the cream-like surface of curds — that solidified, became compacted, being cooked internally and externally by heat. Or, by interchange of gender: 'that which was their froth solidified.' That became the earth — that solidified mass became this earth. From those waters, the cosmic egg was produced — this is the meaning. On that earth, once it was produced, <s>Mṛtyu</s> <s>Prajāpati</s> exerted himself, became fatigued. For everyone in the world becomes weary after performing work. And that great work of <s>Prajāpati</s> was the creation of the earth.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,2.3
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.2.3]

children.text:
sa tredhātmānaṃ vyakurutādityaṃ tṛtīyaṃ vāyuṃ tṛtīyam |
sa eṣa prāṇas tredhāvihitaḥ |
tasya prācī dik śiro 'sau cāsau cermau |
athāsya pratīcī dik puccham asau cāsau ca sakthyau |
dakṣiṇā codīcī ca pārśve |
dyauḥ pṛṣṭham antarikṣam udaram iyam uraḥ |
sa eṣo 'psu pratiṣṭhitaḥ |
yatra kva caiti tad eva pratitiṣṭhaty evaṃ vidvān || BrhUp_1,2.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'He divided himself threefold — a third as the sun, a third as wind. He is this <s>prāṇa</s> distributed threefold. His head is the eastern direction, and those two are his forelegs. His tail is the western direction, and those two are his hind legs. The south and the north are his flanks. The sky is his back, the atmosphere is his belly, this [earth] is his chest. He is established in the waters. Wherever he goes, there indeed he is established — one who knows thus.' // BṛhUp 1.2.3 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,2.3 sa ca jātaḥ prajāpatistredhā triprakāramātmānaṃ svayameva kāryakaraṇasaṃghātaṃ vyakuruta vyabhajadityetat /
kathaṃ tredhā? ityāha ādityaṃ tṛtīyamagnivāyvapekṣayā trayāṇāṃ pūraṇam akurutetyanuvartate /
tathāgnyādityāpekṣayā vāyuṃ tṛtīyam /
tathā vāyvādityāpekṣayāgniṃ tṛtīyamiti draṣṭavyam /
sāmarthyasya tulyatvāttrayāṇāṃ saṃkhyāpūraṇatve /
sa eṣa prāṇaḥ sarvabhūtānāmātmāpy agnivāyvādityarūpeṇa viśeṣataḥ svenaiva mṛtyvātmanā tredhā vihito vibhakto na virāṭ svarūpopamardanena /
tasyāsya prathamajasyāgneraśvamedhopayogikasyārkasya virājaścityātmakasya aśvasyeva darśanamucyate /
sarvā hi pūrvoktotpattirasya stutyarthetyavocāmaitthamasau śuddhajanmeti /
tasya prācī dikśiro viśiṣṭatvasāmānyāt /
asau cāsau caiśānyāgneyyau īrmau bāhū /
īrayatergatikarmaṇaḥ /
athāsyāgneḥ pratīcī dikpucchaṃ jaghanyobhāgaḥ, prāṅmukhasya pratyagdiksambandhād /
asau cāsau ca vāyavyanairṛtyau sakthyausakthinī pṛṣṭhakoṇatvasāmānyāt /
dakṣiṇā codīcī ca pārśe ubhayadiksambandhasāmānyāt /
dyauḥ pṛṣṭhamantarikṣamudaramiti pūrvavat /
iyamuraḥ adhobhāgasāmānyāt /
children.translated_text: This [earth] is his chest, due to the commonality of being the lower part.

children.text: sa eṣo 'gni prajāpatirūpo lokādyātmako 'gnirapsu pratiṣṭhitaḥ"evamime lokā apsvantaḥ"iti śruteḥ /
children.translated_text: He, this <s>Agni</s> in the form of <s>Prajāpati</s>, having the worlds and such as his body — <s>Agni</s> is established in the waters, because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'Thus these worlds are within the waters.'

children.text: yatra kka ca yasminkasmiṃścideti gacchati tadeva tatraiva pratitiṣṭhati sthitiṃ labhate /
children.translated_text: Wherever he goes, there indeed he is established, obtains stability.

children.text: ko 'sau? evaṃ yathoktamapsu pratiṣṭhitatvamagnevidvānvijānan guṇaphalametat //3//
children.translated_text: Who is he? One who knows thus — who knows that <s>Agni</s> is established in the waters as described — this [stability] is the fruit of that [knowledge]. // 3 //

[Commentary:] And he, <s>Prajāpati</s>, once born, divided himself — his own self, the aggregate of body and organs — threefold, in three ways. How threefold? He says: the sun as a third — in relation to fire and wind, he made it complete the triad; 'he made' is to be supplied. Similarly, wind as a third in relation to fire and the sun. And fire as a third in relation to wind and the sun — this is how it should be understood. Because the capacity of all three is equal in completing the number three. He, this <s>prāṇa</s> (life-force) of all beings, who is also the self, specifically in the forms of fire, wind, and the sun, was distributed, divided threefold by his own nature as <s>Mṛtyu</s> — not [that] <s>Virāj</s> [was divided] by destruction of his own essential nature. Of this first-born <s>Agni</s>, who serves the <s>Aśvamedha</s> sacrifice, who is the <s>arka</s>, who is <s>Virāj</s>, who has the nature of a sacrificial altar — a description is given as if of a horse. For all the previously described creation is for the purpose of praise of this [fire] — as we have said: 'thus is his pure birth.' His head is the eastern direction, due to the commonality of eminence. Those two — the northeast and southeast — are his forelegs, his arms. [This is derived] from the root '<s>īr</s>' meaning 'to move.' And his tail, the hindmost part, is the western direction, since he faces east and thus the western direction is behind him. Those two — the northwest and southwest — are his hind legs, due to their commonality of being rear corners. The south and the north are his two flanks, due to the commonality of being related to both directions. The sky is his back, the atmosphere is his belly — as before.

children.text:
yo 'sau mṛtyuḥ so 'bādikrameṇātmanātmānam aṇḍasyāntaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātavantaṃ virājamagnimasṛjata, tredhā cātmānamakurutetyuktam /
sa kiṃvyāpāraḥ sannasṛjata? ityucyate-
children.translated_text: He who is <s>Mṛtyu</s> — through the sequence beginning with water, by himself, created himself within the cosmic egg as <s>Virāj</s>, the fire, endowed with the aggregate of body and organs, and divided himself threefold — this has been stated. What was he engaged in when he created? It is said:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,2.4
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.2.4]

children.text:
so 'kāmayata -- dvitīyo ma ātmā jāyeteti |
sa manasā vācaṃ mithunaṃ samabhavad aśanāyā mṛtyuḥ |
tad yad reta āsīt sa saṃvatsaro 'bhavat |
na ha purā tataḥ saṃvatsara āsa |
tam etāvantaṃ kālam abibhar yāvānt saṃvatsaraḥ |
tam etāvataḥ kālasya parastād asṛjata |
taṃ jātam abhivyādadāt |
sa bhāṇ akarot |
saiva vāg abhavat || BrhUp_1,2.4 ||
children.translated_text: 'He desired: "May a second self be born for me." He, <s>Mṛtyu</s> identified with hunger, united mind with speech in a coupling. That which was the seed became the year. Before that, there was no year. He bore him for as long a time as the year. After that length of time, he emitted him. When he was born, he opened his mouth at him. He made the sound "bhāṇ." That itself became speech.' // BṛhUp 1.2.4 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,2.4 sa mṛtyurakāmayata kāmitavān /
kim? dvitīyo me mamātmā śarīraṃ yenāhaṃ śarīrī syāṃ sa jāyetotpadyeta ityevametadakāmayata /
sa evaṃ kāmayitvā manasā pūrvotpannena vācaṃ lakṣaṇāṃ mithunaṃ dvandvabhāvaṃ samabhavatsambhavanaṃ kṛtavānmanasā trayīmālocitavān /
trayīvihitaṃ sṛṣṭikramaṃ manasānvālocayadityarthaḥ /
ko 'sau? aśanāyayā lakṣito mṛtyuḥ /
aśanāyā mṛtyurityuktam /
tameva parāmṛśatyanyatra prasaṅgo mā bhūditi /
tadyadreta āsīt-tattatra mithune yadreta āsīt, prathamaśarīriṇaḥ prajāpaterutpattau kāraṇaṃ reto bījaṃ jñānakarmarūpam,trayyālocanāyāṃ yaddṛṣṭavānāsījjanmāntarakṛtam;tadbhāvabhāvito 'paḥ sṛṣṭvā tena retasā bījenāpsvanupraviśya aṇḍarūpeṇa garbhībhūtaḥ sa saṃvatsaro 'bhavat, saṃvatsarakālanirmātā saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatirabhavat /
na ha, purā pūrvam, tatastasmātsaṃvatsarakālanirmātuḥ prajāpateḥ, saṃvatsaraḥ kālo nāma nāsa na babhūva ha /
children.translated_text: Indeed, before, prior to that <s>Prajāpati</s> who was the creator of the time-measure called a year, a time called 'year' did not exist.

children.text: taṃ saṃvatsarakālanirmātāramantargarbhaprajāpatim, yāvāniha prasiddhaḥ kāla etāvantametāvatsaṃvatsaraparimāṇaṃ kālamabibhaḥ bhṛtavānmṛtyuḥ /
children.translated_text: That creator of the time-measure called a year, <s>Prajāpati</s> within the embryo — for as long a period as is well-known here, for that much time equal to a year's measure, <s>Mṛtyu</s> bore him, carried him.

children.text: yāvānsaṃvatsara iha prasiddhaḥ, tataḥ parastātkiṃ kṛtavān? tametāvataḥ kālasya saṃvatsaramātrasya parastād ūrdhvamasṛjata sṛṣṭavān, aṇḍamabhinadityarthaḥ tamevaṃ kumāraṃ jātamagniṃ prathamaśarīriṇam, aśanāyavattvānmṛtyurabhivyādadānmukhavidāraṇaṃ kṛtavānattum;sa ca kumāro bhītaḥ svābhāvikyāvidyayā yukto bhāṇityevaṃ śabdamakarot /
children.translated_text: After the duration of a year — what did he do? After that length of time, the measure of one year, he emitted him, created him — meaning he split open the cosmic egg. When that child was born, the first embodied <s>Agni</s>, <s>Mṛtyu</s>, being hungry, opened his mouth at him — made a gaping motion of the mouth, intending to eat him; and that child, frightened, endowed with natural <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), made the sound 'bhāṇ.'

children.text: saiva vāgabhavat, vāk-śabdo 'bhavat //4//
children.translated_text: That itself became speech — it became the word 'speech.' // 4 //

[Commentary:] He, <s>Mṛtyu</s>, desired, wished. What? 'May a second self, a body, be born for me, by which I would become an embodied one' — thus he desired. Having desired thus, with his mind, which had arisen previously, he united with speech, characterized [by the <s>Vedas</s>], in coupling, in a paired state — he accomplished the union; with his mind he contemplated the three <s>Vedas</s>. He contemplated with his mind the order of creation as prescribed in the three <s>Vedas</s> — this is the meaning. Who was he? <s>Mṛtyu</s> characterized by hunger. 'Hunger is death' was stated [before]. He refers back to him [again], lest there be a digression to something else. That which was the seed — there, in that coupling, the seed, the germ in the form of knowledge and action that was the cause of the first embodied <s>Prajāpati</s>'s production, which he had seen in his contemplation of the three <s>Vedas</s>, [which was] created in a previous birth — imbued with that tendency, having created the waters and having entered them with that seed, having become embryonic in the form of the cosmic egg, he became the year, the creator of the measure of time called a year, he became <s>Prajāpati</s> the year.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,2.5
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.2.5]

children.text:
sa aikṣata yadi vā imam abhimaṃsye kanīyo 'nnaṃ kariṣya iti |
sa tayā vācā tenātmanedaṃ sarvam asṛjata yad idaṃ kiñca -- ṛco yajūṃṣi sāmāni chandāṃsi yajñān prajāṃ paśūn |
sa yad-yad evāsṛjata tattad attum adhriyata |
sarvaṃ vā attīti tad aditer adititvam |
sarvasyāttā bhavati sarvam asyānnaṃ bhavati ya evam etad aditer adititvaṃ veda || BrhUp_1,2.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'He reflected: "If I devour this one, I will make less food." With that speech and with that self [mind], he created all this, whatever there is — the <s>Ṛg</s> [verses], the <s>Yajus</s> [formulae], the <s>Sāman</s> [chants], the meters, the sacrifices, the creatures, and the animals. Whatever he created, he began to devour. Because he eats (<s>atti</s>) everything, therefore is [<s>Mṛtyu</s> called] <s>Aditi</s>, and that is the <s>Aditi</s>-nature of <s>Aditi</s>. One who knows this <s>Aditi</s>-nature of <s>Aditi</s> becomes the eater of all; everything becomes his food.' // BṛhUp 1.2.5 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,2.5 sa aikṣata-sa evaṃ bhītaṃ kṛtaravaṃ kumāraṃ dṛṣṭvā mṛtyuraikṣatekṣitavān aśanāyāvānapi-yadā kadācidvā imaṃ kumāramapimaṃsye-abhipūrvomanyatirhiṃsārthaḥ-hiṃsiṣya ityarthaḥ;kanīyo 'nnaṃ kariṣye kanīyo 'lpamannaṃ kariṣya iti /
evamīkṣitvā tadbhakṣaṇādupararāma bahu hyannaṃ kartavyaṃ dīrghakālabhakṣaṇāya naḥ kanīyaḥ /
tadbhakṣaṇe hi kanīyo 'nnaṃ syādbījabhakṣaṇa iva sasyābhāvaḥ /
sa evamprayojanamannabāhulyamālocya tayyaiva trayyā vācā pūrvoktayā tenaiva cātmanā manasā mithunībhāvamālocanamupagamyopagamyedaṃ sarvaṃ sthāvaraṃ jaṅgamaṃ cāsṛjata yadidaṃ kiñcayatkiñcedam /
kiṃ tat? ṛco yajūṃṣi sāmāni chandāṃsi ca saptagāyatryādīdīni stotraśastrādikarmāṅgabhūtāṃstrividhān mantrāngāyatryādicchandoviśiṣṭān yajñāṃśca tatsādhyānprajāstatkartrīḥ paśūṃśca grāmyānāraṇyānkarmasādhanabhūtān /
nanu trayyā mithunībhūtayāsṛjatetyuktam, ṛgādīneha kathamasṛjateti? naiṣa doṣaḥ, manasastvavyakto 'yaṃ mithunībhāvastrayyā, bāhyastu ṛgādīnāṃ vidyamānānāmeva karmasu viniyogabhāvena vyaktībhāvaḥ sarga iti /
sa prajāpatirevamannavṛddhiṃ buddhvā yadyadeva kriyāsādhanaṃ phalaṃ vā kiñcidasṛjata tattadattuṃ bhakṣayitumadhriyata dhṛtavānmanaḥ /
sarvaṃ kṛtsnaṃ vai yasmādattīti tattasmādaditeraditināmno mṛtyoradititvaṃ prasiddham /
tathā ca mantraḥ-"aditirdyairaditirantarikṣamaditirmātā sa pitā"(yajuḥ.saṃ.25 / 23) ityādiḥ /
sarvasyaitasya jagato 'nnabhūtasyāttā sarvātmanaivabhavatyanyathā virodhāt /
children.translated_text: He who eats everything in this food-constituted universe becomes everything in its entirety — otherwise there would be a contradiction.

children.text: na hi kaścitsarvasyaiko 'ttā dṛśyatetasmātsarvātmā bhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For no one is seen to be a single eater of everything; therefore, he becomes the self of all — this is the meaning.

children.text: sarvamasyānnaṃ bhavati;ata eva sarvātmano hyattuḥ sarvamannaṃ bhavatītyupapadyate /
children.translated_text: Everything becomes his food; precisely because, for the eater who is the self of all, everything indeed becomes food — this is established.

children.text: ya evametadyathoktamaditermṛtyoḥ prajāpateḥ sarvasya adanādadititvaṃ veda tasyaitat phalam //5//
children.translated_text: One who knows this — as described — the <s>Aditi</s>-nature of <s>Aditi</s>, i.e., <s>Mṛtyu</s> <s>Prajāpati</s>, [the nature that arises] from eating everything — for him, this is the fruit. // 5 //

[Commentary:] He reflected — having seen the child thus frightened and crying, <s>Mṛtyu</s>, although hungry, reflected. When — if at any time I devour this child — '<s>abhimanyate</s>' with the prefix '<s>abhi</s>' has the meaning of 'to harm,' i.e., if I harm him — I will make less food, I will produce very little food. Having reflected thus, he refrained from devouring him, for much food should be produced for long-term consumption, not little. If he devoured him, there would be little food — like the absence of crops from eating the seed. Having thus considered the advantage of abundant food, with that very speech of the three <s>Vedas</s> mentioned before, and with that very self, the mind, having approached, having entered into the coupling state of contemplation — he created all this, stationary and moveable, whatever there is. What was that? The <s>Ṛg</s> [verses], the <s>Yajus</s> [formulae], the <s>Sāman</s> [chants], and the meters — the seven [meters] beginning with <s>Gāyatrī</s>, the three types of mantras distinguished by meters like <s>Gāyatrī</s> that serve as components of ritual acts such as <s>stotra</s> and <s>śastra</s>; and sacrifices, the means to be accomplished by those [mantras]; the creatures, the performers of those [sacrifices]; and the animals, both domestic and wild, that serve as instruments of ritual action. Now, it was stated that he created [them] through coupling with the three <s>Vedas</s> — how then did he create the <s>Ṛg</s> verses and so forth mentioned here? There is no fault in this, for this coupling with the three <s>Vedas</s> by the mind is unmanifest; but externally, the manifestation of the <s>Ṛg</s> verses and others, which already existed, through their application in ritual acts — that is [what is meant by] 'creation.' That <s>Prajāpati</s>, having thus understood the increase of food, began to devour, to eat, whatever he created — whether the means of action or its fruit.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,2.6
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.2.6]

children.text:
so 'kāmayata -- bhūyasā yajñena bhūyo yajeyeti |
so 'śrāmyat |
sa tapo 'tapyata |
tasya śrāntasya taptasya yaśo vīryam udakrāmat |
prāṇā vai yaśo vīryam |
tat prāṇeṣūtkrānteṣu śarīraṃ śvayitum adhriyata |
tasya śarīra eva mana āsīt || BrhUp_1,2.6 ||
children.translated_text: 'He desired: "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice." He exerted himself. He performed austerity. From him, wearied and heated, glory and vigor departed. The <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths) indeed are glory and vigor. When the <s>prāṇas</s> departed, the body began to swell. His mind was still in the body.' // BṛhUp 1.2.6 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,2.6 so 'kāmayatetyaśvāśvamedhayornirvacanārthamidamāha- bhūyasā mahatā yajñena bhūyaḥ punarapi yajñeyeti /
janmāntarakaraṇāpekṣayā bhūyaḥ- śabdaḥ /
sa prajāpatiḥ janmāntare 'śvamedhenāyajata /
sa tadbhāvabhāvita eva kalpādau vyāvartata /
so 'śvamedhakriyākārakaphalātmatvena nirvṛttaḥ sannakāmayata bhūyasā yajñena bhūyo yajeyeti /
evaṃ mahatkāryaṃ kāmayitvā lokavadaśrāmyat /
sa tapo 'tapyata /
tasya śrāntasya taptasyeti pūrvavat, yaśo vīryamudakrāmaditi /
children.translated_text: 'From him, wearied and heated' — as before — 'glory and vigor departed.'

children.text: svayameva padārthamāha- prāṇāścakṣurādayo vai yaśo yaśohetutvāt teṣu hi yatsukhyātirbhavati, tathā vīryaṃ balamasmiñśarīre /
children.translated_text: He himself explains the meaning of the words: the <s>prāṇas</s> — the eye and other [organs] — are indeed glory, because they are the cause of glory; for whatever happiness one has is due to them. Similarly, vigor means strength in this body.

children.text: tadevaṃ prāṇalakṣaṇaṃ yaśo vīryamudakrāmadutkrāntavat /
children.translated_text: Thus, that glory and vigor characterized by <s>prāṇa</s> departed, went forth.

children.text: tadevaṃ yaśovīryabhūteṣu prāṇeṣūtkrānteṣu śarīrānniṣkrānteṣu taccharīraṃ prajāpateḥ śvayitumucchūnabhāvaṃ gantumadhriyatāmedhyaṃ cābhavat tasya prajāpateḥ śarīrānnirgatasyāpi tasminneva śarīre mana āsīdyathā kasyacitpriye viṣaye dūraṃ gatasyāpi mano bhavati tadvat //6//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Thus, when the <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths) — which are [the repositories of] glory and strength — had departed, had gone out from the body, that body of <s>Prajāpati</s> began to swell — to become bloated — and it became impure. Yet, even though <s>Prajāpati</s> had departed from the body, his mind remained fixed on that very body — just as the mind of someone who has gone far away remains attached to a beloved object. (6)

[Commentary:] 'He desired' — this is said for the purpose of etymologizing '<s>aśva</s>' (horse) and '<s>aśvamedha</s>' (horse sacrifice). [He desired:] 'May I sacrifice again with a greater, grand sacrifice.' The word 'again' (<s>bhūyaḥ</s>) is in reference to performing [sacrifice] in another birth. That <s>Prajāpati</s> sacrificed with the <s>Aśvamedha</s> in a previous birth. He, imbued with that tendency, manifested at the beginning of the [new] cosmic cycle. He, having come into existence as the essence of the action, agent, and fruit of the <s>Aśvamedha</s>, desired: 'May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice.' Having desired such a great undertaking, like any [being] in the world, he became weary. He performed austerity.

children.text: sa tasminneva śarīre gatamanāḥ sankimakarot? ityucyate-
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] He, with his mind fixed on that very body — what did he do? It is stated:

children.text:
so 'kāmayata -- medhyaṃ ma idaṃ syād ātmanvy anena syām iti |
tato 'śvaḥ samabhavat |
yad aśvat tan medhyam abhūd iti tad evāśvamedhasyāśvamedhatvam |
eṣa ha vā aśvamedhaṃ veda ya enam evaṃ veda |
tam anavarudhyaivāmanyata |
taṃ saṃvatsarasya parastād ātmana ālabhata |
paśūn devatābhyaḥ pratyauhat |
tasmāt sarvadevatyaṃ prokṣitaṃ prājāpatyam ālabhante |
eṣa vā aśvamedho ya eṣa tapati |
tasya saṃvatsara ātmā |
ayam agnir arkaḥ |
tasyeme lokā ātmānaḥ |
tāv etāv arkāśvamedhau |
so punar ekaiva devatā bhavati mṛtyur eva |
apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati |
nainaṃ mṛtyur āpnoti |
mṛtyur asyātmā bhavati |
sarvam āyur eti |
etāsāṃ devatānām eko bhavati || BrhUp_1,2.7 ||
children.translated_text: He desired: 'May this [body] of mine become fit for sacrifice; may I be embodied through this.' Then the horse came into being. Because it swelled (<s>aśvat</s>), it became fit for sacrifice — that indeed is the <s>aśvamedha</s>-ness of the <s>Aśvamedha</s>. One who knows this truly knows the <s>Aśvamedha</s>. He let it stand without restraining it. After a year, he sacrificed it to himself. He consigned the [other] animals to the deities. Therefore they sacrifice the consecrated [animal] that belongs to all deities as belonging to <s>Prajāpati</s>. This indeed is the <s>Aśvamedha</s> — that which shines [the sun]. The year is its body. This fire is the <s>arka</s>. These worlds are its bodies. These two are the <s>arka</s> and the <s>Aśvamedha</s>. And again, it becomes one single deity — Death itself. One conquers recurring death; death does not reach him; death becomes his self; he lives the full span of life; he becomes one with these deities. (BṛUp 1.2.7)

children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Lest one apprehend that even though conquered, death might again reach him, [the text] says: death does not reach him.

children.text: kasmāt? mṛtyurasya evaṃvida ātmā bhavati /
children.translated_text: Why? Because death becomes the very self of such a knower.

children.text: kiñca mṛtyureva phalarūpaḥ sanne tāsāṃ devatānāmeko bhavati /
children.translated_text: Moreover, death itself, being in the form of the fruit, becomes one with these deities — he becomes one with them.

children.text: tasyaitat phalam //7//
children.translated_text: This is the fruit thereof. (7)

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.2.7:] 'He desired' — how? 'May this body of mine become <s>medhya</s> (fit for sacrifice), worthy of the <s>medha</s> (sacrifice). And moreover, may I become embodied, possessing a body through this body' — [so thinking,] he entered it. Because that body, having lost its glory and strength due to separation from him, had swelled (<s>aśvat</s>), therefore the horse (<s>aśva</s>) came into being. Therefore [the text says] <s>Prajāpati</s> himself, named '<s>aśva</s>,' is directly [that horse] — thus it is praised. And because, through his re-entering, what had become impure due to the loss of glory and strength became fit for sacrifice — that indeed is the reason for the <s>Aśvamedha</s> sacrifice bearing the name '<s>aśvamedha</s>.' For a sacrifice (<s>kratu</s>) consists of action, agents, and fruit. And that [sacrifice] is <s>Prajāpati</s> himself — thus it is praised. The identity of the horse that accomplishes the sacrifice with <s>Prajāpati</s> has been stated [earlier] beginning with '<s>uṣā</s> is [the head] of the sacrificial horse.' The meditation combining that very sacrificial horse in the form of <s>Prajāpati</s> with the fire as described is now begun, [since it is] to be enjoined in the form of the fruit of the sacrifice. Because in the earlier portion no injunctive verb was heard, and because the section requires an injunctive verb, this meaning is understood. 'One who knows this truly knows the <s>Aśvamedha</s> sacrifice' — whoever knows this horse in the form of fire, the <s>arka</s>, as described, qualified by the particular characteristics to be shown in the composite [meditation] — he knows the <s>Aśvamedha</s>, and no one else. Therefore, one should know it thus — this is the meaning. How? First, regarding the animal, the vision is stated. <s>Prajāpati</s>, having desired 'may I sacrifice with a greater sacrifice,' having made himself the sacrificial animal, fit for sacrifice — he let that animal stand without restraining it, without placing it under restraint, uncontrolled, with loosened reins — he contemplated. After the completion of a year, he sacrificed it to himself — that is, with <s>Prajāpati</s> as the deity — he performed the sacrificial immolation. The other animals — domestic and wild — he consigned to the deities according to their respective presiding deities. And because <s>Prajāpati</s> contemplated thus, therefore another person also, having made himself the sacrificial animal, the horse, fit for sacrifice according to the prescribed method, [should know]: 'I am the sacrifice belonging to all deities; I, who am to be consecrated and sacrificed, belong to my own deity alone; the other animals — domestic and wild — are sacrificed to other deities, who are indeed portions of myself, according to their respective presiding deities' — thus one should know. For this very reason, the ritualists (<s>yājñikas</s>) now sacrifice the consecrated [animal] that belongs to all deities as belonging to <s>Prajāpati</s>. 'This indeed is the <s>Aśvamedha</s> — that which shines' — the sacrifice that is thus accomplished through the animal is here directly indicated as the fruit: 'this indeed is the <s>Aśvamedha</s>.' Who is that? That very <s>Savitṛ</s> (sun) who shines, who illumines the world with his radiance. Of this [sun], who is the embodiment of the fruit of the sacrifice, the year — a particular division of time — is the body, because the year is produced by it. And of this very [sacrifice] in its essential nature as the ritual, because the fruit is accomplished through fire, and for the purpose of indicating it in the form of the sacrifice — this earthly fire is the <s>arka</s>, the instrumental [element]. And of this <s>arka</s>, these three worlds too are the bodies, the limbs of the body in the ritual arrangement. And thus it has been explained [earlier] beginning with 'its eastern direction.' These two — fire and sun — as thus specified, are the <s>arka</s> and the <s>Aśvamedha</s>, the sacrifice and its fruit. The <s>arka</s>, the earthly fire, is directly the embodiment of the sacrifice, consisting of action. Because the sacrifice is accomplished through fire, it is indicated in that very form. And because the fruit is accomplished through the sacrifice, it too is indicated in the form of the sacrifice — thus the sun is the <s>Aśvamedha</s>. These two — the means and the end, the sacrifice and its fruit embodied as fire and sun — that again becomes one single deity. Which one? Death itself. Previously too, it was one alone — [but] it was divided for the differentiation of action, means, and fruit. And thus it has been stated: 'He divided himself threefold' (BṛUp 1.2.3). And again, after the completion of the ritual action, it becomes one single deity — Death itself, in the form of the fruit. Now, one who thus knows this <s>Aśvamedha</s> as Death, as one deity — [knowing] 'I myself am Death, I am the <s>Aśvamedha</s>, one deity whose nature is myself, [consisting of] the horse and fire as means and end' — he conquers recurring death; having died once, he is not born again for the purpose of dying again — this is the meaning.

children.text: iti prathamādhyāye dvitīyamagnibrāhmaṇam //2//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second <s>Agni Brāhmaṇa</s> in the first <s>adhyāya</s>. (2)

children.text:
dvayā hetyādyasya kaḥ sambandhaḥ? karmaṇāṃ jñānasahitānāṃ parā gatiruktā mṛtyvātmabhāvo 'śvamedhagatyuktyā /
athedānīṃ mṛtyvātmabhāvasādhanabhūtayoḥ karmajñānayoryata udbhavastatprakāśanārthamudgīthabrāhmaṇamārabhyate /
nanu mṛtyvātmabhāvaḥ pūrvatra jñānakarmaṇoḥ phalamuktam /
udgīthajñānakarmaṇostumṛtyvātmabhāvātikramaṇaṃ phalaṃ vakṣyati ato bhinnaviṣayatvātphalasya na pūrvakarmajñānodbhavaprakāśanārthamiti cet /
nāyaṃ doṣaḥ;agnyādityātmabhāvatvādudgīthaphalasya /
pūrvatrāpyetadeva phalamuktam'etāsāṃ devatānāmeko bhavati'iti /
nanu'mṛtyumatikrāntaḥ'ityādi viruddham;na svābhāvikapapmāsaṅgaviṣayatvādatikramaṇasya /
ko 'sau svābhāvikaḥ papmāsaṅgo mṛtyuḥ? kuto vā tasyodbhavaḥ? kena vā tasyātikramaṇam? kathaṃ vā? ityetasyārthasya prakāśanāyākhyāyikārabhate /
katham-
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] '<s>Dvayā ha</s>' and so forth — what is its connection [to the preceding]? The supreme destination of actions combined with knowledge has been stated — the attainment of identity with Death — through the exposition of the path of the <s>Aśvamedha</s>. Now, the <s>Udgītha Brāhmaṇa</s> is begun for the purpose of elucidating the source from which the two — action and knowledge — that are the means of attaining identity with Death, arise. But was not the attainment of identity with Death stated earlier as the fruit of knowledge and action? And [here] the fruit of the <s>Udgītha</s> knowledge and action will be stated as the transcending of identity with Death — so, since the fruits are of different domains, [the <s>Udgītha Brāhmaṇa</s> is] not for the purpose of elucidating the source of the preceding knowledge and action? This objection does not hold, because the fruit of the <s>Udgītha</s> consists in identity with fire and sun. The same fruit was stated earlier too: 'he becomes one with these deities.' But does not [the statement] 'he has transcended death' and the like contradict [this]? No, because the transcending pertains to the natural contact with evil. What is that natural contact with evil, that death? And what is its source? And by what means is it transcended? And how? For the purpose of elucidating this meaning, the narrative begins. How?

te ha devā ūcur hantāsurān yajña udgīthenātyayāmeti || BrhUp_1,3.1 ||
children.translated_text: There were two kinds of offspring of <s>Prajāpati</s> — the gods and the <s>Asuras</s>. Of these, the gods were the younger, the <s>Asuras</s> the elder. They competed for these worlds. The gods said: 'Come, let us overcome the <s>Asuras</s> at the sacrifice through the <s>Udgītha</s>.' (BṛUp 1.3.1)

brahmadṛṣṭireva kevalā nāsti brameti cet /
etena pratimābrāhmaṇādiṣu viṣṇvādidevapitrādidṛṣṭīnāṃ tulyatā /
na;ṛgādiṣu pṛthivyādidṛṣṭidarśanāt /
vidyamānapṛthivyādivastudṛṣṭīnāmeva ṛgādiviṣaye kṣepadarśanāt /
tasmāttatsāmānyānnāmādiṣu brahmādidṛṣṭīnāṃ vidyamānabrahmādiviṣayatvasiddhiḥ /
etena pratimābrāhmaṇādiṣu viṣṇvādidevapitrādibuddhīnāṃ ca satyavastuviṣayatvasiddhiḥ /
mukhyāpekṣatvācca gauṇatvasya /
pañcāgnyādiṣu cāgnitvādergauṇatvād mukhyāgnyādisadbhāvavannāmādiṣu bahmatvasya gauṇatvānmukhyabrahmasadbhāvopapattiḥ /
kriyārthaiścāviśeṣādvidyārthānām yathā ca darśapaurṇamāsādikriyedamphalā viśiṣṭaitikartavyatākā evaṅkramaprayuktāṅgā ca ityetadalaukikaṃ vastu pratyakṣādyaviṣayaṃ tathābhūtaṃ ca vedavākyaireva jñāpyate /
tathā, paramātmeśvaradevatādivastu asthūlādidharmakamaśanāyādyatītaṃ cetyevamādiviśiṣṭamiti vedavākyaireva jñāpyate, ityalaukikatvāttathābhūtameva bhavitumarhatīti /
na ca kriyārthairvākyairjñānavākyānāṃ buddhyutpātakatve viśeṣo 'sti /
na cāniścitā viparyastā vā paramātmādivastuviṣayā buddhirutpadyate /
anuṣṭheyābhāvādayuktamiti cet kriyārthairvākyaistryaṃśābhāvanānuṣṭheyā jñāpyate 'laukikyapi /
na tathā paramātmeśvarādivijñāne 'nuṣṭheyaṃ kiñcitasti /
ataḥ kriyārthaiḥ sādharmyamityayuktamiti cet? na, jñānasya tathābhūtārthaviṣayatvāt na hyanuṣṭheyatvāttathātvam, kiṃ tarhi? pramāṇasamadhigatatvāt /
na ca tadviṣayāyā buddheranuṣṭheyaviṣayatvāttathārthatvam, kiṃ tarhi? vedavākyajanitatvādeva /
vedavākyādhigatasya vastunastathātve satyanuṣṭheyatvaviśiṣṭhaṃ cedanutiṣṭhati /
no cedanuṣṭheyatvaviśiṣṭhaṃ nānu tiṣṭhati /
ananuṣṭheyatve vākyapramāṇatvānupapattiriti cet /
na hyanuṣṭheye 'sati padānāṃ sahatirupapadyate /
anuṣṭheyatve tu sati tādarthyena padāni saṃhanyante /
tatrānuṣṭheyaniṣṭhaṃ vākyaṃ pramāṇaṃ bhavati idamanenaivaṃ kartavyamiti /
na tvidamanenaivamityevaṃ prakārāṇāṃ padaśatānāmapi vākyatvamasti'kuryātkriyeta kartavyaṃ bhavetsyāditi pañcamam'ityevamādīnāmanyatame 'sati /
ataḥ paramātmeśvarādīnāmavākyapramāṇatvam, padārthatve ca pramāṇāntaraviṣayatvam /
ato 'sadetaditi cet? na,'asti merurvarṇacatuṣṭayopetaḥ'ityevamādyananuṣṭheye 'pi vākyadarśanāt /
na ca'merurvarṇacatuṣṭayopetaḥ'ityevamādivākyaśravaṇe mervādāvanuṣṭheyatvabuddhirutpadyate /
tathā astipadasahitānāṃ paramātmeśvarādipratipādakavākyapadānāṃ viśeṣaṇa viśeṣyabhāvena saṃhatiḥ kena vāryate /
mervādijñānavatparamātmajñāne prayojanābhāvādayuktamiti cet? na,"brahmavidāpnoti param"(tai.u.2 / 1 / 1) "brahmavidāpnoti param bhidyate hṛdayagranthiḥ"(mu.u.2 / 2 / 8) iti phalaśravaṇāt, saṃsārabījāvidyādidoṣanivṛttidarśanācca /
ananyaśeṣatvācca tajjñānasya, juhvāmiva phalaśruterarthavādatvānupapatti /
pratiṣiddhāniṣṭaphalasambandhaśca vedādeva vijñāyate /
na cānuṣṭheyaḥ saḥ /
na ca pratiṣiddhaviṣaye pravṛttakriyasya akaraṇādanyadanuṣṭheyamasti /
akartavyatājñānaniṣṭhataiva hi paramārthataḥ pratiṣedhavidhīnāṃ syāt /
kṣudhārtasya pratiṣedhajñānasaṃskṛtasya abhakṣye 'bhojye vā pratyupasthite kalajjābhiśastānnādau'idaṃ bhakṣyamado bhojyam'iti vā jñānamutpannam, tadviṣayayā pratiṣedhajñānasmṛtyā bādhyate /
mṛgatṛṣṇikāyāmiva peyajñānaṃ tadviṣayayāthātmyavijñānena /
tasminbādhite snābhāvikanarthakarītadbhakṣaṇabhojanapravṛttirna bhavati /
viparītajñānanimittāyāḥ pravṛtternivṛttireva, na punaryatnaḥ kāryastadabhāve /
tasmāt pratiṣedhavidhīnāṃ vastuyāthātmyajñānaniṣṭhataiva, na puruṣavyāpāraniṣṭhatāgandho 'pyasti /
tathehāpi paramātmādiyāthātmyajñānavidhīnāṃ tāvanmātraparyavāsanataiva syāt /
tathā tadvijñānasaṃskṛtasya tadviparītārthajñānanimittānāṃ pravṛttīnāmanarthārthatvena jñāyamānatvāt paramātmādiyāthātmyajñānasmṛtyā svābhāvike tannimittavijñāne bādhite 'bhāvaḥ syāt /
nanu kalañjādibhakṣaṇāderanarthārthatvavastuyāthātmyajñānasmṛtyā svābhāvike tadbhakṣyatvādiviṣayaviparītajñāne nivartite tadbhakṣaṇādyanarthapravṛttyabhāvavadapratiṣedhaviṣayatvācchāstravihitapravṛttyabhāvo na yukta iti cet /
na, viparītajñānanimittatvānarthārthatvābhyāṃ tulyatvāt /
kalañjabhakṣaṇādipravṛtteḥ mithyājñānanimittatvam /
anarthārthatvaṃ ca yathā, tathā śāstravihitapravṛttīnāmapi /
tasmāt paramātmayāthātmyavijñānavataḥ śāstravihitapravṛttīnāmapi mithyājñānanimittatvena anarthārthatvena ca tulyatvāt paramātmajñānena viparītajñāne nivartite yukta evābhāvaḥ /
nanu tatra yuktaḥ, nityānāṃ tu kevalaśāstranimittatvāt, anarthārthatvābhāvaccābhāvo na yukta iti cet? na avidyārāgadveṣādidoṣavato vihitatvāt /
yathā svargakāmādidoṣavato darśapūrṇamāsādīni kāmyāni karmāṇi vihitāni tathā sarvānarthabījāvidyādidoṣavatastajjaniteṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihārarāgadveṣādidoṣavataśca tatpreritāviśeṣapravṛtteriṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihārārthino nityāni karmāṇi vidhīyante, na kevalaṃ śāstranimittānyeva /
na cāgnihotradarśapūrṇamāsacāturmāsyapaśubandhasomānāṃ karmaṇāṃ svataḥ kāmyanityatvavivekosti /
kartṛgatena hi svargādikāmadoṣeṇa kāmārthatā /
tathā avidyādidoṣavataḥ svabhāvaprāpteṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihārārthinaḥ tadarthānyeva nityāni iti yuktam, taṃ prati vihitatvāt /
na paramātmayāthātmyavijñānavataḥ śamopāyavyatirekeṇa kiñcitkarma vihitamubhalabhyate /
karmanimittadevatādisarvasādhanavijñānopamardena hyātmajñānaṃ vidhīyate, na copamarditakriyākārakādivijñānasya karmapravṛttirupapadyate /
viśiṣṭakriyāsādhanādijñānapūrvakatvātkriyāpravṛtteḥ /
na hi deśakālādyanavacchinnāsthūladvayādibrahmapatyayadhāriṇaḥ karmāvasaro 'sti /
bhojanādipravṛttyavasaravatsyāditi cet? na, avidyādikevaladoṣanimittatvādbhojanādi pravṛtterāvaśyakatvānupapatteḥ /
na tu tathāniyataṃ kadācitkriyate kadācinna kriyate ceti nityaṃ karmopapadyate /
kevaladoṣanimittatvāttu bhojanādikarmaṇo 'niyatatvaṃ syāt /
doṣodbhavābhibhavayoraniyatatvāt kāmānāmiva kāmyeṣu /
śāstranimittakālādyapekṣatvācca nityānāmaniyatatvānupapattiḥ /
doṣanimittatve satyapi yathā kāmyāgnihotrasya śāstravihitatvāt sāyaṃprātaḥ kālādyapekṣatvamevam /
children.translated_text: Even when the defect is the cause, just as the <s>kāmyāgnihotra</s> (desire-motivated fire-ritual), because of being ordained by scripture, depends on the evening and morning times and the like, so too [the injunction of knowledge has such conditions].

children.text: tadbhojanādipavṛttau niyamavatsyāditi cet? na, niyamasākriyatvāt kriyāyāścaprayojakatvānnāsau jñānasyāpavādakaraḥ /
children.translated_text: If it be objected that upon the cessation of eating and the like, there would be a restrictive rule [limiting knowledge] — no, because a restrictive rule is not an [independent] action, and because action is not a motivating [factor for knowledge], that [restriction] does not sublate knowledge.

children.text: tasmāt paramātmāyāthātmyajñānavidherapi tadviparītasthūladvaitādijñānanivartakatvāt sāmarthyātsarvakarmapratiṣedhavidhyarthatvaṃ sampadyate;karmapravṛttyabhāvasya tulyatvād yathā pratiṣedhaviṣaye /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even for the injunction of the knowledge of the true nature of the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self), because of its capacity to remove the contrary cognition of gross duality and the like, through its inherent power, the purpose of the injunction prohibiting all action is accomplished — just as in the domain of prohibition, because of the equal [result of] the absence of engagement in action.

children.text: tasmāt pratiṣedhavidhivacca vastupratipādanaṃ tatparatvaṃ ca siddhaṃ śāstrasya //1//
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as with a prohibitive injunction, the establishment of a real entity and the scripture's having that as its purport are established. (1)

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.3.1:] '<s>Dvayā</s>' means of two kinds. The particle '<s>ha</s>' is used to recall a past event. It brings to mind through the word '<s>ha</s>' what took place in the previous birth of the present <s>Prajāpati</s>. '<s>Prājāpatyāḥ</s>' — the offspring of <s>Prajāpati</s> in his past birth-state are the <s>Prājāpatyas</s>. Who are they? The gods (<s>devas</s>) and the demons (<s>asuras</s>). The <s>prāṇas</s> (vital functions) — speech and the rest — belong to that very <s>Prajāpati</s>. But how is it that they have the nature of gods and demons? It is explained: those cultivated by knowledge and action born of scripture become gods, because of their radiance (<s>dyodana</s>). Those very same [vital functions], when cultivated by knowledge and action that are natural, born of perception and inference, and directed toward visible purposes, become demons — because they delight in their own vital breaths (<s>asu</s>), or because they are different from the gods (<s>suras</s>). And since the demons are cultivated by knowledge and action directed toward visible purposes, therefore the gods are '<s>kānīyasāḥ</s>' — fewer in number; '<s>kānīyāṃsa eva kānīyasāḥ</s>' — the <s>vṛddhi</s> augment is applied in the reflexive sense. The gods are fewer, i.e. smaller in number. The demons are '<s>jyāyasāḥ</s>' — greater, more numerous. For the natural inclination toward action and knowledge of the vital functions is greater than the scripture-born inclination toward action and knowledge, because [the natural inclination] is directed toward visible purposes. For this very reason the gods are fewer, because the scripture-born inclination is smaller in extent, for it is achievable only through extreme effort. These gods and demons, situated within the body of <s>Prajāpati</s>, contended — competed — in these worlds that serve as their fields, which are to be attained through natural and scripture-born knowledge and action. The contention of the gods and demons consists in the rise and suppression of their respective activities. Sometimes the activity of the vital functions in the form of scripture-born cultivation of knowledge and action arises. And when it arises, the activity of those very vital functions in the form of cultivation of knowledge and action born of perception and inference and directed toward visible purposes — the demonic [activity] — is suppressed. That is the victory of the gods and the defeat of the demons. Sometimes, conversely, the activity of the gods is suppressed and the demonic [activity] arises. That is the victory of the demons and the defeat of the gods. Thus, when the gods are victorious, because of the predominance of <s>dharma</s>, there is an upward course up to the attainment of <s>Prajāpati</s>-hood. When the demons are victorious, because of the predominance of <s>adharma</s>, there is a downward course up to the attainment of the state of immovable beings. When both are equal, there is the attainment of human birth. Those gods, being thus overcome by the demons on account of being fewer — because of the preponderance of the demons — what did they do? It is said: those gods, being overcome by the demons, said — spoke. How? 'Come, let us now, in this sacrifice — the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> — overcome [them] through the <s>udgītha</s>, by taking recourse to the true nature of the agent of the <s>udgītha</s> ritual act and its meaning' — let us transcend the demons, overcome them, and regain our own divine state as revealed by scripture — thus they spoke to one another. And the taking recourse to the true nature of the agent of the <s>udgītha</s> ritual act and its meaning is through both knowledge and action. The action is the one to be enjoined hereafter, characterized by the chanting of mantras, as will be prescribed in 'Let him chant these.' But the knowledge is precisely this that is being expounded here. [Objection:] Is not this [passage] merely a glorification (<s>arthavāda</s>) [consisting of] the recounting of a legend and a particular chanting procedure, rather than an exposition of knowledge? No — because of the statement 'He who thus knows.' [Objection:] Since at the beginning of the <s>udgītha</s> [section] an ancient legend is heard, [this passage] is primarily about the injunction of the <s>udgītha</s>. No — because [the <s>udgītha</s>] is not the topic here [in this section]. And because the <s>udgītha</s> is already enjoined elsewhere. And because this [passage] has knowledge as its topic. And because the legend of the chanting is non-eternal [and hence not injunctive], and because it can be separated [from the knowledge portion]; and because knowledge is heard as if eternal [in its validity]. And from the <s>śruti</s>: 'That indeed is the conqueror of worlds' (BṛUp 1.3.28). And because the purity and impurity of <s>prāṇa</s> and speech and the rest are stated. For it is not the case that the purity of <s>prāṇa</s> is stated merely for the purpose of meditation on something else, while the impurity of speech and the rest, which are presented alongside it, is [also merely for that purpose]. And the praise of the chief <s>prāṇa</s> through the censure of speech and the rest is also intended and is appropriate [here]. And there are also statements of fruit such as 'Having transcended death, it shines forth.' For the fruit is the attainment of the true nature of <s>prāṇa</s> — namely, the states of fire and the rest that belong to speech and the others. [Objection:] Granted that the meditation on <s>prāṇa</s> [exists], but it does not possess qualities such as purity and the rest. [Response:] Indeed it should, since [purity] is stated in the <s>śruti</s>. [Objection:] It should not [be taken literally], since if [purity] is taken as the object of meditation, it serves the purpose of praise [alone]. No — because [the passage] conveys a non-erroneous meaning, and because the attainment of the highest good is tenable [on this basis], just as in the world. For one who apprehends a non-erroneous meaning in the world attains what is desired or avoids what is undesired — not through the apprehension of an erroneous meaning. Similarly here too, when the meaning apprehended from the words heard in the <s>śruti</s> is correct, the attainment of the highest good is tenable — not in the contrary case. And there is no means of proof (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for establishing the falsity of the content of the cognition arising from the words heard in the context of meditation. Nor is any sublation (<s>apavāda</s>) of that cognition heard [in the śruti]. Therefore, from observing the attainment of the highest good, we conclude its truth; and from observing the attainment of evil in the contrary case. For one who apprehends the meaning in a contrary fashion in the world — [mistaking] a post for a person, or an enemy for a friend — is seen to attain evil. If the grasping of <s>Ātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, deities, and the like from the <s>śruti</s> were of unreal objects, then the scripture would certainly turn out to be for the attainment of evil, just as in the world — and that is not desirable. Therefore, the scripture causes one to grasp <s>Ātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, deities, and the like as they truly are, for the purpose of meditation. [Objection:] From the fact that the perception of <s>Brahman</s> is taught regarding name and the like [which are not <s>Brahman</s>], this is inappropriate. [Response:] It is clear that name and the like are not <s>Brahman</s>; there the scripture is seen to make one grasp the erroneous perception of <s>Brahman</s> in name and the like, just like the perception of a person in a post. Therefore, from scripture one grasps the real meaning alone, and the highest good [follows] — if you say this, no — because of the analogy with an idol. The scripture does not cause one to grasp the erroneous perception of <s>Brahman</s> in name and the like, which are not <s>Brahman</s>, just as [it does not cause] the perception of a person in a post. This is not well said. Why? Because, having apprehended name and the like as objects distinct from <s>Brahman</s>, the perception of <s>Brahman</s> is enjoined regarding name and the like — just as the perception of <s>Viṣṇu</s> in an idol. For the apprehension of name and the like is merely as a support, just like an idol — not that name and the like are themselves <s>Brahman</s>. Just as when a post is not [properly] ascertained, one mistakenly apprehends it as 'This is indeed a person' — but the perception of <s>Brahman</s> in name and the like is not erroneous in that way. [Objection:] There is simply no perception of <s>Brahman</s> [at all in name and the like]. [Response:] By this [argument], the perceptions of <s>Viṣṇu</s> and the like in idols, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, and the like, and of <s>devas</s>, <s>Pitṛs</s>, and the like, are equally [refuted]. No — because the perception of earth and the like in the <s>Ṛg</s> [Veda] and the rest is observed. Since we see the attribution of perceptions of real objects like earth and the rest to the <s>Ṛg</s> and the rest as their domain, therefore, by analogy with that, the perception of <s>Brahman</s> and the like in name and the rest is established as having a real object of <s>Brahman</s> and the like. By this, the reality of the perceptions of <s>Viṣṇu</s> and other <s>devas</s>, <s>Pitṛs</s>, and the like in idols, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, and the like is also established. And because the secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>) sense presupposes the primary (<s>mukhya</s>) sense. And just as in the five-fire meditation and the like, from the secondary nature of fire-hood and the rest, the existence of primary fire and the rest [is established] — similarly, from the secondary nature of <s>Brahman</s>-hood in name and the like, the existence of primary <s>Brahman</s> is tenable. And there is no difference between knowledge-sentences and action-sentences in their capacity to generate cognition. Just as the ritual of <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> and the like — having such-and-such a fruit, qualified by such-and-such procedural requirements, performed with such-and-such a sequence of subsidiary acts — this extraordinary reality, beyond the scope of perception and the like, of such a nature, is made known by Vedic sentences alone; similarly, the reality of <s>Paramātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, deities, and the like — characterized as 'not gross' and the like, transcending hunger and the rest — of such a nature, is made known by Vedic sentences alone. Being extraordinary, it is fitting that it should be exactly as [described]. And there is no difference between action-sentences and knowledge-sentences in their capacity to generate cognition. Nor does the cognition that arises regarding <s>Paramātman</s> and the like turn out to be uncertain or erroneous. [Objection:] Because there is nothing to be done [as a result], it is inappropriate [to compare knowledge-sentences with action-sentences]. [Response:] The action-sentences make known what is to be done — the bringing-about of three components [agent, act, result] — even though it is extraordinary. But in the knowledge of <s>Paramātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, and the like, there is nothing to be done. Therefore the analogy with action-sentences is inappropriate — if you say so, no — because knowledge has an object of such a nature. For the truth [of knowledge] does not depend on there being something to be done; rather, [it derives] from being apprehended by a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). Nor is the truth of the cognition regarding its object [established] because its object is something to be done; rather, simply because it is generated by a Vedic sentence. When the reality apprehended from a Vedic sentence is true, if it is qualified by something to be done, one acts [accordingly]. If it is not qualified by something to be done, one does not act. [Objection:] If there is nothing to be done, the sentence cannot be a valid means of knowledge. For without something to be done, the syntactic unity of the words is not tenable. But when there is something to be done, the words are unified for that purpose. There, the sentence whose culmination is the thing to be done becomes a valid means of knowledge: 'This is to be done by him in this manner.' But without even one of the [injunctive] forms — '<s>kuryāt</s>, <s>kriyeta</s>, <s>kartavyam</s>, <s>bhavet</s>, <s>syāt</s>' — being the fifth [element], even hundreds of words do not constitute a sentence. Therefore, <s>Paramātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, and the like are not the object of sentence-knowledge, and being mere word-meanings, they are objects of other means of knowledge. Therefore this is not so — if you say, no — because we observe sentences about non-injunctive matters too, such as 'There exists [Mount] <s>Meru</s>, endowed with four colors.' And upon hearing such a sentence as '<s>Meru</s> is endowed with four colors,' no cognition of something to be done arises regarding <s>Meru</s> and the like. Similarly, who can prevent the syntactic unity — through the relation of qualifier and qualified — of the words of sentences that contain the word '<s>asti</s>' (exists) and that convey <s>Paramātman</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, and the like? [Objection:] Just as knowledge about <s>Meru</s> and the like [has no practical purpose], knowledge of <s>Paramātman</s> too has no purpose — hence it is inappropriate. No — because of the <s>śruti</s> statements of fruit: 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (TaiUp 2.1.1), 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme; the knot of the heart is cut' (MuṇḍUp 2.2.8); and because the cessation of the defects of <s>avidyā</s> and the like, which are the seed of <s>saṃsāra</s>, is observed. And because that knowledge has no other purpose [beyond itself], the statement of fruit cannot be explained away as <s>arthavāda</s> (mere praise), unlike [the case of] an oblation and its fruit-statement. And the connection with prohibited undesirable fruits is also known from the <s>Veda</s> alone. And that [prohibited action] is not something to be done. And for one who has refrained from prohibited action, there is nothing else to be done as a separate practice. For the ultimate purport of prohibitive injunctions is indeed the knowledge of the true nature of what should not be done. Just as when a hungry person, endowed with the impression of prohibitive knowledge, is confronted with a forbidden or inedible [substance] — when the cognition arises 'This is edible, that is fit for eating' — it is counteracted by the recollection of prohibitive knowledge regarding that object; just as in [the case of] a mirage, the cognition of something drinkable is counteracted by the knowledge of the true nature of that [mirage]. When that [false cognition] is counteracted, the natural harmful inclination toward eating or consuming that [substance] does not arise. The cessation of the activity that was caused by the erroneous cognition [is all that is required] — no further effort is needed when that [erroneous cognition] is absent. Therefore, the culmination of prohibitive injunctions is in the knowledge of the true nature of things, and there is not even a trace of [their] culminating in human activity. Similarly here too, the injunctions regarding the true nature of <s>Paramātman</s> and the like should culminate in just that much [knowledge alone]. Similarly, for one endowed with the impression of that knowledge [of <s>Paramātman</s>], the activities caused by the cognition contrary to it — being known as having evil as their purpose — upon the counteraction of the natural cognition that causes them by the recollection of the true knowledge of <s>Paramātman</s> and the like, there would be cessation [of those activities]. [Objection:] For activities like eating food from forbidden sources, the cessation [follows] from the knowledge of the true nature and from the recollection [of prohibition]; but for activities enjoined by scripture, cessation is not appropriate, because they are based on scripture alone and because there is no [imputation of] evil purpose [to them]. No — because they are enjoined for one who possesses the defects of <s>avidyā</s>, <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and the like. Just as optional (<s>kāmya</s>) rituals like <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> and the rest are enjoined for one who possesses the defect of desiring heaven and the like, similarly the obligatory (<s>nitya</s>) rites are enjoined for one who possesses the defects of <s>avidyā</s> and the like — the seed of all evil — and the defects of desire and aversion for obtaining the desired and avoiding the undesired that are generated by those [defects] — and for one who is impelled by those [defects] to a non-discriminating activity aimed at obtaining the desired and avoiding the undesired. [The obligatory rites] are for that very purpose and are enjoined for such a person — they are not based on scripture alone. And there is no intrinsic distinction between the optional and the obligatory nature of the rituals of <s>Agnihotra</s>, <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, <s>Cāturmāsya</s>, <s>Paśubandha</s>, and <s>Soma</s> sacrifices. For their optional character [comes] from the defect of desire for heaven and the like that belongs to the agent. Similarly, it is fitting that the obligatory rites are for the very purpose of [addressing] the naturally obtained desire of the one possessing the defects of <s>avidyā</s> and the like to obtain the desired and avoid the undesired — because they are enjoined for such a person. No <s>karma</s> whatsoever is found to be enjoined for one who possesses the knowledge of the true nature of <s>Paramātman</s>, apart from the means of tranquility (<s>śama</s>). For the knowledge of <s>Ātman</s> is enjoined through the annulment of the knowledge of all means [of action] — deities, ritual accessories, and the like — that are the causes of <s>karma</s>. And for one whose knowledge of action, agent, and instrument has been annulled, engagement in action is not tenable — because engagement in action presupposes the prior knowledge of the specific action, its means, and the like. For there is no occasion for <s>karma</s> for one who holds [the view] that <s>Brahman</s> is not gross, not dual, unlimited by space, time, and the like. [Objection:] There would be occasion [for karma], just as there is occasion for activities like eating and the like. No — because activities like eating and the like are caused solely by defects [like hunger and the like] and are not obligatory [in the ritual sense]. But what is sometimes done and sometimes not done — [that] cannot be [considered] an obligatory rite. And because activities like eating are caused solely by defects [like hunger], their non-regularity would follow — because of the non-regularity of the arising and suppression of defects, just as desires [are non-regular] regarding optional rites. And because the obligatory rites depend on time and other conditions established by scripture, their non-regularity is not tenable.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,3.2
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 1.3.2]

children.text:
te ha vācam ūcus tvaṃ na udgāyeti |
tatheti tebhyo vāg udagāyat |
yo vāci bhogas taṃ devebhya āgāyat |
yat kalyāṇaṃ vadati tad ātmane |
te 'vidur anena vai na udgātrātyeṣyantīti |
tam abhidrutya pāpmanāvidhyan |
sa yaḥ sa pāpmā yad evedam apratirūpaṃ vadati |
sa eva sa pāpmā || BrhUp_1,3.2 ||
children.translated_text: They said to Speech: 'You chant the <s>Udgītha</s> for us.' 'So be it,' [said Speech]. Speech chanted the <s>Udgītha</s> for them. Whatever enjoyment there is in speech, that it chanted for the gods; whatever beautiful thing it speaks, that [it kept] for itself. They [the <s>Asuras</s>] knew: 'By this <s>Udgātṛ</s> (chanter) they will surpass us.' They rushed upon it and pierced it with evil. That evil which [makes one] speak what is improper — that is that evil. (BṛUp 1.3.2)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,3.2 te devā haivaṃ viniścitya, vācaṃ vāgabhimāninīṃ devatāmucuruktavantaḥ /
tvaṃ no 'smabhyamudgāyaudgātraṃ karma kuruṣva /
vāgdevatānirvarttyamaugātraṃ kama dṛṣṭavantaḥ, tāmeva ca devatāṃ japamantrābhidhāyām"asato mā sadgamaya"(bṛ.u.1 / 3 / 28) iti /
atra copāsanāyāḥ karmaṇaśca kartṛtvena vāgādaya eva vivakṣyante /
kasmāt? yasmātparamārthatastat kartṛkastadviṣaya eva ca sarvo jñānakarmasaṃvyavahāraḥ /
vakṣyati hi"dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva"ityātmakartṛkatvābhāvaṃ vistarataḥ ṣaṣṭe /
ihāpi cādyāyānte upasaṃhariṣyati avyākṛtādikriyākārakaphalajātam,"trayaṃ vā idaṃ nāma rūpaṃ karma"(1 / 6 / 1) iti avidyāviṣayam /
avyākṛtāttu yatparaṃ paramātmākhyaṃ vidyāviṣayam anāmarūpakarmātmakam"neti neti"(2 / 3 / 6) iti itarapratyākhyānenopasaṃhariṣyati pṛthak /
yastu vāgādisamāhāropādhiparikalpitaḥ saṃsāryātmā taṃ ca vāgādisamāhārapakṣapātinameva darśayiṣyati"etebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya tānyevānuvinaśyati"(2 / 4 / 12) iti /
tasmādyuktā vāgādīnāmeva jñānakarmakartṛtvaphalaprāptivivakṣā /
tatheti tathāstviti devairuktā vāktebhyo 'rthibhyor'thāya udakāyadudgānaṃ kṛtavatī /
kaḥ punarasau devebhyor'thāya udgānakarmaṇā vācā nirvartitaḥ kāryaviśeṣaḥ? ityucyate- yo vācī nimittabhūtāyāṃ vāgādisamudāyasya ya upakāro niṣpadyate vadanādivyāpāreṇa, sa eva /
sarveṣāṃ hyasau vāgvadanābhinirvṛtto bhogaḥ phalam /
taṃ bhogaṃ sā tṛṣu pavamāneṣu kṛtvā avaśiṣṭeṣu navasu stotreṣu vācanikamārtvijyaṃ phalaṃ yatkalyāṇaṃ śobhanaṃ vadati varṇānabhinirvartayati tad ātmane mahyameva /
taddhyasādhāraṇaṃ vāgdevatāyāḥ karma yatsamyagvarṇānāmuccāraṇam /
atastadeva viśeṣyate yatkalyāṇaṃ vadatīti /
yattu vadanakāryaṃ sarvasaṃghātopakārātmakaṃ tadyājamānameva /
tatra kalyāṇavadanātmasambandhāsaṅgāvasaraṃ devatāyā randhraṃ pratilamya te vidurasurāḥ, katham? anenodgātrāno 'smānsvābhāvikaṃ jñānaṃ cābhibhūyātītya śāstrajanitakarmajñānarūpeṇa jyotiṣodgātrātmanā atyeṣvantyatigamiṣyanti /
ityevaṃ vijñāya samudgātāramabhidrutyābhigamya svena āsaṅgalakṣaṇena pāpmanāvidhyaṃstāḍitavantaḥ saṃyojitavanta ityarthaḥ /
sa yaḥ sa pāpmā prajāpateḥ pūrvajanmāvasthasya vāci kṣiptaḥ sa eṣa pratyakṣīkriyate /
children.translated_text: That evil which was cast upon speech by <s>Prajāpati</s> in its former birth-state — that is now made manifest.

children.text: ko 'sau? yadevamapratirūpamananurūpaṃ śāstrapratiṣiddhaṃ vadati yena prayukto 'sabhyabībhatsānṛtādyanicchannapi vadati /
children.translated_text: What is it? That which [makes one] speak what is improper — what is unfitting, what is prohibited by scripture — by which, being impelled, one speaks obscene, disgusting, and false things even unwillingly.

children.text: anena kāryeṇāpratirūpavadanena anugamyamānaḥ prajāpateḥ kāryabhūtāsu prajāsu vāci vartate /
children.translated_text: Through this effect — the speaking of improper things — [the evil], being inferred, exists in speech among the creatures who are the products of <s>Prajāpati</s>.
