children.text: guṇavijñānaphalamidamucyate - yathāyamātmātmā nāmarūpānupraveśena khyātiṃ gata ātmetyādināmarūpābhyāṃ prāṇādisaṃhatiṃ ca ślokaṃ prāptavānityevaṃ yo veda,sa kīrtiṃ khyātiṃ ślokaṃ ca saṅghātamiṣṭaiḥ saha vindate labhate /
children.translated_text: The fruit of the knowledge of this quality is stated: just as this self, by name the <s>Ātman</s>, having entered into name and form, attained renown as 'the self,' and attained association (<s>śloka</s>) with the aggregate of <s>prāṇa</s> and so forth through name and form — one who knows thus attains fame, renown, and association (<s>śloka</s>), i.e., community with desirable [beings].

children.text: yadvā yathoktaṃ vastu yo veda mumukṣūṇāmapekṣitaṃ kīrtiśabditamaikyajñānaṃ tatphalaṃ ślokaśabditāṃ muktimāpnotīti mukhyameva phalam //7//
children.translated_text: Alternatively, one who knows the thing as described — the knowledge of oneness, designated by the word '<s>kīrti</s>' (fame), which is sought by those who desire liberation — attains as its fruit liberation, designated by the word '<s>śloka</s>' — and this is indeed the principal fruit. // 7 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.7:] 'That' — this word 'that' (<s>tat</s>) refers to the world in its seed-state prior to manifestation, at that time; it is denoted by the pronoun 'that,' which is an indirect designation using an indefinite pronoun, because of the remoteness [of that state], and because the world in its unmanifest condition belongs to the past. The word '<s>ha</s>' is used in the sense of tradition for ease of comprehension. When it is said 'thus indeed it was at that time,' one easily apprehends that seed-state of the world, even though it is remote — just as when it is said '<s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> was indeed a king.' The word 'this' (<s>idam</s>) refers to the manifest world constituted by name and form, characterized by ends and means, as previously described. From the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of the words 'that' and 'this' — which denote the world in its remote and immediately present states respectively — the identity of the world in its unmanifest and manifest states is understood: that very thing is this, and this very thing is that which was unmanifest. And this being so, it is ascertained that there is no origination from non-being, nor destruction of being, with respect to the effect. That world, being of such nature, which was unmanifest, became manifest precisely through name and form — through name and through form alone. The verb 'became manifest' (<s>vyākriyata</s>) is used in the <s>karma-kartṛ</s> construction (middle voice where the object acts upon itself), meaning that it — the <s>Ātman</s> itself — manifested itself; it became distinctly manifest, attaining the state of manifestation with the determination of particular names and forms as its limit, the governing agent, instrumental cause, action, and occasioning factor being implied by its own inherent power. 'Of such-and-such a name' — by designating with an indefinite pronoun without specifying, it indicates mere name. 'His name is <s>Devadatta</s>' or '<s>Yajñadatta</s>' — thus 'he is of such-and-such a name.' Similarly, 'this' is the non-specification of white, black, and so forth. 'This is his white form' or 'this is his black form' — thus 'he is of this form.' That thing which was unmanifest becomes manifest even now, at the present time too, through name and form alone: 'he is of such-and-such a name, he is of this form.' That for the sake of which all scriptural enterprise is undertaken; upon which, through beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the superimposition of agent, action, and result has been made; which is the cause of the entire world; in which — as its own nature — name and form, which were previously unmanifest, become manifest like foam or impurity arising from clear water; and which is distinct from those two — name and form — being by its own nature eternally pure, awakened, and free (<s>nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāva</s>) — that <s>Ātman</s>, manifesting the unmanifest name and form which constitute its own [apparent] body, has entered into bodies here in this world, from <s>Brahmā</s> down to a clump of grass, which are the substrata of the fruits of action and which are subject to hunger and the rest. But it was said that the unmanifest manifested itself — how then is it now said that the supreme <s>Ātman</s> itself, manifesting the unmanifest, entered here? This is not a fault, because even the supreme <s>Ātman</s> is intended to be spoken of as having the unmanifest world as its own nature. We have said that the unmanifest world becomes manifest, the governing agent, instrumental cause, action, and occasioning factor being implied by its inherent power. And because of the co-referentiality of the unmanifest with 'this' [world]: just as this world is manifest with the diversity of particular agents such as the controller, and multiple causes and conditions, so too that unmanifest [world] possessed the same diversity, without having abandoned any of those particular features. The only distinction is between the manifest and unmanifest states. And in the world, the use of words is observed to vary according to the speaker's intention — 'the village has arrived' and 'the village is empty.' Sometimes the word 'village' is used when one intends merely the habitation, and 'the village is empty' is the expression used; sometimes when one intends the inhabitants, 'the village has arrived' is used; and sometimes the word 'village' is used when both are intended, as in 'one should not enter the village.' Similarly here too, when the identity of the <s>Ātman</s> and the non-self is intended, the designation applies to both the manifest and unmanifest world. Similarly, 'this world is subject to origination and destruction' is a designation pertaining to the world alone. Likewise, 'The great unborn <s>Ātman</s>' (BṛUp 4.4.22), 'Not gross, not subtle... this is "not this, not this"' (BṛUp 3.9.26) and the like are designations pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s> alone. But if the entire world, which has been manifested by the supreme Manifester, is pervaded by Him always and everywhere — how is it imagined that He 'entered' here? For an unpenetrated place can be entered by a delimited entity, just as a village can be entered by a person. But nothing can be entered by space (<s>ākāśa</s>), since it is never not-entered. If it be said: like a snake in a stone, or water in a coconut — [the Self exists there] by virtue of a different attribute — [we say:] even so, the supreme <s>Ātman</s> did not enter in His own essential form. Rather, while remaining right there, He is born with a different attribute, and by that He is figuratively said to have 'entered' — like a snake inherent within a stone, or water within a coconut. No — because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'Having created that, He entered into that very thing' (TaiUp 2.6.1). For it is heard that the very creator, without undergoing any change of state, having created the effect, subsequently entered it — just as 'having eaten, he goes,' where the eater and goer are the same undifferentiated agent, and the two actions of eating and going are distinguished only by temporal sequence. But this cannot be the case for one who is already present there and merely undergoes a change of attribute. Nor has entry — defined as disconnecting from one place and connecting with another — ever been observed for something partless and unlimited. If it be said that entry is heard only of something with parts — no, because of <s>śrutis</s> such as 'The divine, formless <s>Puruṣa</s>' (MuUp 2.1.2), 'Partless, actionless' (ŚveUp 6.19), and because of <s>śrutis</s> that negate all attributable properties. If it be said: like the entry of a reflection — no, because separation from another substance is impossible [for the all-pervading Self]. If it be said: like a quality entering a substance — no, because [the Self] is not dependent. Only a quality that is eternally dependent and supported is figuratively said to 'enter' a substance. But since <s>Brahman</s> is heard to be independent, such entry is not tenable. If it be said: like a seed in a fruit — no, because that would entail the faults of having parts, growth, decay, origination, destruction, and the like. And <s>Brahman</s> does not have such attributes, because of the contradiction with <s>śruti</s> and reasoning such as 'Unborn, undecaying.' Therefore, a different, limited, transmigrating entity has entered — if this be said — no, because of the <s>śruti</s> beginning with 'This deity reflected' (ChUp 6.3.2) and continuing to 'Let me manifest name and form' (ChUp 6.3.2), which attributes the agency of entry and manifestation to that very [supreme deity]. Similarly, 'Having created that, He entered into that very thing' (TaiUp 2.6.1); 'He split open this very seam and entered by this door' (AiUp 3.12); 'The wise one, having created all forms, having made names, goes on calling [them]'; 'You are a boy and also a girl; you totter as an old man with a staff' (ŚveUp 4.3); 'He made two-footed bodies' (BṛUp 2.5.18); 'form after form' (KaUp 2.2.9) — from these <s>mantra</s> passages, entry belongs to none other than the Supreme. If it be said that because of the mutual difference among those who have entered, the Supreme must be many — no, because of <s>śrutis</s> such as 'The one God has entered in many ways' (ŚveUp 6.11), 'Being one, He moved about in many ways,' 'You are one, having entered into many,' 'The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings.' Let the question whether entry is tenable or not stand aside for now. If it be said that since those who have entered are transmigrators, and the Supreme is non-different from them, the Supreme too would be a transmigrator — no, because of the <s>śruti</s> that [He] transcends hunger and the rest. If it be objected that He is observed to experience pleasure and pain — no, because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'He is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external [to it]' (KaUp 2.2.11). If it be said this is untenable because of contradiction with perception and the like — no, because perception and the like pertain to distinctions generated by dependence on limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>). From <s>śrutis</s> such as 'You cannot see the seer of seeing' (BṛUp 3.4.2), 'By what would one know the knower?' (BṛUp 4.5.15), 'The knower is unknown' (BṛUp 3.8.11), knowledge does not have the <s>Ātman</s> as its object. Rather, perceptual knowledge such as 'I am happy' or 'I am suffering' has as its object only the reflection of the <s>Ātman</s> in the limiting adjuncts of intellect and the like. By the figurative co-referential usage of the object with the subject — 'I am this' — and because of the negation of any other self — 'There is no other seer than this' (BṛUp 3.8.11) — and because pleasure and pain are qualified by particular bodily parts, they are properties of the object [not the subject]. If it be said that the <s>śruti</s> 'For the sake of the <s>Ātman</s> indeed' (BṛUp 2.4.5) implies that things are for the <s>Ātman</s>'s purpose, and hence [the <s>Ātman</s> has desires and suffering] — no, because of the admission that 'Where, as it were, there is another' (BṛUp 4.5.15) pertains to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>; and because of the negation thereof in the domain of <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) by such passages as 'By what would one see whom?' (BṛUp 4.5.15), 'There is no diversity here whatsoever' (BṛUp 4.4.19), 'Where is delusion, where is sorrow for the one who sees oneness?' (ĪśUp 7) — therefore [suffering] is not an attribute of the <s>Ātman</s>. If it be said this is untenable because of contradiction with the system of the logicians (<s>tārkikas</s>) — no, because even by reasoning, the <s>Ātman</s>'s being a sufferer is untenable. For suffering, which is an object of perception, cannot qualify the <s>Ātman</s>, since [the <s>Ātman</s>] is not an object of perception. If it be said that the <s>Ātman</s>'s being a sufferer is like space having the quality of sound — no, because it is untenable for them to be objects of a single cognition. For it is not tenable that the <s>Ātman</s>, which is always an object of inference, be objectified by that very perceptual cognition which apprehends pleasure; and if it were so objectified, since the <s>Ātman</s> is one, the absurd consequence would be that the subject would become an object. If it be said: like a lamp, a single thing can be both object and subject — no, because they cannot occur simultaneously, and because parts in the <s>Ātman</s> are untenable. By this, the claim that consciousness has the dual nature of being both apprehended and apprehender is also refuted. And between suffering, which is an object of perception, and the <s>Ātman</s>, which is an object of inference, the relation of quality and substrate is not established by inference. Because suffering is always an object of perception, and because of its co-referentiality with form and the like [which are properties of objects]. Even if suffering were generated by contact with the mind, to attribute it to the <s>Ātman</s> would entail the absurd consequences of the <s>Ātman</s> having parts, being subject to modification, and being non-eternal. For no quality has ever been observed to approach or depart from a substance without modifying that substance. And nothing partless has been observed to undergo modification, nor has anything been observed to be both eternal and the substrate of non-eternal qualities. Nor is space accepted as eternal by the āgama-theorists, and there is no other example. If it be said that even though modified, [the <s>Ātman</s>] is eternal because the cognition of it does not cease — no, because modification of a substance is impossible without alteration of its parts. If it be said that even something with parts can be eternal — no, because something with parts, being preceded by the conjunction of its parts, is susceptible to disjunction. If it be said this is not observed in the case of diamonds and the like — no, because the precedence of conjunction is to be inferred. Therefore, it is not tenable that the <s>Ātman</s> is the substrate of non-eternal qualities such as suffering. If it be objected that if the Supreme is free from suffering and there is no other sufferer, the undertaking of scripture for the alleviation of suffering would be purposeless — no, because [scripture's purpose is] the removal of the erroneous notion of being a sufferer, which is superimposed through <s>avidyā</s> — just as [scripture removes] the erroneous notion of numbers superimposed upon the <s>Ātman</s> under discussion. And because the suffering self is accepted as imagined. The entry of the <s>Ātman</s> is like the reflection of the sun and the like in water — like a reflection, it is perceived within the manifest effect. The <s>Ātman</s>, not perceived prior to creation, and subsequently perceived within the created, manifest effect, within the intellect — appearing like a reflection of the sun in water — having created the effect, appears as if He has entered; He is designated thus: 'This [<s>Ātman</s>] has entered here' (BṛUp 1.4.7); 'Having created that, He entered into that very thing' (TaiUp 2.6.1); 'He split open this very seam and entered by this door' (AiUp 3.12); 'This deity reflected: Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self' (ChUp 6.3.2) — by such [statements]. But for the all-pervading, partless [<s>Ātman</s>], entry — defined as departing from one place and arriving at another — is never tenable. Nor is there any other self besides the Supreme — 'There is no other seer than this; there is no other hearer than this' (BṛUp 3.8.11) — so we have said. And because the statements about creation, entry, sustenance, and dissolution have the purpose of realizing [the oneness of] the <s>Ātman</s>, and because it is heard that realization is of the highest human purpose: '<s>Ātmānam evāvet</s>' — 'He knew the <s>Ātman</s> alone' (BṛUp 1.4.10); 'Therefore he became all' (BṛUp 1.4.10); 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (TaiUp 2.1.1); 'He who knows that supreme <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (MuUp 3.2.9); 'A person who has a teacher knows' (ChUp 6.14.2); 'For him there is that much delay only' (ChUp 6.14.2) — from such <s>śrutis</s>; and from <s>smṛtis</s> such as: 'Knowing Me in truth, he enters that thereafter' (BhG 18.55); 'This is the foremost of all sciences; from it immortality is attained.' And because the statements about creation and the like are sublated by [the teaching of] the vision of difference being [merely apparent], it is tenable that they have the purpose of the vision of the oneness of the <s>Ātman</s>. Therefore, perceivability within the effect alone is figuratively called 'entry.' The consciousness of the <s>Ātman</s> is perceived from the tips of the toenails to the tips of the fingernails. How, as it were, has He entered there? [The text] says: just as in the world, a razor is contained (<s>avahita</s>) in a razor-case — a razor-case (<s>kṣuradhāna</s>) is that in which a razor is placed, i.e., in that barber's equipment-case, the razor inside is perceived as contained, as placed within. Or just as fire — <s>Viśvambhara</s> (all-sustaining), so called because it sustains all — is contained in its abode, its nest, i.e. in wood and the like — '<s>avahita</s>' ('contained') is carried forward [from the previous clause]. For there [in wood], fire is perceived when [the wood] is churned. Just as a razor is situated in one part of the razor-case, and just as fire is situated pervading wood and the like in their entirety — so too the <s>Ātman</s> is situated pervading the body both generally and particularly. For there [in the body], it is perceived as possessing the activities of breathing and the like, and of seeing and the like. Therefore, that <s>Ātman</s> which has thus entered — endowed with the particular activities of breathing and the like — they do not see, do not perceive. But is not this negation of seeing already established [i.e., there is nothing new to negate], since seeing [of the <s>Ātman</s>] is not the topic under discussion? This is not a fault, because the statements about creation and the like have the purpose of the realization of the oneness of the <s>Ātman</s>, and therefore the seeing of it is indeed the topic. [This follows] from the <s>mantra</s> passage: 'Form after form He became; that is His form, for the sake of making Him visible' (BṛUp 2.5.19). There, the reason for not seeing [the <s>Ātman</s>] as qualified by the activities of breathing and the like is stated: because it is incomplete (<s>akṛtsna</s>), not whole. Why is it incomplete? It is said: when performing the activity of breathing alone, it becomes [known as] <s>prāṇa</s> — the one designated as <s>prāṇa</s>, bearing the name <s>prāṇa</s>. For it is called '<s>prāṇa</s>' because of being the agent of the activity of breathing — it is not called [<s>prāṇa</s>] while performing another activity. Just as [one is called] a reaper or a cook [only when performing that function]. Therefore, because the other qualifying activities are not included, it is incomplete. Similarly, when speaking, performing the activity of speaking, it speaks — [it is called] speech (<s>vāk</s>). When seeing, [it is called] the eye — 'the eye sees.' When hearing, [it is called] the ear — 'the ear hears.' By 'when breathing, it is <s>prāṇa</s>' and 'when speaking, it is speech,' the origin of the power of action is demonstrated. By 'when seeing, it is the eye' and 'when hearing, it is the ear,' the origin of the power of knowledge is demonstrated, because the power of knowledge pertains to name and form. The ear and eye are the instruments of knowledge, while knowledge is the means of [apprehending] name and form. For there is nothing knowable apart from name and form. And the eye and ear are the instruments for perceiving these two. Action, which is to be accomplished through name and form and is conjoined with <s>prāṇa</s> — speech is the instrument for the expression of that [action], which depends on <s>prāṇa</s>. Similarly, [the organs called] hand, foot, excretory organ, and reproductive organ. Speech is mentioned as representative of all [action-organs]. For this alone is the entirety of what is manifest: 'This is threefold indeed — name, form, and action' (BṛUp 1.6.1) — so [the text] will say. 'The thinker' — the mind is called the one who thinks (<s>manvāna</s>); knowledge-capacity and its particular developments — for these, the mind is the common instrument: 'one thinks by it.' But the person (<s>puruṣa</s>), being the agent, while thinking, is called 'the thinker' (<s>manvāna</s>). These — <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest — are the action-names of this <s>Ātman</s>: names born from action, names pertaining to action alone, not designating the mere reality [of the <s>Ātman</s>]. Therefore, they do not illuminate the <s>Ātman</s> in its completeness. For thus this <s>Ātman</s>, though being manifested, illuminated, through the activities of breathing and the like, through the name-and-form generated by each respective activity — yet one who, from this aggregate of activities of breathing and the like, takes each one individually — [thinking] 'this <s>Ātman</s> is <s>prāṇa</s>' or 'it is the eye' — and meditates upon it as qualified by a specific [function] without including the other qualifying activities — he does not know <s>Brahman</s>. Why? Because this <s>Ātman</s> is incomplete when taken separately from this aggregate of breathing and the like. Therefore, being divided, qualified by each individual qualification without the inclusion of the other attributes, it becomes [incomplete]. As long as one knows thus — 'I see,' 'I hear,' 'I touch' — knowing [the <s>Ātman</s>] as qualified by a naturally occurring specific activity — so long one does not directly know the complete <s>Ātman</s>. How then does one know it properly? [The text] says: as the <s>Ātman</s> alone — '<s>Ātman</s>' means that which attains the qualifying attributes such as <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest that have been mentioned. Not thus [individually qualified], but by including all qualifications, does it become complete. For it attains the qualifications — the specific activities generated by the particular limiting adjuncts of <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest — in its mere essential nature. And thus [the text] will say: 'It appears to think, appears to move' (BṛUp 4.3.7). Therefore, one should meditate upon it as the <s>Ātman</s> alone. For thus, apprehended in its own essential nature, it becomes complete. Why is it complete? To this anticipated question [the text] says: because in this <s>Ātman</s>, all the particular attributes created by the limiting adjuncts of <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest — designated by the action-names such as <s>prāṇa</s> — they all become one, attain non-differentiation — just as the distinctions caused by sun-reflections in water merge in the sun when no limiting adjunct [remains]. '<s>Ātmety evopāsīta</s>' — 'One should meditate upon it as the <s>Ātman</s> alone' — is not a new injunction (<s>apūrvavidhi</s>). Because, on the alternative view, it is already accomplished: 'That which is directly and immediately <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 3.4.1); 'Which is the <s>Ātman</s>? That which consists of knowledge' (BṛUp 4.3.7) — by such <s>śrutis</s> directed at establishing the <s>Ātman</s>, knowledge pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s> has been produced. When, through knowledge of the essential nature of the <s>Ātman</s>, the <s>avidyā</s> — consisting of the superimposition of agent, action, and result upon the non-self — pertaining to that very [<s>Ātman</s>] has been removed, then, since defects such as desire and the like become untenable [when <s>avidyā</s> is removed], thinking about the non-self becomes untenable. Therefore, on this view, the meditation [on the <s>Ātman</s>] need not be enjoined, since it is already accomplished. Let the question stand whether the attainment of <s>Ātman</s>-meditation on this alternative view is eternal — [if so], it would be a new injunction, since knowledge and meditation, being identical, are not yet accomplished. [The objection continues:] since [the text] first presents 'he does not know' with reference to knowledge, and then says '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>' (one should meditate upon it as the <s>Ātman</s> alone), the identity of meaning of the words 'know' and 'meditate' is understood. And from <s>śrutis</s> such as 'By this, one knows all' and '<s>ātmānam evāvet</s>' ('he knew the <s>Ātman</s> alone,' BṛUp 1.4.10), knowledge is [identical with] meditation. And since that [meditation] is not yet accomplished, it is fit to be enjoined. And since exertion by a person is not possible with respect to a mere description of the nature of a thing, therefore this is indeed a new injunction. And because of the analogy with injunctions of action: just as 'one should sacrifice,' 'one should offer oblations,' and the like are injunctions of action — from these, no distinction is understood between them and the injunction of meditation on the <s>Ātman</s> such as '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.7) and '<s>ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ</s>' ('the <s>Ātman</s> is to be seen,' BṛUp 2.4.5). And because knowledge, being a mental activity, [can be enjoined]: just as the mental activity 'one should meditate upon the deity for whom the oblation has been taken up, while about to pronounce <s>vaṣaṭ</s>' is enjoined, so too '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>' and '<s>mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>' ('it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon,' BṛUp 2.4.5) — this very activity, consisting of knowledge, is enjoined. And thus we have said that 'know' and 'meditate' are identical in meaning. And because of the tenability of the three components of injunction: just as in the injunction 'one should sacrifice,' the three components — by what? how? — are understood as removing the expectation regarding what is to be accomplished — so too, in the injunction 'one should meditate,' when it is being enjoined — 'what should one meditate upon? by what should one meditate?' — in response to this expectation: 'one should meditate upon the <s>Ātman</s>, by the mind, equipped with the requisite practices of renunciation, <s>brahmacarya</s>, tranquility, self-control, withdrawal, and forbearance' — thus the three components are established by scripture itself. And just as the entire section on the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> and the like has its utility as serving the injunction of the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, so too the Upaniṣadic sections have their utility as serving the injunction of <s>Ātman</s>-meditation. The passages 'not this, not this' (BṛUp 2.3.6), 'not gross' (BṛUp 3.8.8), 'One alone, without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1), 'transcending hunger and the rest' — such sentences have their utility in specifying the essential nature of the <s>Ātman</s> that is to be meditated upon. And the fruit is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), or the cessation of <s>avidyā</s>. Others explain: through meditation, one should produce a special, distinct knowledge pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s>; by that, the <s>Ātman</s> is known; and that very [knowledge] is what removes <s>avidyā</s> — not the knowledge generated by the Vedic sentences pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s>. In support of this view, there are also statements such as: 'Having known, one should cultivate <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom)' (BṛUp 4.4.21); '<s>draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ</s>' — 'It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and deeply meditated upon' (BṛUp 2.4.5); 'It is to be sought, it is to be desired to be known' (ChUp 4). [We say:] no, because there is no other thing [to be produced by meditation, apart from knowledge]. And '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>' is not a new injunction. Why? Because apart from the knowledge generated by the sentences that describe the essential nature of the <s>Ātman</s> and negate the non-self, there is no mental or external [activity possible]. For an injunction is fruitful only where, apart from the knowledge generated merely by hearing the injunctive sentence, a person's exertion is understood [to be required]. As in the case of 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>' — for the knowledge generated by the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> injunctive sentence is not itself the performance of the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, and that [performance] requires qualification and other [conditions]. But apart from the knowledge generated by the <s>Ātman</s>-establishing sentences such as 'not this, not this,' no human activity is possible — as with the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> [performance]. Because the knowledge generated by those sentences is the cause of the cessation of all activity. For dispassionate knowledge does not generate activity, and because the sentences such as 'One alone, without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1) and 'You are That' (ChUp 6.8–16) remove the knowledge of non-<s>Brahman</s> and non-<s>Ātman</s>. And when that [false knowledge] is removed, activity is not tenable — because of contradiction. If it be said that the knowledge generated merely by the sentence does not remove the knowledge of non-<s>Brahman</s> and non-<s>Ātman</s> — no, because the sentences 'You are That' (ChUp 6.8–16), 'Not this, not this' (BṛUp 2.3.6), 'The <s>Ātman</s> alone is all this' (ChUp 7.25.2), 'One alone, without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1), '<s>Brahman</s> alone is this immortal' (MuUp 2.2.11), 'There is no other seer' (BṛUp 3.8.11), 'Know that very <s>Brahman</s>' (KeUp 1.4) — these sentences are declaratory of precisely that [removal]. If it be said these are merely specifiers of the object for the injunction 'it is to be seen' — no, because, as stated, there is no other thing [beyond knowledge]. Since the very sentences 'You are That' and the like accomplish the seeing [of truth] simultaneously with the time of hearing, the injunction 'it is to be seen' does not require any further performance — this has been stated as the answer. If it be said that mere description of the essential nature of the <s>Ātman</s> does not, without an injunction, cause knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> to arise — no, because knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> is generated by hearing the <s>Ātman</s>-declaring sentences — what is the point of performing what has already been accomplished? If it be said that even hearing does not produce [knowledge] without an injunction — no, because of the absurd consequence of infinite regress. Just as one does not engage in hearing the meaning of <s>Ātman</s>-declaring sentences without an injunction, so too one will not engage in hearing the meaning of injunctive sentences without [another] injunction — and so the expectation of another injunction [would lead to regress]. And similarly for hearing the meaning of that [further injunction] — infinite regress would follow. If it be said that the continuous stream of memory-knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> is something different from the knowledge generated merely by hearing the sentence — no, because it is already entailed. The moment knowledge pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s> arises from hearing the <s>Ātman</s>-establishing sentence, at that very moment it arises as destroying the false knowledge pertaining to that [<s>Ātman</s>]. And when the false knowledge pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s> is removed, the memories born from it — which naturally pertain to the diversity of non-<s>Ātman</s> objects — do not arise. And because purposelessness is understood: when the <s>Ātman</s> is known, every other thing is understood as purposeless, being endowed with the many faults of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and the like, and the <s>Ātman</s>-reality being of the opposite character. Therefore, the memories and cognitions of non-<s>Ātman</s> things are destined to cease upon the knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s>. By elimination, the continuous stream of memory-knowledge of the oneness of the <s>Ātman</s> comes about of its own accord — it need not be enjoined, since it also removes the defects of suffering such as sorrow, delusion, fear, and the like. For the defects of sorrow, delusion, and the like are born from false knowledge. And thus: 'Where is delusion, where is sorrow for the one who sees oneness?' (ĪśUp 7); 'The wise one does not fear from anything' (TaiUp 2.9.1); 'O <s>Janaka</s>, you have attained fearlessness' (BṛUp 4.2.4); 'The knot of the heart is split' (MuUp 2.2.8) — such <s>śrutis</s>. If it be said that cessation of mental activity (<s>nirodha</s>) is something different [and hence can be enjoined] — even if the cessation of mental modifications (<s>cittavṛttinirodha</s>) is indeed different from the knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> generated by the Vedic sentences, and even though it is understood as something to be practiced in other systems — it can be enjoined? No — because it is not understood as a means to liberation [in the Vedānta]. For in the Vedānta, nothing other than the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>-<s>Ātman</s> is understood as a means to the highest human goal. From hundreds of <s>śrutis</s> such as: '<s>ātmānam evāvet</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.10); 'Therefore he became all' (BṛUp 1.4.10); 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (TaiUp 2.1.1); 'He who knows that supreme <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (MuUp 3.2.9); 'A person who has a teacher knows' (ChUp 6.14.2); 'For him there is that much delay only' (ChUp 6.14.2); 'One who knows <s>Brahman</s> thus becomes <s>Brahman</s>; fearlessness indeed is <s>Brahman</s> for one who knows thus' (BṛUp 4.4.25). And because <s>nirodha</s> has no other means [than knowledge itself]. For there is no means of cessation of mental modifications other than the knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s> and the continuous stream of memory thereof. This has been said by way of concession; in truth, no means to liberation other than the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is understood. And because of the absence of expectation, there is no [operative] injunction (<s>bhāvanā</s>): what was said — that in 'one should sacrifice' and the like, the removal of expectation regarding fruit, means, and procedure by the three components of the injunction is possible, and similarly here too in the injunction of <s>Ātman</s>-knowledge — that is wrong, because all expectation ceases simultaneously with the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence 'One alone, without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1), 'You are That' (ChUp 6.8–16), 'Not this, not this' (BṛUp 2.3.6), 'Without interior, without exterior' (BṛUp 2.5.19), 'This <s>Ātman</s> is <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 2.5.19). And one does not engage in knowing the meaning of the sentence under compulsion of an injunction — and we have stated the fault of infinite regress if [one requires] another injunction. And in the sentences 'One alone, without a second, is <s>Brahman</s>' and the like, no injunction is understood — because they are exhausted in merely describing the essential nature of a thing. If it be said that because they merely describe the nature of a thing, they lack authority (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) — even if it were so, that just as in 'He wept; because he wept, that is the <s>Rudra</s>-ness of <s>Rudra</s>' and the like, since they merely describe the nature of a thing, they lack authority — similarly, the <s>Ātman</s>-sentences would also [lack authority]? No — because of a distinction. It is not the case that a sentence's authority or lack thereof is caused by its describing a thing or describing an action. Rather, [authority is determined by] its capacity to produce definite and fruitful knowledge. Where this [capacity] exists, the sentence is authoritative; where it does not, it is not. Moreover, we ask you: in the sentences directed at describing the essential nature of the <s>Ātman</s> — does definite and fruitful knowledge arise, or not? If it does arise — how can they lack authority? Or do you not see the cessation of the defects that are the seeds of <s>saṃsāra</s> — <s>avidyā</s>, sorrow, delusion, fear, and the like — as the fruit of that knowledge? Or do you not hear the hundreds of Upaniṣadic sentences such as: 'Where is delusion, where is sorrow for the one who sees oneness?' (ĪśUp 7); 'I am a knower of mantras, not a knower of the <s>Ātman</s>; I, sir, grieve; may you, revered sir, take me beyond sorrow' (ChUp 7.1.3)? Now, does definite and fruitful knowledge arise in the case of 'He wept' and the like? If it does not — then let them lack authority. But if those [<s>Ātman</s>-sentences] that produce definite and fruitful knowledge are denied authority — why should they lack it? And if those were denied authority, what confidence could there be in the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> sentences and the like? You say the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> sentences are authoritative because they produce knowledge that impels human activity. And this is absent in the <s>Ātman</s>-knowledge sentences. True — this is not a fault. Because the criterion of authority applies as stated, and no other. And this is an ornament [rather than a defect]: that the <s>Ātman</s>-establishing sentences produce knowledge whose fruit contradicts the seed of all activity — this is not a cause of non-authority. As for the statement that sentences like 'Having known, one should cultivate <s>prajñā</s>' (BṛUp 4.4.21) have the purpose of meditation distinct from the knowledge of the sentence's meaning — that is true. But it does not serve as a new injunction; on the alternative view, it serves merely as a regulation (<s>niyama</s>) of what is already accomplished. But how is meditation already accomplished [on that view]? We have said that, by elimination, the continuous stream of <s>Ātman</s>-knowledge memory is indeed eternal. Even so — because of the definiteness of the fruit of the <s>karma</s> that initiated the current body, even after the attainment of right knowledge, the activity of speech, mind, and body inevitably continues, owing to the greater force of <s>karma</s> already set in motion — like the whirling of a potter's wheel [after the potter's hand is removed]. Therefore, on this alternative view, the weakness of the flow of knowledge-activity is entailed. Hence, with the support of the strength of means such as renunciation, dispassion, and the like, the continuous stream of <s>Ātman</s>-knowledge memory must be regulated — but it is not newly to be produced, since it is already accomplished — so we have said. Therefore, the sentences 'Having known, one should cultivate <s>prajñā</s>' and the like serve as regulations of the already attained continuous stream of knowledge-memory — no other meaning being possible. [Objection:] But is this not meditation on the non-self, because of the use of the word '<s>iti</s>'? Just as in 'One should meditate upon this as dear' and the like, the qualities of dearness and the like are not themselves the object of meditation, but rather <s>prāṇa</s> and the like, which possess the qualities of dearness, are the object of meditation — so here too, because of the use of '<s>iti</s>' after '<s>ātman</s>,' it would be understood that a non-self entity possessing the quality of <s>Ātman</s> is the object of meditation. And because of the dissimilarity with sentences stating that the <s>Ātman</s> is the object of meditation — [the text] will say later: '<s>ātmānam eva lokam upāsīta</s>' — 'One should meditate upon the <s>Ātman</s> alone as the world' (BṛUp 1.4.15). In that sentence, the <s>Ātman</s> itself is intended as the object of meditation, since the accusative case is heard — '<s>ātmānam eva</s>.' But here, no accusative is heard. The word '<s>ātman</s>' follows '<s>iti</s>': '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>.' Therefore, it is not the <s>Ātman</s> that is to be meditated upon, but some other entity with the quality of <s>Ātman</s> — this is the understanding. No — because from the remainder of the sentence, the <s>Ātman</s> is understood as the object of meditation. In the continuation of this very sentence, the <s>Ātman</s> itself is understood as the object of meditation: 'This alone is that which is to be sought, of all this — that which is this <s>Ātman</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.7); 'More inward is that which is this <s>Ātman</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.8); '<s>ātmānam evāvet</s>' — 'He knew the <s>Ātman</s> alone' (BṛUp 1.4.10). [Objection:] Because of the negation of seeing with respect to the one who has entered, [the <s>Ātman</s>] is not fit to be meditated upon. The seeing of that very <s>Ātman</s> whose entry was stated is negated — 'they do not see Him' (BṛUp 4.3.23) — because it is the one under discussion that is taken up [for negation]. Therefore, the <s>Ātman</s> is not fit for meditation? No — because of the fault of incompleteness (<s>akṛtsnatva</s>). The negation of seeing has the intention of [pointing to] the fault of incompleteness — not [the intention of] negating the <s>Ātman</s>'s fitness for meditation. [The negation is] on account of qualification by the specific activities of breathing and the like. For if the <s>Ātman</s>'s fitness for meditation were not intended, the statement of the <s>Ātman</s>'s incompleteness when qualified by each individual activity of breathing and the like — 'for He is incomplete when [taken] as each one individually' (BṛUp 1.4.7) — would be purposeless. Therefore, when qualified not individually but collectively, the <s>Ātman</s> is indeed fit for meditation, because of its completeness — this is established. As for the use of the word '<s>ātman</s>' followed by '<s>iti</s>' — that is for the purpose of knowing that the word '<s>ātman</s>' and its conceptual content are not, in the ultimate analysis, applicable to the reality of the <s>Ātman</s>; otherwise, [the text] would have simply said '<s>ātmānam upāsīta</s>' ('one should meditate upon the <s>Ātman</s>'). And if so, the word and concept pertaining to the <s>Ātman</s> would be sanctioned as applicable — and that is undesirable, because of <s>śrutis</s> such as 'Not this, not this' (BṛUp 2.3.6); 'By what would one know the knower?' (BṛUp 2.4.14); 'The knower is unknown' (BṛUp 3.8.12); 'From which words return, along with the mind, without reaching' (TaiUp 2.4.1). As for the sentence '<s>ātmānam eva lokam upāsīta</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.15) — that is directed at preventing meditation on the non-self, and is therefore not a separate [injunctive] sentence. Because both the <s>Ātman</s> and the non-self share the commonality of not being ascertained — [one might think] the <s>Ātman</s> is to be known, and the non-self too. Among these, why is effort directed only toward meditation on the <s>Ātman</s> — '<s>ātmety evopāsīta</s>' — and not toward knowledge of the other [the non-self]? To this it is said: this very [<s>Ātman</s>] under discussion is that which is to be sought, to be reached — nothing else. 'Of all this' — the genitive case is used in the partitive sense: 'in all this,' that is the meaning. 'That which is this <s>Ātman</s>' — that which is the reality of the <s>Ātman</s>. Is the other [non-self] then not to be known at all? No — rather, even though it is to be known, it does not require a separate, additional act of knowledge apart from the knowledge of the <s>Ātman</s>. Why? Because by this <s>Ātman</s>, once known — all this non-self, whatever other thing there is — all that one knows. But how can one thing be known through the knowledge of another? The answer to this we shall give in the passage on the drum and the like. How then is this said to be 'that which is to be sought'? Just as in the world, a footprint — a spot marked by the hoof of a cow or the like — is called <s>pada</s> (track, trace); by that track, one who is searching for, wanting to find, a lost animal, following the track, would find, would obtain [it]. So too, when the <s>Ātman</s> is found, everything is found — this is the meaning. But if knowing the <s>Ātman</s> [means] knowing all — and knowledge is the topic — how is 'finding' (<s>lābha</s>), which is not the topic, being mentioned? No — because the identity of meaning between knowledge and finding is intended. For the 'not-finding' of the <s>Ātman</s> is nothing but ignorance of it. Therefore, knowledge alone is the 'finding' of the <s>Ātman</s> — not a finding characterized by the acquisition of something previously unattained, as in the case of finding a non-self [object]; because there is no distinction between finder and found. For where there is [a case of] the <s>Ātman</s> finding a non-self, the non-self is [what is] to be found. And that, being previously unattained, is to be found through producing a particular action mediated by particular instrumental means. And that [finding] — characterized by the attainment of something previously unattained — is impermanent, because it is born of desire and action generated by false knowledge, like finding a son in a dream. But this [<s>Ātman</s>] is the opposite. Being the <s>Ātman</s> itself, it is not mediated by actions such as production and the like. Even though its essential nature is eternally attained, the only obstruction is <s>avidyā</s> alone. Just as a shell being perceived, but misperceived through error as silver — the non-apprehension is merely the obstruction of false knowledge; and the apprehension is merely knowledge, for the purpose of removing the obstruction of false knowledge. So here too, the 'not-finding' of the <s>Ātman</s> is merely the obstruction of <s>avidyā</s>. Therefore, the removal of that through <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) alone is the 'finding' — no other [finding] is ever tenable. Therefore, the purposelessness of any means other than knowledge for the finding of the <s>Ātman</s> — this we shall explain. (7)

children.text: kutaścātmatattvameva jñeyamanāhatyānyadityāha -
children.translated_text: And why is the self-reality alone to be known, to the exclusion of everything else? He says:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.8
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.4.8]

children.text:
tad etat preyaḥ putrāt preyo vittāt preyo 'nyasmāt sarvasmād antarataraṃ yad ayam ātmā |
sa yo 'nyam ātmanaḥ priyaṃ bruvāṇaṃ brūyāt priyaṃ rotsyatītīśvaro ha tathaiva syāt |
ātmānam eva priyam upāsīta |
sa ya ātmānam eva priyam upāste na hāsya priyaṃ pramāyukaṃ bhavati || BrhUp_1,4.8 ||
children.translated_text: 'This [self] is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than all else, and is the innermost — this self. If someone were to say to one who speaks of anything other than the self as dear: "You will lose what is dear to you" — that would indeed come to pass. One should meditate on the self alone as dear. For one who meditates on the self alone as dear — what is dear to him does not perish.' // BṛhUp 1.4.8 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.8 tadetadātmatattvaṃ preyaḥ priyataraṃ putrāt /
putro hi loke priyaḥ prasiddhastasmādapi priyataramiti niratiśayapriyatvaṃ darśayati /
tathā vittāddhiraṇyaratnādeḥ, tathā anyasyādyalloke priyatvena prasiddhaṃ tasmātsarvasmādityarthaḥ /
tatkasmādātmatattvameva priyataraṃ na prāṇādi? ityucyate - antarataraṃ bāhyātputravittādeḥ prāṇapiṇḍasamudāyo hyantaro 'bhyantaraḥ sannikṛṣṭa ātmanaḥ /
tasmādapyantarādantarataraṃ yadayamātmā yadetadātmatattvam /
yo hi loke niratiśayapriyaḥ sa sarvaprayatnena labdhavyo bhavati /
tathāyamātmā sarvalaukikapriyebhyaḥ priyatamaḥ /
tasmāttallābhe mahānyatna āsthena ityarthaḥ, karttavyatāprāptamapyanyapriyalābhe yatnamujjhitvā /
kasmātpunaḥ ātmānātmapriyayoranyatarapriyahānena itarapriyopādānaprāptau ātmapriyopādānenaivetarahānaṃ kriyate na viparyayaḥ? ityucyate - sa yaḥ kaścidanyamanātmamamamamaviśeṣaṃ putrādikaṃ priyataramātmānaḥ sākāśād brūvāṇaṃ brūyādātmapriyavādī /
kim? priyaṃ tavābhimataṃ putrādilakṣaṇaṃ rotsyatyāvaraṇaṃ prāṇasaṃrodhaṃ prāpsyati /
vinaṅkṣyatīti /
sa kasmādevaṃ bravīti? yasmādīśvaraḥ samarthaḥ paryāpto 'sāvevaṃ vaktuṃ ha yasmāttasmāttathaiva syādyattenoktaṃ prāṇasaṃrodhaṃ prāpsyati /
yathābhūtavādī hi saḥ, tasmātsa īśvaro vaktum /
īśvaraśabdaḥ kṣipravācīti kecit /
bhavedyadi prasiddhiḥ syāt /
tasmādujjhitvānyatpriyamātmānameva priyamupāsīta /
sa ya ātmānameva priyamupāste, ātmaiva priyo nānyo 'stīti pratipadyate 'nyallaukikaṃ priyamapyapriyameveti niścitya upāste cintayati, na hāsyaivaṃvidaḥ priyaṃ pramāyukaṃ pramaraṇaśīlaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: One who thus meditates on the self alone as dear — who understands 'the self alone is dear, nothing else is' — having ascertained that even worldly dear things are in fact not dear, he meditates, reflects. For such a knower, what is dear does not become subject to perishing, does not have the nature of dying.

children.text: nityānuvādamātrametat, ātmavido 'nyasya priyasyāpriyasya cābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: This is merely a restatement of what is eternally the case, since for the knower of the self there is no [separate] existence of what is dear or not dear.

children.text: ātmapriyagrahaṇastutyarthaṃ vā priyaguṇaphalavidhānārthaṃ mandātmadarśinaḥ /
children.translated_text: Or, the mention of 'the dear self' is for the purpose of praise, or for enjoining the meditation on the quality of dearness for one whose vision of the self is still incomplete.

children.text: tācchīlyapratyayopādānāt //8//
children.translated_text: Because of the use of the suffix indicating habitual disposition (<s>tācchīlyapratyaya</s>). // 8 //

[Commentary:] This self-reality is dearer, more beloved, than a son. For a son is well known in the world as dear; [the self] is dearer even than that — [the text] shows its surpassing dearness. Similarly, [dearer] than wealth — gold, jewels, and such. And [dearer] than whatever else is well known in the world as dear — than all that — this is the meaning. Why is the self-reality alone dearer than <s>prāṇa</s> and such? It is said: because it is more interior — a son, wealth, and such are external; the aggregate of <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest is interior, closer, more proximate to the self. Even more interior than that interior is this self, this self-reality. For whoever is supremely dear in the world is sought after with all effort. Similarly, this self is the dearest of all worldly dear things. Therefore, great effort should be applied to attaining it — this is the meaning, even abandoning the effort to attain other dear things. But why, when one must choose between the dear self and the dear non-self, giving up one to obtain the other — why is it the case that by adopting the dear self alone, the other is given up, and not the reverse? It is said: if someone — anyone — were to say to another who speaks of a non-self thing, something undifferentiated as 'mine,' such as a son, as dearer than the self — if a proponent of the self's dearness were to say to him, what? 'What is dear to you, your cherished object in the form of a son and such, will suffer obstruction, confinement of the vital breath — it will perish.' Why does he say this? Because he is '<s>īśvara</s>' (capable, authoritative) — he is competent and qualified to say this. Indeed, it would come to pass just as he has said — that [the dear thing] would suffer confinement of the vital breath. For he speaks in accordance with reality; therefore, he is competent to say so. Some say the word '<s>īśvara</s>' means 'soon, swiftly.' That [interpretation] would [hold] if there were established usage [to that effect]. Therefore, abandoning other dear things, one should meditate on the self alone as dear.

children.text:
sūtritā brahmavidyā ātmetyevopāsīta iti yadarthopaniṣatkṛtasnāpi /
tasyaitasya sūtrasya vyācikhyāsuḥ prayojanābhidhitsayopojjighāṃsati /
children.translated_text: The knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> has been summarized: 'one should meditate as the self alone' — this is the purpose for which the <s>Upaniṣad</s> was composed. Wishing to elaborate on this summarizing <s>sūtra</s>, [the text] introduces [the discussion] by expressing the purpose as a question:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.9
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.4.9]

children.text:
tad āhur yad brahmavidyayā sarvaṃ bhaviṣyanto manuṣyā manyante |
kim u tad brahmāved yasmāt tat sarvam abhavad iti || BrhUp_1,4.9 ||
children.translated_text: 'They say: "Since human beings think that by the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> they will become everything — what then did <s>Brahman</s> know, from which it became all this?"' // BṛhUp 1.4.9 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.9 taditi vakṣyamāṇamanantaravākye 'vadyotyaṃ vastvāhuḥ /
brāhmaṇā brahma vividiṣavo janmajarāmaraṇaprabandhacakrabhramaṇakṛtāyāsaduḥkhodakāpāramahodadhiplavabhūtaṃ gurumāsādya tattīramuttitīrṣavo dharmādharmasādhanatatphalalakṣaṇāt sādhyasādhanarūpānnirviṇṇāḥ tadvilakṣaṇanityaniratiśayaśreyaḥ pratipitsavaḥ /
kimāhurityāha - yadbrahmavidyayā brahma paramātmā tayā brahmavidyayā, sarvaṃ niravaśeṣaṃ bhaviṣyanto bhaviṣyāma ityevaṃ manuṣyā yanmanyante /
manuṣyagrahaṇaṃ viśeṣato 'dhikārajñāpanārtham /
manuṣyā eva hi viśeṣato 'bhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhane 'dhikṛtā ityabhiprāyaḥ /
yathā karmaviṣaye phalaprāptiṃ dhruvāṃ karmabhyo manyante, tathā brahmavidyāyā sarvātmabhāvaphalaprāptiṃ dhruvāmeva manyante /
vedaprāmāṇyasyobhayatrāviśeṣāt /
tatra vipratiṣiddhaṃ vastu lakṣyate 'taḥ pṛcchāmaḥ - kimu tadbrahma yasya vijñānātsarvaṃ bhaviṣyanto manuṣyā manyante? tatkimavedyasmādvijñānāttadbrahma sarvamabhavat? brahma ca sarvamiti śrūyate /
tadyadyavijñāya kiñcitsarvamabhavattathānyeṣāmapyastu, kiṃ brahmavidyayā? atha vijñāya sarvamabhavat, vijñānasādhyatvātkarmaphalena tulyamevetyanityatvaprasaṅgaḥ sarvabhāvasya brahmavidyāphalasya /
children.translated_text: If without knowing, [<s>Brahman</s>] became everything, then let it be so for others too — what need is there for the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>? But if by knowing it became everything, then since [the becoming of everything] is accomplished through knowledge, it would be on par with the fruit of ritual action — and thus the fault of impermanence would apply to the becoming of everything, the fruit of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: anavasthādoṣaścatadapyanyadvijñāya sarevamabhavattataḥ pūrvamapyanyadvijñāyeti /
children.translated_text: And there would be the fault of infinite regress — [<s>Brahman</s>] knew something else and became everything; prior to that too, it knew something else [and so on].

children.text: na tāvadavijñāya sarvamabhavat, śāstrārthavairūpyadoṣāt /
children.translated_text: [Response:] Firstly, it is not the case that without knowing, [<s>Brahman</s>] became everything — because of the fault of contradicting the meaning of scripture.

children.text: phalānityatvadoṣastarhi? naiko 'pi doṣor'thaviśeṣopapatteḥ //9//
children.translated_text: Then is there the fault of impermanence of the fruit? No, there is not a single fault, because of the cogency of the specific meaning [intended]. // 9 //

[Commentary:] 'That' — [the text] indicates the matter to be presented in the immediately following sentence. 'They say' — <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, those desiring to know <s>Brahman</s>, wearied by the affliction of rotating in the cycle of birth, old age, and death, having found a teacher who serves as a vessel for crossing the vast ocean of [that cycle], desiring to reach the other shore — [these are] those who have become disenchanted with the [means and ends] in the form of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, their instruments, and their fruits, characterized by what is to be accomplished and the means of accomplishing it, and who desire to attain the eternal, unsurpassed good that is different from all that. What do they say? 'Since by the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>' — <s>Brahman</s> is the <s>Paramātman</s> — through that knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, 'everything' — without remainder — 'we will become' — they think thus — these are humans. The use of the word 'humans' (<s>manuṣya</s>) specifically indicates [their] qualification [for this knowledge]. The intended meaning is that humans specifically are qualified for the means of attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good. Just as in the domain of ritual action they consider the attainment of fruit from actions as certain, so too they consider the attainment of the fruit of becoming the self of all from the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> as equally certain. Because the authority of the <s>Veda</s> is the same in both cases. There, a contradictory matter is perceived, hence we ask: what is that <s>Brahman</s>, through whose knowledge humans think they will become everything? Did that <s>Brahman</s> not know — from whose knowledge that <s>Brahman</s> became everything? And <s>śruti</s> declares that <s>Brahman</s> is everything.

children.text:
yadi kimapi vijñāyaiva tadbrahma sarvamabhavatpṛcchāmaḥ - kimu tadbrahmāvet? yasmāttatsarvamabhavaditi /
evaṃ codite sarvadoṣānāgandhitaṃ prativacanamāha-
children.translated_text: If indeed <s>Brahman</s> became everything only by knowing something — we ask: what did that <s>Brahman</s> know, from which it became all this? When the question has been thus raised, [the text] gives an answer untouched by any of the faults:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.10
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.4.10]

children.text:
brahma vā idam agra āsīt |
tad ātmānam evāvet |
ahaṃ brahmāsmīti |
tasmāt tat sarvam abhavat |
tad yo yo devānāṃ pratyabudhyata sa eva tad abhavat |
tatharṣīnām |
tathā manuṣyāṇām |
tad dhaitat paśyann ṛṣir vāmadevaḥ pratipede 'haṃ manur abhavaṃ sūryaś ceti |
tad idam apy etarhi ya evaṃ vedāhaṃ brahmāsmīti sa idaṃ sarvaṃ bhavati |
tasya ha na devāś canābhūtyā īśate |
ātmā hy eṣāṃ sa bhavati |
atha yo 'nyāṃ devatām upāste 'nyo 'sāv anyo 'ham asmīti na sa veda |
yathā paśur evaṃ sa devānām |
yathā ha vai bahavaḥ paśavo manuṣyaṃ bhuñjyur evam ekaikaḥ puruṣo devān bhunakti |
ekasminn eva paśāv ādīyamāne 'priyaṃ bhavati kim u bahuṣu |
tasmād eṣāṃ tan na priyaṃ yad etan manuṣyā vidyuḥ || BrhUp_1,4.10 ||
children.translated_text: '<s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning. It knew only itself: "I am <s>Brahman</s>." Therefore it became all. Whoever among the gods awakened to this — he indeed became that. Likewise among the sages. Likewise among humans. Seeing this, the sage <s>Vāmadeva</s> understood: "I became <s>Manu</s> and <s>Sūrya</s>." And even now, whoever thus knows "I am <s>Brahman</s>" — he becomes this all. Even the gods cannot prevent him, for he becomes their very self. But whoever worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another" — he does not know. He is like an animal to the gods. Just as many animals serve a person, so each person serves the gods. If even one animal is taken away, it causes displeasure — how much more when many are taken? Therefore, it is not pleasing to the gods that humans should know this.' // BṛhUp 1.4.10 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.10 brahmāparam, sarvabhāvasya sādhyatvopapatteḥ /
na hi parasya brahmaṇaḥ sarvabhāvāpattirvijñānasādhyā /
vijñānasādhyāṃ ca sarvabhāvāpattirvijñānasādhyā /
vijñānasādhyāṃ ca sarvabhāvāpattimāha -'tasmāttatsarvamabhavat'iti /
tadasmādbrahma vā idamagra āsīdityaparaṃ brahmeha bhavitumarhati /
manuṣyādhikārādvā tadbhāvī brāhmaṇaḥ syāt /
'sarvaṃ bhaviṣyanto manuṣyā manyante'iti hi manuṣyāḥ prakṛtāḥ, teṣāṃ cābhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhane viśeṣato 'dhikāra ityuktam, na parasya brahmaṇo nāpyaparasya prajāpateḥ /
ato dvaitaikatvāparabrahmavidyayā karmasahitayā aparabrahmabhāvamupasampanno bhojyādapāvṛttaḥ sarvaprāptyocchinnakāmakarmabandhanaḥ parabrahmabhāvī brahmavidyāhetorbrahmetyabhidhīyate /
dṛṣṭaśca loke bhāvinīṃ vṛttimāśritya śabdaprayogaḥ - yathā'odanaṃ pacati'iti, śāstre ca -'parivrājakaḥ sarvabhūtābhayadakṣiṇām'ityādi, tatheheti kecit - brahma brahmabhāvī puruṣo brāhmaṇaḥ - iti vyācakṣate /
tanna, sarvabhāvāpatteranityatvadoṣāt /
na hi so 'sti loke paramārthato yo nimittavaśādbhāvāntaramāpadyate nityaśceti /
tathā brahmavijñānanimittakṛtā cetsarvabhāvāpattiḥ, nityā ceti viruddham /
anityatve ca karmaphalatulyatetyukto doṣaḥ /
avidyākṛtāsarvatvanivṛttiṃ cetsarvabhāvāpattiṃ brahmavidyāphalaṃ manyase, brahmabhāvipuruṣakalpanā vyarthā syāt;prāgbrahmavijñānādapi sarvo jantubrahmatvānnityameva sarvabhāvāpannaḥ paramārthataḥ, avidyayā tvabrahmatvamasarvatvaṃ cādhyāropitam yathā śuktikāyāṃ rajatam, vyomni vā talamalavattvādi, tatheha brahmaṇyadhyoropitamavidyayā abrahmatvamasarvatvaṃ ca brahmavidyayā nivartyata iti manyase yadi, tadā yuktam yatparamārthata āsītparaṃ brahma, brahmaśabdasya mukhyārthabhūtam'brahma vā idamagra āsīt'ityasminvākye ucyate iti vaktum;yathābhūtārthavāditvādvedasya /
na tviyaṃ kalpanā yuktā, brahmaśabdārthaviparīto brahmabhāvī puruṣo brahmetyucyata iti śrutahānyaśrutakalpanāyā anyāyyatvānmahattare prayojanāntare 'sati /
avidyākṛtavyatirekeṇābrahmatvamasarvatvaṃ ca vidyata eveti cenna, tasya brahmavidyayāpohānupapatteḥ /
na hi kvacitsākṣādvastudharmasyāpoḍhrī dṛṣṭā kartrī vā brahmavidyā /
avidyāyāstu sarvatraiva nivartikā dṛśyate /
tathehāpyabrahmatvamasarvatvaṃ cāvidyākṛtameva nivartyatāṃ brahmavidyayā /
na tu pāramārthikaṃ vastu kartuṃ nivartayituṃ vārhati brahmavidyā /
tasmādvyarthaiva śrutahānyaśrutakalpanā /
brahmaṇyavidyānupapattiriti cet? na, brahmaṇi vidyāvidhānāt /
na hi śuktikāyāṃ rajatādhyāropaṇe 'sati śuktikātvaṃ jñāpyate cakṣurgocarāpannāyām - iyaṃ śuktikā na rajatam, iti /
tathā"sadevedaṃ sarvam" "brahmaivedaṃ sarvam" "ātmaivedaṃ sarvam" "nedaṃ dvaitamastyabrahma"iti brahmaṇyekatvavijñānaṃ na vidhātavyaṃ brahmaṇyavidyādhyāropaṇāyāmasatyām /
na brūmaḥ - śuktikāyāmiva brahmaṇyataddharmādhyāropaṇā nāstīti, kiṃ tarhi? na brahma svātmanyataddharmādhyāropanimittam, avidyākartṛ ceti /
bhavatvevaṃ nāvidyākartṛ bhrāntaṃ ca brahma /
kiṃntu naivābrahmāvidyākartā cetano bhrānto 'nya iṣyate /
"nānyo 'to 'sti vijñātā" (bṛ.u.3 / 7 / 23) "nānyadato 'sti vijñātṛ"(3 / 8 / 11) "tattvamasi"(chā.u.6 / 8 -13)"ātmānamevāvet /
ahaṃ brahmāsmi"(bṛ.u.1 / 4 / 10) "anyo 'sāvanyo 'hamasmīti na sa veda"(1 / 4 / 10) ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
smṛtibhyaśca -"samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu"(gītā 13 / 27) "ahamātmāguḍākeśa"(gītā 10 / 20) "śuni caiva śvapāke ca"(gītā 5 / 18) "yastu sarvāṇi bhūtāni"ityādibhyaḥ /
"yasminsarvāṇi bhūtāni" (īśā.u.7) iti ca mantravarṇāt /
nanvevaṃ śāstropadeśānarthakyamiti /
bāḍhamevam avagate 'stvevānarthakyam /
avagamanarthakyamiti cet? na, anavagamanivṛtterdṛṣṭatvāt /
tannivṛtterapyanupapattirekatva iti cet? na dṛṣṭavirodhāt /
dṛśyate hyekatvavijñānādevānavagamanivṛttiḥ, dṛśyamānamapyanupapannamiti bruvato dṛṣṭavirodhaḥ syāt;na ca dṛṣṭavirodhaḥ kenacidapyabhyupagamyate /
na ca dṛṣṭe 'nupapannaṃ nāma, dṛṣṭatvādeva /
darśanānupapattiriti cettatrāpyeṣaiva yuktiḥ /
"puṇyaṃ vai puṇyena karmaṇā bhavati"(bṛ.u.3 / 2 / 13) "taṃ vidyākarmaṇī samanvārabhete" (4 / 4 / 2) ityevamādiśrutismṛtinyāyebhyaḥ parasmādvilakṣaṇo 'nyaḥ saṃsāryavagamyate /
tadvilakṣaṇaśca paraḥ"sa eṣa neti neti"(bṛ.u.3 / 9 / 23) "aśanāyādyatyeti" "ya ātmāpahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyuḥ"(chā.u.8 / 7 / 1) "etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane"(bṛ.u.3 / 8 / 9) ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
kaṇādākṣapādāditarkaśāstreṣu ca saṃsāravilakṣaṇa īśvara upapattitaḥ sādhyate /
saṃsāraduḥkhāpanayārthitvapravṛttidarśanātsphuṭamanyatvamīśvarātsaṃsāriṇo 'vagamyate /
"avākyanādaraḥ"(chā.u.3 / 14 / 2) "na me pārthāsti" (gītā3 / 22) iti śrutibhyaḥ /
"so 'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ"(chā.u.8 / 7 / 1) "taṃ viditvā na lipyate"(bṛ.u.4 / 4 / 23) "brahmavidāpnoti param"(tai.u.2 / 1 / 1) "ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyametat"(bṛ.u.4 / 4 / 20) "yo vā etadakṣaraṃ gārgyaviditvā"(3 / 8 / 10) "tameva dhīro vijñāya"(4 / 4 / 21) "praṇavo dhanuḥ śaro hyātmā brahma tallakṣyamucyate" (mu.u.2 / 2 / 4) ityādikarmakartṛnirdeśācca /
mumukṣośca gatimārgaviśeṣadeśopadeśāt /
asati bhede kasya kuto gatiḥ syāt? tadabhāve ca dakṣiṇottaramārgaviśeṣānupapattiḥ, gantavyadeśānupapattiśceti /
bhinnasya tu parasmādātmanaḥ sarvametadupapannam /
karmajñānasādhanopadeśācca - bhinnaścedbrahmaṇaḥ saṃsārī syāt, yuktastaṃ pratyabhyudayaniḥśreyasādhanayoḥ karmajñānayorupadeśo neśvarasyāptakāmatvāt /
tasmādyuktaṃ brahmeti brahmabhāvī puruṣa ucyata iti cet? na, brahmopadeśānarthakyaprasaṅgāt /
saṃsārī ced - brahmabhāvyabrahma san viditvātmānamevāhaṃ brahmāsmīti sarvamabhavattasya saṃsāryātmavijñānādeva sarvātmabhāvasya phalasya siddhatvātparabrahmopadeśasya dhruvamānarthakyaṃ prāptam /
tadvijñānasya kvacitpuruṣārthasādhane 'viniyāgātsaṃsāriṇa evāhaṃ brahmāsmīti brahmatvasampādanārtha upadeśa iti cet /
anirjñāte hi brahmasvarūpe kiṃ sampādayedahaṃ brahmāsmīti /
nirjñātalakṣaṇe hi brahmaṇi śakyā sampatkartum /
na; "ayamātmā brahma"(bṛ.u.2 / 5 / 19) catsākṣādaparokṣādbrahma (3 / 4 / 1) ya ātmā (chā.u.8 / 7 / 1) tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā (chā.u.6 / 8 / 7) brahmavidāpnoti param (tai.u.2 / 1 / 1 / ) iti prakṛtya tasmādvā etasmādātmanaḥ (2 / 1 / 1) iti sahasraśo brahmātmaśabdayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyādekārthatvamevetyavagamyate /
anyasya hyanyatve sampatkriyate naikatve /
idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā (bṛ.u.2 / 4 / 6) iti ca prakṛtasyaiva draṣṭavyasyātmana ekatvaṃ darśayati /
tasmānnātmano brahmatvasampadupapattiḥ /
na cāpyanyatprayojanaṃ brahmopadeśasya gamyate, brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati (mu.u.3 / 2 / 9) abhayaṃ vai janaka prāpto 'si (bṛ.u.4 / 2 / 4) abhayaṃ hi vai brahma bhavati (4 / 4 / 25) iti ca tadāpattiśravaṇāt /
sampattiścettadāpattirna syāt /
na hyanyasyāmyabhāva upapadyate /
vacanāt sampatterapi tadbhāvāpattiḥ syāditi cet? na, sampatteḥ pratyayamātratvāt /
vijñānasya ca mithyājñānanivartakatvavyatirekeṇākārakatvamityavocāma /
na ca vacanaṃ vastunaḥ sāmarthyajanakam /
jñāpakaṃ hi śāstraṃ na kārakamiti sthitiḥ /
sa eṣa iha praviṣṭaḥ (bṛ.u.1 / 4 / 7) ityādivākyeṣu ca parasyaiva praveśa iti sthitam /
tasmādbrahmeti na brahmabhāvipuruṣakalpanā sādhvī /
iṣṭārthabādhanācca /
saindhavadhanavadanantaramabāhyamekarasaṃ brahmeti vijñānaṃ sarvasyāmupaniṣadi pratipipādayiṣitor'thaḥ /
kāṇḍadvaye 'pyante 'vadhāraṇādavagamyate ityanuśāsanam etāvadare khalvamṛtatvam iti. tathā sarvaśākhopaniṣatsu ca brahmaikatvavijñānaṃ niścitor'thaḥ /
tatra yadi saṃsārī brahmaṇo 'nya ātmānamevāvediti kalpyeta, iṣṭasyārthasya nādhanaṃ syāt /
tathā ca śāstramupakramopasaṃhārayorvirodhādasamañjasaṃ kalpitaṃ syāt /
vyapadeśānupapatteśca /
yadi ca ātmānamevāvet iti saṃsārī kalpyeta, brahmavidyā iti vyapadeśo na syāt /
ātmānamevāvediti saṃsāriṇa eva vedyatvopapatteḥ /
ātmeti vedituranyaducyata iti cenna, ahaṃ brahmāsmīti viśeṣaṇāt /
anyaścedvedyaḥ syādayamasāviti vā viśeṣyeta na tvahamasmīti /
ahamasmīti viśeṣaṇādātmānamevāvediti cāvadhāraṇānniścitamātmaiva brahmetyavagamyate /
tathā ca satyupapanno brahmavidyāvyapadeśo nānyathā /
saṃsārividyā hyanyathā syāt /
na ca brahmatvābrahmatve hyekasyopapanne paramārthataḥ, tamaḥprakāśāviva bhānorviruddhatvāt /
na cobhayanimittatve brahmavidyeti niścito vyapadeśo yuktaṃ tattvajñānavivakṣāyām, śrotuḥ saṃśayo hi tathā syāt /
niścitaṃ ca jñānaṃ puruṣārthasādhanamiṣyate"yasya syādddhā na vicikitsāsti" (chā.u.3 / 14 / 4) "saṃśayātmā vinaśyati"(gītā 4 / 40) iti śrutismṛtibhyām /
ato na saṃśayito vākyārtho vācyaḥ parahitārthinā /
brahmaṇi sādhakatvakalpanā asmadādiṣviva apeśalā'tadātmānamevāvettasmāttatsarvamabhavat'iti - iti cet? na, śāstropālambhāt /
na hyasmātkalpaneyam, śāstrakṛtā tu;tasmācchāstrasyāyamupālambhaḥ /
na ca brahmaṇa iṣṭaṃ cikīrṣuṇā śāstrāthaviparītakalpanā svārthaparityāgaḥ kāryaḥ /
na caitāvatyevākṣamā yuktā bhavataḥ /
sarvaṃ hi nānātvaṃ brahmaṇi kalpitameva"ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyam"(bṛ.u.4 / 4 / 20) "neha nānāsti kiñcana" (4 / 4 / 19) "yatra hi dvaitamiva bhavati" (2 / 4 / 14) "ekamevādvitīyam"(chā.u.6 / 2 / 1) ityādivākyaśatebhyaḥ /
sarvo hi lokavyavahāro brahmaṇyeva kalpito na paramārthaḥ san, ityatyalpamidamucyate'iyameva kalpanā apeśalā'iti /
tasmād yatpraviṣṭaṃ sraṣṭrṛ brahma tadbrahma /
vaiśabdo 'vadhāraṇārthaḥ /
idaṃ śarīrasthaṃ yad gṛhyate, agre prākpratibodhādapi brahmaivāsīt, sarvaṃ cedam /
kintvapratibodhāt abrahmāsmyasarvaṃ ca ityātmanyadhyāropāt'kartāhe kriyāvānphalānāṃ ca bhoktā sukhī duḥkho saṃsārī'iti cādhyāropayati /
paramārthatastu brahmaiva tadvilakṣaṇaṃ sarvaṃ ca /
tatkathañcidācāryeṇa dayālunā pratibodhitam'nāsi saṃsārī'ityātmānamevāvetsvābhāvikam /
avidyādhyāropitaviśeṣavarjitamiti eva śabdasyārthaḥ /
brūhi ko 'sāvātmā svābhāvikaḥ, yamātmānaṃ viditavadbrahma /
nanu na smarasyātmānam, darśito hyasau, ya iha praviśya prāṇityapāniti vyānityudāniti samānitīti /
nanu'asau gauḥ, asāvaśvaḥ'ityevamasau vyapadiśyate bhavatā nātmānaṃ pratyakṣaṃ darśayasi /
evaṃ tarhi draṣṭā śrotā mantā vijñātā, sa ātmeti /
nanvatrāpi darśanādikriyākartuḥ svarūpaṃ na pratyakṣaṃ darśayasi /
na hi gamireva gantuḥ svarūpaṃ chidirvā chettuḥ /
evaṃ tarhi dṛṣṭerdraṣṭā śruteḥ śrotā matermantā vijñātervijñātā, sa ātmeti /
nanvatra ko viśeṣo draṣṭari? yadi dṛṣṭardraṣṭā. yadi vā ghaṭasya draṣṭā, sarvathāpi draṣṭaiva /
draṣṭavya eva tu bhavānviśeṣamāha dṛṣṭerdraṣṭeti draṣṭā tu yadi dṛṣṭeḥ, yadi vā ghaṭasya, draṣṭā draṣṭaiva /
na, viśeṣopapatteḥ /
astyatra viśeṣaḥ dṛṣṭerdraṣṭā sa dṛṣṭim, na kadācidapi dṛṣṭirna dṛśyate draṣṭā;tatra draṣṭurdṛṣṭyā nityayā bhavitavyam, anityā ced draṣṭurdṛṣṭiḥ, tatra dṛśyā yā dṛṣṭiḥ sā kadācinna dṛśyetāpi, yathānityayā dṛṣṭyā ghaṭādi vastu /
na ca tadvad dṛṣṭerdraṣṭā kadācidapi na paśyati dṛṣṭim /
kiṃ dve dṛṣṭī draṣṭuḥ - nityā adṛśyā, anyā anityā dṛśyeti? bāḍham;prasiddhā tāvadanityā dṛṣṭiḥ, andhānandhatvadarśanāt /
nityaiva cetsarvo 'nandha eva syāt /
draṣṭastu nityā dṛṣṭiḥ"na hi draṣṭurdṛṣṭerviparilopo vidyate" -iti śruteḥ /
anumānācca - andhasyāpi ghaṭādyābhāsaviṣayā svapne dṛṣṭirupalabhyate, sā tarhītaradṛṣṭināśe na paśyati, sā draṣṭurdṛṣṭiḥ /
tayāvipariluptayā nityayā dṛṣṭyā svarūpabhūtayā svayañjyotiḥsamākhyathetāmanityāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ svapnavuddhāntayorvāsanāpratyayarūpāṃ nityameva paśyandṛṣṭerdraṣṭā bhavati /
evaśca sati dṛṣṭireva svarūpamasyāgnyauṣṇyavat, na kāṇādānāmiva dṛṣṭivyatirikto 'nyaścetano draṣṭā /
tadbrahma ātmānameva nityadṛgrūpamadhyāropitānityadṛṣṭyādivarjitamevāvedviditavat /
nanu vipratiṣiddhaṃ"na vijñātevijñātāraṃ vijānīyāḥ"(bṛ.u.3 / 4 / 2) iti śruteḥ, vijñāturvijñānam /
na, evaṃ vijñānānna vipratiṣedhaḥ /
evaṃ dṛṣṭerdraṣṭeti vijñāyata eva /
anyajñānānapekṣatvācca - na ca draṣṭurnityaiva dṛṣṭirityevaṃ vijñāte draṣṭriviṣayāṃ dṛṣṭimanyāmākāṅkṣate /
nivartate hi draṣṭuviṣayadṛṣṭyākāṅkṣā tadasambhavādeva /
na hyavidyamāne viṣaya ākāṅkṣā kasyacidupajāyate /
na ca dṛśyā dṛṣṭirdraṣṭāraṃ viṣayīkartumutsahate, yatastāmākāṅkṣeta /
na ca svarūpaviṣayākhāṅkṣāsvasyaiva /
tasmādajñānādhyāropaṇanivṛttireva'atmānamevāvet ityuktam,nātmano viṣayīkaraṇam' /
tatkathamavet? ityāha - ahaṃ dṛṣṭerdraṣṭā ātmā brahmāsmi bhavāmīti brahmeti - yatsākṣādaparokṣātsarvāntara ātmā aśanāyādyatīto neti netyasthūlamanaṇvityevamādi lakṣaṇam, tadevāhamasmi, nānyaḥ saṃsārī, yathā bhavānāheti /
tasmādevaṃ vijñānāttadbrahma sarvamabhavat /
tasmādyuktameva manuṣyā manyante yadbrahmavidyayā sarvaṃ bhaviṣyāma iti /
yatpṛṣṭam,'kimu tadbrahmāved yasmāttatsarvamabhavat'iti, tannirṇītam -'brahma vā idamagra āsīt tadātmānamevāvedahaṃ brahmāsmīti tasmāttatsarvamabhavat'iti /
tattatra yo yo devānāṃ madhye pratyabudhyata pratibuddhvānātmānaṃ yathoktena ātmā tadbrahmābhavat /
tatharpīṇāṃ tathā manuṣyāṇāṃ ca madhye /
devānāmityādi lokadṛṣṭyapekṣayā na brahmatvabuddhyocyate /
'puraḥ puruṣa āviśat'iti sarvatra brahmaivānupraviṣṭamityādyucyate /
paramārthatastu tatra tatra brahmaivāgra āsītprākpratibodhād devādiśarīreśvanyathaiva vibhāvyamānam /
tadātmānamevāvettathaiva ca sarvamabhavat /
asyā brahmavidyāyāḥ sarvabhāvāpattiḥ phalamityetasyārthasya draḍhimne mantrānudāharati śrutiḥ /
katham? tad brahma etadātmānameva'ahamasmi'iti paśyannetasmādeva brahmaṇo darśanādṛṣṭirvāmadevākhyaḥ pratipede ha pratipannavānkila /
sa etasminmantrāndadarśa -'ahaṃ manurabhavaṃ sūryaśca'ityādīn /
tadetadbrahma paśyan iti brahmavidyā parāmṛśyate /
'ahaṃ manurabhavaṃ suryaśca'ityādinā sarvabhāvāpattiṃ brahmavidyāphalaṃ parāmṛśati /
paśyansarvātmabhāvaṃ phalaṃ pratipeda ityasmātprayogād brahmavidyāsahāyasādhanasādhyaṃ mokṣaṃ darśayati;bhuñjānastṛpyatīti yadvat /
seyaṃ brahmavidyayā sarvabhāvāpattirāsīnmahatāṃ devādīnāṃ vīryātiśayāt /
nedānīmaidaṃyugīnānāṃ viśeṣato manuṣyāṇām, alpavīryatvāditi syātkasyacidbuddhiḥ, tadutthāpanāyāha- tadidaṃ prakṛtaṃ brahma yatsarvabhūtānupraviṣṭaṃ dṛṣṭikriyādiliṅgam, etarhyetasminnapi vartamānakāle yaḥ kaścidvyāvṛttabāhyautsukya ātmānamevaivaṃ veda'ahaṃ brahmāsmi'iti apohyopādhijanitabhrāntivijñānādhyāropitānviśeṣān saṃsāradharmānāgandhitamanantaramabāhyaṃ brahyevāhamasmi kevalamiti-so 'vidyākṛtāsarvatvanivṛtterbrahāvijhānādidaṃ sarva bhavati /
na hi mahāvīryeṣu vāmaḍhevādiṣu hīnavīryeṣu vā vārtamānikeṣu manuṣyeṣubrahyaṇo viśeṣastadvijhānasya vāsti /
vārtamānikeṣu puruṣeṣu tu bahyavidyāphale anaikāntikatā śaḍkyata ityata āha-tasya ha brahyavijhāturyathotkena vidhinā devā mahāvīryāśca nāpi abhūtatya.abhavanāya brahyāsarvamāvasya, neśate na paryāptāḥ, kimutānye /
brahyāvidyāphalaprāpyau vidhnakaraṇe devādaya īśata iti kā śaḍkā? ityucyate-devādīnprati ṛṇavattvānmartyānām /
"brahyacaryeṇa ṛpibhyo yajhena devabhyaḥ prajayā pitṛbhyaḥ"iti hi jāyamānamevarṇavantaṃ puruṣaṃ darśayati śrutiḥ /
paśunidarśanācca"atho 'yaṃ vā"(bṛ.u. 1 / 4 / 16) ityādlokaśruteścātmano vṛttiparipipālayiṣayādhamarṇānivaṃ devāḥ paratantrānmanuṣyānpratyamṛtatvaprāptiṃ prati vidhnaṃ kuryuriti nyāyyaivaiṣā śaḍkā /
svapaśūnsvaśarīrāṇīva ca rakṣanti devāḥ /
mahattarāṃ hi vṛttiṃ karmādhīnāṃ darśayṣyati devādīnāṃ bahupaśusamatayaikaikasya puruṣasya /
"tasmāndepāṃ tanna priyaṃ yadetanmanudhyā vidyāḥ"(1 / 4 / 10) iti hahi vakṣyati /
"yathā ha vai svāya lokāyāriṣṭimicchedevaṃ haivaṃvide sarvāṇi bhūtānyariṣṭimicchanti"(1 / 4 / 16) iti ca /
brahyāviśve pārārthyanivṛtterna svalokatvaṃ paśutvañcetyamiprāyo 'priyāriṣṭivacanābhyāmavagamyate /
tasmādbrahyāvido brahyavidyāphalarprāpta prati kuryureva vidhnaṃ devāḥ, prabhāvavantaśca hi te /
nanvevaṃ satyanyāsvapi karmaphalaprāptipudevānāṃ vidhnakaraṇaṃpeyapānasamam /
hanta tarhyāvisrambho 'bhyudayaniḥśreyasasādhanā. nuṣṭhāneṣu /
tatheśvarasyācintaya. śaktitvādvidhnakaraṇe prabhutvam /
tathā kālakarmamantrauṣadhitapasām /
eṣāṃ hi phalasampattivipattihetutvaṃ śāstre loke ca prasidvam /
ato 'pyanāśvāsaḥ śāstrārthānuṣṭhāne /
na;sarvapadārthānāṃ niyatanimittopādānāt, jagadvaicitryadarśanācca /
svabhāvapakṣe ca tadubhayānupapatteḥ /
'sukhaduḥkhādi phalanimittaṃ karma'ityetasminpakṣe sthite vedasmṛtinyāyalokaparigṛhīte, deveśvarakālāstāvanna karmaphalaviparyāsakartāraḥ, karmaṇāṃ kāṅkṣitakārakatvāt /
karma hi śubhāśubhaṃ puruṣāṇāṃ devakāleśvarādikārakamanapekṣya nātmānaṃ prati labhate, labdhātmakamapi phaladāne 'samartham, kriyāyā hi kārakādyanekanimittopādānasvābhāvyāt /
tasmātkriyānuguṇā hi deveśvarādaya iti karmasu tāvanna phalaprāptiṃ pratyavisrambhaḥ /
karmaṇāmapyeṣāṃ vaśānigatvaṃ kvacit, svasāmarthyasyāpraṇodyatvāt /
karmakāladaivadravyādisvabhāvānāṃ guṇapradhānabhāvastvaniyato durvijñeyaśceti tatkṛto moho lokasya - karmaiva kārakaṃ nānyatphalaprāptāviti kecitaṃ;daivamevetyapare;kāla ityeke;dravyādisvabhāva iti kecit;sarva ete saṃhatā evetyapare /

children.translated_text: [Continuing commentary on BṛUp 1.4.10:] 'These <s>Indra</s> and other [gods] are different from me; they are my rulers; I am like a servant to them — having propitiated them through praise, obeisance, worship, and other acts of devotion, I shall obtain prosperity and the supreme good, the fruit granted by them' — such is the intention [of the ignorant person].

children.text: tatra loke bahupaśumato yathaikasminneva paśāvādīyamāne vyāghrādināpahiyamāṇe mahadapriyaṃ bhavati, tathā bahupaśusthānīya ekasminpuruṣe paśubhāvād vyuttiṣṭhatyapriyaṃ bhavatīti, kiṃ citraṃ devānāṃ bahupaśvapaharaṇa iva kuṭuṃbinaḥ /
children.translated_text: In that regard, just as in the world, when a man who has many animals has even one animal being seized or carried away by a tiger and the like, great displeasure arises — similarly, when even one person, who occupies the place of many animals, rises above his animal-status, displeasure arises [for the gods]. What wonder then [that displeasure arises] for the gods, like the loss of many animals for a householder?
