children.translated_text: Therefore, it is not pleasing to these gods — what is that? — that humans should somehow come to know this truth of <s>Brahman</s> as the self. And thus the <s>smṛti</s> of the blessed <s>Vyāsa</s> in the <s>Anugītā</s>: 'For the world of the gods is filled by those who perform rituals, O son of <s>Kuntī</s>;

children.text: na caitadiṣṭaṃ devānāṃ maryairupari vartanam //
children.translated_text: and this is not desired by the gods — that mortals should rise above [them].'

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.10:] '<s>Brahman</s>' — [here means] the lower (<s>apara</s>) [<s>Brahman</s>], because it is tenable that the state of being everything is something to be accomplished [through knowledge]. For the supreme <s>Brahman</s>'s becoming everything is not something to be accomplished through knowledge. And [the text] states that the becoming of everything is to be accomplished through knowledge: 'Therefore it became all.' Hence, '<s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning' — the lower <s>Brahman</s> is appropriate here. Or, because of the qualification pertaining to human beings, [the word '<s>Brahman</s>'] would refer to a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who is destined to become that [<s>Brahman</s>]. For 'humans think they will become everything' — humans are the subject under discussion, and it has been stated that they in particular are qualified for the means of worldly prosperity and the supreme good — not the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, nor the lower <s>Prajāpati</s>. Therefore, having attained the state of the lower <s>Brahman</s> through the knowledge of the lower <s>Brahman</s> — [the knowledge] of duality-and-unity — combined with action, having turned away from what is to be enjoyed, having had the bonds of desire and action severed through the attainment of everything — [such a person,] being destined to become the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, is called '<s>Brahman</s>' because of being the cause of <s>Brahmavidyā</s> (the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>). And in the world, the usage of words based on a future state is observed — as in 'he is cooking rice' [where the rice is not yet cooked], and in scripture — 'the wandering ascetic [gives] the gift of fearlessness to all beings' and such. Similarly here, some explain — '<s>Brahman</s>' means a person destined to become <s>Brahman</s>, i.e., a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. That is not so, because of the fault of impermanence of the becoming of everything. For there exists no thing in the world that, in the ultimate sense, undergoes a transformation into another state due to some cause and yet is permanent. Similarly, if the becoming of everything is brought about by the cause of <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge, [the claim that] it is permanent — this is contradictory. And if it is impermanent, there is the stated fault that it would be on par with the fruit of ritual action. If, on the other hand, you hold that the becoming of everything — [understood as] the removal of the non-everythingness created by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — is the fruit of <s>Brahmavidyā</s>, then the postulation of a person 'destined to become <s>Brahman</s>' would be pointless. For even before the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, every living being, being <s>Brahman</s> [in reality], has eternally attained the state of being everything in the ultimate sense. But non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-everythingness are superimposed through <s>avidyā</s> — just as silver [is superimposed] on a mother-of-pearl, or [qualities like] being dirty upon the sky. Similarly here, non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-everythingness, superimposed on <s>Brahman</s> through <s>avidyā</s>, are removed by <s>Brahmavidyā</s> — if you hold this, then it is proper to say that what was there in the ultimate sense is the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, which is the primary meaning of the word '<s>Brahman</s>,' [and that this supreme <s>Brahman</s>] is spoken of in the sentence '<s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning' — because the <s>Veda</s> speaks of things as they truly are. But the postulation that a person whose nature is contrary to the meaning of the word '<s>Brahman</s>' — a person 'destined to become <s>Brahman</s>' — is called '<s>Brahman</s>' is not proper, because it is illegitimate to abandon what is heard [in scripture] and postulate what is not heard, in the absence of a greater purpose [requiring it]. [Objection:] But non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-everythingness exist as real distinctions from <s>Brahman</s>, not merely created by <s>avidyā</s>. No — because in that case their removal by <s>Brahmavidyā</s> would be untenable. For <s>Brahmavidyā</s> is never seen anywhere to directly remove or create a real property of a thing. But it is seen everywhere to remove <s>avidyā</s>. Similarly here too, let non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-everythingness, being created by <s>avidyā</s> alone, be removed by <s>Brahmavidyā</s>. But <s>Brahmavidyā</s> cannot create or remove an ultimately real entity. Therefore, the abandonment of what is heard and the postulation of what is not heard is entirely pointless. [Objection:] <s>Avidyā</s> in <s>Brahman</s> is untenable. No — because <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) is enjoined with regard to <s>Brahman</s>. For when silver has not been superimposed on a mother-of-pearl, the mother-of-pearl-ness [of the shell] is not [separately] made known — even when it has come within the range of the eye — [by the cognition] 'This is a mother-of-pearl, not silver.' Similarly, the knowledge of oneness with regard to <s>Brahman</s> — '[All] this is indeed Being,' '<s>Brahman</s> indeed is all this,' 'The Self alone is all this,' 'There is no duality here, no non-<s>Brahman</s>' — would not need to be enjoined if there were no superimposition of <s>avidyā</s> upon <s>Brahman</s>. We do not say that there is no superimposition of non-<s>Brahman</s> properties upon <s>Brahman</s>, as [there is superimposition] of silver upon a mother-of-pearl. Rather, [we say] <s>Brahman</s> does not in its own self have the superimposition of non-<s>Brahman</s> properties as its cause, and <s>Brahman</s> is not the agent of <s>avidyā</s>. [Objection:] Let it be so — <s>Brahman</s> is not the agent of <s>avidyā</s>, nor is it deluded. But then, there is no other conscious being apart from <s>Brahman</s> who is a non-<s>Brahman</s> agent of <s>avidyā</s> and who is deluded — this [follows] from <s>śruti</s> passages such as: 'There is no knower other than this' (BṛUp 3.7.23), 'There is no knower other than this' (BṛUp 3.8.11), 'You are That' (ChāUp 6.8-13), 'He knew the Self: I am <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.10), 'He who thinks "He is one and I am another" — he does not know' (BṛUp 1.4.10), and such. And from <s>smṛtis</s>: 'Equal in all beings' (BhG 13.27), 'I am the Self, O <s>Guḍākeśa</s>' (BhG 10.20), 'In a dog and in a dog-eater' (BhG 5.18), 'He who [sees] all beings' and such. And from the <s>mantra</s>: 'In whom all beings' (ĪśāUp 7). [Objection:] If so, the teaching of scripture would be purposeless. [Response:] Indeed, when [the truth] is [already] comprehended, let there be purposelessness [of scripture]. [Objection:] If [there is] purposelessness of comprehension? No — because the removal of non-comprehension is observed. [Objection:] But the removal [of non-comprehension] too is untenable, given [the view of] oneness. No — because of contradiction with what is observed. For we see that the removal of non-comprehension [occurs] precisely through the knowledge of oneness; to say that what is observed is untenable would be to contradict what is directly seen. And no one accepts contradiction with direct experience. And what is directly observed cannot be called 'untenable,' precisely because it is observed. [Objection:] But the observation [itself] is untenable. [Response:] To this too, the very same reasoning applies. [Objection:] From <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, reasoning, and common experience such as 'One becomes meritorious through meritorious action' (BṛUp 3.2.13), 'Knowledge and actions follow him' (BṛUp 4.4.2), and the like, a transmigrating self different from the Supreme is understood. And the Supreme is different from that — from <s>śrutis</s> such as 'He is "not this, not this"' (BṛUp 3.9.23), 'transcends hunger' and such, 'The Self free from evil, ageless, deathless' (ChāUp 8.7.1), 'Under the rule of this Imperishable' (BṛUp 3.8.9), and so forth. And in the logical treatises of <s>Kaṇāda</s>, <s>Akṣapāda</s>, and others, <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), different from <s>saṃsāra</s>, is established through reasoning. And from the observation that beings are impelled by the desire to remove the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, the otherness of the transmigrating self from <s>Īśvara</s> is clearly understood. [And] from <s>śrutis</s>: 'Without speech, without care' (ChāUp 3.14.2), 'Nothing that should be done exists for Me, O <s>Pārtha</s>' (BhG 3.22). [And:] 'He is to be sought, He is to be known' (ChāUp 8.7.1), 'Having known Him, one is not tainted' (BṛUp 4.4.23), 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (TaiUp 2.1.1), 'It should be seen as one alone' (BṛUp 4.4.20), 'He who, O <s>Gārgī</s>, knows this Imperishable' (BṛUp 3.8.10), 'The wise one, having known this' (BṛUp 4.4.21), '<s>Praṇava</s> is the bow, the Self is the arrow, <s>Brahman</s> is said to be the target' (MuṇḍUp 2.2.4) — and from the grammatical indication of object and agent. And from the teaching of specific paths, destinations, and places for the one desiring liberation. If there is no difference, whose movement to where would there be? And in the absence [of movement], the distinction between the southern and northern paths would be untenable, and the destination to be reached would be untenable. But for a self that is different from the Supreme, all this is tenable. And because of the teaching of the means of <s>karma</s> and <s>jñāna</s> — if the transmigrating self is different from <s>Brahman</s>, then the teaching of <s>karma</s> and <s>jñāna</s> as means for worldly prosperity and the supreme good would be appropriate for that [self], but not for <s>Īśvara</s>, because He has all desires fulfilled. Therefore, it is proper that '<s>Brahman</s>' refers to a person destined to become <s>Brahman</s> — if you say this, no — because of the consequence that the teaching about <s>Brahman</s> would be purposeless. If the transmigrating self — being a non-<s>Brahman</s> destined to become <s>Brahman</s> — having known the Self, [thinking] 'I am <s>Brahman</s>,' became everything — since the state of being the Self of all would be accomplished through the very self-knowledge of the transmigrating self, the teaching about the supreme <s>Brahman</s> would certainly become purposeless. [Objection:] Since the knowledge of that [<s>Brahman</s>] is not applied anywhere as a means to human ends, the teaching is for the purpose of the transmigrating self's accomplishment [of identifying as] '<s>Brahman</s>' — 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.' But without the true nature of <s>Brahman</s> being ascertained, what would one accomplish with 'I am <s>Brahman</s>'? For the identification can only be made when <s>Brahman</s>'s defining characteristics are ascertained. No [this doesn't work] — from 'This Self is <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 2.5.19), 'the directly perceived, non-remote <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 3.4.1), 'that Self' (ChāUp 8.7.1), 'That is the truth, that is the Self' (ChāUp 6.8.7), 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> attains the Supreme' (TaiUp 2.1.1), followed by 'From that Self indeed' (TaiUp 2.1.1) — from the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) of the words '<s>Brahman</s>' and '<s>Ātman</s>' in thousands of places, their identity of meaning alone is understood. For identification (<s>sampat</s>) is made between two different things, not when [they are] one. And 'All this is what this Self is' (BṛUp 2.4.6) shows the oneness of the very Self that is the subject under discussion, that is to be seen. Therefore, the identification of the Self with <s>Brahman</s> is not tenable. Nor can any other purpose of the teaching about <s>Brahman</s> be conceived, since from [śrutis] such as 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself' (MuṇḍUp 3.2.9), 'Fearlessness have you attained, O <s>Janaka</s>' (BṛUp 4.2.4), 'For <s>Brahman</s> is without fear' (BṛUp 4.4.25), we hear of the attainment of that [<s>Brahman</s>]. And if [the 'becoming <s>Brahman</s>'] were merely an identification (<s>sampatti</s>), the [actual] attainment would not occur. For it is not tenable that one [truly] becomes another [merely through identification]. [Objection:] By the force of the [scriptural] statement, even from identification, the attainment of that state would follow. No — because identification is a mere mental cognition. And we have said that the function of knowledge is solely the removal of false knowledge, not the production [of anything new]. And a [mere] statement cannot generate the capacity of a thing. For scripture is an informer, not a producer — this is the established position. And in sentences such as 'He entered here' (BṛUp 1.4.7) and the like, it is established that it is the Supreme alone that has entered. Therefore, the postulation that '<s>Brahman</s>' refers to a person destined to become <s>Brahman</s> is not correct. And because it would contradict the intended meaning. The intended meaning of the entire <s>Upaniṣad</s>, which wishes to convey that <s>Brahman</s> is like a lump of salt — without interior, without exterior, of one taste throughout — [is the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness]. That this is determined at the conclusion of both sections [of the <s>Veda</s>] is understood from the teaching: 'This much alone is immortality.' Similarly, in all the <s>Upaniṣads</s> of all <s>Vedic</s> branches, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness is the established meaning. If a transmigrating self different from <s>Brahman</s> were postulated as the one who 'knew the Self,' then the intended meaning would not be established. And the scripture, having contradiction between its opening and conclusion, would become incoherent — a [mere] fabrication. And because of the impossibility of the designation [as '<s>Brahmavidyā</s>']: if a transmigrating self were postulated in 'he knew the Self,' the designation '<s>Brahmavidyā</s>' (knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>) would not be appropriate — since it would be tenable that the transmigrating self alone is the object to be known in 'he knew the Self.' [Objection:] The word '<s>Ātman</s>' (Self) refers to something other than the knower. No — because of the qualification 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.' If something else were the object to be known, it would be qualified as 'this one' or 'that one,' not as 'I am.' From the qualification 'I am' and from the emphatic restriction in 'he knew the Self alone,' it is definitely understood that the Self alone is <s>Brahman</s>. And when this is so, the designation '<s>Brahmavidyā</s>' is justified — not otherwise. Otherwise it would be '<s>saṃsāravidyā</s>' (knowledge of <s>saṃsāra</s>). And <s>Brahman</s>-hood and non-<s>Brahman</s>-hood cannot both be ultimately true of one [entity], because they are contradictory — like darkness and light for the sun. And if both were the basis [of the designation], the definite designation '<s>Brahmavidyā</s>' would not be appropriate when the intention is to convey the knowledge of reality, for the listener would then have doubt. And definite knowledge is desired as the means of the highest human good — from <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>: 'If one has certainty, without hesitation' (ChāUp 3.14.4), 'The doubting self perishes' (BhG 4.40). Therefore, the sentence-meaning should not be stated as doubtful by one who wishes the welfare of others. [Objection:] The postulation of agency in <s>Brahman</s> — as in us [ordinary beings] — is unseemly, given [the passage] 'It knew the Self: from that it became all.' No — because [the postulation] is supported by scripture. For this postulation is not from us [our invention]; it is made by scripture. Therefore, this is a criticism of scripture [not of us]. And one who wishes to accomplish the desired meaning of <s>Brahman</s> should not fabricate something contrary to the meaning of scripture — [that would be] abandoning one's own purpose. Nor should you be impatient about only this much [seeming absurdity]. For all the manifoldness [of the world] is superimposed on <s>Brahman</s> alone — from hundreds of passages such as 'It should be seen as one alone' (BṛUp 4.4.20), 'There is no plurality here whatsoever' (BṛUp 4.4.19), 'Where there is, as it were, duality' (BṛUp 2.4.14), 'One alone, without a second' (ChāUp 6.2.1), and so forth. For all worldly transaction is superimposed on <s>Brahman</s> alone and is not ultimately real — thus, it is saying very little to say 'this postulation [of agency] is unseemly.' Therefore, that <s>Brahman</s> which has entered [all beings] and which is the creator — that is <s>Brahman</s> [in this passage]. The particle '<s>vai</s>' is for emphasis. What is grasped as dwelling in this body — even before awakening [to the truth], it was <s>Brahman</s> alone, and all this [is <s>Brahman</s>]. But because of non-awakening, [one thinks] 'I am not <s>Brahman</s>, and not everything' — superimposing [these ideas] upon the Self — and further superimposes: 'I am an agent, I am one who acts, I am an enjoyer of fruits, I am happy, I am miserable, I am a <s>saṃsārin</s> (transmigrating being).' But in the ultimate sense, it is <s>Brahman</s> alone — different from all that — and is everything. That [<s>Brahman</s>], having been somehow awakened by a compassionate teacher — [with the teaching] 'You are not a <s>saṃsārin</s>' — knew the Self, its own natural [Self]. The word '<s>eva</s>' (alone) means: devoid of the distinctions superimposed by <s>avidyā</s>. Tell me, what is that natural Self which <s>Brahman</s> knew? Do you not remember the Self? For it has been shown — that which, having entered here, breathes in, breathes out, diffuses, ascends, and equalizes. [Objection:] But 'that is a cow, that is a horse' — in this way you designate it [externally]; you do not directly show the Self itself. If so, then: the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower — that is the Self. [Objection:] But even here you do not directly show the essential nature of the agent of seeing and other activities. For going is not the essential nature of the goer, nor is cutting [the nature] of the cutter. If so, then: the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing, the thinker of thinking, the knower of knowing — that is the Self. [Objection:] But what difference does this make regarding the seer? Whether one is the seer of seeing or the seer of a pot, in either case one is simply the seer. The difference should be stated about what is to be seen — [you say] 'the seer of seeing' — but the seer, whether of seeing or of a pot, is simply the seer. No — because a difference is tenable. There is a difference here: the seer of seeing — he is [the witness of] seeing [itself]. Never is seeing not seen [by the seer]; the seer's seeing must be permanent. If the seer's seeing were impermanent, then that seeing which is the object of sight might sometimes not be seen — just as a pot and such things [are sometimes not seen] by impermanent seeing. But the seer of seeing never at any time fails to see seeing. [Question:] Does the seer then have two seeings — one permanent and invisible, the other impermanent and visible? Indeed — the impermanent seeing is well known, from the observation that the blind and the non-blind [differ]. If [seeing] were always permanent, everyone would be non-blind. But the seer's seeing is permanent — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'For the seeing of the seer is never lost' (BṛUp 4.3.23). And from inference — even for a blind person, seeing whose object is the appearance of pots and such is experienced in dreams. That [seeing], then, when the other [empirical] seeing is destroyed, does not [itself] see [external objects] — that is the seer's seeing. With that unfailing, permanent seeing — which is its own nature — being self-luminous by designation, always seeing this impermanent seeing, which in waking and dream has the form of impressions and cognitions — [the self] is the seer of seeing. And this being so, seeing itself is its essential nature, like heat of fire — not, as the followers of <s>Kaṇāda</s> [hold], is the seer a conscious entity different from seeing. That <s>Brahman</s> knew the Self alone — of the nature of eternal seeing — devoid of the distinctions of impermanent seeing and the like superimposed [by <s>avidyā</s>]. [Objection:] But this is contradictory — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'You cannot know the knower of knowing' (BṛUp 3.4.2) — [it would follow that] the knower's knowing [itself] [is impossible]. No — knowing in this manner is not contradictory. For it is known precisely in this way — as the seer of seeing. And because it does not require another knowledge — when it is known that the seer's seeing is eternal, one does not desire another seeing pertaining to the seer. For the desire for a seeing pertaining to the seer ceases, precisely because it is impossible [to have such a thing]. For no desire arises in anyone with regard to a non-existent object. And visible seeing cannot make the seer its object, such that one would desire it. Nor is there desire for one's own essential nature regarding oneself. Therefore, what is stated as 'he knew the Self alone' is merely the removal of the superimposition of ignorance — not the objectification of the Self. How then did he know? This is stated: 'I — the seer of seeing — am the Self, am <s>Brahman</s>' — that which is directly perceived, non-remote, the innermost Self of all, transcending hunger and the rest, characterized as 'not gross, not subtle' and so forth — that alone I am, not a <s>saṃsārin</s> different [from <s>Brahman</s>], as you [might think]. Therefore, from such knowledge, that <s>Brahman</s> became everything. Therefore, it is indeed proper that humans think: 'Through <s>Brahmavidyā</s> we will become everything.' The question that was asked — 'What indeed did that <s>Brahman</s> know, from which it became all this?' — that has been resolved: '<s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning; it knew the Self alone — "I am <s>Brahman</s>" — therefore it became all.' Now, among the gods, whoever awakened to this — having awakened, [understood:] the Self, that <s>Brahman</s>, as described — he indeed became that. Similarly among the sages. Similarly among humans. The mention of 'among the gods' and so forth is from the standpoint of worldly [conventional] perspective, not from the standpoint of <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge. 'He entered into bodies' — everywhere <s>Brahman</s> alone has entered — this and such has been stated. But in the ultimate sense, <s>Brahman</s> alone was there in each place, in the beginning, before awakening, being perceived otherwise in the bodies of gods and the rest. That [<s>Brahman</s>] knew the Self alone, and thus became everything. To strengthen this meaning — that the becoming of everything is the fruit of this <s>Brahmavidyā</s> — the <s>śruti</s> cites mantras. How? That <s>Brahman</s>, seeing this Self alone as 'I am' — from this very vision of <s>Brahman</s>, the seer named <s>Vāmadeva</s> attained understanding. He perceived these mantras: 'I became <s>Manu</s> and <s>Sūrya</s>' and so forth. 'That <s>Brahman</s>, seeing' — by this, <s>Brahmavidyā</s> is referenced. 'I became <s>Manu</s> and <s>Sūrya</s>' and so forth — by this, the becoming of everything, the fruit of <s>Brahmavidyā</s>, is referenced. 'Seeing [and thereby] attaining the fruit of becoming the Self of all' — from this usage, [the text] shows that liberation, which is to be accomplished through the auxiliary means of <s>Brahmavidyā</s>, [follows directly from knowledge] — just as 'one who eats is satisfied.' This becoming of everything through <s>Brahmavidyā</s> was [attainable] because of the surpassing power of the great ones — gods and the like. [One might think:] Not now for those of this present age, especially humans, because of their meager power. To remove this [doubt, the text] says: that very <s>Brahman</s> which is the subject here, which has entered all beings, whose mark is the activity of seeing and the like — even now, in the present time, whoever, having turned away from external preoccupations, knows the Self thus: 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' — having removed the distinctions of <s>saṃsāra</s>, the properties superimposed through the deluded cognition born of limiting adjuncts — [knowing] 'I am <s>Brahman</s> alone, without interior, without exterior, of one taste' — he, through the removal of the non-everythingness created by <s>avidyā</s>, from <s>Brahman</s>-knowledge, becomes all this. For there is no distinction in <s>Brahman</s> between the great-powered ones like <s>Vāmadeva</s> and the humans of lesser power in the present age, nor is there any [distinction] in the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>. But regarding humans of the present age, doubt might be entertained about the non-certainty of the fruit of <s>Brahmavidyā</s>, and therefore [the text] says: of that knower of <s>Brahman</s>, by the method described, even the gods — who are of great power — were not able to prevent [him from becoming everything]. Because of the rule that the fruit of <s>Brahman</s>-attainment immediately follows the time of <s>vidyā</s>. How? Just as in the world, the moment the eye comes into contact with light is the very moment color becomes manifest — so too, the very time when the knowledge pertaining to the Self [arises] is the very time when the concealment of knowledge pertaining to that [Self] would [be removed]. Therefore, when <s>Brahmavidyā</s> is present, the effects of <s>avidyā</s> are untenable — like the effects of darkness when a lamp [is present]. To whom and by whom would the gods create obstruction — when the gods' very selfhood belongs to the knower of <s>Brahman</s>? This is what [the text] states: the Self — the nature to be contemplated — that which is to be known through all scriptures, that <s>Brahman</s> — because (<s>hi</s>) — of these gods — the knower of <s>Brahman</s> becomes [their very Self]. We have said that simultaneously with <s>Brahmavidyā</s>, through the removal of the mere veil of <s>avidyā</s>, the mother-of-pearl nature [becomes manifest], as it were, when the silver-appearance upon the mother-of-pearl [is removed]. Therefore, no effort of the gods adverse to the Self is possible. For one whose fruit is a non-Self [entity], separated by space, time, and other causes — in that domain pertaining to the non-Self, the gods' effort to create obstruction is fruitful. But not here, where [the fruit] is the Self, is simultaneous with knowledge, and is not separated by space, time, and causes — because there is no opportunity [for obstruction]. [Objection:] If so, then since a continuous stream of <s>vidyā</s>-cognitions does not [always] obtain, and since contrary cognitions and their effects are observed [even after knowledge], only the final cognition of the Self removes <s>avidyā</s>, not the earlier ones. No — because of non-certainty regarding the first [cognition]. For if the first cognition pertaining to the Self does not remove <s>avidyā</s>, neither does the final one, since they have the same object. [Objection:] If so, then the continuous [stream] removes <s>avidyā</s>, not the interrupted [one]. No — because a continuous stream is untenable when life-activities and the like persist. For when cognitions that are the causes of life-activities and the like exist, a continuous stream of <s>vidyā</s>-cognitions is untenable, because of contradiction. [Objection:] Then let the continuous stream of <s>vidyā</s> persist by suppressing the cognitions of life-activities and the like, until death. No — because of the fault of not determining the specific number of cognitions and hence not determining the meaning of scripture. Since one cannot determine that 'a continuous stream of this many cognitions removes <s>avidyā</s>,' the meaning of scripture would remain undetermined — and that is undesirable. [Objection:] When it is determined that a mere continuous stream [is required]? No — because there is no difference between the first and the last. Since there is no specific difference [between] the first and last cognitions in the stream of <s>vidyā</s>-cognitions — [whether] the stream ends at death or not — the faults stated earlier regarding the first and last cognitions would apply. [Objection:] If so, then [knowledge] is simply non-removing [of <s>avidyā</s>]. No — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'Therefore it became all' (BṛUp 1.4.10). And from <s>śrutis</s> such as 'The knot of the heart is cut' (MuṇḍUp 2.2.8), 'Where then is delusion?' (ĪśāUp 7), and so forth. [Objection:] These are <s>arthavāda</s> (mere praise). No — [they are found] in all the <s>Upaniṣads</s> of all <s>Vedic</s> branches. [Objection:] Because the Self, which is the object of [these statements], is established by perception, [knowledge of it] certainly exists [already]. No — because the answer has [already] been given. The answer given is: because the removal of the defects of <s>avidyā</s>, sorrow, delusion, fear, and the like is directly perceived. Therefore, this [objection] — whether the first, the last, the continuous, or the non-continuous [cognition removes avidyā] — is not a valid criticism, because the injunction [of knowledge] terminates in the result of removing the defects of <s>avidyā</s> and the like. Whatever cognition — whether the first, the last, continuous, or non-continuous — produces the fruit of removing the defects of <s>avidyā</s> and the like, that is accepted as <s>vidyā</s> — and hence there is not even a trace of grounds for criticism. As for what was said — that contrary cognitions and their effects are observed [even after knowledge] — no, because [those effects] are the cause of the persistence of the remaining [<s>prārabdha karma</s>]. The <s>karma</s> by which the [current] body was initiated — that [<s>karma</s>], being caused by the defect of contrary cognition, has the capacity to give fruit only in that very state [while the body lasts]. Therefore, for as long as the body lasts, as an accessory to the experience of [that <s>karma</s>'s] fruit, it draws out just that much contrary cognition and the defect of desire and the like — because the <s>karma</s> that caused it has already begun to bear fruit, like a released arrow. Therefore, <s>vidyā</s> does not counteract that [<s>prārabdha</s>], because there is no contradiction [between them]. Rather, it blocks only that which is about to arise in its own domain — the effects of <s>avidyā</s> that are contrary to itself — because they are [still] future. The other [<s>prārabdha</s> effects] are past. Moreover, a contrary cognition does not arise for the knower as [a genuine cognition] — because it is objectless. For a contrary cognition, which arises by taking recourse to mere generality without having ascertained the specific nature of its object, arises [only] when the specific object has not been determined — as [the cognition] 'silver' upon a mother-of-pearl. But since the entire basis of contrary cognition has been destroyed through the ascertainment of the specific object, [such cognition] cannot occur as before — just as, in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, it [does not recur] once the correct cognition has arisen, as seen [from experience]. But sometimes, memories — having the appearance of contrary cognitions, arising from impressions produced by prior contrary cognitions — generate, for the one possessing <s>vidyā</s>, the illusion of contrary cognition unexpectedly — just as even for one who knows the directions, there may unexpectedly arise the confusion of reversed directions. And if, for one possessing correct knowledge, a contrary cognition were to arise as before, then, because of lack of trust even in correct knowledge, engagement in ascertaining the meaning of scripture would become incoherent, and all means of valid knowledge would become invalid — because of the impossibility of distinguishing between valid and invalid means of knowledge. By this, the [question] 'Why does the body not fall immediately after correct knowledge?' is also answered. The destruction of [karmas] accumulated before and after the arising of knowledge, as well as those from other births, is established from the very <s>śruti</s> that denies obstruction to the attainment of the fruit — [from passages such as:] 'His <s>karmas</s> are destroyed' (MuṇḍUp 2.2.8), 'For him the delay is just that long' (ChāUp 6.14.2), 'All evils are scattered' (ChāUp 5.24.3), 'Having known Him, one is not tainted by evil <s>karma</s>' (BṛUp 4.4.23), 'They do not cross beyond this' (BṛUp 4.4.22), 'Neither done nor undone [actions] torment him' (BṛUp 4.4.22), 'That indeed does not torment him' (TaiUp 2.9.1), 'He fears nothing from anywhere' (TaiUp 2.9.1), and such <s>śrutis</s>. And from <s>smṛtis</s> such as: 'The fire of knowledge reduces all <s>karmas</s> to ashes' (BhG 4.37), and so forth. As for what was said — that [humans] are obstructed because of being debtors [to the gods] — that is not so, because that [debtorship] pertains only to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>. For it is one who possesses <s>avidyā</s> who is a debtor, because agency and the like are tenable for him. For [the text] will state: 'Where there is, as it were, another' (BṛUp 4.3.31). Where, when <s>avidyā</s> is present, there appears to be another — like a second moon produced by an eye-disease — there [the text] shows that action such as seeing and the like, which requires multiple agents produced by <s>avidyā</s>, and its fruit, are [produced by <s>avidyā</s>], by 'there one sees another' and the like. But where, when <s>vidyā</s> is present, the delusion of plurality created by <s>avidyā</s> has been destroyed — [there the text] shows the impossibility of action by 'with what would one see whom?' (BṛUp 4.5.15). Therefore, debtorship pertains only to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>, because action is possible [only there] — not otherwise. This we will demonstrate at length with the very passages to be explained hereafter. Now, as for this very [present passage] — whoever, not knowing <s>Brahman</s>, worships another deity — distinct from the Self — any deity whatsoever — through praise, salutation, sacrifice, offerings, dedication, and the like — [thinking] 'He is one, different from me, not the Self; I am another, the qualified [agent]; I must repay him as a debtor' — one who has such a cognition, who knows [things] thus. He is not merely such an ignorant person, afflicted by the defect of <s>avidyā</s> — but rather, just as an animal — a cow and the like — is utilized through the services of carrying, milking, and so forth, so he, being one to be utilized by each of the gods through the many services of sacrifice and the like — therefore, like an animal, he is employed in all activities of <s>karma</s> — this is the meaning. For this ignorant person — differentiated by <s>varṇa</s> (class) and <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life), qualified [for ritual] — the result of <s>karma</s> — whether combined with knowledge or by itself — as prescribed by scripture, is the ascent from the human state up to the state of <s>Brahmā</s>. And the result of action contrary to scripture — natural [action] — is the descent from the human state down to the state of immovable beings. How this is so, we will explain with the entire remainder of this chapter, beginning with 'Now there are three worlds' (BṛUp 1.5.16). And the result of <s>vidyā</s> is the attainment of the state of being the Self of all — this has been shown in summary. This entire <s>Upaniṣad</s> is concluded by the demonstration of the distinction between <s>vidyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s>. How this meaning applies to the entire scripture, we will demonstrate. Since this is so, with regard to a person who possesses <s>avidyā</s>, the gods are indeed capable of creating obstruction as well as bestowing grace — this is what [the text] demonstrates: just as in the world many animals — cows, horses, and such — serve a human being, their owner, their master — so, each ignorant person, standing in the position of many animals, serves the gods. The word 'gods' is used to indicate the ancestors and others as well.

children.text: " ato devāḥ paśūniva vyāghrādibhyo brahmavijñānādvighnamācikīrṣanti;asmadupabhogyatvānmāvyuttiṣṭheyuriti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the gods, like tigers and the like [guarding] animals, wish to create obstacles to the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> — [thinking] 'since they are objects of our enjoyment, let them not rise above [their station].'

children.text: yaṃ tu mumocayiṣanti taṃ śraddhādibhiryokṣyanti viparītamaśraddhādibhiḥ /
children.translated_text: But the one whom they wish to liberate, him they endow with faith and the like; the one [they wish to keep bound], with the opposite — lack of faith and the like.

children.text: tasmānmumukṣurdevārādhanaparaḥ śraddhābhaktiparaḥ praṇayo 'pramādī syādvidyāprāptiṃ ati vidyāṃ pratīti vā kākvaitatpradarśitaṃ bhavati devāpriyavākyena //10//
children.translated_text: Therefore, one who seeks liberation should be devoted to the worship of the gods, devoted to faith and devotion, reverential, and vigilant — for the attainment of knowledge. Or, 'he surpasses knowledge' — this [alternative reading] is indicated with irony by the sentence about what is displeasing to the gods. // 10 //

children.text:
brahma vā idam agra āsīd ekam eva |
tad ekaṃ san na vyabhavat |
tac chreyo rūpam atyasṛjata kṣatraṃ, yāny etāni devatrā kṣatrāṇīndro varuṇaḥ somo rudraḥ parjanyo yamo mṛtyur īśāna iti |
tasmāt kṣatrāt paraṃ nāsti |
tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ kṣatriyaṃ adhastād upāste rājasūye |
kṣatra eva tad yaśo dadhāti |
saiṣā kṣatrasya yonir yad brahma |
tasmād yady api rājā paramatāṃ gacchati brahmaivāntata upaniśrayati svāṃ yonim |
ya u enaṃ hinasti svāṃ sa yonim ṛcchati |
sa pāpīyān bhavati yathā śreyāṃsaṃ hiṃsitvā || BrhUp_1,4.11 ||
children.translated_text: <s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning, one alone. Being one, it did not flourish. It created a superior form — the <s>Kṣatra</s> (warrior class): those that are the <s>Kṣatras</s> (rulers) among the gods — <s>Indra</s>, <s>Varuṇa</s>, <s>Soma</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, <s>Parjanya</s>, <s>Yama</s>, <s>Mṛtyu</s>, <s>Īśāna</s>. Therefore there is nothing higher than the <s>Kṣatra</s>. Therefore the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> worships the <s>Kṣatriya</s> from below at the <s>Rājasūya</s> sacrifice. He places that glory in the <s>Kṣatra</s> alone. This — <s>Brahman</s> (the priestly class) — is the womb of the <s>Kṣatra</s>. Therefore, even if the king attains the highest position, at the end he takes refuge in <s>Brahman</s> (the priestly class) alone — his own womb. Whoever injures him [the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>] — he injures his own womb. He becomes more sinful, as one who has injured a superior. // BṛhUp 1.4.11 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.11 sūtritaḥ śāsrārthaḥ"ātmetyevopāsīta"iti /
tasya ca vyācikhyāsitasyasārthavādena"tadāhuryadbrahmavidyayā" ityādinā sambandhaprayojane abhihite /
avidyāyāścasaṃsārādhikārakāraṇatvamuktam"atha yo 'nyāṃ devatāmupāste"ityādinā /
tatrāvidvānṛṇī paśavaddevādikarmakartavyatayā paratantra ityuktam /
kiṃ punardevādikarmavyatvenimittam? varṇā āśramāśca /
tatra ke varṇāḥ? ityataidamārabhyate /
yannimittasambaddheṣu karmasvayaṃ paratantra evādhikṛtaḥ saṃsārīti /
etasyaivārthasya pradarśanāyāgnisargānantaramindrādisargo noktaḥ /
agnestu sargaḥ prajāpateḥ sṛṣṭiparipūraṇāya pradarśitaḥ /
ayaṃ ca indrādisargastatraiva draṣṭavyastaccheṣatvāt /
iha tu sa evāmidhīyate 'viduṣaḥ karmādhikārahetupradarśanāya- brahma vā idamagra āsīdyadagniṃ sṛṣṭvā agnirūpāpannaṃ brahma /
brāhmaṇajātyamimānād brahmetyabhidhīyate /
vai idaṃ kṣatrādijjātaṃ brahmaivābhinnamāsīdekameva /
nāsītkṣatrādibhedaḥ /
tadbrahmaikaṃ kṣatrādiparipālayitrādiśūnyaṃ sadaṃ na vyabhavat- na vibhūtavat, karmaṇe nālamāsīdityarthaḥ /
tatastadbrahma'brāhmaṇo 'smi mametthaṃ kartavyam'iti brāhmaṇajātinimittaṃ karma cikīrṣu-ātmanaḥ karmakartṛtvavibhūtyai śreyorūpaṃ praśastarūpam atyasṛjatātiśayenāsṛjata-sṛṣṭavat /
kiṃ punastadyatsṛṣṭam? kṣatraṃ kṣatriyajātiḥ, tadvyaktibhedena pradarśayati-yānyetāni prasiddhāni loke devatrā deveṣu kṣatrāṇīti /
jātyākhyāyāṃ pakṣe bahuvacanasmaraṇād vyaktibahutvādvā bhedopacāreṇa bahuvacanam /
kāni punastāni? ityāhatatrābhipiktā eva viśeṣato nirdiśyante-indro devānāṃ rājā, varuṇo yādasām, somo brāhmaṇānām, rudraḥ paśūnām, parjanyo vidyudādīnām, yamaḥ pitṝṇām, mṛtyurogādīnām, īśānobhāsām-ityevamādīni deveṣukṣatrāṇi /
tadanu, indrādikṣatradevatādhiṣṭhitāni purūravaḥprabhṛtīni sṛṣṭānyeva draṣṭavyāni /
tadartha eva hi devakṣatrasargaḥ prastutaḥ /
yasmādbrahmaṇātiśayena sṛṣṭaṃ kṣatraṃ tasmātkṣatrātparaṃ nāsti brāhmaṇajāterapi niyansṛ /
tasmādbrāhmaṇaḥ kāraṇabhāto 'pi kṣatriyasya kṣatriyamadhastādvyavasthitaḥ sannuparisthitamupāste /
kka? rājasūye /
kṣatra eva tadātmīyaṃ yaśaḥ khyātirūpaṃ brahmeti dadhāti sthāpayati /
rājasūyābhiṣiktenāsandyāṃ sthitena rājñā āmantrito brahmanniti ṛtvikpunastaṃ pratyāha"tvaṃ rājanbrahmāsi"iti /
tadetadabhidhīyate -"kṣatra eva tadyaśo dadhāti"iti /
saiṣā prakṛtā kṣatrasya yonireva yadbrahma /
tasmādyadyati rājā paramatāṃ rājasūyābhiṣekaguṇaṃ gacchatyāpnoti brahmaiva brāhmaṇajātimedha, antato 'nte karmaparisamāptāvupanikṣayatyāśrayati svāṃ yonim, purohitaṃ puro nidhatta ityarthaḥ /

yastu punarbalābhimānātsvāṃ yoniṃ brāhmaṇajātiṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ya u enaṃ hinasti hiṃsati nyagbhāvena paśyati, svāmātmāyāmeva sa yonimṛcchati-svaṃ prasavaṃ vicchinatti vināśayati-svaṃ prasavaṃ vicchinatti vināśayati /
children.translated_text: But whoever, out of pride of strength, injures his own womb — the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> class, the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> — whoever harms him, looks down upon him — he injures his own womb, he severs his own origin, he destroys [it].

children.text: sa etatkṛtvā pāpīyānpāpataro bhavati /
children.translated_text: Having done this, he becomes more sinful — more wicked.

children.text: pūrvamapi kṣatriyaḥ pāpa eva krūratvādātmaprasavahiṃsayā sutarām /
children.translated_text: Even previously, the <s>Kṣatriya</s> is sinful indeed, because of his cruelty — all the more so through the injury to his own origin.

children.text: yathā loke śreyāṃsaṃ praśastataraṃ hiṃsitvā paribhūya pāpataro bhavati tadvat //11//
children.translated_text: Just as in the world, one who has injured, disrespected one who is superior — more praiseworthy — becomes more sinful, so too [here]. // 11 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.11:] The meaning of the scripture has been aphoristically stated: 'One should meditate as the self alone.' And the connection and purpose of that [teaching] which is to be elaborated upon have been stated through the <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) beginning with 'They say: since by the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>...' And the causality of <s>avidyā</s> for the qualification [to be in] <s>saṃsāra</s> has been stated through 'But whoever worships another deity...' and so on. There it was stated that the ignorant person, being indebted [to the gods] like an animal, is dependent upon them through the obligation to perform rituals for the gods and the like. What then is the occasion for the obligation to perform rituals for the gods and the like? The <s>varṇas</s> (social classes) and <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life). Of these, what are the <s>varṇas</s>? For the purpose of showing this, [the text] commences — [to show] that this [individual], being qualified in and dependent upon the rituals connected with the causes [of varṇa], is indeed a transmigrating being. It is for the demonstration of this very meaning that the creation of <s>Indra</s> and the others was not stated immediately after the creation of fire. The creation of fire, however, was presented for the completion of <s>Prajāpati</s>'s creative work. And this creation of <s>Indra</s> and the others is to be viewed as belonging to that same [earlier creation], being subsidiary to it. But here it is mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the basis of the qualification for ritual action of the ignorant person. '<s>Brahman</s> indeed was this in the beginning' — that <s>Brahman</s> which, having created fire, had assumed the form of fire. It is called '<s>Brahman</s>' due to its contempt for the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> class [i.e., its identity with the priestly class]. Indeed this — all that was born from the <s>Kṣatra</s> and the rest — was <s>Brahman</s> alone, undifferentiated, one only. There was no differentiation into <s>Kṣatra</s> and the rest. That <s>Brahman</s>, being one, devoid of a ruler of the <s>Kṣatra</s> and the rest, did not flourish — did not become powerful; the meaning is: it was not sufficient for [performing] action. Then that <s>Brahman</s>, desiring action on the basis of [thinking] 'I am a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, this is my duty,' and wishing for the manifestation of its own capacity for being an agent of action — created exceedingly a superior form, a praiseworthy form. What is that which was created? The <s>Kṣatra</s>, the <s>Kṣatriya</s> class. He demonstrates it with specific instances: those that are well-known in the world as <s>Kṣatras</s> (rulers) among the gods. In the interpretation where [<s>Kṣatra</s>] denotes the class-name, the plural is either from the recollection [in scripture] of the plural, or figuratively due to the plurality of individuals. What are those? He lists them — among these, the specifically anointed ones are named: <s>Indra</s> is the king of the gods, <s>Varuṇa</s> of the waters, <s>Soma</s> of the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, <s>Rudra</s> of the animals, <s>Parjanya</s> of lightning and the like, <s>Yama</s> of the ancestors, <s>Mṛtyu</s> of diseases and the like, <s>Īśāna</s> of luminaries — such are the <s>Kṣatras</s> among the gods. Following upon them, the human [<s>Kṣatras</s>] such as <s>Purūravas</s> and the rest, presided over by these <s>Kṣatra</s>-deities like <s>Indra</s> and the rest, are to be understood as having been created. For the creation of the divine <s>Kṣatra</s> is introduced precisely for that purpose. Since the <s>Kṣatra</s> was created exceedingly by <s>Brahman</s>, therefore there is nothing higher than the <s>Kṣatra</s>, since it is the controller even of the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> class. Therefore the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, though being the causal [class] of the <s>Kṣatriya</s>, worships the <s>Kṣatriya</s>, being positioned below the one positioned above. Where? At the <s>Rājasūya</s> sacrifice. In the <s>Kṣatra</s> alone he places that glory of his — his fame-like [glory] which is <s>Brahman</s> (the priestly status). The king, consecrated through the <s>Rājasūya</s> abhiṣeka, seated on the throne, addresses [the priest] 'O <s>Brahman</s>!' — and the <s>Ṛtvik</s> (priest) in turn says to him: 'You, O King, are <s>Brahman</s>.' This is what is referred to by: 'He places that glory in the <s>Kṣatra</s> alone.' This well-known <s>Brahman</s> (priestly class) under discussion is the very womb of the <s>Kṣatra</s>. Therefore, even if the king attains the highest position — the distinction of the <s>Rājasūya</s> consecration — at the end, at the conclusion of the ritual, he takes refuge in <s>Brahman</s> alone — the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> class — his own womb; [meaning] he places the <s>Purohita</s> (family priest) in front [of himself]; this is the meaning.

children.text: kṣatre sṛṣṭe 'pi-
children.translated_text: Even after the <s>Kṣatra</s> was created —

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.12
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,4.12

children.text:
sa naiva vyabhavat |
sa viśam asṛjata |
yāny etāni devajātāni gaṇaśa ākhyāyante vasavo rudrā ādityā viśve devā maruta iti || BrhUp_1,4.12 ||
children.translated_text: It [<s>Brahman</s>] still did not flourish. It created the <s>Viś</s> (commoner class) — those divine classes that are named in groups: the <s>Vasus</s>, <s>Rudras</s>, <s>Ādityas</s>, <s>Viśvedevas</s>, and <s>Maruts</s>. // BṛhUp 1.4.12 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,4.12 sa naiva vyabhavat, karmaṇe brahma tathā navyabhavat, vittopārjayiturabhāvāt /
sa viśamasṛjata karmasādhanavittopārjanāya /
children.translated_text: It created the <s>Viś</s> (commoner class) for the purpose of earning wealth, which is the means for [performing] action.

children.text: kaḥ punarasau viṭ? yānyetāni devajātāni-svārthe niṣṭhā, ya ete devajātibhedā ityarthaḥ;gaṇaśo gaṇaṃ gaṇam, ākhyāyante kathyante /
children.translated_text: Who then is this <s>Viś</s>? 'Those divine classes' — the suffix is used in its own sense [reflexively]; the meaning is: those distinctions of divine classes. In groups, group by group, they are named — spoken of.

children.text: gaṇaprāyā hi viśaḥ, prāyeṇa saṃhatā hi vittopārjane samarthāḥ na ekaikaśaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the <s>Viś</s> mostly consists of groups — generally, those who are united together are capable of earning wealth, not individually.

children.text: vasavaḥ aṣṭasaṅkhyo gaṇaḥ, tathaikādaśa rudrāḥ, dvādaśādityāḥ, viśvedevāsrayodaśa viśvāyā apatyāni, sarve vā devāḥ, marutaḥ sapta sapta gaṇāḥ //12//
children.translated_text: The <s>Vasus</s> — a group of eight; similarly, eleven <s>Rudras</s>, twelve <s>Ādityas</s>, thirteen <s>Viśvedevas</s> — the offspring of <s>Viśvā</s>, or all the gods [collectively]; the <s>Maruts</s> — seven groups of seven. // 12 //
[Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.12:] 'It still did not flourish' — <s>Brahman</s> even then did not flourish for [the purpose of] action, because there was no one to earn wealth.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.13
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,4.13

children.text:
sa naiva vyabhavat |
sa śaudraṃ varṇam asṛjata pūṣaṇam |
iyaṃ vai pūṣā |
iyaṃ hīdaṃ sarvaṃ puṣyati yad idaṃ kiñca || BrhUp_1,4.13 ||
children.translated_text: It still did not flourish. It created the <s>Śūdra</s> class — <s>Pūṣan</s>. This [earth] indeed is <s>Pūṣan</s>. For this [earth] nourishes all this — whatever there is. // BṛhUp 1.4.13 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,4.13 sa paricārakabhāvātpunarapi naiva vyabhavat, sa śaudraṃ varṇamasṛjata- śūdra eva śaudraḥ, svārthe 'ṇi vṛddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.13:] Due to the absence of a servant-class, it again still did not flourish. It created the <s>Śūdra</s> class — '<s>Śaudra</s>' means pertaining to the <s>Śūdra</s>; the <s>vṛddhi</s> augment is used in its own [reflexive] sense.

children.text: kaḥ punarasau śaudro varṇo yaḥ sṛṣṭaḥ? pūṣaṇam- puṇyatīti pūṣā kaḥ punarasau pūṣā? iti viśeṣatastannirdiśati- iyaṃ pṛthivī pūpā /
children.translated_text: Who then is this <s>Śūdra</s> class that was created? <s>Pūṣan</s> — one who nourishes (<s>puṣṇāti</s>) is <s>Pūṣan</s>. Who then is this <s>Pūṣan</s>? He specifies it particularly: this earth is <s>Pūṣan</s>.

children.text: svayameva nirvacanamāha- iyaṃ hīdaṃ sarvaṃ puṣyati yadidaṃ kiñca //13//
children.translated_text: [The text] itself provides the etymology: 'For this [earth] nourishes (<s>puṣyati</s>) all this, whatever there is.' // 13 //

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.14
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,4.14

children.text:
sa naiva vyabhavat |
tac chreyo rūpam atyasṛjata dharmam |
tad etat kṣatrasya kṣatraṃ yad dharmaḥ |
tasmād dharmāt paraṃ nāsti |
atho abalīyān balīyāṃsam āśaṃsate dharmeṇa |
yathā rājñaivam |
yo vai sa dharmaḥ satyaṃ vai tat |
tasmāt satyaṃ vadantam āhur dharmaṃ vadatīti |
dharmaṃ vā vadantaṃ satyaṃ vadatīti |
etad dhy evaitad ubhayaṃ bhavati || BrhUp_1,4.14 ||
children.translated_text: It still did not flourish. It created a superior form — <s>Dharma</s> (righteousness, law). This is the <s>Kṣatra</s> (ruling power) of the <s>Kṣatra</s> — namely <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore there is nothing higher than <s>Dharma</s>. Hence a weaker man hopes [to prevail over] a stronger one through <s>Dharma</s> — as through a king. That which is <s>Dharma</s> is indeed <s>Satya</s> (truth). Therefore, of one who speaks truth, they say: 'He speaks <s>Dharma</s>.' Or of one who speaks <s>Dharma</s>, they say: 'He speaks truth.' For both of these are the same. // BṛhUp 1.4.14 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.14 sa caturaḥ sṛṣṭvāpi varṇānnaiva vyabhavat, ugratvātkṣatrasyāniyatāśaṅkayā /
tacchreyorūpamatyasṛjata, kiṃ tat? dharmam;tadetacchreyorūpaṃ sṛṣṭaṃ kṣatrasya kṣatraṃ kṣatrasyāpi niyantṛ, ugrādapyugram, yaddharmo yo dharmaḥ;tasmātkṣatrasyāpi niyantṛtvāddharmātparaṃ nāsti;tena hi niyamyante sarve /
tatkatham? ityucyate- atho apyabalīyāndurbalataro balīyāṃsamātmano balavattaramapyāśaṃsate kāmayate jetuṃ dharmeṇa balena;yathā loke rājñā sarvabalavattamenāpi kuṭumbikaḥ; evam;tasmātsiddhaṃ dharmasya sarvabalavattaratvātsarvaniyantṛtvam /
yo vai sa dharmo vyavahāralakṣaṇo laukikairvyavahriyamāṇaḥ satyaṃ vai tat;satyamiti yathāstrārthatā;sa evānuṣṭhīyamāno dharmanāmā bhavati, śāstrārthatvena jñāyamānastu satyaṃ bhavati /
yasmādevaṃ tasmātsatyaṃ yathāśāstraṃ vadantaṃ vyavahārakāla āhuḥ samīpasthā ubhayavivekajñāḥ- dharma vadatīti, prasiddhaṃ laukikaṃ nyāyaṃ vadatīti /
tathā viparyayeṇa dharma vā laukikaṃ vyavahāraṃ vadantamāhuḥ- satyaṃ vadati, śāstrādanapetaṃ vadatīti /
etadyaduktamubhayaṃ jñāyamānamanuṣṭhīyamānaṃ caitaddharma eva bhavati /
tasmātsa dharmo jñānānuṣṭānalakṣaṇaḥ śāstrajñānanitarāṃśca sarvāneva niyamayati /
children.translated_text: Therefore, that <s>Dharma</s>, characterized by knowledge and practice, restrains all others — especially those ignorant of scriptural knowledge.

children.text: tasmātsa kṣatrasyāpi kṣatram /
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is the <s>Kṣatra</s> (ruling power) even of the <s>Kṣatra</s>.

children.text: atastadabhimāno 'vidvāṃstadviśeṣānuṣṭhānāya brahmakṣatraviṭśūdranimittaviśeṣamabhimanyate /
children.translated_text: Hence, the ignorant one, possessing the conceit of that [<s>Dharma</s>], for the purpose of performing its specific observances, identifies himself with the specific causes of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, <s>Kṣatriya</s>, <s>Vaiśya</s>, and <s>Śūdra</s> [classes].

children.text: tāni ca nisargata eva karmādhikāranimittāni //14//
children.translated_text: And those [class distinctions] are indeed the causes of the natural qualification for ritual action. // 14 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.4.14:] It, having created even the four <s>varṇas</s>, still did not flourish — because of the apprehension that the <s>Kṣatra</s>, being fierce, might be unrestrained. It created a superior form. What is that? <s>Dharma</s>. This superior form that was created is the <s>Kṣatra</s> of the <s>Kṣatra</s> — the controller even of the <s>Kṣatra</s>; more formidable than even the formidable — namely <s>Dharma</s>, that which is <s>Dharma</s>. Therefore, because it controls even the <s>Kṣatra</s>, there is nothing higher than <s>Dharma</s>; for by it, all are restrained. How so? It is said: hence, even a weaker person — one of lesser strength — hopes, i.e. desires to conquer even one stronger than himself — one more powerful than him — through <s>Dharma</s> as his strength; just as in the world, [one prevails] through a king — even the most powerful of all — so does the householder. Thus the all-surpassing controlling power of <s>Dharma</s>, being stronger than all, is established. That which is this <s>Dharma</s>, characterized by worldly conduct and practiced by worldly people, is indeed <s>Satya</s> (truth) — <s>satya</s> means conformity with the scripture. That very same [principle], when being practiced, bears the name <s>Dharma</s>; but when known as the meaning of scripture, it becomes <s>Satya</s>. Since this is so, therefore when someone speaks truth — speaks in accordance with scripture — during the course of worldly conduct, those nearby who know the distinction between both say: 'He speaks <s>Dharma</s>' — meaning he states the well-known worldly norm. Similarly, in reverse, when one speaks <s>Dharma</s> — worldly conduct — they say: 'He speaks truth — he speaks what is not deviant from scripture.' This that has been stated — both [<s>Dharma</s> and <s>Satya</s>], when known and when practiced — are indeed <s>Dharma</s> alone.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.15
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,4.15

children.text:
tad etad brahma kṣatraṃ viṭ śūdraḥ |
tad agninaiva deveṣu brahmābhavad brāhmaṇo manuṣyeṣu, kṣatriyeṇa kṣatriyaḥ, vaiśyena vaiśyaḥ, śūdreṇa śūdraḥ |
tasmād agnāv eva deveṣu lokam icchante brāhmaṇe manuṣyeṣu |
etābhyāṃ hi rūpābhyāṃ brahmābhavat |
atha yo ha vā asmāl lokāt svaṃ lokam adṛṣṭvā praiti sa enam avidito na bhunakti yathā vedo vānanūkto 'nyad vā karmākṛtam |
yadi ha vā apy anevaṃvin mahatpuṇyaṃ karma karoti tad dhāsyāntataḥ kṣīyata eva |
ātmānam eva lokam upāsīta |
sa ya ātmānam eva lokam upāste na hāsya karma kṣīyate |
asmād dhy evātmano yadyat kāmayate tattat sṛjate || BrhUp_1,4.15 ||
children.translated_text: So this is <s>Brahman</s> (priestly class), <s>Kṣatra</s> (warrior class), <s>Viś</s> (commoner class), <s>Śūdra</s>. Among the gods, <s>Brahman</s> became [manifest] through <s>Agni</s> alone; among humans, as the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>; through the <s>Kṣatriya</s> [divine form], as a <s>Kṣatriya</s>; through the <s>Vaiśya</s> [divine form], as a <s>Vaiśya</s>; through the <s>Śūdra</s> [divine form], as a <s>Śūdra</s>. Therefore, among the gods one desires a world through <s>Agni</s> alone, and among humans through the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>. For through these two forms <s>Brahman</s> became [manifest]. Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world — it, being unknown, does not benefit him, just as the <s>Veda</s> unrecited or any other deed undone [does not benefit]. Even if one who does not know this performs a great and meritorious deed — that will certainly be exhausted for him in the end. One should meditate on the self alone as [one's] world. Whoever meditates on the self alone as [one's] world — his deed does not become exhausted. For from this very self he creates whatever he desires. // BṛhUp 1.4.15 //

children.translated_text: 'Whether he performs other [rites] or not — one who is friendly [to all] is called a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>.'

[Commentary on BṛhUp 1.4.15:] This four-fold class system was created — <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, <s>Kṣatriya</s>, <s>Vaiśya</s>, and <s>Śūdra</s>. A summation is made for the sake of what follows: that creator <s>Brahman</s> became <s>Brahman</s> (the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> class) among the gods in the form of <s>Agni</s> alone, in no other form, and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> caste [arose]. Among humans, <s>Brahman</s> became [manifest] in the form of the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>; in the other classes, having undergone different modifications — he became a <s>Kṣatriya</s> through the <s>Kṣatriya</s> [form], presided over by deities such as <s>Indra</s>; a <s>Vaiśya</s> through the <s>Vaiśya</s> [form]; a <s>Śūdra</s> through the <s>Śūdra</s> [form]. Since in the <s>Kṣatriya</s> and other classes, the creator <s>Brahman</s> underwent modification, but in <s>Agni</s> and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> it remained unmodified — therefore, among the gods, people desire the fruits of action connected with <s>Agni</s> alone, by performing rituals connected with fire — this is the meaning. For that very purpose did that <s>Brahman</s> take its position in the form of <s>Agni</s> as the substratum of ritual action. Therefore, having performed ritual action in that fire and praying for its fruit — this is well-established.

children.translated_text: Or, it is for showing that one becomes the self of all, as before.

children.translated_text: For if it is indeed the supreme self that is attained, then the use of the word '<s>ātman</s>' in 'from this very self' is appropriate — the meaning being 'from one's own world, the self, which is the topic.'

children.text: na hyasminprakṛte viśeṣite 'śrutāntarālāvasthāpratipattuṃ śakyate //15//
children.translated_text: For when the topic has been specified, one cannot import an intermediate state not heard [in the text]. // 15 //

(<s>Manu</s> 2.87). And because of the scriptural evidence for the <s>parivrājya</s> (renunciant) way of life. Therefore, among humans, people desire the fruits of action only in the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> state. Since it is through these two — in the forms of <s>Agni</s> and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, serving as the agent and substratum of ritual action — that the creator <s>Brahman</s> directly manifested. However, some [commentators] say that here they desire the world of the <s>Paramātman</s> in <s>Agni</s> and the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>. That is incorrect, because the topic is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and the class-distinction is introduced for the purpose of the domain of ritual action, and because of the specification [given] later. For if the word '<s>loka</s>' (world) here referred to the supreme self, then the later specification 'without seeing one's own world' would be purposeless. But if the 'world' under discussion, which is sought through dependence on fire [and the like], is different from one's own [world], then the specification 'one's own' is appropriate, because it serves to negate the world under discussion. And because the word '<s>sva</s>' (one's own) never deviates [in meaning] with respect to the world of the <s>Paramātman</s>, while the sense of 'own-ness' does deviate for things created by <s>avidyā</s>. And [the <s>śruti</s>] states the deviation of those produced by <s>karma</s>: 'it is exhausted indeed.' The classes (<s>varṇas</s>) were created by <s>Brahman</s> for the purpose of action; and that action, called <s>dharma</s>, either controls all [classes] as obligatory, or is the means to human goals. Therefore, if by that very action itself one's own world, called the <s>Paramātman</s>, were attained — even without knowing it — what purpose would there be in its being separately sought? Hence [the text] says: 'now' — this is for the purpose of refuting the objection. Whoever — any person whatsoever — from this world that is foreign, not one's own, which arises from <s>saṃsāric</s> desires and actions, or from the conceit of dependence on rituals connected with fire, or from the conceit of mere <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-class identity and action — from this adventitious, non-inherent world — 'one's own world,' called the self, which is unfailing because of its identity with the self — not having seen it, [i.e., not having realized] 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' — departs, dies. Although it is one's own world, unknown due to being concealed by <s>avidyā</s>, it is as if not one's own, unrecognized — it does not benefit him, does not protect him, by removing the defects of grief, delusion, fear, and so forth — just as in the world, the <s>Veda</s> when not recited, not studied, does not benefit [one] by revealing the knowledge of ritual action and such; or just as worldly action such as agriculture, when not performed, not manifested by one's own effort, does not benefit [one] by yielding its fruit. Similarly, the self, one's own world, when not manifested by its own eternal self-nature through the removal of <s>avidyā</s> and the like, does not benefit at all. But what use is there in protecting through the vision of one's own world? Since the attainment of fruit through action is certain, and since the action that is the cause of desired fruit is abundant, the protection resulting from that will be inexhaustible. Not so, because what is produced is subject to exhaustion. This is what [the text] says: if here, in <s>saṃsāra</s>, as if miraculously, even some great soul — one who does not know thus, who does not know his own world by the method described — performs great, abundant meritorious action such as the <s>Aśvamedha</s>, whose fruit is only the desired [worldly] fruit, continuously [thinking] 'by this, I shall attain infinity' — that action, for one who has <s>avidyā</s>, because it is caused by desire born of <s>avidyā</s>, like prosperity arising from the delusion of a dream-vision, is indeed exhausted at the end, when the enjoyment of its fruit [is complete]. Because both its causes — <s>avidyā</s> and desire — are unstable, the impossibility of what is produced [being] destructive of exhaustion is established. Therefore, there is no hope of infinity from the protection of the fruit of meritorious action. Hence, one should meditate on the self alone as one's own world — 'the self' is in the sense of 'one's own world,' since the topic is 'one's own world,' and the word '<s>sva</s>' (own) is not used again here. One who meditates on the self alone as his world — what [happens] for him? It is said: his <s>karma</s> is not exhausted. Because <s>karma</s> is simply absent [for him] — this is merely a restatement of what is eternally the case. Just as for the ignorant, the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s> characterized by the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> is perpetual, it is not so for this [knower] — this is the meaning. Just as: 'When <s>Mithilā</s> is burning, nothing of mine is burnt.' For the wise one who meditates on the self as his own world, because of the connection with knowledge, <s>karma</s> itself is not exhausted — so others interpret. And they construct the meaning of the word '<s>loka</s>' (world) in two ways as associated with <s>karma</s>: one is the manifest state, the world dependent on <s>karma</s>, called <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>'s [world]; one who meditates on that <s>karma</s>-associated world in its manifest, limited [form] — for him, being one who sees <s>karma</s> and self as limited, <s>karma</s> is exhausted. But one who meditates on that same <s>karma</s>-associated world having reduced it to its unmanifest state, its causal form — for him, because he sees <s>karma</s> and self as unlimited, his <s>karma</s> is not exhausted. This is an attractive construction, but it is not based on <s>śruti</s>. Because the word '<s>svaloka</s>' (one's own world) refers to the <s>Paramātman</s> under discussion. Having introduced the topic with 'one's own world' and then dropping the word '<s>sva</s>' and substituting the word '<s>ātman</s>' in the re-statement of the same [idea] — 'one should meditate on the self alone as [one's] world' — there is no occasion at all for constructing a world associated with <s>karma</s>. And because of the later specification, which pertains exclusively to knowledge: 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this self is this world?' (BṛhUp 4.4.22). For [that text] distinguishes 'this self is our world' from the worlds created by sons, <s>karma</s>, and lower knowledge. And: 'His world is not diminished by any <s>karma</s> — this is his supreme world.' The syntactical unity of this [passage] with those qualified [texts] is appropriate, and here too the specification 'one's own world' is seen. [Objection:] '[The text says] from this [world] he desired' — [if one's own world is the <s>Paramātman</s>], this is inappropriate. [Reply:] Here, one's own world is the <s>Paramātman</s>. Since through meditation on that one becomes that very thing — when this is established — whatever he desires, he creates from that very self — this statement of a result other than the attainment of the self is inappropriate, [you say]. Not so, because it is for the purpose of praising the meditation on one's own world: the meaning is that from one's own world itself, all that is desired is accomplished — nothing other than that need be sought, because of the attainment of all desires — as in the other <s>śruti</s>: 'From the self [comes] <s>prāṇa</s>, from the self [comes] hope' (<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 7.23.1).

What then are those actions by whose compulsion one becomes subservient like an animal? And who are those gods and others whom one serves through actions like an animal? Both of these are now elaborated:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,4.16
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 1.4.16]

children.text:
atho ayaṃ vā ātmā sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ lokaḥ |
sa yaj juhoti yad yajate tena devānāṃ lokaḥ |
atha yad anubrūte tena ṛṣīṇām |
atha yat pitṛbhyo nipṛṇāti yat prajām icchate tena pitṝṇām |
atha yan manuṣyān vāsayate yad ebhyo 'śanaṃ dadāti tena manuṣyāṇām |

yad asya gṛheṣu śvāpadā vayāṃsy ā pipīlikābhya upajīvanti tena teṣāṃ lokaḥ |
yathā ha vai svāya lokāyāriṣṭim icchet |
evaṃ haivaṃvide sarvadā sarvāṇi bhūtāny ariṣṭim icchanti |
tad vā etad viditaṃ mīmāṃsitam || BrhUp_1,4.16 ||
children.translated_text: 'Now, this self is the world of all beings. Insofar as he offers oblations and performs sacrifices — thereby he becomes the world of the gods. Insofar as he recites [the <s>Vedas</s>] — thereby [he becomes the world] of the sages. Insofar as he offers libations to the ancestors and desires offspring — thereby [he becomes the world] of the ancestors. Insofar as he gives shelter to people and gives them food — thereby [he becomes the world] of humans. Insofar as he provides grass and water for the animals — thereby [he becomes the world] of the animals. Insofar as beasts, birds, down to the ants live in his house — thereby he is their world. Just as one would wish safety for one's own world, so indeed all beings wish safety for one who knows thus. This indeed is known and investigated.' // BṛhUp 1.4.16 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,4.16 atho ityayaṃ vākyopanyāsārthaḥ /
ayaṃ yaḥ prakṛto gṛhī karmādhikṛto 'vidvāñcharīrendriyasaṅghātādiviśiṣṭaḥ piṇḍa ātmetyucyate;sarveṣāṃ varṇāśramādivihitaiḥ karmabhirupakāritvāt /

atha yadanubrūte svādhyāyamadhīte 'harahastena ṛṣīṇāṃ lokaḥ /

atha yatpitṛbhyo nipṛṇāti prayacchati piṇḍodakādi, yacca prajāmicchati prajārthamudyamaṃ karoti - icchā cotpattyupalakṣaṇārthā - prajāṃ cotpādayatītyarthaḥ, tena karmaṇāvaśyakartavyatvena pitṛṇāṃ bhogyatvena paratantro lokaḥ /
children.translated_text: Insofar as he offers to the ancestors — gives them offerings of rice-balls, water, and the like — and insofar as he desires offspring, i.e., makes effort for the purpose of progeny — and 'desire' here is indicative of [actual] production — he also produces offspring, this is the meaning — by that action, being bound by its obligatory nature, he is the world of the ancestors, subservient as their object of enjoyment.

children.text: atha yanmanuṣyānvāsayate gṛhe, yacca tebhyo vasadbhyo 'vasadbhyo vā arthibhyo 'śanaṃ dadāti, tena manuṣyāṇām;atha yatpaśubhyastṛṇodakaṃ vindati lambhayati, tena paśūnām;yadasya gṛheṣu śvāpadā vayāṃsi ca pipīlikābhiḥ saha kaṇabalibhāṇḍakṣālanādyupajīvanti, tena teṣāṃ lokaḥ /
children.translated_text: Insofar as he gives shelter to people in his house, and insofar as he gives food to those dwelling [there] or not dwelling [there], to those who are needy — thereby [he is the world] of humans. Insofar as he provides — makes available — grass and water for animals, thereby [he is the world] of animals. Insofar as beasts and birds, together with ants, live in his house on grain-offerings, vessel-washings, and such — thereby he is their world.

children.text: yasmādayametāni karmāṇi kurvannupakaroti devādibhyaḥ, tasmādyathā ha vai loke svāpya lokāya svasmai dehāyāriṣṭamavināśaṃ svatvabhāvāpracyutimicchet svatvabhāvapracyutibhayātpoṣaṇarakṣaṇādibhiḥ sarvataḥ paripālayet, evaṃ haivaṃvide'sarvabhūtabhogyo 'hamanena prakāreṇa mayā avaśyamṛṇivatpratikartavyam'ityevamātmānaṃ parikalpitavate sarvāṇi bhūtāni devādīni yathoktāni ariṣṭimavināśamicchanti svatvāpracyutyai sarvataḥ saṃrakṣanti kuṭumbina iva paśūn -"tasmādeṣāṃ tanna priyam"ityuktam /
children.translated_text: Since this [householder] renders service to gods and others by performing these actions, therefore, just as in the world one would wish safety — non-destruction, non-loss of one's own status — for one's own body, one's own world, out of fear of the loss of [that] status, by nurturing and protecting it from all sides — so indeed, for one who knows thus — '[I am] the object of enjoyment of all beings, and in this manner I must make repayment as if of a debt' — all beings, gods and the rest, as described, wish safety, non-destruction, for him, protecting him from all sides in order that his status may not be lost, just as a householder [protects] his animals. As was said: 'Therefore it is not pleasing to them [that humans should know this].'

children.text: tadvā etattadetadyathoktānāṃ karmaṇām ṛṇavadavaśyakartavyatvaṃ pañcamahāyajñaprakaraṇe viditaṃ kartavyatayā mīmāṃsitaṃ vicāritaṃ cāvadānaprakaraṇe //16//
children.translated_text: That is this — regarding the obligatory nature, like a debt, of the actions described above — this was known in the section on the Five Great Sacrifices (<s>pañcamahāyajña</s>), and was examined and investigated as obligatory in the section on portions (<s>avadāna</s>). // 16 //

[Commentary:] The word '<s>atho</s>' serves to introduce the sentence. This one — this one who is the topic, the householder, qualified for ritual action, ignorant, the aggregate designated as 'self,' distinguished by body, sense-organs, and the like — [is the world] of all [beings], because he renders service through the actions prescribed for class, life-stage, and so forth. By what particular actions does he serve, and of which particular beings is he the world? It is said: this householder — insofar as he offers oblations and performs sacrifices — a sacrifice (<s>yāga</s>) being the relinquishment of ownership directed toward a deity, and that very relinquishment, when exceptionally [performed], is an oblation (<s>homa</s>) — by that action characterized as oblation and sacrifice, being bound by its obligatory nature in a subservient manner like an animal, he is the world, the support, of the gods. Insofar as he recites — studies the <s>Veda</s> day by day — thereby he is the world of the sages.

children.text:
brahma vidvāṃścettasmātpaśubhāvātkartavyatābandhanarūpātpratimucyate, kenāyaṃ kāritaḥ karmavandhanādhikāre 'vaśa iva pravartate, na punastadvimokṣṇopāye vidyādhikāra iti nanūktaṃ devā rakṣantīti /
bāḍham, karmādhikārasvagocarārūḍhāneva te 'pi rakṣanti, anyathākṛtābhyāgamakṛtanāśaprasaṅgāt /
na tu sāmānyaṃ puruṣamātraṃ viśiṣṭādhikārānārūḍham;tasmādbhavitavyaṃ tena, yena prerito 'vaśa eva bahirmukho bhavati svasmāllokāt /
nanvavidyāsā, avidyāvānihi bahirmukhībhūtaḥ pravartate /
sāpi naiva pravartikā;vastusvarūpāvarṇātmikā hi sā;pravartakabījatvaṃ tu pratipadyate 'ndhatvamiva gartādipatanapravṛttihetuḥ /
evaṃ tarhyucyatāṃ kiṃ tad yatpravṛttiheturiti? tadihābhidhīyate - eṣaṇā kāmaḥ saḥ ,'svābhāvikyāmavidyāyāṃ vartamānā bālāḥ parācaḥ kāmānanuyanti'iti kāṭhakaśrutau, smṛtau ca -"kāma eṣa krodha eṣaḥ"(gītā 3 / 37) ityādi, mānave ca sarvā pravṛttiḥ kāmahetukyeveti /
sa eṣor'thaḥ savistaraḥ pradarśyata iha ā adhyāyaparisamāpteḥ -
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] If one who knows <s>Brahman</s> is released from that animal-like condition characterized by bondage through obligatory duties — then by what is this [person] made to engage helplessly, as it were, in the sphere of bondage to action, rather than in the sphere of knowledge, which is the means of liberation from that? [Response:] Was it not already said that the gods protect [him, keeping him in bondage]? True, they too protect only those who have already entered the sphere of the entitlement to action — otherwise there would be the fault of acquiring what was not acquired and destroying what was acquired. But they do not [protect] an ordinary person who has not yet entered into a specific entitlement. Therefore, there must be something by which one is impelled, helplessly becoming outward-turned from one's own world. [Objection:] That is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — for the one possessed of ignorance, being outward-turned, engages [in action]. [Reply:] Even that [<s>avidyā</s>] is not the actual cause of engagement; for its nature is the concealment of the true nature of things. But it becomes the seed of engagement — just as blindness becomes the cause of falling into pits and the like. [Objection:] If so, then let it be said: what is that which is the cause of engagement? [Reply:] This is stated here: it is desire (<s>eṣaṇā</s>), which is <s>kāma</s> (longing). As the <s>Kāṭhaka</s> <s>śruti</s> says: 'The childish, dwelling in natural ignorance, outward-turned, pursue desires.' And in <s>smṛti</s>: 'This is desire, this is anger' (<s>Gītā</s> 3.37) and so forth. And in <s>Manu</s>: all activity is caused by desire alone. This very meaning is now presented in detail here, until the end of the chapter.

tasyo kṛtsnatā |
mana evāsyātmā |
vāg jāyā |
prāṇaḥ prajā |
cakṣur mānuṣaṃ vittam |
cakṣuṣā hi tad vindate |
śrotraṃ daivam |
śrotreṇa hi tac chṛṇoti |
ātmaivāsya karma |
ātmanā hi karma karoti |
sa eṣa pāṅkto yajñaḥ |
pāṅktaḥ paśuḥ |
pāṅktaḥ puruṣaḥ |

children.translated_text: The self alone was this in the beginning, one only. He desired: 'May I have a wife, so that I may procreate. May I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action.' This much indeed is desire. Even if one wishes, one cannot obtain more than this. Therefore, even now, one who is alone desires: 'May I have a wife, so that I may procreate. May I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action.' As long as he does not obtain each of these, he considers himself incomplete. His completeness [is as follows]: the mind is his self; speech is his wife; <s>prāṇa</s> (breath) is his offspring; the eye is his human wealth — for one finds it with the eye; the ear is his divine [wealth] — for one hears it with the ear; the body itself is his ritual action — for one performs action with the body. This is the five-fold sacrifice; the sacrificial animal is five-fold; the person is five-fold; all this, whatever there is, is five-fold. One who knows this obtains all this. // BṛhUp 1.4.17 //

BrhUpBh_1,4.17 ātmaivedamagra āsīt /

te ete eṣaṇe sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇe kāmaḥ, yena prayukto 'vidvānavaśa eva kośakāravadātmānaṃ veṣṭayati - karmamārga evātmānaṃ praṇidadhadbahirmukhībhūto na svaṃ lokaṃ pratijānāti /

kathaṃ punaretāvattvamavadhāryate kāmānām? anantatvāt /

so 'bibhedavidyayā, tataḥ kāmaprayukta ekākyaramamāṇo 'styupaghātāya striyamaicchat, tāṃ samabhavat tataḥ sargo 'yamāsīditi hyuktam /

yathā jāyādīnāṃ kuṭumbapatirātmeva tadanukāritvāñjāyādi catuṣṭyasya;evamihāpi mana ātmā parikalpate kṛtsnatāyai /

vāgiti śabdaścodanādilakṣaṇaḥ, manasā śrotradvāreṇa gṛhyate 'vadhāryate prasṛjyate ca, iti manaso jāyeva vāk /
tābhyāṃ ca vāṅmanasābhyāṃ jāyāpatisthānīyābhyāṃ prasūyate prāṇaḥ karmārtham, iti prāṇaḥ prajeva /
tatra prāṇaceṣṭādilakṣaṇaṃ karma cakṣurmānuṣaṃ vittam /
tad dvividhaṃ vittaṃ mānuṣamitaracca;ato viśinaṣṭītaravittanivṛttyartha mānuṣamiti /
gavādi hi manuṣyasambandhi vittaṃ cakṣurgrāhyaṃ karmasādhanam;tasmāttatsthānīyam, tena sambandhāccakṣurgrāhyaṃ vittam;cakṣuṣā hi yasmāttanmānuṣaṃ vittaṃ vindate gavādyupalabhata ityarthaḥ /
kiṃ punaritaradvittam? śrotraṃ daivaṃ devaviṣayatvādvijñānasya /
vijñānaṃ daivaṃ vittam;tadiha śrotrameva sampattiviṣayam /
