kathaṃ karmahetutvam? ātmanā hi śarīreṇa yataḥ karma karoti /
tasyākṛtsnatvābhimānina evaṃ kṛtsnatā sampannā - yathā bāhyā jāyādilakṣaṇā evam /
tasmātsa eṣa pāṅktaḥ pañcabhirnirvṛttaḥ pāṅkto yajño darśanamātranirvṛtto 'karmiṇo 'pi /
kathaṃ punarasya pañcatvasampattimātreṇa yajñatvam? ucyate - yasmādbāhyo 'pi yajñaḥ paśupuruṣasādhyaḥ, sa ca paśuḥ puruṣaśca pāṅkta eva yathoktamanaādipañcatvayogāt /
children.translated_text: But how does mere attainment of five-fold-ness make it a sacrifice? It is said: because even the external sacrifice is accomplished through the animal and the person (<s>puruṣa</s>); and both the animal and the person are indeed five-fold, as stated, through the five-fold composition of mind and the rest.

children.text: tadāha - pāṅktaḥ paśugarvādiḥ, pāṅktaḥ puruṣaḥ paśutve 'pyadhikṛtatvenāsya viśeṣaḥ puruṣasyeti pṛthakpuruṣagrahaṇam /
children.translated_text: Therefore [the text] says: the animal — cattle and the like — is five-fold. The person too is five-fold. The person is mentioned separately from the animal because, though [he shares] the state of being an animal, he is distinguished by being the one entitled [to perform the sacrifice].

children.text: kiṃ bahunā? pāṅktamidaṃ sarvaṃ karmasādhanaṃ phalaṃ ca, yadidaṃ kiñca yatkiñcididaṃ sarvam /
children.translated_text: In short: all this — both the instrument of action and the fruit — whatever there is, all this is five-fold.

children.text: evaṃ pāṅktaṃ yajñamātmānaṃ yaḥ sampādayat sa tadidaṃ sarvaṃ jagadātmatvenāpnoti ya evaṃ veda //17//
children.translated_text: One who thus accomplishes the five-fold sacrifice as the self — he attains all this world as his own self. One who knows this. // 17 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.4.17: 'The self alone was this in the beginning.' The self — the natural, ignorant one characterized by the aggregate of body and organs, the one in the <s>varṇa</s> [system] — in the beginning, before marriage, is called 'the self.' Therefore, the desired things — wife and the rest, differentiated from the self — did not exist [for him]; he alone was one — possessed of ignorance, the seed of desire for wife and the rest, was alone. Being imbued with the natural <s>avidyā</s> tendency (<s>vāsanā</s>) characterized by the superimposition on his own self of the nature of agent, instruments, action, and fruit — he desired. How? 'May I have a wife who would be the basis for my entitlement to ritual action; without her, I would indeed be unentitled to ritual action. Therefore, for the sake of attaining entitlement to action, may there be a wife. And then may I procreate — may I myself be born in the form of progeny. And then may I have wealth — of the form of cattle and the like, as instruments of ritual action. Then may I perform action — the means of attaining worldly prosperity and the supreme good — by which, having become free from debt to the gods and the rest, I may attain their worlds; and also desire-prompted [actions] which are the means of attaining sons, wealth, heaven, and the like.' 'This much indeed is desire' — this much is the extent of the object [of desire] — this is the meaning. For this much alone is the desirable object — namely, wife, son, wealth, and action as the means; and the three worlds — the human world, the ancestral world, and the divine world — as the fruits. The desire for the means is [implicit in] the desire for the worlds. Therefore, the desire for the worlds is essentially one single desire. That single desire, being dependent on means, becomes twofold. Hence [the text] will determine: 'These are indeed both desires' (BṛUp 3.5.1). Since all undertaking is for the sake of fruit, the desire for the worlds is already implied [in what has been stated]. 'This much' — this much alone is desire — this is determined. When food has been mentioned, satisfaction need not be separately stated, since food is for that purpose. These two desires — characterized by the end and the means — constitute <s>kāma</s>, impelled by which, the ignorant one, helplessly, like a silkworm, envelops himself — placing himself on the path of action alone, becoming outward-turned, he does not recognize his own world. And thus in the <s>Taittirīyaka</s>: 'Like one stupefied by fire, with smoke around him, he does not recognize his own world.' How then is this extent of desire determined, since desires are infinite? Anticipating this objection, [the text] gives the reason: because even if not wishing, even without desiring, one cannot obtain, cannot acquire, anything more than this extent characterized by fruit and means. For in the world, neither anything seen nor unseen is obtainable beyond fruit and means. For desire has as its object what can be obtained, and since that does not exist beyond this [extent], it is proper to say 'this much indeed is desire.' What is stated is this: the twofold desire — characterized by end and means, whether pertaining to the seen or the unseen — which constitutes the sphere of entitlement of the ignorant person, is <s>kāma</s>; from this, the knower must rise above. Because thus the ignorant self, as <s>kāma</s>, desired formerly, and so too in even earlier [cycles] — this is the established order of the world, and this was <s>Prajāpati</s>'s creation. He was afraid due to <s>avidyā</s>; then, impelled by desire, being alone and finding no delight, for the sake of removing [his] distress he desired a woman, and united with her — from that, this creation came about — for thus it has been stated. Therefore, in that creation, even now, in the present time too, one who is alone, before the rite of marriage, desires: 'May I have a wife; then may I procreate; then may I have wealth; then may I perform action' — this statement has been explained. He, thus desiring and obtaining wife and the rest — as long as he does not obtain each and every one of these described things — wife and the rest — he considers himself incomplete, unfulfilled. Through the process of elimination, when he obtains all of them, then there is his completeness. But when he is unable to bring about [external] completeness, then, for the purpose of accomplishing his completeness, [the text] says: his completeness is as follows — this is how it comes about. The aggregate of body and organs is divided [as follows]: therein, the mind — since everything else, the aggregate of body and organs, is known through mind, it follows [from mind] — therefore, because of its preeminence, the mind is the self itself. Just as the head of a household is the very self of wife and the other four members, because they follow him — so here too, the mind is figuratively treated as the self for the sake of completeness. Similarly, speech is his wife, because of the commonality of following the mind. The word 'speech' denotes the injunctive statements and such — [speech] is grasped, determined, and produced by the mind through the medium of the ear — thus speech is like the wife of the mind. And from those two — speech and mind, who are like wife and husband — <s>prāṇa</s> is produced for the purpose of action — thus <s>prāṇa</s> is like offspring. There, wealth — characterized by action involving the activity of <s>prāṇa</s> and the like — is the eye, which is human wealth. That wealth is of two kinds: human and the other [divine]. Therefore, to distinguish it and exclude the other wealth, [the text] says 'human.' For cattle and such — wealth connected with humans — is graspable by the eye and serves as an instrument of action; therefore it is analogous [to the eye], and because of its connection [with it], the eye is [treated as] wealth graspable by the eye. Because one finds — one perceives — that human wealth, namely cattle and the like, with the eye — this is the meaning. But what is the other wealth? The ear is the divine [wealth], since knowledge pertains to the divine realm. Knowledge is the divine wealth; here, the ear alone is its symbolic equivalent. Why? Because one hears — because one hears that divine wealth, that knowledge, with the ear. Therefore, the ear is that [divine wealth]. And what action [is performed] by these — self, wife, and the rest up to wealth? This is stated: the self itself — the word 'self' here denotes the body. But how is the body analogous to action? Because it is the cause of action. How is it the cause of action? Because one performs action with the body — with the body. For this one who considers himself incomplete, completeness is thus accomplished — just as [with] the external wife and the rest, so [with] these internal equivalents. Therefore, he is five-fold. That sacrifice composed of five [parts] is five-fold. The sacrificial animal too is five-fold.

children.text: iti prathamādhyāye caturthaṃ sṛṣṭyādisarvātmatābrāhmaṇam //4//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth [section] in the first chapter — the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> on creation and the self of all. // 4 //

yatsaptānnāni medhayā /
avidyā prastutā, tatrāvidvānanyāṃ devatāmupāste'anyo 'sāvanyo 'hamasmi'iti /
sa varṇāśramābhimānaḥ karmakartavyatayā niyato juhotyādikarmabhiḥ kāmaprayukto devādīnāmupakurvansarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ loka ityuktam /
yathā ca svakarmabhirekaikena sarvairbhūtairasau loko bhojyatvena sṛṣṭaḥ, evamasāvapi juhotyādipāṅktakarmabhiḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni sarvaṃ ca jagadātmabhojyatvenāsṛjat /
evamekaikaḥ svakarmavidyānurūpyeṇa sarvasya jagato bhoktā bhojyaṃ ca, sarvasya sarvaḥ kartā kāryaṃ cetyarthaḥ /
etadeva ca vidyāprakaraṇe madhuvidyāyāṃ vakṣyāmaḥ -'sarvaṃ sarvasya kāryaṃ madhu'ityātmaikatvavijñānārtham /
yadasau juhotītyādinā pāṅktena kāmyena karmaṇā ātmabhojyatvena jagadasṛjata vijñānena ca, tajjagatsarvaṃ saptadhā pravibhajyamānaṃ kāryakāraṇatvena saptānnānyucyante, bhojyatvāt;tenāsau pitā teṣāmannānām /
eteṣāmannānāṃ saviniyogānāṃ sūtrabhūtāḥ saṅkṣepataḥ prakāśakatvādime mantrāḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary on BṛUp 1.5.1:] 'The seven foods produced by wisdom' — <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) has been introduced [as the topic]. There, the ignorant one worships another deity [thinking] 'he is one and I am another.' He, identified with <s>varṇa</s> and <s>āśrama</s>, bound by the obligatoriness of action, impelled by desire, performing ritual acts such as offering oblations, serving the gods and others — is called the world of all beings. And just as this world was created by each individual being through their own actions as something to be enjoyed — so too this person, through the five-fold ritual actions of offering oblations and the like, created all beings and the entire world as objects of his own enjoyment. Thus, each individual, in accordance with their own actions and knowledge, is both the enjoyer and the enjoyed of the entire world, and the agent and the effect of all — this is the meaning. And this very [topic] will be stated in the section on knowledge, in the <s>Madhu Vidyā</s>: 'Everything is the <s>madhu</s> (honey, i.e. the effect) of everything' — for the purpose of [establishing] the knowledge of the oneness of the self. When that [being], through the five-fold desire-prompted actions beginning with offering oblations, created the world as the object of his own enjoyment, and [created it] through knowledge — that entire world, when analyzed as seven-fold, in terms of cause and effect, is called the seven foods, because it is the object of enjoyment. Of these, he is the father, the progenitor. These <s>mantras</s> serve as <s>sūtras</s> (threads, i.e. summarizing statements) for these foods together with their application, being concise illuminators.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.1
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.1]

children.text:
yat saptānnāni medhayā tapasājanayat pitā |
ekam asya sādhāraṇaṃ dve devān abhājayat |
trīṇy ātmane 'kuruta paśubhya ekaṃ prāyacchat |
tasmin sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ yacca prāṇiti yacca na |
kasmāt tāni na kṣīyante adyamānāni sarvadā |
yo vai tām akṣitiṃ veda so 'nnam atti pratīkena |
sa devān apigacchati sa ūṛjam upajīvati |
iti ślokāḥ || BrhUp_1,5.1 ||
children.translated_text: The seven foods which the father produced by wisdom and austerity — one of them is common [to all]; two he assigned to the gods; three he made for himself; one he gave to the animals. In that [food] is established everything — whatever breathes and whatever does not. Why then do they not diminish, though they are always being eaten? One who knows this imperishability — he eats food with his face [turned toward the gods]; he goes to the gods; he lives on vigor. Thus the verses. // BṛhUp 1.5.1 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.1 yatsaptānnāni, yad ajanayaditi kriyāviśeṣaṇam;medhayā prajñayā vijñānena tapasā ca karmaṇā;jñānakarmaṇī eva hi medhātapaḥ śabdavācye, tayoḥ prakṛtatvāt;netare medhātapasī, aprakaraṇāt;pāṅktaṃ hi karma jāyādisādhanam; 'ya evaṃ veda'iti cānantarameva jñānaṃ prakṛtam;tasmānna prasiddhayormedhātapasorāśaṅkā kāryā;ato yāni saptānnāni jñānakarmabhyāṃ janitavānpitā tāni prakāśayiṣyāma iti vākyaśeṣaḥ //1//
children.translated_text: [Commentary on BṛUp 1.5.1:] 'The seven foods which' — '<s>yat</s>' in '<s>yat ajanayaditi</s>' is an adverbial qualifier of the verb. 'By <s>medhā</s>' (wisdom) means by <s>prajñā</s>, by <s>vijñāna</s> (knowledge); 'and by <s>tapas</s>' means by <s>karma</s> (action). For knowledge and action alone are denoted by the words '<s>medhā</s>' and '<s>tapas</s>,' since both are the topic [here]. Not the commonly known [meanings of] '<s>medhā</s>' (intelligence) and '<s>tapas</s>' (austerity), since they are not the topic [under discussion]. For the five-fold action — having wife and the rest as its means — is [the topic]; and 'he who knows thus' — immediately after that, knowledge is the topic. Therefore, there should be no apprehension [that the well-known meanings of] '<s>medhā</s>' and '<s>tapas</s>' [are intended]. Hence, the seven foods which the father produced through knowledge and action — these we shall elucidate — this is the remainder of the sentence. // 1 //

children.text: tatra mantrāṇāmarthastirohitatvāttprāyeṇa durvijñeyo bhavatīti tadarthavyākhyānāya brāhmaṇaṃ pravartate -
children.translated_text: Now, since the meaning of the <s>mantras</s> (Vedic verses) is generally hidden and difficult to understand, the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> (prose explanatory text) is introduced for the purpose of explaining their meaning:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.2
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,5.2

children.text:
yat saptānnāni medhayā tapasājanayat piteti |
medhayā hi tapasājanayat pitaikam asya sādhāraṇam iti |
idam evāsya tat sādhāraṇam annaṃ yad idam adyate |
sa ya etad upāste na sa pāpmano vyāvartate |
miśraṃ hy etat |
dve devān abhājayad iti |
hutaṃ ca prahutaṃ ca |
tasmād devebhyo juhvati ca pra ca juhvati |
atho āhur darśapūrṇamāsāv iti |
tasmān neṣṭiyājukaḥ syāt |
paśubhya ekaṃ prāyacchad iti |
tat payaḥ |
payo hy evāgre manuṣyāś ca paśavaś copajīvanti |
tasmāt kumāraṃ jātaṃ ghṛtaṃ vaivāgre pratilehayanti stanaṃ vānudhāpayanti |
atha vatsaṃ jātam āhus tṛṇād iti |
tasmin sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ yacca prāṇiti yacca neti |
payasi hīdaṃ sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ yacca prāṇiti yacca na |
tad yad idam āhuḥ saṃvatsaraṃ payasā juhvad apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayatīti |
na tathā vidyāt |
yad ahar eva juhoti tad ahaḥ punarmṛtyum apajayaty evaṃ vidvān |
sarvaṃ hi devebhyo 'nnādyaṃ prayacchati |
kasmāt tāni na kṣīyante adyamānāni sarvadeti |
puruṣo vā akṣitiḥ |
sa hīdam annaṃ punaḥ punar janayate |
yo vaitām akṣitiṃ vedeti |
puruṣo vā akṣitiḥ |
sa hīdam annaṃ dhiyādhiyā janayate karmabhiḥ |
yad dhaitan na kuryāt kṣīyeta ha |
so 'nnam atti pratīkeneti |
mukhaṃ pratīkaṃ mukhenety etat |
sa devān apigacchati sa ūrjam upajīvatīti praśaṃsā || BrhUp_1,5.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'The seven foods which the father produced by wisdom and austerity' — 'by wisdom indeed and by austerity the father produced [them].' 'One of them is common' — this indeed is that common food of his — that which is eaten. He who meditates on this [food alone] does not turn away from sin, for it is mixed. 'He assigned two to the gods' — these are the <s>huta</s> (what is offered into fire) and the <s>prahuta</s> (what is offered by placement). Therefore, one offers to the gods both the <s>huta</s> and the <s>prahuta</s>. They also say these are the <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> (new-moon and full-moon sacrifices). Therefore one should not be one who performs <s>iṣṭi</s>-sacrifices for material gain. 'He gave one to the animals' — that is milk. For in the beginning, both humans and animals live on milk alone. Therefore, they make a newborn child first lick ghee, or they put it to the breast. And they call a newborn calf 'one [who lives] on grass.' In that [milk] everything is established — whatever breathes and whatever does not. For in milk indeed everything is established — whatever breathes and whatever does not. Now, regarding what they say: 'By offering with milk for a year, one conquers redeath' — one should not understand it thus. On the very day one offers, on that very day one who knows thus conquers redeath. For one offers all that is to be eaten to the gods. 'Why do they not diminish, though they are always being eaten?' — the person (<s>puruṣa</s>) indeed is the imperishable. For he produces this food again and again. 'One who knows this imperishability' — the person indeed is the imperishable. For he produces this food by thought after thought, through [ritual] actions. If he were not to do this, it would indeed be exhausted. 'He eats food with his face' (<s>pratīka</s>) — the face is the <s>pratīka</s>; [that is,] with the mouth — this is what it means. 'He goes to the gods; he lives on vigor' — this is praise. // BṛhUp 1.5.2 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.2 tatra'yatsaptānnāni medhayā tapasājanayatpitā'ityasya kor'tha ucyate? ithi hi śabdenaiva vyācaṣṭe prasiddhārthāvadyotakena /
prasiddho hyasya mantrasyārtha ityarthaḥ /
yadajanayaditi cānuvādasvarūpeṇa mantreṇa prasiddhārthataiva prakāśitā /
ato brāhmaṇamaviśaṅkyaivāha -'medhayā hi tapasājanayatpitā'iti? nanu kathaṃ prasiddhātāsyārthasya? ityucyate - jāyādikarmāntānāṃ lokaphalasādhanānāṃ pitṛtvaṃ tāvat pratyakṣameva, abhihitaṃ ca'jāyā me syāt'ityādinā /
tatra ca daivaṃ vittaṃ vidyā karma putraśca phalabhūtānāṃ lokānāṃ sādhanaṃ sraṣṭṛtvaṃ pratītyabhihitam, vakṣyamāṇaṃ ca prasiddhameva;tasmādyuktaṃ vaktuṃ medhayetyādi /
eṣaṇā hi phalaviṣayā prasiddhaiva ca loke /
eṣaṇā ca jāyādītyuktam'etāvānvai kāmaḥ'ityanena /
brahmavidyāviṣaye ca sarvaikatvātkāmānupapatteḥ /
etenāśāstrīyaprajñātapobhyāṃ svābhāvikābhyāṃ jagatsraṣṭṛtvamuktameva bhavati;sthāvarāntasya cāniṣṭaphalasya karmavijñānanimittatvāt /
vivakṣitastu śāstrīya eva sādhyasādhanabhāvo brahmavidyāvidhitsayā tadvairāgyasya vivakṣitatvāt /
sarvo hyaṃ vyaktāvyaktalakṣaṇaḥ saṃsāro 'suddho 'nityaḥ sādhyasādhanarūpo duḥkho 'vidyāviṣaya ityetasmādviraktasya brahmavidyā ārabdhavyeti /
tatrānnānāṃ vibhāgena viniyoga ucyate-'ekamasya sādhāraṇma'iti mantrapadam, tasya vyākhyānam'idamevāsya tasmādhāraṇamannam'ityuttkam /
asya bhottkṛsamudāyasya, kiṃ tat? yadidamadyate bhujyate sarvaiḥ prāṇibhirahanyahani, tasmādhāraṇaṃ sarvabhoktrarthamakalpayatpitā sṛṣṭvānnam /
sa ya etatsādhāraṇaṃ sarvaprāṇabhṛtsthitikaraṃ bhujyamānamannamupāste tatparo bhavatītyarthaḥ-- upāsanaṃ hi nāma tātparya dṛṣṭaṃ loke'gurumupāste' 'rājānamupāste'ityādau--tasmāccharīrasthityarthannopabhogapradhānonādṛṣṭārthakarmapradhāna ityarthaḥ;sa evaṃ bhūto na pāpmano 'dharmadvayāvartate--na vimucyata ityetat /
tathā ca mantravarṇaḥ---"moghamannaṃvindate"ityādiḥ /
smṛtirapi-"nātmārtha pācayedannam" "apradāyaibhyo yo bhūṅkte stena eva saḥ" "annāde bhrūṇahā mārṣṭi" ityādiḥ /
kasmātpunaḥ pāpmano na vyāvartate? miśraṃ hyetasmarseṣāṃ hi svaṃ tadapravibhaktaṃ yatprāṇibhirbhujyate /
sarvabhojyatpādeva yo mukhe prakṣipyamāṇo 'pi grāsaḥ parasya pīḍākaro dṛśyate,'mamedaṃ syāt'iti hi sarveṣāṃ tatrāśā prativadvā /
tasmānna paramapīḍaytvā grasitumapi śakyate /
"duṣkṛtaṃ hi manuṣyāṇām"ityādismaraṇācca /
gṛhiṇā vaiśvadevākhyamannaṃ yadahanyahani nirūpyata iti kecit, tatra, sarvabhottakṛsādhāraṇatvaṃ vaiśvadevākhyasyānnasya na sarvaprāṇabhṛdbhujyamānānnavatpratyakṣam, nāpi'yadidamadyate'iti tadviṣayaṃ vacanamanukūlam /
sarvaprāṇabhṛdbhapajyamānāṃnānnāntaḥpātitvācca vaiśvadevākhyasya yuttakaṃ śvacāṇḍālādyādhasyānnasya grahaṇam, vaiśvadevavyatirekeṇāpi śvacāṇḍālādyādhāśvadarśanāt, tatra yutkam,'yadidamadyate'iti vacanam /
yadi hi tanna gṛhyeta, sādhāraṇaśabdena pitrāsṛṣṭatvāviniyuttkatve tasya prasajyeyātām /
iṣyate hi tatsṛṣṭavaṃ tadviniyuttkatvaṃ ya sarvasyānnajātasya /
na ca vaiśvadevākhyaṃ śāstroktaṃ karma kurvataḥ pāpmano 'vinivṛttiryuktā, na ca tasya pratiṣedho 'sti, na ca matsyabandhanādikarmavatsvabhāvajugupsitametat, śiṣṭanirvartyatvāt, akaraṇe ca pratyavāyaśravaṇāt /
itaratra ca pratyavāyopapatteḥ"ahamannamannamadantamā3ṅmi"(tai.u.3 / 10 / 6) iti mantravarṇāt /
dve devānabhājayat iti mantrapadam, ye dve anne sṛṣṭvā devānabhājayat /
ke te dve? ityucyate - hutaṃ ca prahutaṃ ca /
hutamityagnau havanam, prahutaṃ hutvā baliharaṇam /
yasmād dve ete anne hutaprahute devānabhājayatpitā /
tasmādetarhyapi gṛhiṇaḥ kāle dvebhyo(? ) juhvati devebhya idamannamasmābhirdīyamānamiti manvānā juhvati, prajuhvati ca hutvā baliharaṇaṃ ca kurvata ityarthaḥ /
atho apyanya āhurdve anne pitrā devebhyaḥ pratte na hutaprahute, kiṃ tarhi? darśapūrṇamāsāviti /
dvitvaśravaṇāviśeṣādatyantaprasiddhatvācca hutaprahute iti prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ /
yadyapi dvitvaṃ hutaprahutayoḥ sambhavati, tathāpi śrautayoreva tu darśapūrṇamāsayordevānnatvaṃ prasiddhataram, mantra prakāśitatvāt /
guṇapradhānaprāptau ca pradhāne prathamatarā avagatiḥ, darśapūrṇamāsayośca prādhānyaṃ hutaprahutāpekṣayā /
tasmāttayoreva grahaṇaṃ yuktam'dve devānabhājayat'iti /
yasmāddevātamete pitrā prakḷpte darśapūrṇamāsākhye anne, tasmāttayordevārthatvāvighātāya neṣṭiyājuka iṣṭiyajanaśīlaḥ, iṣṭiśabdena kila kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ, śātapathīyaṃ prasiddhiḥ, tācchīlyapratyayaprayogātkāmyeṣṭiyajanapradhāne na syādityarthaḥ /
paśubhya ekaṃ prāyacchaditi - yatpaśubhya ekaṃ punastadannam? tatpayaḥ /
kathaṃ punaravagamyate paśavo 'syānnasya svāminaḥ? ityata āha - payo hyagre prathamaṃ yasmānmanuṣyāśca paśavaśca payaḥ evopajīvantīti /
ucitaṃ hi'tapo tadannam'anyathā kathaṃ tadevāgre niyamenopajīveyuḥ? kathamagre tadevopajīvanti? ityucyate - manuṣyāśca paśavaśca yasmāttenaivānnena vartante 'dyatve 'pi, yathā pitrā ādau viniyogaḥ kṛtastathā /
tasmātkumāraṃ bālaṃ jātaṃ ghṛtaṃ vā traivarṇikā jātakarmaṇi jātarūpasaṃyuktaṃ pratilehayanti paścāt pāyayanti /
yathāsambhavamanyeṣāṃ stanamevāgre dhāpayanti manuṣyebhyo 'nyeṣāṃ paśūnām /
atha vatsaṃ jātamāhuḥ'kiyatpramāṇo vatsaḥ'? ityevaṃ pṛṣṭā- santo 'tṛṇāda iti /
nādyāpi tṛṇamatti, atīva bālaḥ, payasaivādyāpi vartata ityarthaḥ /
yaccāgre jātakarmādau ghṛtamupajīvanti, yaccetare paya eva, tatsarvathāpi paya evopajīvanti;ghṛtasyāpi payovikāratvātpayastvameva kasmātpunaḥ saptamaṃ satpaśvannaṃ caturthatvena vyākhyāyate? karmasādhanatvāt /
karma hi payaḥsādhanāśrayaṃ agnihotrādi /
tacca karma sādhanaṃ vittasādhyaṃ vakṣyamāṇasyānnatrayasya sādhyasya, yathā darśapūrṇamāsau pūrvoktāvanne /
ataḥ karmapakṣatvāt karmaṇā saha piṇḍīkṛtyopadeśaḥ /
sādhanatvāviśeṣādarthasambandhādānantaryamakāraṇamiti cāvyākhyāne pratipattisaukaryācca /
sukhaṃ hi nairantaryeṇa vyākhyātu śakyante 'nnāni vyākhyātāni ca sukhaṃ pratīyante /
tasminsarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ yacca prāṇiti yacca netyasya kor'thaḥ? ityucyate - tasminpaśvanne payasi sarvamadhyātmādhibhūtādhidaivalakṣaṇaṃ kṛtsnaṃ jagatpratiṣṭhitaṃ yacca prāṇiti prāṇaveṣṭāvadyacca na sthānaraṃ śailādi /
tatra hi śabdenaiva prasiddhāvadyotakena vyākhyātam /
kāraṇatvāpapatteḥ /
kāraṇatvaṃ cāgnihotrādikarmasamavāyitvam /
agnihotrādyāhutivipariṇāmātmakaṃ ca jagatkṛtsnamiti śrutismṛtivādāḥ śataśo vyavasthitāḥ /
ato yuktameva hi śabdena vyākhyānam /
yattadbrāhmaṇāntareṣvidamāhuḥ - saṃvatsaraṃ payasā juhvadapa punarmṛtyuṃ jayatīti, saṃvatsareṇa kila trīṇi ṣaṣṭiśatānyāhutīnāṃ sapta ca śatāni viṃśatiśceti yājuṣmatīriṣṭakā abhisampadyamānāḥ saṃvatsarasya cāhorātrāṇi, saṃvatsaramagniṃ prajāpatimāpnuvanti;evaṃ kṛtvā saṃvatsaraṃ juhvadapajayati punaḥ mṛtyum, itaḥ pretya deveṣu sambhūtaḥ punarna mriyata ityarthaḥ /
ityevaṃ brāhmaṇavādā āhuḥ, na tathā vidyānna tathā draṣṭavyam;yadahareva juhoti tadahaḥ punarmṛtyumapajayati, na saṃvatsarābhyāsamapekṣate /
evaṃ vidvānsan, yaduktam - payasi hīdaṃ sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ paya āhutivipariṇāmātmakatvātsarvasyeti, tadekenaivāhvā jagadātmatvaṃ pratipadyate;taducyate - apajayati punarmṛtyuṃ punarmaraṇam, sakṛnmṛtvāviddhāñcharīreṇa viyujya sarvātmā bhavati na punarmaraṇāya paricchinnaṃ śarīraṃ gṛhṇātītyarthaḥ /
kaḥ punarhetuḥ sarvātmāptyā mṛtyumapajayati? ityucyate - sarvaṃ samastaṃ hi yasmāddevebhyaḥ sarvebhyo 'nnādyamannameva tadādyaṃ ca sāyaṃprātarāhutiprakṣepeṇa prayacchati /
tadyuktaṃ sarvamāhutimayamātmānaṃ kṛtvā sarvadevānnarūpeṇa sarvairdevairekātmabhāvaṃ gatvā sarvadevamayo bhūtvā punarna mriyata iti /
athaitadapyuktaṃ brāhmaṇena -"brahma vai svayambhū tapo 'tapyata tadaikṣata na vai tapasyānantyamasti, hantāhaṃ bhūteṣvātmānaṃ juhavāni bhūtāni cātmanīti, tatsarveṣu bhūteṣvātmānaṃ hutvā bhūtāni cātmani sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ śraiṣṭhyaṃ svārājyagādhipatyaṃ paryet"iti /
kasmāttāni na kṣīyante 'dyamānāni sarvadeti /
yadā pitrā annāni sṛṣṭvā sapta pṛthakpṛthagbhoktṛbhiradyagānāni - tannimittatvātteṣāṃ sthiteḥ - sarvadā nairantaryeṇa;kṛtakṣayopapatteśca yuktasteṣāṃ kṣayaḥ /
na ca tāni kṣīyamāṇāni, jagato 'vibhraṣṭarūpeṇaivāvasthānadarśanāt /
bhavitavyaṃ cākṣayakāraṇena;tasmātkasmātpunastāni na kṣīyanta iti praśnaḥ /
tasyedaṃ prativacanam -'puriṣo vā akṣitiḥ' /
yathāsau pūrvamannānāṃ sraṣṭāsītpitā medhayā jāyādisambandhena ca pāṅktakarmaṇā bhoktā ca, tathā yebhyo dattānyannāni te 'pi teṣāmannānāṃ bhoktāro 'pi santaḥ pitara eva, medhayā tapasā ca yato janayanti tānyannāni /
tadetadabhidhīyate puruṣo vai yo 'nnānāṃ bhoktā so 'kṣitirakṣayahetuḥ /
kathamasyākṣititvam? ityucyate - sa hi yasmādidaṃ bhujyamānaṃ saptavidhaṃ kāryakaraṇalakṣaṇaṃ kriyāphalātmakaṃ punaḥ punarbhūyo bhūyo janayata utpādayati dhiyā dhiyā tattatkālabhāvinyā tayā tayā prajñayā, karmabhiśca vāṅmanaḥkāyaveṣṭitaiḥ yadyadi ha yadyetatsaptavidhamannamuktaṃ kṣaṇamātramapi na kuryātprajñayā karmabhiśca, tato vicchidyeta bhujyamānatvātsātatyena kṣīyeta ha /
tasmādyathaivāyaṃ puruṣo bhoktā annānāṃ nairantaryeṇa, yathāprajñe yathākarma ca karotyapi /
tasmātpuruṣo 'kṣitiḥ sātatyena kartṛtvāt /
tasmād bhujyamānānyapyannāni na kṣīyanta ityarthaḥ /
ataḥ prajñākriyālakṣaṇaprabandhārūḍhaḥ sarvo lokaḥ sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇaḥ kriyāphalātmakaḥ saṃhatānekaprāṇikarmavāsanāsantānāvaṣṭabdhatvātkṣaṇiko 'śuddho 'sāro nadīsrotaḥ pradīpasantānakalpaḥ kadalīstambhavadasāraḥ phenamāyāmarīcyambhaḥsvapnādisamastadātmagatadṛṣṭīnāmavikīryamāṇo nityaḥ sāravāniva lakṣyate /
tadetadvairāgyārthamucyate - dhiyā dhiyā janayate karmabhiryaddhaitanna kuryātkṣīyeta heti - viraktānāṃ hyasmādbrahmavidyā ārabdhavyā caturthapramukheṇeti /
yo vaitāmakṣitiṃ vedeti;vakṣyamāṇānyapi trīṇyannānyasminnavasare vyakhyātānyeveti kṛtvā teṣāṃ yāthātmyavijñānaphalamupasaṃhriyate - yo vā etām akṣitim akṣayahetuṃ yathoktaṃ veda, puruṣo vā akṣitiḥ sa hīdamannaṃ dhiyā dhiyā janayate karmabhiryaddhaitanna kuryātkṣīyate heti /
so 'nnamatti pratīkenetyasyārtha ucyate - mukhaṃ mukhyatvaṃ prādhānyamityetat /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'He eats food with his face' — the meaning of this is stated: 'face' means preeminence, primacy — this is the sense.

children.text: prādhānyevānnānāṃ pituḥ puruṣasyākṣititvaṃ yo veda so 'nnamatti nānnaṃ prati guṇabhūtaḥ san /
children.translated_text: One who knows the imperishability of the foods — being their preeminent master, the <s>puruṣa</s> — he eats food, not being subsidiary to the food.

children.text: yathājño na tathā vidvānannānāyātmabhūtaḥ, bhoktaiva bhavati, na bhojyatāmāpādyate /
children.translated_text: Unlike the ignorant, the knower does not become subsidiary to food — he is the enjoyer alone, he is not reduced to being the enjoyed.

children.text: sa devānapi gacchati sa ūrjamupajīvati, devānapi gacchati devātmabhāvaṃ pratipadyate, ūrjamamṛtaṃ copajīvatīti yaduktaṃ sā praśaṃsā, nāpūrvārtho 'nyo 'sti //2//
children.translated_text: 'He goes to the gods and lives on vigor' — he goes to the gods, attains the state of being the self of the gods; and lives on vigor, on the immortal — what was stated [above] is praise, not [conveying] any other unprecedented meaning. // 2 //

[Commentary on BṛhUp 1.5.2:] In regard to the [mantra-verse] 'The seven foods which the father produced by wisdom and austerity' — what is its meaning said to be? The word '<s>iti</s>' here itself explains, being an illuminator of the well-known meaning. For the meaning of this mantra is well-known — this is the intent. And the mantra, being in the form of a restatement ('he produced'), itself reveals its established meaning. Therefore, the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> (explanatory prose) says without hesitation: 'by wisdom and austerity the father produced.' But how is the meaning of this well-known? It is said: the fatherhood of [<s>Prajāpati</s>], who, through activities beginning with [desiring] a wife and ending with action, [creates] the means for attaining the worlds as fruit — is directly perceptible; and it has been stated [in the text] 'may I have a wife' and so forth. And therein, the creatorship [of <s>Prajāpati</s>] as the means for the worlds that are the fruit — through divine [wealth], material wealth, knowledge, action, and sons — has been stated as inferred, and what is about to be stated is already well-known. Therefore, it is proper to say 'by wisdom' and so on. For desire has the fruit as its object and is well-known in the world. And desire pertains to wife and the rest — this was stated by 'this much indeed is desire.' And in the domain of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, since all is one, desire is impossible. By this, it is established that creatorship of the world is through natural [i.e., non-scriptural] intelligence and austerity; and because the undesirable fruit down to immovable beings is caused by [prior] action and knowledge. But what is intended [here] is the scriptural relationship of end and means alone, because the desire is to teach the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> [and for that] the teaching of dispassion toward that [world] is intended. For all this <s>saṃsāra</s>, characterized by the manifest and unmanifest, impure, impermanent, of the nature of what is to be accomplished and its means, suffering, the domain of <s>avidyā</s> — the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is to be undertaken by one who has become dispassionate toward this. There, the application of the foods by division is stated: 'one of them is common' — this is the mantra-text; its explanation is 'this indeed is the common food for him,' as has been stated. For this entire aggregate of enjoyers — what is that? Whatever is eaten, consumed by all living beings day after day — the father, having created that common food intended for all enjoyers, assigned it. He who devotes himself to, who makes the primary focus, this common food that sustains all living beings — 'devotion' (<s>upāsana</s>) means 'primary commitment,' as seen in worldly usage: 'he is devoted to the teacher,' 'he is devoted to the king' — therefore, [such a person's commitment is] merely for the sake of bodily sustenance, not primarily for enjoyment or primarily for unseen religious merit — this is the meaning. Such a person does not turn away from, is not released from, evil, i.e., the twofold <s>adharma</s>. And thus the mantra-text: 'He obtains food in vain' and so forth. And <s>smṛti</s> also: 'One should not cook food for oneself alone'; 'He who eats without giving to these [beings] is a thief indeed'; 'One who eats food [from another] wipes away the [sin of] embryo-killing' and so forth. Why does he not turn away from evil? Because it is mixed — for this is their common [property], undivided, which is consumed by living beings. The very morsel that, though being placed in one's mouth, is seen to cause pain to another due to its being consumable by all — for everyone's hope is directed toward it, [thinking] 'may this be mine.' Therefore, without harming another, one cannot even take a morsel. And from <s>smṛti</s>: 'Evil indeed for humans' and so forth. Some say that the food called <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> (the offering to all gods) is what is daily dedicated by the householder. But there, the commonality of the food called <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> with all enjoyers is not directly perceived like the food eaten by all living beings, nor is the statement 'whatever is eaten here' favorable to that [interpretation]. And because the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> food falls within [the category of] food eaten by all living beings, the [alternative] interpretation that it refers to the food given to dogs, outcasts, and such is appropriate — since the giving of food to dogs, outcasts, and such is observed even apart from the <s>Vaiśvadeva</s> [ritual], the statement 'whatever is eaten here' is fitting for that. For if that [interpretation] were not accepted, then because of the word 'common' and [the idea that it was] created by the father, [the faults of] non-application would arise regarding that. For the creatorship and application of all classes of food by [the father] is indeed intended. And it is not appropriate that there be no turning away from evil for one performing the scriptural rite called <s>Vaiśvadeva</s>; nor is there any prohibition of it; nor is it inherently repugnant like the action of catching fish and the like, because it is performed by the virtuous; and because the omission [of it] is heard to result in sin. And because sin is entailed in the opposite case [of not giving], from the mantra-text: 'I am food, I eat the eater of food' (<s>Taittirīyopaniṣad</s> 3.10.6). 'Two he assigned to the gods' — this is the mantra-text: having created these two foods, he assigned them to the gods. Which two are they? It is said: the <s>huta</s> (oblation into fire) and the <s>prahuta</s> (offering after the oblation). '<s>Huta</s>' means the offering into fire; '<s>prahuta</s>' means the offering of <s>bali</s> (food-offering) after the fire-oblation. Since the father assigned these two foods, the <s>huta</s> and <s>prahuta</s>, to the gods — therefore, even now, householders at the proper time offer oblations to the two [classes of] gods, thinking 'this food is being given by us,' and also make <s>bali</s>-offerings after the fire-oblation — this is the meaning. But others say the two foods assigned by the father to the gods are not the <s>huta</s> and <s>prahuta</s> but the <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> [new-moon and full-moon sacrifices]. Since there is no distinction in the mention of 'two' and because both [interpretations] are extremely well-known — the first view [holds for] the <s>huta</s> and <s>prahuta</s>. Although 'two-ness' applies to <s>huta</s> and <s>prahuta</s> as well, nevertheless the status of food for the gods is more well-known for the <s>Śrauta</s> [Vedic] <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> sacrifices, because it is illuminated by the mantra. And when there is a choice between the secondary and the primary, the primary is understood first; and the <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> are primary in comparison with the <s>huta</s> and <s>prahuta</s>. Therefore, the interpretation in terms of those two alone is appropriate for 'two he assigned to the gods.' Since these two foods called <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> were assigned for the gods by the father — therefore, so that their purpose for the gods may not be obstructed, the <s>iṣṭiyājuka</s> (one habitually performing <s>iṣṭi</s> sacrifices) — the word '<s>iṣṭi</s>' refers specifically to the optional (<s>kāmya</s>) <s>iṣṭi</s> sacrifices, as is the well-known usage in the <s>Śatapatha</s> — should not primarily be one who performs optional sacrifices, since the suffix indicating habitual disposition is used — this is the meaning. 'One he gave to the animals' — the one [food] he gave to the animals, what is that food? It is milk. But how is it known that the animals are the owners of this food? Hence [the text] says: because milk is the first thing — in the beginning — by which both humans and animals subsist. For it is fitting — 'austerity is its food' — otherwise, how would they inevitably subsist on that very [milk] at first? How do they subsist on it at first? It is said: humans and animals, because they subsist even now on that very food as [they did when] created by the father. Therefore, when a child is born, members of the three upper classes, at the <s>jātakarma</s> (birth-ceremony), make [the infant] lick ghee mixed with gold; afterwards they give [the infant] milk. For other [beings], as applicable, they first give the breast to suckle — for animals other than humans. And when a calf is born, they say: 'How big is the calf?' — when asked thus, [they reply]: '[It is still] not grass-eating' — meaning it does not yet eat grass, it is very young, it still subsists on milk alone. And the ghee on which [humans] subsist at first during the birth-ceremony and so forth, and the milk on which the others [subsist] — in every case it is milk alone that they subsist on, because ghee too is a transformation of milk, hence it is [essentially] milk. But why is milk, being the seventh [food], explained as the fourth? Because it is the means of [ritual] action. For ritual action such as the <s>Agnihotra</s> depends on milk as its [material] basis. And that action is the means — dependent on wealth — of the three foods about to be described, which are to be accomplished, just as the <s>Darśa</s> and <s>Pūrṇamāsa</s> mentioned earlier are foods [for the gods]. Therefore, because of being on the side of action, it is taught together with action as a group. And because there is no distinction in being a means, the proximity of connection does not constitute a [separate] reason — and for the ease of understanding if not explained [in this order]. For when explained continuously, the foods are easily explained and easily understood. 'In that is everything established, whatever breathes and whatever does not' — what is the meaning of this? It is said: in that food of the animals, milk, everything is established — the entire universe characterized as <s>ādhyātma</s> (pertaining to the individual self), <s>adhibhūta</s> (pertaining to beings), and <s>adhidaiva</s> (pertaining to deities) — whatever breathes, that which possesses <s>prāṇa</s> (life-breath), and whatever does not — what is stationary, such as mountains and the like. For the word '<s>hi</s>' indeed explains, being an illuminator of the well-known [meaning]. Because of the applicability of causality. And causality means being concomitant with [ritual] action such as the <s>Agnihotra</s>. And [the doctrine] that the entire universe is a transformation of the oblations of the <s>Agnihotra</s> and such — <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> statements to this effect are established in hundreds. Therefore, the explanation by the word '<s>hi</s>' is indeed fitting. As is said in other <s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts: 'One who offers oblations with milk for a year conquers recurring death.' In a year, the number of oblations amounts to three hundred and sixty and seven hundred and twenty — these correspond to the <s>yājuṣmatī</s> bricks, and the days and nights of the year — [thus] one attains the fire that is the year, that is <s>Prajāpati</s>. Having done this, one who offers for a year conquers recurring death — meaning that, having departed from here, having been born among the gods, one does not die again. Thus the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-statements say. [But] one should not understand it that way, one should not view it that way. On the very day that one offers the oblation, on that very day one conquers recurring death — it does not require the practice [sustained] over a year. Being such a knower, [the meaning of] what was stated — 'in milk everything is established, because the entire [universe] is a transformation of the oblations' — by a single oblation alone one attains identity with the universe. This is what is said: one conquers recurring death, i.e., dying again. Having died once, having separated from the body with which one identified, one becomes the self of all — one does not again take up a limited body for the purpose of dying again — this is the meaning. What then is the reason that through becoming the self of all one conquers death? It is said: because all the food for all the gods — i.e., what is to be eaten — he gives that very [food] by the casting of the morning and evening oblations. Thus it is fitting: having made his entire self consisting of oblations, having attained identity with all the gods in the form of food, having become constituted of all the gods — he does not die again. And this too is stated by the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>: '<s>Brahman</s>, the self-existent, performed austerity. It reflected: "There is no infinity in austerity. Come, let me offer myself in beings and beings in myself." Having offered itself in all beings and all beings in itself, it attained the sovereignty, self-rule, and overlordship of all beings.' Why then do those [foods] not diminish, though they are always being eaten? Since the father, having created the seven foods, assigned them separately to separate enjoyers — because [the foods'] continued existence is dependent on those [enjoyers] — continuously, without interruption — and since what is produced is subject to exhaustion, the exhaustion of those [foods] is expected. Yet they do not diminish — because the world is observed to remain in an unchanged form. There must be some cause of imperishability; therefore, 'why do they not diminish?' is the question. The answer to this is: 'The person (<s>puruṣa</s>) indeed is the imperishability.' Just as that father was formerly the creator of the foods, by wisdom and by the connection with wife and the rest, performing the five-fold action, and was also the enjoyer — so too those to whom the foods were given, though being enjoyers of those foods, are themselves also fathers, since by wisdom and austerity they produce those very foods. This is what is stated: the person (<s>puruṣa</s>), whoever is the enjoyer of the foods — he is the imperishability, the cause of non-exhaustion. How is he the cause of imperishability? It is said: because he, since he produces this sevenfold [food] — characterized as body-and-organs, of the nature of action and fruit — again and again, more and more, by each successive cognition, by each successive intelligence arising at each successive moment, and by actions performed through speech, mind, and body. If this sevenfold food as described were not produced even for a moment by intelligence and actions, then it would be cut off, would be continuously exhausted due to being always consumed. Therefore, just as this person is a continuous enjoyer of the foods, so also, according to his knowledge and according to his action, he produces [them]. Therefore the person is the imperishability, because of being a continuous creator. Therefore, even though the foods are being consumed, they are not exhausted — this is the meaning. Hence, this entire world, characterized as what is to be accomplished and its means, of the nature of action and fruit — being mounted upon the continuous flow characterized by cognition and action, held together by the aggregate stream of <s>karma</s>-impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) of many living beings — is momentary, impure, insubstantial, like the current of a river, like the continuity of a lamp-flame, like the trunk of a plantain tree that is without pith, like foam, illusion, mirages, water, dreams, and the like — yet to those whose vision remains within it, it appears as if eternal and substantial, without being dissipated. This is said for the purpose of dispassion: 'by each successive cognition he produces, by actions; if he did not produce this, it would be exhausted' — for those who have become dispassionate toward this [world], the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is to be undertaken, beginning with the fourth [<s>āśrama</s>, i.e., renunciation]. 'One who knows this imperishability' — the three foods yet to be described are also explained in this context; therefore, the fruit of the knowledge of the true nature of all [seven foods] is summarized: one who indeed knows this imperishability as described — 'the person is the imperishability; he produces this food by each successive cognition, by actions; if he did not produce this, it would be exhausted.'

children.text: pāṅktasya karmaṇaḥ phalabhūtāni yāni trīṇyannāpyupakṣiptāni tāni kāryatvādvistīrṇaviṣayatvācca pūrvabhyo 'nnebhyaḥ pṛthagutkṛṣṭāni, teṣāṃ vyākhyānārtha uttaro grantha ā brāhmaṇaparisamāpteḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The three foods that are the fruits of five-fold action, which were briefly alluded to — being effects and having an extensive scope — are distinguished separately from the previous foods. The subsequent text, up to the end of the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, is for the purpose of explaining those.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.3
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.3]

children.text:
trīṇy ātmane 'kuruteti:
mano vācaṃ prāṇaṃ tāny ātmane 'kuruta |
anyatramanā abhūvaṃ nādarśam anyatramanā abhūvaṃ nāśrauṣam iti manasā hy eva paśyati manasā śṛṇoti |
kāmaḥ saṃkalpo vicikitsā śraddhāśraddhā dhṛtir adhṛtir hrīr dhīr bhīr ity etat sarvaṃ mana eva |
tasmād api pṛṣṭhata upaspṛṣṭo manasā vijānāti |
yaḥ kaśca śabdo vāg eva sā |
eṣā hy antaṃ āyattaiṣā hi na |
prāṇo 'pāno vyāna udānaḥ samāno 'na ity etat sarvaṃ prāṇa eva |
etanmayo vā ayam ātmā |
vāṅmayo manomayaḥ prāṇamayaḥ || BrhUp_1,5.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'He made three for himself' — mind, speech, and <s>prāṇa</s> — these he made for himself. 'My mind was elsewhere; I did not see. My mind was elsewhere; I did not hear' — for one sees indeed with the mind, one hears with the mind. Desire, intention, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, fear — all this is indeed the mind. Therefore, even when touched from behind, one cognizes with the mind. Whatever sound there is — that is speech alone. For this [speech] comes to a terminus; and this does not [i.e., speech itself is not an object of another speech]. <s>Prāṇa</s> (in-breath), <s>apāna</s> (out-breath), <s>vyāna</s> (diffused breath), <s>udāna</s> (upward breath), <s>samāna</s> (equalizing breath), <s>ana</s> (general breath) — all this is indeed <s>prāṇa</s>. This self is indeed made of these. It is made of speech, made of mind, made of <s>prāṇa</s>. // BṛhUp 1.5.3 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.3 trīṇyātmane 'kuruteti ko 'syārtha ityucyate - manovākprāṇā etāni trīṇyannāni, tāni mano vācaṃ prāṇaṃ cātmane ātmārthamakuruta - kṛtavān sṛṣṭvā ādau pitā /
teṣāṃ saṃśaya ityata āha - asti tāvanmanaḥ śrotrādibāhyakaraṇavyatiriktam, yata evaṃ prasiddham - bāhyakaraṇaviṣayātmasambandhe satyapyabhimukhībhūtaṃ viṣayaṃ na gṛhṇāti,'kiṃ dṛṣṭavānasīdaṃ rūpam'? ityukto vadati -'anyatra me gataṃ mana āsītso 'hamanyatramanā āsaṃ nādarśam' /
tathā'idaṃ śrutavānasi madīyaṃ vacaḥ'ityuktaḥ'anyatramanā abhūvaṃ nāśrauṣaṃ na śrutavānasmi'iti /
tasmād yasyāsannidhau rūpādigrahaṇasamarthasyāpi sataścakṣurādeḥ svasvaviṣayasambandhe rūpāśabdādijñānaṃ na bhavati, yasya ca bhāve bhavati, tadanyadasti mano nāmāntaḥkaraṇaṃ sarvakāraṇaviṣayayogi ityavagabhyate /
tasmātsarvo hi lokāṃ manasā hyeva paśyati manasā śṛṇoti, tadvayagratve darśanādyabhāvāt /
astitve sidve manasaḥ svarūpārthamidamucyatekāmaḥ strīcyatikarābhīlāṣādiḥ, saṃkalpaḥ pratyupasthitavipayavikalpanaṃ śuklanīlādibhedena, vicikitsā saṃśayajñānam, śradvā adṛṣṭārtheṣu karmasvāstikyavudvidaivayādipu ca, aśradvā tadviparītā vudviḥ, dhṛtirdhāraṇaṃ dehādyavasāde uttambhan, adhṛtistadviparyayaḥ, hrīrlajjā, dhīḥ prajñā, bhīrbhayma, ityetadevamādikaṃ sarvaṃ mana eva;manaso 'ntaḥkaraṇasya rūpāṇyetāni /
mano 'stitvaṃ pratyanyacca kāraṇamucyate-tasmānmano nāmāstayantaḥ karaṇam, yasmāccakṣuṣo hyagocare pṛṣṭhapto 'pyupaspṛṣṭhaḥ kenicid hastasyāyaṃ sparśo jānerayamiti vivekena pratipadyate /
yadi vivekakṛnmano nāma nāsti tarhi tvaṅmātreṇa kuto vivekapratipattiḥ syāt? tanmanaḥ /
asti tāvanmanaḥ, svarūpaṃ ca tasyāpādhigatam /
trīṇyannānīha phalabhūtāni karmaṇāṃ manovākprāṇākhyāni adhpātmamadhibhūtamadhidaivaṃ ca vyācikhyāsitāni /
tatra ādhyātmikānāṃ vāṅmanaḥ prāṇānāṃ mano vyākhyātam /
athedārnīvāgvattkavyetyāraṃmaḥ- yaḥ kaśca loke śabdo dhavanistālvādivyaṅgyaḥ prāṇibhirvarṇādilakṣaṇa itaro vā vāditramedhādinimittaḥ sarvo dhvanirvāgeva sā /
idaṃ tāvadvācaḥ svarūpamuttkam? atha tasyāḥ kāryamucyate-eṣā vāgghi yasmādantamabhidheyāvasānamabhidheyanirṇayamāyattānugatā /
eṣā punaḥ svayaṃ nābhidheyavatprakāśyā abhidheyaprakāśikaiv prakāśātmakatvāt pradīpādivat /
na hi pradīpādiprakāśaḥ prakāśāntareṇa prakāśyate, tadvadvākprakāśikaiva svayaṃ na prakāśyetyanavasthāṃ śrutiḥ pariharati - eṣā hi na prakāśyā /
prakāśakatvameva vācaḥ kāryamityarthaḥ /
atha prāṇa ucyate - prāṇo mukhanāsikāsañcāryā hṛdayavṛttiḥpraṇayanātprāṇaḥ apanayanānmūtrapurīṣāderapānano 'dhovṛttirānābhisthānaḥ;vyānano vyāyamanakarmā vyānaḥ prāṇāpānayoḥ sandhirvīryavatkarmahetuśca;udāna utkarṣordhvagamanādiheturāpādatalamastakasthāna ūrdhvavṛttiḥ, samānaḥ samaṃ nayanād bhuktasya pītasya ca koṣṭhasthāno 'nnapaktā, ana ityeṣāṃ vṛttiviśeṣāṇāṃ sāmānyabhūtā sāmānyadehaceṣṭābhisambandhinī vṛttiḥ, evaṃ yathoktaṃ prāṇādivṛttijātametatsarvaṃ prāṇa eva /
prāṇa ithi vṛttimānādhyātmiko 'na uktaḥ /
karma cāsya vṛttibhedapradarśanenaiva vyākhyātam /
vyākhyātānyādhyātmikāni manovākprāṇākhyānyannāni /
children.translated_text: Thus, the three foods called mind, speech, and <s>prāṇa</s> in the individual [sphere] have been explained.

children.text: etanmaya etadvikāraḥ prājāpatyairetairvāṅmanaḥ prāṇairārabdhaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Made of these' — constituted by these, transformed from these — the <s>prājāpatya</s> [being], constituted by speech, mind, and <s>prāṇa</s>.

children.text: ko 'sau? athaṃ kāryakaraṇasaṅghāta ātmā piṇḍa ātmasvarūpatvenābhimato 'vivekibhiḥ /
children.translated_text: Who is that? This aggregate of body and organs, the self — the physical form, which is falsely identified as the self by the undiscriminating.

children.text: aviśeṣeṇaitanmaya ityuktasya viśeṣeṇa vāṅmayo manomayaḥ prāṇamaya iti sphuṭīkaraṇam //3//
children.translated_text: What was stated without specification as 'made of these' is now clarified with specification: 'made of speech, made of mind, made of <s>prāṇa</s>.' // 3 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.3: 'He made three for himself' — what is the meaning of this? It is said: mind, speech, and <s>prāṇa</s> — these are the three foods. He — the father — made these three for himself, for his own sake, having created [them] at the beginning. Regarding the doubt about these, [the text] says: there does exist mind, distinct from the external organs like the ear and the rest, since this is well known — when the connection between the external organ, its object, and the self exists, yet [the organ, though] facing the object, does not grasp it. [When asked] 'Did you see this form?' one says: 'My mind had gone elsewhere; I was absent-minded — I did not see.' Similarly, [when told] 'You heard my words,' [one says]: 'My mind was elsewhere; I did not hear.' Therefore, that in whose absence — even when the eye and other organs are capable of grasping form and the like, and are in contact with their respective objects — knowledge of form, sound, and the like does not arise, and in whose presence it does arise — that is something distinct, an internal organ called mind, connected with the objects of all [external] organs. Therefore, everyone in the world sees indeed with the mind, hears with the mind — because in its absence, seeing and the like do not occur. The existence of mind being established, [the text] states its essential nature: desire — longing for women, pleasure, and the like; intention (<s>saṃkalpa</s>) — the differentiation of a present object into alternatives such as white, blue, and the like; doubt (<s>vicikitsā</s>) — doubtful cognition; faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) — confidence in matters pertaining to unseen fruits, actions, the existence of gods, and the like; lack of faith — the opposite of that; steadfastness (<s>dhṛti</s>) — firmness, supporting [the body and mind] when the body and the like are sinking; lack of steadfastness — the opposite of that; shame (<s>hrī</s>) — modesty; intelligence (<s>dhī</s>) — wisdom; fear (<s>bhī</s>) — this and other such [states] — all this is indeed mind; these are the forms of the internal organ called mind. Another proof for the existence of mind is stated: therefore — because there is this internal organ called mind — even when touched from behind, outside the range of the eye, by someone [one cognizes] — 'this is the touch of a hand on such-and-such [part]' — one discerns with discrimination. If there were no discriminating [faculty] called mind, how could such discriminative cognition occur through touch alone? Therefore, mind [exists]. Thus, mind exists, and its essential nature has been ascertained. Three foods — the fruits of action — called mind, speech, and <s>prāṇa</s> — are intended to be explained in terms of the individual (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), the elemental (<s>adhibhūta</s>), and the divine (<s>adhidaiva</s>) [aspects]. Among those, of the individual-level mind, speech, and <s>prāṇa</s>, mind has been explained. Now the explanation of speech begins: whatever sound in the world — any vibration produced by the palate, teeth, and other articulators by living beings, whether in the form of phonemes and the like, or produced by musical instruments, clouds, and the like — all vibration is speech alone. This much is stated about the essential nature of speech. Then its function is stated: this speech indeed comes to a terminus — it rests upon, follows after, the determination of what is to be expressed, i.e., the ascertainment of the object to be expressed. But speech itself is not expressible like the objects it expresses — it is by nature a means of expression, like a lamp and the like. For the light of a lamp and the like is not illuminated by another light; similarly, speech is an illuminator alone and is not itself illuminated — thus the <s>śruti</s> averts an infinite regress: this [speech] indeed does not [need further expression]. The function of speech is to illuminate — this is the meaning. Now <s>prāṇa</s> is described: <s>prāṇa</s> — the activity moving through the mouth and nose, based in the heart, [called] <s>prāṇa</s> from its leading forth (<s>praṇayana</s>). <s>Apāna</s> — the downward activity, based in the area around the navel, [called so] from its leading away (<s>apanayana</s>) of urine, feces, and the like. <s>Vyāna</s> — the activity of exertion (<s>vyāyamana</s>), the junction of <s>prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s>, the cause of powerful actions. <s>Udāna</s> — the cause of elevation, upward movement, and the like, based from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, the upward activity. <s>Samāna</s> — the digestive fire based in the torso, [called so] from its equalizing (<s>sama nayana</s>) distribution of food and drink that has been consumed. <s>Ana</s> — the general activity related to bodily movement in general, being the common element among these particular functions. Thus, all the activities of <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest as described — all this is indeed <s>prāṇa</s>. <s>Prāṇa</s>, the possessor of these functions, in the individual sense, has been described as '<s>ana</s>.' And its function has been explained through the demonstration of the various functions.

children.text: teṣāmeva prājāpatyānāmannānāmādhibhautiko vistāro 'bhidhīyate
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The elemental (<s>adhibhūta</s>) expansion of those very <s>prājāpatya</s> foods is now stated:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.4
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.4]

children.text:
trayo lokā eta eva |
vāg evāyaṃ loko mano 'ntarikṣalokaḥ prāṇo 'sau lokaḥ || BrhUp_1,5.4 ||
children.translated_text: These are the three worlds. Speech alone is this world. Mind is the intermediate world. <s>Prāṇa</s> is that [yonder] world. // BṛhUp 1.5.4 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.4 traya lokā eta eva vāgevāyaṃ loko mano 'ntarikṣalokaḥ, prāṇo 'sau lokaḥ //4//
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.4: These are the three worlds. Speech alone is this [earthly] world. Mind is the intermediate world. <s>Prāṇa</s> is that [yonder, heavenly] world. // 4 //

children.text: tathā -
children.translated_text: Similarly:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.5-7
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.5-7]

children.text:
trayo vedā eta eva |
vāg evargvedo mano yajurvedaḥ prāṇaḥ sāmavedaḥ || BrhUp_1,5.5 ||
children.translated_text: These are the three <s>Vedas</s>. Speech alone is the <s>Ṛgveda</s>. Mind is the <s>Yajurveda</s>. <s>Prāṇa</s> is the <s>Sāmaveda</s>. // BṛhUp 1.5.5 //

children.text:
devā pitaro manuṣyā eta eva |
vāg eva devā manaḥ pitaraḥ, prāṇo mānuṣyāḥ || BrhUp_1,5.6 ||
children.translated_text: Gods, ancestors, and humans — these are [the three]. Speech alone is the gods. Mind is the ancestors. <s>Prāṇa</s> is the humans. // BṛhUp 1.5.6 //

children.text:
pitā mātā prajaita eva |
mana eva pitā vāṅ mātā prāṇaḥ prajā || BrhUp_1,5.7 ||
children.translated_text: Father, mother, and offspring — these are [the three]. Mind alone is the father. Speech is the mother. <s>Prāṇa</s> is the offspring. // BṛhUp 1.5.7 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.5-7 trayo vedā ityādīni vākyāni ṛjvarthāni //5-7//
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.5-7: 'These are the three <s>Vedas</s>' and the other statements — their meaning is straightforward. // 5-7 //

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.8
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.8]

children.text:
vijñātaṃ vijijñāsyam avijñātam eta eva |
yat kiñca vijñātaṃ vācas tad rūpam |
vāg ghi vijñātā |
vāg enaṃ tad bhūtvāvati || BrhUp_1,5.8 ||
children.translated_text: The known, the to-be-known, and the unknown — these are [the three]. Whatever is known — that is the form of speech. For speech is the knower. Speech, having become that, protects him. // BṛhUp 1.5.8 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.8 vijñātaṃ vijijñāsyamavijñātameta eva /
tatra viśeṣaḥ - yatkiñca vijñātaṃ vispaṣṭaṃ jñātaṃ vācastadrūpam /
tatra svayameva hetunāha - vāgdhi vijñātā prakāśātmakatvāt /
kathamavijñātā bhaved yānyānapi vijñāpayadi"vācaiva samrāḍbandhuḥ prajñāyate"(4 / 1 / 2) iti hi vakṣyati /
vāgviśeṣavida idaṃ phalamucyate - vāgevainaṃ yathoktavāgvibhūtividaṃ tadvijñātaṃ bhūtvā avati pālayati, vijñātarūpeṇevāsyānnaṃ bhojyatāṃ pratipadyata ityarthaḥ //8//
children.translated_text: The fruit for one who knows the specific quality of speech is stated: speech itself, having become that known [object], protects him — the one who knows the qualities of speech as described. The meaning is: in the form of the known, speech becomes food for him, i.e., assumes the nature of something to be enjoyed. // 8 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.8: The known, the to-be-known, and the unknown — these are [the three]. Therein is the distinction: whatever is known — clearly ascertained — that is the form of speech. [The text] itself gives the reason: for speech is the knower, because it is by nature a means of expression. How could that be unknown which makes even other things known? As [the text] will say: 'Through speech alone, O King, the associate is recognized' (BṛUp 4.1.2).

children.text: tathā -
children.translated_text: Similarly:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.9
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.9]

children.text:
yat kiñca vijijñāsyaṃ manasas tad rūpam |
mano hi vijijñāsyam |
mana enaṃ tad bhūtvāvati || BrhUp_1,5.9 ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is to be known — that is the form of mind. For mind is the to-be-known. Mind, having become that, protects him. // BṛhUp 1.5.9 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.9 yatkiñca vijijñāsyam, vispaṣṭaṃ jñātumiṣṭaṃ vijijñāsyam, tatsarvaṃ manaso rūpam;mano hi yasmāsyam /
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.9: Whatever is to be known — desired to be clearly known, i.e., the to-be-known — all that is the form of mind; for mind is indeed the to-be-known.

children.text: pūrvamanmanovibhūtividaḥ phalam - mana enaṃ tadvijijñāsyaṃ bhūtvā avati vijijñāsyasvarūpeṇaivānnatvamāpadyate //9//
children.translated_text: As before, the fruit for one who knows the specific quality of mind: mind, having become that to-be-known, protects him — it assumes the nature of food in the very form of the to-be-known. // 9 //

children.text: tathā -
children.translated_text: Similarly:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.10
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.10]

children.text:
yat kiñcāvijñātaṃ prāṇasya tad rūpam |
prāṇo hy avijñātaḥ |
prāṇa enaṃ tad bhūtvāvati || BrhUp_1,5.10 ||
children.translated_text: Whatever is unknown — that is the form of <s>prāṇa</s>. For <s>prāṇa</s> is the unknown. <s>Prāṇa</s>, having become that, protects him. // BṛhUp 1.5.10 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.10 yatkiñcāvijñātaṃ vijñānāgocaraṃ na ca sandihyamānam, prāṇasya tadrūpam prāṇo hyavijñāto 'niruktaśruteḥ /
vijñātavijijñāsyāvijñātabhedena vāṅmanaḥprāṇavibhāge sthite trayo lokā ityādayo vācanikā eva /
children.translated_text: Since the division into speech, mind, and <s>prāṇa</s> has been established based on the distinction of the known, to-be-known, and unknown, the statements 'these are the three worlds' and so forth are indeed based on scriptural authority alone.

children.text: sarvatra vijñātādirūpadarśanādvacanādeva niyamaḥ smartavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Since the known and other [categories] are seen everywhere [as forms of speech and the rest], the restriction [to a particular correspondence] should be understood from the scriptural statement alone.

children.text: prāṇa enaṃ tadbhūtvā avati - avijñātarūpeṇaivāsya prāṇo 'nnaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Prāṇa</s>, having become that, protects him — in the very form of the unknown, <s>prāṇa</s> becomes food for him — this is the meaning.

children.text: śiṣyaputrādibhiḥ sandihyamānāvijñātopakārā apyācāryapitrādayā dṛśyante;tathā manaḥprāṇayorapi sandihyamānāvijñātayorannatvopapattiḥ //10//
children.translated_text: Even teachers and fathers, whose benefit is doubted or unknown, are seen [to exist]; similarly, even for mind and <s>prāṇa</s>, whose [contributions are] doubted or unknown, the property of being food is reasonable. // 10 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.10: Whatever is unknown — beyond the range of cognition and not even the subject of doubt — that is the form of <s>prāṇa</s>. For <s>prāṇa</s> is the unknown, because the <s>śruti</s> does not define it [explicitly].

children.text:
vyākhyāto vāṅmanaḥprāṇānāmādhibhautiko vistāraḥ /
athāyamādhidaivikārya ārambhaḥ -
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The elemental (<s>adhibhūta</s>) expansion of speech, mind, and <s>prāṇa</s> has been explained. Now the divine (<s>adhidaivika</s>) exposition begins:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.11
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.11]

children.text:
tasyai vācaḥ pṛthivī śarīram |
jyotīrūpam ayam agniḥ |
tad yāvaty eva vāk tāvatī pṛthivī tāvān ayam agniḥ || BrhUp_1,5.11 ||
children.translated_text: Of that speech, the earth is the body; the luminous form is this fire. As far as speech extends, so far extends the earth, and so far this fire. // BṛhUp 1.5.11 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_1,5.11 tasyai tasyāḥ vācaḥ prajāpaterannatvena prastutāyāḥ pṛthivī śarīraṃ brahma ādhāraḥ, jyotīrūpaṃ prakāśātmakaṃ karaṇaṃ cādheyaṃ prakāśaḥ, tadubhayaṃ pṛthivyagni vāgeva prajāpateḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.11: Of that speech — the speech of <s>Prajāpati</s> that was introduced as food — the earth is the body, i.e. the <s>Brahman</s> (support, substratum). The luminous form — the illuminating instrument, the light that is the content [of the support] — is this fire. Both — the earth and fire — are speech of <s>Prajāpati</s>.

children.text: tattatra yāvatyeva yāvatparimāṇaiva adhyātmādhibhūtabhedabhinnā satī vāgbhavati, tatra sarvatra ādhāratvena pṛthivī vyavasthitā, tāvatyeva bhavati kāryabhūtā;tāvānayamagniḥ, ādheyaḥ karaṇarūpo jyotirūpeṇa pṛthivīmanupraviṣṭastāvāneva bhavati /
children.translated_text: There, the extent — the measure — to which speech exists, being differentiated into its individual (<s>adhyātma</s>) and elemental (<s>adhibhūta</s>) aspects — to that extent, everywhere, the earth is established as the substratum, being the effect; and this fire, the content, the instrument in the form of light, having entered the earth, is of that same extent.

children.text: samānamuttaram //11//
children.translated_text: The rest is the same [as before]. // 11 //

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.12
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 1.5.12]

children.text:
athaitasya manaso dyauḥ śarīram |
jyotīrūpam asāv ādityaḥ |
tad yāvad eva manas tāvatī dyaus tāvān asāv ādityaḥ |
tau mithunaṃ samaitām |
tataḥ prāṇo 'jāyata |
sa indraḥ |
sa eṣo 'sapatnaḥ |
dvitīyo vai sapatnaḥ |
nāsya sapatno bhavati ya evaṃ veda || BrhUp_1,5.12 ||
children.translated_text: Now of this mind, heaven is the body; the luminous form is that sun. As far as mind extends, so far extends heaven, and so far that sun. Those two — [speech and mind, fire and sun] — joined as a pair. From that, <s>prāṇa</s> was born. He is <s>Indra</s>. He is without a rival. A second indeed is a rival. One who knows this has no rival. // BṛhUp 1.5.12 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.12 athaitasya prājāpatyānnoktasyaiva manaso dyaurdyulokaḥ śarīraṃ kāryamādhāraḥ, jyotīrūpaṃ karaṇamādheyo 'sāvādityaḥ /
tattatra yāvatparimāṇameva adhyātmamadhibhūtaṃ vā manastāvatī tāvadvistārā tāvatparimāṇā manaso jyotīrūpasya karaṇasya ādhāratvena vyavasthitā dyauḥ, tāvānasāvādityo jyotīrūpaṃ karaṇamādheyam /
tāvavagnyādityau vāṅmanase ādhidaivike bhātāpitarau, mithunaṃ maithunyamitaretarasaṃsarga samaitāṃ samagacchetām /
'manasā ādityena prabhūtaṃ pitrā, vācāgninā mātrā prakāśitaṃ karma kariṣyāmi'iti, antarā rodasyoḥ /
tatastayoreva saṅgamanātprāṇo vāyurajñāyata parispandāya karmaṇe /
children.translated_text: Then, from the union of those very two [speech and mind], <s>prāṇa</s> — wind — was born, for the purpose of movement and action.

children.text: yo jātaḥ sa indraḥ parameśvaraḥ, na kevalamindra evāsapatno 'vidyamānaḥ sapatno yasya;kaḥ punaḥ sapatnano nāma? dvitīyo vai pratipakṣatvenopagataḥ sa dvitīyaḥ sapatna ityucyate /
children.translated_text: He who was born is <s>Indra</s>, the Supreme Lord. Not merely <s>Indra</s> alone is without an adversary — one who has no adversary (<s>sapatna</s>). But who then is called an adversary? Indeed, a second [entity] encountered as an opponent — that second is called an adversary.

children.text: tena dvitīyatve 'pi sati vāṅmanase na sapatnatvaṃ bhajete, prāṇaṃ prati guṇabhāvopagate eva hi te adhyātmamiva /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even though [speech and mind] exist as a second, they do not partake of the nature of being adversaries to <s>prāṇa</s>, for they have assumed the status of subordinates [to <s>prāṇa</s>] — just as in the individual self (<s>adhyātma</s>).

children.text: tatra prāsaṅgikāsapatnavijñānaphalamidam - nāsyaviduṣaḥsapatnaḥ pratipakṣo bhavati, ya evaṃ yathoktaṃ prāṇamasapatnaṃ veda //12//
children.translated_text: In that regard, the incidental fruit of the knowledge that [<s>prāṇa</s>] is without adversary is this: for one who knows <s>prāṇa</s> as being without adversary in the manner described, no adversary — no opponent — arises. // 12 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 1.5.12: Now of this mind — the same <s>prājāpatya</s> food just described — heaven, the celestial world, is the body, the effect, the substratum; the luminous form, the instrument, the content — is that sun. There, the extent — the measure — to which mind extends, whether in the individual or elemental sense — to that extent, to that measure, to that expanse — heaven is established as the substratum of mind's luminous instrumental form; that sun is the luminous instrument, the content. Those two — fire and the sun, i.e. speech and mind — as the <s>adhidaivika</s> (divine) [aspects], like mother and father, joined as a pair, came together in mutual conjunction. [The meaning is:] 'With mind, through the sun, illuminated by the father; with speech, through fire, illuminated by the mother — I shall perform action' — in the space between heaven and earth.

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.13
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,5.13

children.text:
athaitasya prāṇasyāpaḥ śarīram |
jyotīrūpam asau candraḥ |
tad yāvān eva prāṇas tāvatya āpas tāvān asau candraḥ |
ta ete sarva eva samāḥ sarve 'nantāḥ |
sa yo haitān antavata upāste 'ntavantaṃ sa lokaṃ jayati |
atha yo haitān anantān upāste 'nantaṃ sa lokaṃ jayati || BrhUp_1,5.13 ||
children.translated_text: Now, the body of this <s>prāṇa</s> is water. Its luminous form is the moon yonder. As far as <s>prāṇa</s> extends, so far extend the waters, and so far extends the moon yonder. All these are indeed equal; all are infinite. One who meditates on these as finite wins a finite world. But one who meditates on these as infinite wins an infinite world. // BṛhUp 1.5.13 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.13 athaitasya prakṛtasya prajāpatyānnasya prāṇamasya, na prajoktasyāntaranirdiṣṭasya, āpaḥ śarīraṃ kāryaṃ karaṇādhāraḥ, pūrvavajjayotīrūpamasau candraḥ /
tatrayāvaneva prāṇo yāvatparimāṇo 'dhyātmādibhedeṣu, tāvadvyāptimatya āpaḥ tāvatparimāṇāḥ, tāvānasau candro 'bādheyastāsvapsvanupraviṣṭaḥ karaṇabhūto 'dhyātmamadhibhūtaṃ ca tāvadvyāptimāneva /
tānyetāni pitrā pāṅktena karmaṇā sṛṣṭāni trīṇyannāni vāṅmanaḥprāṇākhyāni /
adhyātmamadhibhūtaṃ ca jagatsamastametairvyāptam, naitebhyo 'nyadatiriktaṃ kiñcidasti kāryātmakaṃ karaṇātmakaṃ vā /
samastāni tvetāni prajāpatiḥ /
ta ete vāṅmanaḥprāṇāḥ sarve eva samāstulyā vyāptimanto yāvatprāṇigocaraṃ sādhyātmādhibhūtaṃ vyāpya vyavasthitāḥ /
ata evānantā yāvatsaṃsārabhāvinano hi te /
na hi kāryakaraṇapratyākhyānena saṃsāro 'vagamyate /
children.translated_text: For <s>saṃsāra</s> is not comprehended through the rejection of effects and instruments.

children.text: kāryakaraṇātmakā hi ta ityuktam /
children.translated_text: For it has been stated that they are of the nature of effects and instruments.

children.text: sa yaḥ kaścid haitānprajāpaterātmabhūtānantavataḥparicchinnānadhyātmarūpeṇa vā adhibhūtarūpeṇa vā adhibhūtarūpeṇa vopāste, sa ca tadupāsanānurūpameva phalamantavantaṃ lokaṃ jayati, paricchinna eva jāyate naiteṣāmātmabhūto bhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, whoever meditates on these — which are the very self of <s>Prajāpati</s> — as finite, as limited, either in the form of the individual self or in the form of the cosmic realm — he wins a finite world, a corresponding fruit; he is born as limited alone and does not become the self of these [beings] — this is the meaning.

children.text: atha punaryo haitānanantānsarvātmakānsarvaprāṇyātmabhūtān aparicchinnānupāste so 'ntameva lokaṃ jayati //13//
children.translated_text: But on the other hand, whoever meditates on these as infinite, as the self of all, as constituting the self of all living beings, as unlimited — he wins an infinite world. // 13 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.5.13:] Now, the body — the effect, the support of the instruments — of this <s>prāṇa</s> under discussion, which is the food of <s>Prajāpati</s>, not the one mentioned and specified in the intermediate [passage] — is water. As before, its luminous form is the moon yonder. In that regard, as far as <s>prāṇa</s> extends — as much as its measure in the divisions of the individual self (<s>adhyātma</s>) and the rest — so far the waters pervade, having that same measure; so far the moon yonder, which is irrefutable, having entered into those waters as their instrumental [aspect], pervades the individual self (<s>adhyātma</s>) and the cosmic realm (<s>adhibhūta</s>) to that same extent. These three foods created by the father through five-fold action, called speech, mind, and <s>prāṇa</s> — the entire world, both the individual self and the cosmic realm, is pervaded by them; there is nothing whatsoever beyond them, whether of the nature of effects or of instruments. But all of these together constitute <s>Prajāpati</s>. These — speech, mind, and <s>prāṇa</s> — are all equal, co-extensive, pervading everything that falls within the domain of living beings, both the individual self and the cosmic realm. For this very reason they are infinite, for they endure as long as <s>saṃsāra</s> endures.

children.text:
pitā pāṅktena karmaṇā saptānnāni sṛṣṭvā trīṇyannānyātmārthaṅkarodityuktam /
tānyetāni /
pāṅktakarmaphalabhūtāni vyākhyātāni /
tatra kathaṃ punaḥ pāṅktatāvagamyate, vittakarmaṇamorapi tatra sambhavāt /
tatra pṛthivyagnī mātā, divādityau pitā /
yo 'pyamanayorantarā prāṇaḥ, sa prajeti vyākhyātam /
tatra vittakarmaṇī sambhāvayitavye ityārambhaḥ -
children.translated_text: It has been said that the father, having created the seven foods through five-fold action, made three foods for himself. These are those [three]. They have been explained as fruits of the five-fold action. Now, how is the five-fold nature [of this <s>Prajāpati</s>] to be understood, since wealth and action are also possible here? In that regard, earth and fire are the mother; heaven and the sun are the father. The <s>prāṇa</s> that is between those two [parents] is the offspring — this has been explained. In that regard, wealth and action are to be accounted for — this is the beginning [of the next section]:

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.14
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,5.14

children.text:
sa eṣa saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiṣ ṣoḍaśakalaḥ |
tasya rātraya eva pañcadaśa kalā |
dhruvaivāsya ṣoḍaśī kalā |
sa rātribhir evā ca pūryate 'pa ca kṣīyate |
so 'māvāsyāṃ rātrim etayā ṣoḍaśyā kalayā sarvam idaṃ prāṇabhṛd anupraviśya tataḥ prātar jāyate |
tasmād etāṃ rātriṃ prāṇabhṛtaḥ prāṇaṃ na vicchindyād api kṛkalāsasyaitasyā eva devatāyā apacityai || BrhUp_1,5.14 ||
children.translated_text: This is that year — <s>Prajāpati</s> — of sixteen digits. His nights alone are fifteen digits. His sixteenth digit is fixed. He is filled and diminished by the nights alone. On the new-moon night, having entered through this sixteenth digit into all this that has breath, from there he is born in the morning. Therefore, on this night, one should not cut off the breath of any breathing thing, not even of a lizard — in honor of this very deity. // BṛhUp 1.5.14 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_1,5.14 'sa eṣaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ' -yo 'yaṃ tryannātmā prajāpatiḥ prakṛtaḥ, sa eṣa saṃvatsarātmanā viśeṣato nirdiśyate /
ṣoḍaśakalaḥ ṣoḍaśa kalā avayavā asya so 'yaṃ ṣoḍaśakalaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ saṃvatsarātmākālarūpaḥ /
tasya ca kālātmanaḥ prajāpateḥ rātraya evāhorātrāṇi, tithaya ityarthaḥ, pañcadaśa kalāḥ /
dhruvaiva nityaiva vyavasthitā asya prajāpateḥ ṣoḍaśī ṣoḍaśānāṃ pūraṇī kalā /
sa rātribhireva tithibhiḥ kaloktābhirāpūryate cāpakṣīyate ca /
pratipadādyābhirhi candramāḥ prajāpatiḥ śuklapakṣa āpūryate kalābhirupacīyamānābhirvardhate yāvatsampūrṇamaṇḍalaḥ paurṇamāsyām /
tābhirevāpacīyamānābhiḥ kalābhirapakṣīyate kṛṣṇapakṣe yāvad dhruvaikā kalā vyavasthitā amāvāsyām /
sa prajāpatiḥ kalātmā amāvāsyāmamāvāsyāyāṃ rātriṃrātrau yā vyavasthitā dhruvā kaloktā etayā ṣoḍaśyā kalayā sarvamidaṃ prāṇabhṛtprāṇijātamanupraviśya yadapaḥ pibati yaccaupadhīraśnāti tatsarvameva oṣadhyātmanā sarvaṃ vyāpyāmāvāsyāṃ rātrimavasthāya tato 'paredyuḥ prātarjñāyate dvitīyayā kalayā saṃyuktaḥ /
evaṃ pāṅktātmako 'sau prajāpatiḥ /
divādityau manaḥ pitā;pṛthivyagno vāgjñāyā mātā;tayośca prāṇaḥ prajā /
cāndramasyastithayaḥ kalā vittam, upacayāpacayadharmitvādvittavat /
tāsāṃ ca kalānāṃ kālāvayavānāṃ jagatpariṇāmahetutvaṃ karma /
evameṣa kṛtsnaḥ prajāpatiḥ"jāyā me syādatha prajāyeyātha vittaṃ me syādatha karma kurvīya" (bṛ.u.1 / 4 / 17) ityeṣaṇānurūpa eva pāṅktasya karmaṇaḥ phalabhūtaḥ saṃvṛttaḥ /
kāraṇānuvidhāyi hi kāryamiti loke 'pi sthitiḥ /
children.translated_text: For it is a settled principle in the world too that the effect conforms to the cause.

children.text: yasmādeṣa candra etāṃ rātriṃ sarvaprāṇijātamanupraviṣṭo dhruvayā kalayā vartate, tasmāddhetoretāmamāvāsyāṃ rātriṃ prāṇabhṛtaḥ prāṇinaḥ prāṇaṃ na vicchindyātprāṇinaṃ na pramāpayedityetat, api kṛkalāsasya /
children.translated_text: Since this moon, on this [new-moon] night, having entered into all living beings through the fixed digit, abides [there] — therefore, on this new-moon night, one should not cut off the breath of any living being, i.e. one should not kill any creature — not even a lizard.

children.text: kṛkalāso hi pāpātmā svabhāvenaiva hiṃsyate prāṇibhirdṛṣṭo 'pyamaṅgala iti kṛtvā /
children.translated_text: For a lizard is by nature sinful and is killed by living beings even when merely seen — considering it to be inauspicious.

children.text: bāḍhaṃ pratiṣiddhā, tathāpi nāmāvāsyāyā anyatra pratiprasavārthaṃ vacanaṃ hiṃsāyāḥ kṛkalāsaviṣaye vā, kiṃ tarhi? etasyāḥ somadevatāyā apacityai pūjārtham //14//
children.translated_text: Granted, [killing] is prohibited [generally]. Even so, this statement is not for the purpose of a counter-exception [allowing killing] on other [nights], or [allowing killing] in the case of lizards, but rather: for the honor, for the worship, of this deity — [the deity] <s>Soma</s> (the moon). // 14 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 1.5.14:] 'This is that year' — this <s>Prajāpati</s> under discussion, whose self consists of three foods, is here specifically indicated as having the year for his self. 'Of sixteen digits' — sixteen digits (parts) are his — he is this year of sixteen digits, this <s>Prajāpati</s> whose self is time. And of that <s>Prajāpati</s> whose self is time, the nights — [meaning] the days and nights, i.e. the <s>tithis</s> (lunar days) — these are the fifteen digits. His sixteenth digit — the one that fills up the sixteen — is fixed, permanent, constant. He is filled and diminished by the nights alone, i.e. by the <s>tithis</s> designated as digits. For the moon — <s>Prajāpati</s> — is filled during the bright half [of the month], increasing by these digits from the first day onward, growing until the full-moon day when its disc is complete. And by those very digits diminishing, it wanes during the dark half until only the fixed, single digit remains on the new-moon night. That <s>Prajāpati</s>, whose self consists of digits, on the new-moon night — on the new-moon night — through that established, fixed, sixteenth digit, having entered into all this that has breath, i.e., the totality of living beings — whatever water it drinks and whatever food it consumes — pervading all in the form of plants — having stayed through the new-moon night — thereupon, on the following day, in the morning, it is born, united with the second digit. Thus this <s>Prajāpati</s> is of five-fold nature. Heaven and the sun are the mind, the father; earth and fire are speech, the mother; and <s>prāṇa</s> is the offspring of those two. The lunar <s>tithis</s>, as digits, are the wealth, because they share the property of increase and decrease like [material] wealth. And the property of these digits — which are parts of time — being the cause of the transformation of the world, is the action. Thus this entire <s>Prajāpati</s> has turned out to be the fruit of five-fold action, in accordance with the desires 'May I have a wife, then may I procreate, then may I have wealth, then may I perform action' (BṛUp 1.4.17).

children.text: START BrhUp 1,5.15
children.translated_text: START BrhUp 1,5.15

children.text:
yo vai sa saṃvatsaraḥ prajāpatiḥ ṣoḍaśakālo 'yam eva sa yo 'yam evaṃvit puruṣaḥ |
tasya vittam eva pañcadaśa kalāḥ |
ātmaivāsya ṣoḍaśī kalā |
sa vittenaivā ca pūryate 'pa ca kṣīyate |
