children.text: nanvapādānapakṣe 'pi punaruktatādoṣaḥ sthita eva /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Even on the interpretation of material source (<s>upādāna</s>), the fault of redundancy remains.

children.text:
naiṣa doṣaḥ, praśnābhyām ātmani kriyākārakaphalātmatāpohasya vivakṣitatvāt /
iha hi vidyāvidyāviṣayāvupanyastau /
"ātmetyevopāsīta" "ātmānamevāvet" "ātmānameva lokamupāsīta"iti vidyāviṣayaḥ /
tathā avidyāviṣayaśca pāṅktaṃ karma tatphalaṃ cānnatrayaṃ nāmarūpakarmātmakamiti /
tatrāvidyāviṣaye vaktavyaṃ sarvamuktam /
children.translated_text: [Reply:] This is not a fault, because what is intended by the two questions is the negation of the nature of action, instruments, and fruit in the self. For here, both the domain of knowledge and the domain of ignorance have been presented. 'One should meditate as the self alone,' 'he knew the self,' 'one should meditate on the self alone as one's world' — this is the domain of knowledge. Similarly, the domain of ignorance is the five-fold action, its fruit which is the three foods, [all] having the nature of name, form, and action. Therein, everything to be said about the domain of ignorance has been said.

children.text:
vidyāviṣayastvātmā kevala upanyasto na nirṇītaḥ /
tannirṇayāya ca 'brahma te bravāṇi'iti prakrāntaṃ 'jñapayiṣyāmi'iti ca /
atastadbrahma vidyāviṣayabhūtaṃ jñāpayitavyaṃ yāthātmyataḥ /
tasya ca yāthātmyaṃ kriyākārakaphalabhedaśūnyamatyantaviśuddhamadvaitamityetadvivakṣitam /
atastadanurūpau praśnāvutthāpyete śrutyā 'kvaiṣa tadābhūt' 'kuta etadāgāt'iti /
children.translated_text: But the self, the domain of knowledge, has been introduced but not determined. And for its determination, [the teaching] was begun with 'I shall tell you <s>Brahman</s>' and 'I shall make you know.' Therefore, that <s>Brahman</s>, which is the domain of knowledge, must be made known in its true nature. And its true nature — devoid of the distinctions of action, instruments, and fruit, utterly pure, non-dual — this is what is intended. Therefore, two questions are raised by the <s>śruti</s>, consonant with that: 'Where was this one then?' and 'From where did this come?'

children.text:
tatra yatra bhavati tadadhikaraṇaṃ yadbhavati tadadhikartavyam, yatoścādhikaraṇādhikartavyayorbhedo dṛṣṭo loke /
tathā yata āgacchati tadapādānaṃ ya āgacchati sa kartā tasmādanyo dṛṣṭaḥ /
tathā ātmā kvāpyabhūdanyasminnanyaḥ kutaścidāgādanyasmādanyaḥ kenacidbhinnena sādhanāntareṇetyevaṃ lokavatprāptā buddhiḥ /
sā prativacanena nivartayitavyeti /
nāyamātmā anyo 'nyatrābhūdanyo vā
children.translated_text: There — that in which something exists is the locus; that which exists is the thing located; and the distinction between locus and thing located is seen in the world. Similarly, that from which something comes is the source; he who comes is the agent — and he is seen to be different from the source. Thus, [the thought arises that] the self was somewhere, in some [place] other [than itself]; and it came from somewhere, from some other [place]; and [it acted] through some different instrument — such worldly thinking arises. That [misconception] is to be removed by the answer.

children.text:
anyasmādāgataḥ sādhanāntaraṃ vā ātmanyasti /
kiṃ tarhi? svātmanyevābhūt 'svam (ātmānam) apīto bhavati' 'satā somya tadā sampanno bhavati' 'prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ' /
'para ātmani sampratiṣṭhate'ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
ata eva nānyo 'nyasmādāgacchati /
tacchrutyaiva pradarśyate 'asmādātmanaḥ'iti /
ātmavyatirekeṇa vastvantarābhāvāt /
children.translated_text: This self was not in any other place as something different, nor did it come from elsewhere as something different, nor is there any other instrument in the self. What then? It was in its very own self — 'he goes to his own self,' 'then, O dear one, he has merged with Being,' 'embraced by the <s>Prajña</s> self.' 'The supreme [self] rests in the self' — from such <s>śruti</s> passages. And therefore, nothing comes from elsewhere. This the <s>śruti</s> itself demonstrates: 'from this self.' Because there is no other entity apart from the self.

children.text:
nanvasti prāṇādyātmavyatiriktaṃ vastvantaram /
na, prāṇādestata eva niṣpatteḥ /
tatkatham? ityucyate, tatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ-
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But there do exist other entities apart from the self — <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest. [Reply:] No, because <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest originate from that very [self]. How then? This is stated, with an illustration:

children.text:
sa yathorṇavābhis tantunoccared yathā agneḥ kṣudrā viṣphuliṅgā vyuccaranty evam evāsmād ātmanaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sarve lokāḥ sarve devāḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni vyuccaranti |
tasyopaniṣat satyasya satyam iti |
prāṇā vai satyaṃ teṣām eṣa satyam || BrhUp_2,1.20 ||
children.translated_text: Just as a spider sends forth its thread, and just as small sparks fly forth from a fire — even so, from this self, all <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths), all worlds, all gods, all beings fly forth. Its secret name (<s>Upaniṣad</s>) is 'the truth of the true.' The <s>prāṇas</s> are the true; of them, this [self] is the truth. // BṛhUp 2.1.20 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_2,1.20
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 2.1.20:

children.text:
sa yathā loka ūrṇanābhiḥ /
ūrṇanābhirlūtākīṭa eka eva prasiddhaḥ sansvātmāpravibhaktena tantunoccaredudgacchet /
na cāsti tasyodgamane svato 'tiriktaṃ kārakāntaram /
yathā caikarūpādekasmādagneḥ śrudrā alpā visphuliṅgāsruṭayo 'gnyavayavā vyuccaranti vividhaṃ nānā voccaranti /
yathemau dṛṣṭāntau kārakabhedābhāve 'pi pravṛttiṃ darśayataḥ, prākpravṛtteśca svabhāvata ekatvam, evamevāsmādātmano vijñānamayasya prākpratibodhādyatsvarūpaṃ tasmādityarthaḥ /
sarve prāṇā vāgādayaḥ, sarve lokā bhūrādayaḥ, sarvāṇi karmaphalāni, sarve devāḥ prāṇalokādhiṣṭhātāro 'gnyādayaḥ, sarvāṇi bhūtāni brahmādistambaparyantāni prāṇijātāni, sarva eta ātmāna ityasminpāṭha upādhisamparkajanitaprabudhyamānaviśeṣātmāna ityarthaḥ, vyuccaranti /
children.translated_text: Just as in the world a spider (<s>ūrṇanābhi</s>), a well-known single spider-insect, sends forth, emits, its thread from its own self, without any differentiation — and there is no other causal factor apart from itself for its emission. And just as from a fire of uniform nature, from a single fire, small, minute sparks — particles of fire — fly forth in various ways. Just as these two examples show activity even in the absence of differentiated causal factors, and oneness with [the source] by nature before the activity — even so, 'from this self' — from the self constituted of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>), from the essential nature that exists before the awakening [to differentiation] — this is the meaning. All <s>prāṇas</s> — speech and the rest; all worlds — <s>bhūḥ</s> and the rest; all the fruits of action; all gods — <s>Agni</s> and the rest, who preside over the <s>prāṇas</s> and worlds; all beings — the entire class of living creatures from <s>Brahmā</s> down to a blade of grass — all these selves: in the reading '<s>sarva eta ātmānaḥ</s>,' the meaning is the specific selves that are awakened through contact with limiting adjuncts — they fly forth.

children.text: yasmādātmanaḥ sthāvarajabhgamaṃ jagadidamagnivisphuliṅgavad vyuccaratyaniśam, yasminneva ca pralīyate jalabudbudavat, yadātmakaṃ ca vartate sthitikāle, tasyāsyātmano brahmaṇaḥ, upaniṣad;upa samīpaṃ nigamayatītyabhidhāyakaḥ śabda upaniṣadityucatyate, śāsraprāmāṇyādetacchabdagato viśeṣo 'vasīyata upanigamayitṛtvaṃ nāma /
children.translated_text: Because from this self the world of moveable and immoveable beings flies forth incessantly like sparks from a fire, and dissolves back into it alone like bubbles in water, and during the period of continuance has that [self] as its nature — of this self, of <s>Brahman</s>, the <s>Upaniṣad</s> [is stated]. The word '<s>Upaniṣad</s>' is said [to mean]: that which brings near, that which leads to approach — the <s>Upaniṣad</s>, the designating word, is so called. Because of the authority of scripture, this specific quality of the word is determined — namely, the property of leading one near [to <s>Brahman</s>].

children.text:
kāsāvupaniṣadityāha-satyasya satyamiti /
sā hi sarvatra copaniṣadalaukikārthatvād durvijñeyārthā, iti tadarthamācaṣṭe-prāṇā vai satyaṃ teṣāmeṣa satyamiti /
etasyaiva vākyasya vyākhyānāyottaraṃ brāhmaṇadvayaṃ bhaviṣyati /
children.translated_text: What then is that <s>Upaniṣad</s>? He says: 'the truth of the true.' For the <s>Upaniṣad</s> everywhere, being of an extraordinary meaning, has a meaning that is difficult to know; therefore, [the text] explains its meaning: 'The <s>prāṇas</s> indeed are the true; of them, this [self] is the truth.' For the explanation of this very sentence, the subsequent two <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> will follow.

children.text:
bhavatu tāvadupaniṣadvyākhyānāyottaraṃ brāhmaṇadvayam, tasyopaniṣadityuktam, tatra na jānīmaḥ kiṃ prakṛtasyātmano vijñānamayasya pāṇipeṣaṇotthitasya saṃsāriṇaḥ śabdādibhuja iyamupaniṣadāhosvidasaṃsāriṇaḥ kasyacit? kiñcātaḥ? yadi saṃsāriṇastadā saṃsāryeva vijñeyaḥ, tadvijñānādeva sarvaprāptiḥ /
sa eva brahmaśabdavācyastadvidyaiva brahmavidyeti /
atha asaṃsāriṇaḥ, tadā tadviṣayā vidyā brahmavidyā /
tasmācca brahmavijñānātsarvabhāvāpattiḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Granted that the subsequent two <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> sections serve to explain the <s>Upaniṣad</s>, and that [<s>Ajātaśatru</s>] has said 'this is the <s>Upaniṣad</s>.' But we do not know whether this <s>Upaniṣad</s> pertains to the self that is the topic — the one constituted of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>), aroused by the pressing of the hand, the enjoyer of sound and other [sense-objects], the <s>saṃsārin</s> — or to some non-<s>saṃsārin</s>. What follows from this? If it pertains to the <s>saṃsārin</s>, then it is the <s>saṃsārin</s> alone who is to be known; through knowledge of him alone comes the attainment of all. He alone is denoted by the word '<s>Brahman</s>,' and the knowledge of him is the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>. But if it pertains to a non-<s>saṃsārin</s>, then the knowledge that has him as its object is the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>. And from that knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> comes the attainment of everything.

children.text:
sarvametacchāsraprāmāṇyādbhaviṣyati /
kintvasminpakṣe"ātmetyevopāsīta" "ātmānamevāvedahaṃ brahmāsmi"iti parabrahmaikatvapratipādikāḥ śrutayaḥ kupyeran, saṃsāriṇaścānyasyābhāve upadeśānarthakyāt /
yata evaṃ paṇḍitānāmapyetanmahāmohasthānam anuktaprativacanapraśnaviṣayam; ato yathāśakti brahmavidyāpratipādakavākyeṣu brahma vijijñāsūnāṃ buddhivyutpādanāya vicārayiṣyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: All this will be [resolved] by the authority of scripture. However, on this [first] view, the <s>śruti</s> texts that teach the oneness with the supreme <s>Brahman</s> — 'one should meditate as the self alone' and 'he knew the self: I am <s>Brahman</s>' — would be violated; and since there is no other [entity] apart from the <s>saṃsārin</s>, the teaching would be pointless. Since this matter is the abode of great delusion even for the learned — being the subject of questions whose answers have not been [adequately] stated — therefore we shall, to the best of our ability, investigate the sentences that teach the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, for the purpose of training the intellect of those who desire to know <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text:
na tāvadasaṃsārī paraḥ, pāṇipeṣaṇapratibodhitācchabdādibhujo 'vasthāntaraviśiṣṭādutpattiśruteḥ /
na praśāsitāśanāyādivarjitaḥ paro vidyate, kasmāt? yasmāt 'brahma jñapayiṣyāmi' iti pratijñāya suptaṃ puruṣaṃ pāṇipeṣaṃ bodhayitvā tasyaiva svapnadvāreṇa suṣuptyākhyamavasthāntaramunnīya tasmādevātmanaḥ suṣuptyavasthāviśiṣṭād agnivisphuliṅgorṇanābhidṛṣṭāntābhyāmutpattiṃ darśayati śrutiḥ"evamevāsmāt"ityādinā /
na cānyo jagadutpattikāraṇamantarāle śruto 'sti, vijñānamayasyaiva hi prakaraṇam /
samānaprakaraṇe ca śrutyantare kauṣītakināmādityādipuruṣānprastutya"sa hovāca yo vai bālāka eteṣāṃ puruṣāṇāṃ kartā yasya vaitatkarma sa vai veditavyaḥ"iti prabuddhasyaiva vijñānamayasya veditavyatāṃ darśayati, nārthāntarasya /
children.translated_text: [Thesis 1:] To begin with, there is no transcendent non-<s>saṃsārin</s>, because the <s>śruti</s> teaches the origination [of the world] from [one who is] distinguished by a different state — the enjoyer of sound and the rest, aroused by the pressing of the hand. There exists no transcendent [being] who is a controller, free from hunger and the like. Why? Because, having declared 'I shall make <s>Brahman</s> known,' [<s>Ajātaśatru</s>] awakened the sleeping person by pressing his hand, and through the doorway of the dream-state, having elevated that very self to the state called deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>) — which is a different condition — the <s>śruti</s> shows the origination [of the world] from that very self, distinguished by the state of deep sleep, through the examples of fire-sparks and a spider, by the words 'thus indeed from this self' and so forth. And no other cause of the world's origination is heard in the intervening [passages], for the topic pertains to the one constituted of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>) alone. And in a parallel passage in another <s>śruti</s>, that of the <s>Kauṣītakins</s>, having introduced the <s>puruṣas</s> in the sun and the rest, [the text] says: 'He said: "One who indeed is the maker of these <s>puruṣas</s>, whose work this is — he indeed is to be known"' — showing that it is the awakened <s>vijñānamaya</s> itself that is to be known, not something else.

children.text:
tathā ca"ātmanastu kāmāya sarvaṃ priyaṃ bhavati"ityuktvā, ya evātmā priyaḥ prasiddhastasyaiva draṣṭavyaśrotavyamantavyanididhyāsitavyatāṃ darśayati /
tathā ca vidyopanyāsakāle"ātmetyevopāsīta" "tadetatpreyaḥ putrātpreyo vittāt" "tadātmānamevāvedahaṃ brahmāsmi"ityevamādivākyānāmānulomyaṃ syātparābhāve /
vakṣyati ca -"ātmānaṃ cedvijānīyādayamasmīti pūruṣaḥ"iti /
sarvavedānteṣu ca pratyagātmavedyataiva pradarśyate 'hamiti, na bahirvedyatā śabdādivatpradarśyate 'sau brahmeti /
tathā kauṣītakināmeva"na vācaṃ vijijñāsīta vaktāraṃ vidyāt"ityādinā vāgādikaraṇairvyāvṛttasya kartureva veditavyatāṃ darśayati /
children.translated_text: And thus, having said 'For the self's sake alone, all is dear,' [the <s>śruti</s>] shows that the very self that is well-known as dear is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. And at the time of presenting the <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), the [consistent] usage of sentences such as 'one should meditate as the self alone,' 'this is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth,' 'he knew the self: I am <s>Brahman</s>' — would be appropriate if there is no transcendent [<s>Brahman</s>]. And [the text] will say: 'If a person were to know the self — "this I am"' and so forth. And in all <s>Vedānta</s> texts, the self is shown as knowable as the inner self, [designated by] 'I' — it is not shown as knowable externally, like sound and the rest, as 'that is <s>Brahman</s>.' Likewise, in the <s>Kauṣītaki</s> text: 'One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker' — by [separating] the speaker from the organs such as speech, [the <s>śruti</s>] shows that the agent alone is to be known, not something else.

children.text:
avasthāntaraviśiṣṭo 'saṃsārīti cet-athāpi syādyo jāgarite śabdādibhugvijñānamayaḥ, sa eva suṣuptākhyamavasthāntaraṃ gato 'saṃsārī paraḥ praśāsitā anyaḥ syāditi cenna, adṛṣṭatvāt /
na hyevandharmakaḥ padārtho dṛṣṭo 'nyatra vaināśikasiddhāntāt /
na hi loke gaustiṣṭhan gacchanvā gaurbhavati, śayānastvaśvādijātyantaramiti /
nyāyācca-yaddharmako yaḥ padārdhaḥ pramāṇenāvagato bhavati, sa deśakālāvasthāntareṣvapi taddharmaka eva bhavati /
sa cettaddharmakatvaṃ vyabhicarati, sarvaḥ pramāṇavyavahāro lupyeta /
tathā ca nyāyavidaḥ sāṅkhyamīmāṃsakādayo 'saṃsāriṇo 'bhāvaṃ yuktiśataiḥ pratipādayanti /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] One distinguished by a different state is the non-<s>saṃsārin</s>. [Opponent says:] But perhaps the one who in the waking state is the enjoyer of sound and the rest, the <s>vijñānamaya</s> — that very one, having gone to the different state called deep sleep, becomes the non-<s>saṃsārin</s>, the transcendent, the controller — he would be something different. [Reply:] No, because such a thing is not observed. For an entity with such properties is not observed anywhere except in the <s>Vaināśika</s> (Buddhist momentarist) doctrine. In the world, a cow does not become a cow when standing and then become a horse or another species when lying down. And by logical reasoning: an entity whose properties have been ascertained by a valid means of knowledge retains those very properties in other places, times, and states. If it were to deviate from those properties, all transactional usage based on valid means of knowledge would be destroyed. And thus the logicians — the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s>, <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>, and others — establish the non-existence of a non-<s>saṃsārin</s> [entity] by hundreds of arguments.

children.text:
saṃsāriṇo 'pi jagadutpattisthitilayakriyākartṛtvavijñānasyābhāvād ayuktamiti cet-yanmahatā prapañcena sthāpitaṃ bhavatā, śabdādibhuksaṃsāryevāvasthāntaraviśiṣṭo jagata iha karteti-tadasat; yato jagadutpattisthitilayakriyākartṛtvavijñānaśaktisādhanābhāvaḥ sarvalokapratyakṣaḥ saṃsāriṇaḥ /
sa kathamasmadādiḥ saṃsārī manasāpi cintayitumaśakyaṃ pṛthivyādivinyāsaviśiṣṭaṃ jagannirminuyāt? ato 'yuktamiti cenna, śāsrāt; śāsraṃ saṃsāriṇaḥ"evamevāsmādātmanaḥ"iti jagadutpattyādi darśayati /
tasmātsarvaṃ śraddheyamiti syādayamekaḥ pakṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Even for the <s>saṃsārin</s>, since there is no [capacity for] the knowledge of creating, sustaining, and dissolving the world, [this view] is untenable. [Opponent says:] What was established by you with great elaboration — that the <s>saṃsārin</s> alone, the enjoyer of sound and the rest, distinguished by a different state, is the creator of the world — that is wrong. Because the absence of the power of knowledge for creating, sustaining, and dissolving the world is directly perceived by everyone for the <s>saṃsārin</s>. How could a <s>saṃsārin</s> like us create a universe, distinguished by the arrangement of earth and such, that is inconceivable even to the mind? Therefore, this is untenable. [Reply:] Not so, because of scripture. Scripture shows the origination of the world and the like from the <s>saṃsārin</s> by the words 'thus indeed from this self.' Therefore, everything should be accepted on faith — this would be one position.

children.text: "yaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvavit" "yo 'śanāyāpipāse atyeti" "asaṅgo na hi sajjate" "etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane" "yaḥ sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhannantaryāmyamṛtaḥ" "sa yastānpuruṣānniruhyātyakrāmat" "sa vā eṣa mahānaja ātmā"
children.translated_text: [Thesis 2:] 'He who is omniscient, who knows all' (<s>Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad</s>); 'He who transcends hunger and thirst' (<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>); 'Unattached, for it does not become attached' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'Under the rule of this Imperishable' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'He who, standing in all beings, is the inner controller, the immortal' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'He who, having overcome those <s>puruṣas</s>, transcended' (<s>Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad</s>); 'This is that great, unborn self' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>);

children.text:
"eṣa seturvidharaṇaḥ" "sarvasya vaśī sarvasyeśānaḥ" "ya ātmāpahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyuḥ" "tattejo 'sṛjata" "ātmā vā idameka evāgra āsīt" "na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyaḥ"ityādiśrutiśatebhyaḥ /
smṛteśca"ahaṃ sarvasya prabhavo mattaḥ sarvaṃ pravartate"iti paro 'styasaṃsārī /
śrutismṛtinyāyebhyaśca /
sa ca kāraṇaṃ jagataḥ /
nan"vevamevāsmādātmana"iti
children.translated_text: 'This is the bridge, the upholder' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'The controller of all, the ruler of all' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'That self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless' (<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>); 'That created light' (<s>Taittirīya Upaniṣad</s>); 'The self alone was this, one, in the beginning' (<s>Aitareya Upaniṣad</s>); 'Not tainted by worldly suffering, being external' (<s>Kaṭha Upaniṣad</s>) — from these and hundreds of other <s>śrutis</s>. And from <s>smṛti</s>: 'I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds' (<s>Bhagavadgītā</s> 10.8) — there exists a transcendent non-<s>saṃsārin</s>. And from <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and reasoning. And that [transcendent being] is the cause of the world. [Objection:] But does not 'thus indeed from this self'

children.text:
saṃsāriṇa evotpattiṃ /
darśayatītyuktam /
na /
"ya eṣo 'ntarhṛdaya ākāśa"iti parasya prakṛtatvādasmādātmana iti yuktaḥ parasyaiva parāmarśaḥ /
"kvaiṣa tadābhūdi"tyasya praśnasya prativacanatvenā'kāśaśabdavācyaḥ para ātmokto"ya eṣo 'ntarhṛdaya ākāśastasmiñcheta"iti /
"satā somya tadā sampanno bhavatya" "harahargacchantya etaṃ brahmalokaṃ na vidanti" "prājñenā'tmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ" "para ātmani saṃpratiṣṭhate"ityādiśrutibhya ākāśaśabdaḥ para ātmeti niścīyate /
"daharo 'sminnantarākāśa"iti prastutya tasminnevā'tmaśabdaprayogācca /
prakuta eva para ātmā /
tasmādyuktameva asmādātmana iti paramātmana eva sṛṣṭiriti /
saṃsāriṇaḥ sṛṣṭisthitisaṃhārajñānasāmarthyābhāvaṃ cāvotāma /
children.translated_text: show the origination from the <s>saṃsārin</s> itself? — this was stated. [Reply:] No. Because 'that which is the space within the heart' introduces the transcendent [<s>Brahman</s>] as the topic — the reference 'from this self' is properly a reference to the transcendent alone. For the response to the question 'where did that one go at that time?' — the one denoted by the word 'space' (<s>ākāśa</s>) was stated as the supreme self: 'that which is the space within the heart — in that one sleeps.' And from <s>śruti</s> texts such as: 'O <s>Somya</s>, at that time one is merged with Being (<s>Sat</s>)'; 'Day after day they go to that <s>Brahmaloka</s> and do not know [it]'; 'Embraced by the all-knowing self'; 'One is established in the supreme self' — the word 'space' (<s>ākāśa</s>) is ascertained to refer to the supreme self. And because, having introduced [the topic] with 'the small space within this [heart]' (<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>), the word '<s>ātman</s>' is used in that very [context]. The supreme self is indeed the topic. Therefore, it is entirely proper that 'from this self' refers to the origination from the <s>Paramātman</s> alone. And we have stated the absence of the capacity for creating, sustaining, and dissolving [the world] on the part of the <s>saṃsārin</s>.

children.text:
atra ca"ātmetyevopāsīta" "ātmānamevāvedahaṃ brahmāsmī"ti brahmavidyā prastutā /
brahmaviṣayañca brahmavijñānamiti /
"brahma te bravāṇī"ti"brahma jñapayiṣyāmī"ti prārabdham /
tatredānīmasaṃsāri brahma jagataḥ kāraṇamaśanāyādyatītaṃ nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaṃ tadviparītaśca saṃsārī tasmādahaṃ brahmāsmīti na gṛhṇīyāt /
paraṃ hi devamīśānaṃ nikṛṣṭaḥ saṃsāryātmatvena smarankathaṃ na doṣabhāksyāt /
tasmānnāhaṃ brahmāsmīti yuktam /
children.translated_text: And here, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> has been introduced: 'one should meditate as the self alone'; 'he knew the self: I am <s>Brahman</s>.' And the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> has <s>Brahman</s> as its object. [The teaching] was begun with 'let me tell you about <s>Brahman</s>' and 'I shall make <s>Brahman</s> known.' Now, <s>Brahman</s> — the non-<s>saṃsārin</s>, the cause of the world, beyond hunger and the like, of eternally pure, awakened, and free nature — is one thing, and the <s>saṃsārin</s>, whose nature is the opposite of that, is another. [One might say:] Therefore, one should not grasp 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.' For one who remembers the supreme deity, the Lord, as his own self — being a lowly <s>saṃsārin</s> — how would he not incur fault?

children.text:
tasmātpuṣpodakāñjalistutinamaskārabalyupahārasvādhyāyadhyānayogādibhirār irādhayiṣeta /
ārādhanena viditvā sarveśitṛ brahma bhavati /
na punarasaṃsāri brahma saṃsāryātmatvena cintayedagnimiva śītatvenā'kāśamiva mūrtimatvena /
brahmātmatvapratipādakamapi śāsramarthavādo bhaviṣyati /
sarvatarkaśāsralokanyāyaiścaivamavirodhaḥ syāt /
na, mantrabrāhmaṇavādebhyastasyaiva praveśa śravaṇāt /
"puraścakra"iti prakṛtya"puraḥ puruṣa āviśadi"ti"rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya" "sarvāṇi rūpāṇi vicitya dhoro nāmāni kṛtvābhivadanyadāste"iti sarvaśākhāsu sahasraśo mantravādāḥ sṛṣṭikarturevāsaṃsāriṇaḥ śarīrapraveśaṃ darśayanti /
tathā brāhmaṇavādāḥ /
"tatsṛṣṭvā tadevānuprāviśat" "sa etameva sīmānaṃ vidāryaitayā dvārā prāpadyata" "seyaṃ devatemāstisatro devatā anena jīvenā'tmanānupraviśya" "eṣa sarveṣu bhūteṣu gūḍhātmā na prakāśate"ityādyāḥ /
sarvaśrutiṣu ca brahmaṇyātmaśabdaprayogādātmaśabdasya ca pratyagātmābhidhāyakatvāt"eṣa sarvabhūtāntarātmā"iti ca śruteḥ paramātmavyatirekeṇa saṃsāriṇo 'bhāvāt"ekamevādvitīyam" "brahmaivedam" "ātmaivedam"ityādiśrutibhyo yuktamevāhaṃ brahmāsmītyavadhārayitum /
children.translated_text: Therefore, one should propitiate [<s>Brahman</s>] with flower-offerings, water-oblations, praise, prostration, <s>bali</s>-offerings, donations, <s>svādhyāya</s> (Vedic recitation), meditation, <s>yoga</s>, and the like. Having known the all-ruling <s>Brahman</s> through propitiation, one becomes [<s>Brahman</s>]. But one should not think of the non-<s>saṃsārin</s> <s>Brahman</s> as the self of a <s>saṃsārin</s> — just as one should not think of fire as cold, or of space as having form. Even the scriptural [statements] that teach the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and the self will be [explained as] <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passages). And with all the reasoning of logic, treatises, and worldly norms, there would be no contradiction in this way. [Reply:] No — because in the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> passages, the entry of that very [<s>Brahman</s> into bodies] is heard. Having introduced [the topic] with 'he created the cities' (<s>Aitareya Upaniṣad</s>), [the text says] 'the <s>Puruṣa</s> entered the city'; 'having become a counter-form for each form — that was his form, for recognizing him'; 'having fashioned all forms, the wise one, creating names, sits down calling [things] by name' — in all branches [of the <s>Veda</s>], thousands of <s>mantra</s>-passages show the entry of the non-<s>saṃsārin</s> creator into bodies. Similarly, the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-passages: 'Having created that, he entered into that very thing' (<s>Taittirīya Upaniṣad</s>); 'He broke open this seam and entered through this door' (<s>Aitareya Upaniṣad</s>); 'This deity thought: "Let me enter these three deities with this living self"'; 'He is hidden in all beings; he does not manifest' and so forth. And because in all <s>śrutis</s> the word '<s>ātman</s>' is used for <s>Brahman</s>, and because the word '<s>ātman</s>' denotes the inner self — from the <s>śruti</s> 'he is the inner self of all beings,' and because apart from the <s>Paramātman</s> there is no [separate] <s>saṃsārin</s> — from <s>śrutis</s> such as 'one alone without a second,' '<s>Brahman</s> indeed is all this,' 'the self alone is all this' — it is entirely proper to determine 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text:
yadaivaṃ sthitaḥ śāsrārthastadā paramātmanaḥ saṃsaritvam /
tathā ca sati śāsrānarthakyamasaṃsāritve copadeśānarthakyaṃ spaṣṭo doṣaḥ prāptaḥ /
yadi tāvatparamātmā sarvabhūtāntarātmā sarvaśarīrasamparkajanitaduḥkhānyanubhavatīti spaṣṭaṃ parasya saṃsāritvaṃ prāptam /
tathā ca parasyāsaṃsāritvapratipādikāḥ śrutayaḥ kupyeransmṛtayaśca sarve ca nyāyāḥ /
atha kathañcitprāṇiśarīrasambandhajairduḥkhairna sambadhyata iti śakyaṃ pratipādayituṃ paramātmanaḥ sādhyaparihāryābhāvādupadeśānarthakyadoṣo na śakyate nivārayitum /
atra kecitparihāramācakṣate /
paramātmā na sākṣādbhūteṣvanupraviṣṭaḥ svena rūpeṇa /
kiṃ tarhi vikārabhāvamāpanno vijñānātmatvaṃ pratipede /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If the meaning of scripture is thus established, then the <s>Paramātman</s> would be a <s>saṃsārin</s>. And in that case, the clear defect of scripture being pointless follows — and the teaching too would be pointless if there is no <s>saṃsāra</s> [to be liberated from]. If the <s>Paramātman</s>, being the inner self of all beings, experiences the sufferings born from contact with all bodies — then clearly the <s>Paramātman</s>'s being a <s>saṃsārin</s> follows. And the <s>śruti</s> texts that teach the non-<s>saṃsārin</s>-hood of the transcendent would be violated, as would all <s>smṛtis</s> and all [forms of] reasoning. On the other hand, if it can somehow be established that the <s>Paramātman</s> is not afflicted by the sufferings born from contact with the bodies of living beings — even so, because the <s>Paramātman</s> has nothing to be accomplished and nothing to be removed, the fault of the teaching being pointless cannot be averted. To this, some offer a resolution: the <s>Paramātman</s> has not directly entered into beings in his own form.

children.text:
sa ca vijñānātmā parasmādanyo 'nanyaśca /
yenānyastena saṃsāritvasambandhī yenānanyastenāhaṃ brahmetyavadhāraṇārhaḥ /
evaṃ sarvamaviruddhaṃ bhaviṣyatīti /
children.translated_text: Rather, having undergone modification, he has assumed the nature of the cognizing self (<s>vijñānātman</s>). And that <s>vijñānātman</s> is both different from and non-different from the supreme [self]. Insofar as it is different, it is related to <s>saṃsāra</s>; insofar as it is non-different, it is worthy of the determination 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.' Thus, everything will be free from contradiction.

children.text:
tatra vijñānātmano vikārapakṣe etā gatayaḥ-pṛthivīdravyavadane-kadravyasamāhārasya sāvayavasya paramātmana ekadeśavipariṇāmo vijñānātmā ghaṭādivat /
pūrvasaṃsthānāvasthasya vā parasyaikadeśo vikriyate keśoṣarādivat, sarva eva vā paraḥ pariṇametkṣīrādivat /
children.translated_text: In that case, on the view that the <s>vijñānātman</s> is a transformation [of <s>Brahman</s>], the following possibilities arise: on the view that [<s>Brahman</s>] is a composite of many substances like earth — the <s>vijñānātman</s> is the transformation of one part of the composite <s>Paramātman</s>, like a pot [made from a portion of clay]. Or, [on the view that] the transcendent [<s>Brahman</s>] in its original unmodified state — one part of it is modified, like [grey] hair growing on the [otherwise black] head. Or, the entire transcendent [<s>Brahman</s>] transforms, like milk [transforming into curd].

children.text:
tatra samānajātīyānekadravyasamūhasya kaściddravyaviśeṣo vijñānātmatvaṃ pratipadyate yadā, tadā samānajātīyatvādekatvamupacaritameva na tu paramārthataḥ /
tathā ca sati siddhāntavirodhaḥ /
children.translated_text: In the case where a particular substance from a composite of many substances of the same class assumes the nature of the <s>vijñānātman</s> — then, because of being of the same class, the oneness [with <s>Brahman</s>] would be merely figurative, not in ultimate reality. And in that case, there would be a contradiction with the established conclusion [of Advaita].

children.text:
atha nityāyutasiddhāvayavānugato 'vayavī para ātmā, tasya tadavasthasyaikadeśo vijñānātmā saṃsārī-tadāpi sarvāvayavānugatatvādavayavina evāvayavagato doṣo guṇo veti, vijñānātmanaḥ saṃsāritvadoṣeṇa para evātmā sambadhyata iti, iyamapyaniṣṭā kalpanā /
kṣīravatsarvapariṇāmapakṣe sarvaśrutismṛtikopaḥ, sa cāniṣṭaḥ /
"niṣkalaṃ niṣkriyaṃ śāntam" "divyo hyamūrtaḥ puruṣaḥ sabāhyābhyantaro hyajaḥ" "ākāśavatsarvagataśca nityaḥ" "sa vā eṣa mahānaja ātmājaro 'maro 'mṛtaḥ" "na jāyate mriyate vā kadācit" "avyakto 'yam"ityādiśrutismṛtinyāyaviruddhā ete sarve pakṣāḥ /
children.translated_text: If the supreme self is a composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) pervading eternally conjoined parts — and one part of it in that [unmodified] state is the <s>vijñānātman</s>, the <s>saṃsārin</s> — then too, since the composite pervades all its parts, the defect or quality of any part would belong to the composite itself. Thus, by the defect of <s>saṃsāra</s> belonging to the <s>vijñānātman</s>, the supreme self itself would be afflicted — and this too is an undesirable construction. On the view that [<s>Brahman</s>] entirely transforms, like milk [into curd], all <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> would be violated — and that is undesirable. 'Partless, actionless, tranquil' (<s>Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad</s>); 'The divine <s>Puruṣa</s> is indeed formless, both external and internal, unborn' (<s>Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad</s>); 'Like space, all-pervading and eternal' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'This is that great, unborn self, ageless, undying, immortal' (<s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s>); 'It is never born and never dies' (<s>Kaṭha Upaniṣad</s>/<s>Bhagavadgītā</s>); 'This unmanifest one' (<s>Bhagavadgītā</s>) — all these views are contradicted by <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and reasoning.

children.text:
acalasya paramātmana ekadeśapakṣe vijñānātmanaḥ karmaphalavaddeśasaṃsaraṇānupapattiḥ, parasya vā saṃsāritvam-ityuktam /
parasyaikadeśo 'gnivisphuliṅgavatsphuṭito vijñānātmā saṃsaratīti cet-tathāpi parasyāvayavasphuṭanena kṣataprāptiḥ, tatsaṃsaraṇe ca paramātmanaḥ pradeśāntarāvayavavyūhe chidratāprāptiḥ, avraṇatvavākyavirodhaśca /
ātmāvayavabhūtasya vijñānātmanaḥ saṃsaraṇe paramātmaśūnyapradeśābhāvādavayavāntaranodanavyūhanābhyāṃ hṛdayaśūleneva paramātmano duḥkhitvaprāptiḥ /
children.translated_text: It has been said: on the hypothesis that [the <s>vijñānātman</s>] is a part of the immovable <s>Paramātman</s>, it is untenable that the <s>vijñānātman</s> should migrate from place to place like the fruit of action — or else the Supreme itself would be a transmigrating being. [Objection:] A part of the Supreme, split off like a spark from a fire, transmigrates as the <s>vijñānātman</s>. [Reply:] Even so, the splitting off of a part of the Supreme would result in injury [to the Supreme]; and when that [part] transmigrates, there would be the consequence of a hole in the Supreme — because of the rearrangement of the parts into different locations — and this would contradict the scriptural statement of [<s>Brahman</s> being] without wound. When the <s>vijñānātman</s>, which is a part of the <s>Ātman</s>, transmigrates, since there is no place devoid of the <s>Paramātman</s>, through the pushing aside and rearrangement of other parts, the <s>Paramātman</s> would suffer pain — as if from a heart-piercing [weapon].

children.text:
agnivisphuliṅgādidṛṣṭāntaśruterna doṣa iti cet? na, śruterjñāpakatvāt;na śāsraṃ padārthānanyathā kartuṃ pravṛttam /
kiṃ tarhi? yathābhūtānāmajñātānāṃ jñāpane /
kiñcātaḥ? śṛṇu-ato yadbhavati, yathābhūtā mūrtāmūrtādipadārthadharmā loke prasiddhāḥ /
taddṛṣṭāntopādānena tadavirodhyeva vastvantaraṃ jñāpayituṃ pravṛttaṃ śāsraṃ na laukikavastuvirodhajñāpanāya laukikavastuvirodhajñāpanāya laukikameva dṛṣṭāntamupādatte /
upādīyamāno 'pi dṛṣṭānto 'narthakaḥ syāddārṣṭāntikāsaṅgateḥ /
na hyāgniḥ śīta ādityo na tapatīti vā dṛṣṭāntaśatenāpi pratipādayituṃ śakyam, pramāṇāntareṇānyathādhigatatvādvastunaḥ /
na ca pramāṇaṃ pramāṇāntareṇa virudhyate, pramāṇāntarāviṣayameva hi pramāṇāntaraṃ jñāpayati /
na ca laukikapadapadārthāśrayaṇavyatirekeṇāgamena śakyamajñātaṃ vastvantaramavagamayitum /
tasmātprasiddhanyāyamanusaratā na śakyā paramātmanaḥ sāvayavāṃśāṃśitvakalpanā paramārthataḥ pratipādayitum /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Because of the <s>śruti</s> illustration of fire and sparks and the like, there is no fault. [Reply:] No — because <s>śruti</s> serves to make known [what is unknown]. Scripture is not engaged in making objects otherwise [than they are]. What then? [It is engaged] in making known things as they truly are, when they are unknown. Moreover, what follows from this? Listen — the properties of objects, such as being material, immaterial, and so forth, are well-known in the world as they truly are. Scripture, by employing illustrations consistent with those [well-known properties], is engaged in making known a different reality that is not inconsistent with them — not in making known what contradicts worldly objects, for [then] it would employ worldly illustrations [that contradict worldly objects]. An illustration employed in this way would be pointless, because of the incongruity with the thing being illustrated. For it cannot be established, even with a hundred illustrations, that fire is cold or that the sun does not heat — because the object has been otherwise ascertained by another means of valid knowledge. And one means of knowledge does not contradict another means of knowledge, for a [second] means of knowledge makes known precisely what is beyond the scope of the [first] means of knowledge. And it is not possible for scripture to make known an unknown reality except by relying on words with worldly meanings and their referents. Therefore, by following established reasoning, it is not possible to truly establish the attribution of parts — the part-whole relationship — to the <s>Paramātman</s>.

children.text:
"kṣudrā visphuliṅgāḥ" "mamaivāṃśaḥ"iti ca śrūyate smaryate ceti cenna, ekatvapratyayārthaparatvāt /
agnerhi visphuliṅgo 'gnireva ityekatvapratyayārhe dṛṣṭo loke; tathā cāṃśoṃ'śinaikatvapratyayārhaḥ; tatraivaṃ sati vijñānātmanaḥ paramātmavikārāṃśatvavācakāḥ śabdāḥ paramātmavikārāṃśatvavācakāḥ śabdāḥ paramātmaikatvapratyayādhitsavaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But it is heard in <s>śruti</s> and remembered in <s>smṛti</s>: 'The tiny sparks' and 'My own part' (BhG 15.7). [Reply:] No — because [these statements] have as their purpose the cognition of oneness. For a spark of fire is seen in the world to be worthy of the cognition of identity with fire — 'a spark of fire is fire itself.' Similarly, a part is worthy of the cognition of identity with the whole. This being so, the words that express the <s>vijñānātman</s>'s being a modification or part of the <s>Paramātman</s> are intended to establish the cognition of identity with the <s>Paramātman</s>.

children.text:
upakramopasaṃhārābhyāṃ ca-sarvāsu hyupaniṣatsu pūrvamekatvaṃ pratijñāya, dṛṣṭāntairhetubhiśca paramātmano vikārāṃśāditvaṃ jagataḥ pratipādya, punarekatvamupasaṃharati; tadyathehaiva tāvat"idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā"iti pratijñāya, utpattisthitilayahetudṛṣṭāntairvikāravikāritvādyekatvapratyayahetūnprati pādya"anantaramabāhyam" "ayamātmā brahma"ityupasaṃhariṣyati /
tasmādupakramopasaṃhariṣyati /
tasmādupakramopasaṃhārābhyāmayamartho niścīyate paramātmaikatvapratyayadraḍhimna utpattisthitilayapratipādakāni vākyānīti /
children.translated_text: And from the opening and concluding [statements] — for in all <s>Upaniṣads</s>, first the oneness is declared, then the modification-hood, part-hood, and the like of the world with respect to the <s>Paramātman</s> are established through illustrations and reasons, and then oneness is again concluded at the end. For example, right here [in this <s>Upaniṣad</s>], having first declared 'All this is this self' (BṛUp 2.4.6), [the text] will establish the reasons for the cognition of oneness through illustrations of origination, sustenance, and dissolution, and the relationship of modification and modifier — and will conclude with 'Without an inside, without an outside' and 'This self is <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 2.5.19). Therefore, from the opening and concluding [statements], this meaning is ascertained: the sentences teaching origination, sustenance, and dissolution are for the purpose of strengthening the cognition of the oneness of the <s>Paramātman</s>.

children.text:
anyathā vākyabhedaprasaṅgācca-sarvopaniṣatsu hi vijñānātmanaḥ paramātmanaikatvapratyayo vidhīyata ityavipratipattiḥ sarveṣāmupaniṣadvādinām /
tadvidhyekavākyayoge ca sambhavatyutpattyādivākyānāṃ na pramāṇamasti;phalāntaraṃ ca kalpayitavyaṃ syāt;tasmādutpattyādiśrutaya ātmaikatvapratipādanaparāḥ /
children.translated_text: And because otherwise there would be a splitting of the sentences — for it is undisputed among all proponents of the <s>Upaniṣads</s> that the cognition of the identity of the <s>vijñānātman</s> with the <s>Paramātman</s> is enjoined in all <s>Upaniṣads</s>. And when a syntactical connection with that injunction is possible, there is no independent authority for the sentences on origination and the like; and a separate fruit would have to be postulated [for them]. Therefore, the <s>śrutis</s> on origination and the like have as their purpose the establishing of the oneness of the self.

children.text:
atra ca sampradāyavida ākhyāyikāṃ sampracakṣate-kaścitkila rājapitro jātamātra eva mātāpitṛbhyāmapaviddho vyādhagṛhe saṃvardhitaḥ, so 'muṣya vaṃśyatāmajānanvyādhajātipratyayo vyādhajātikarmāṇyevānuvartate; na rājāsmīti rājajātikarmāṇyanuvartate /
yadā punaḥ kaścitparamakāruṇiko rājaputrasya rājaśrīprāptiyogyatāṃ jānannamuṣya putratāṃ bodhayati-"na tvaṃ vyādho 'muṣya rājñaḥ putraḥ, kathañcidvyādhagṛhamanupraviṣṭaḥ"iti-sa evaṃ bodhitastyaktvā vyādhajātipratyayakarmāṇi pitṛpaitāmahīmātmanaḥ padavīmanuvartate rājāhamasmīti /
tathā kilāyaṃ parasmādagnivisphuliṅgādivattajjātireva vibhakta iha dehendriyādigahane praviṣṭo 'saṃsārī san dehendriyādisaṃsāradharmamanuvartate-"dehendriyasaṅghāto 'smi kṛśaḥ sthūlaḥ sukhī duḥkhī"iti paramātmatāmajānannātmanaḥ /
na tvametadātmakaḥ parameva brahmāsyasaṃsārīti pratibodhita ācāryeṇa hitvaiṣaṇātrayānuvṛttiṃ brahmaivāsmīti pratipadyate /
atra rājaputrasya rājapratyayavadbrahmapratyayo dṛḍhībhavati-visphuliṅgava deva tvaṃ parasmādbrahmaṇo bhraṣṭa ityukte visphuliṅgasya prāgagnerbhraṃśādagnyekatvadarśanāt /
children.translated_text: And here the knowers of the tradition recount an illustrative story: a certain prince, abandoned by his parents at the very moment of birth, was raised in a hunter's house. He, not knowing his lineage, with the conviction 'I am a hunter,' follows the occupations of the hunter class; he does not follow the occupations of the royal class [thinking] 'I am a king.' Then some supremely compassionate person, knowing the prince's fitness for attaining royal glory, awakens him to his [true] sonship — 'You are not a hunter; you are the son of such-and-such a king. Somehow you ended up in the hunter's house.' He, thus awakened, abandoning the convictions and occupations of the hunter class, follows the path of his fathers and grandfathers, [knowing] 'I am a king.' Similarly, it is said, this [<s>vijñānātman</s>], being of the same nature [as the Supreme], split off from the Supreme like a spark from a fire, has entered into the thicket of body, senses, and the like. Though in reality a non-transmigrator, he follows the <s>saṃsāric</s> properties of body, senses, and the like — [thinking] 'I am the aggregate of body and senses; I am thin, fat, happy, unhappy' — not knowing his own nature as the <s>Paramātman</s>. When awakened by the teacher — 'You are not of this nature; you are the Supreme <s>Brahman</s> itself, a non-transmigrator' — he abandons the pursuit of the triple desire and realizes: 'I am <s>Brahman</s> alone.' In this [story], just as the prince's conviction of being a king becomes firm, so too the conviction of being <s>Brahman</s> [becomes firm] — when told 'Like a spark, you have fallen from the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>,' because the spark is seen to be identical with fire before its separation from it.

children.text: tasmādekatvapratyayadārḍhyāya suvarṇamaṇilohāgnivisphuliṅgadṛṣṭāntāḥ, notpattyādibhedapratipādanaparāḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the illustrations of gold, gems, iron, fire-sparks, and the like are for the purpose of strengthening the cognition of oneness — not for the purpose of establishing a difference through origination and the like.

children.text:
saindhavadhanavatprajñaptyekarasanairantaryāvadhāraṇāt"ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyam"iti ca /
yadi ca brahmaṇaścitrapaṭavad vṛkṣasamudrādivaccotpattyādyanekadharmavicitratā vijigrāhayiṣitā, ekarasaṃ saindhavaghanavadanantaramabāhyamiti nopasamahariṣyat,"ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyam"iti ca na prāyokṣyata-"ya iha nāneva paśyati"iti nindāvacanaṃ ca /
tasmādekarūpaikatvapratyayadārḍhyāyaiva sarvavedānteṣūtpattisthitilayādikalpanā, na tatpratyayakaraṇāya /
children.translated_text: And from the determination, through [the illustration of] the lump of salt, that [<s>Brahman</s> is] of one taste, awareness, and continuity — and from [the injunction] 'It should be perceived as one only' (BṛUp 4.4.20). And if the [scripture] intended to make known a variegated multiplicity of properties such as origination and the like in <s>Brahman</s> — like a painted canvas, or like a tree or ocean — it would not conclude with 'Without an inside, without an outside, a mass of salt of one taste alone'; nor would it employ [the statement] 'It should be perceived as one only'; and the censorious statement 'Whoever sees multiplicity here' [would not be made]. Therefore, in all <s>Vedānta</s> texts, the postulation of origination, sustenance, dissolution, and the like is solely for the purpose of strengthening the cognition of oneness of one form — not for the purpose of producing that [multiple] cognition.

children.text:
na ca niravayavasya paramātmano 'saṃsāriṇaḥ saṃsāryekadeśakalpanānyāyyā, svato 'deśatvātparamātmanaḥ /
adeśasya parasya ekadeśasaṃsāritvakalpanāyāṃ para eva saṃsārīti kalpitaṃ bhavet /
atha paropādhikṛta ekadeśaḥ parasya, ghaṭakarakādyākāśavat;na tadā tatra vivekināṃ paramātmaikadeśaḥ pṛthaksaṃvyavahārabhāgiti buddhirutpadyate /
children.translated_text: And it is not proper to postulate that a part of the <s>Paramātman</s> — who is partless and a non-transmigrator — is a transmigrator, because the <s>Paramātman</s> is by nature without spatial division. If one postulates that a part of the spatially undivided Supreme is a transmigrator, it would amount to saying that the Supreme itself is a transmigrator. [Objection:] If the part of the Supreme is produced by the <s>upādhis</s> (limiting adjuncts) of the Supreme — like the space [delimited by] a pot, a water-jug, and the like — [Reply:] then for the discriminating, no cognition arises that the portion of <s>Paramātman</s> [so delimited] is a separate entity subject to independent treatment.

children.text:
avivekināṃ vivekināṃ copacaritā buddhirdṛṣṭeti cet? na;avivekināṃ mithyābuddhitvāt, vivekināṃ ca saṃvyavahāramātrālambanārthatvāt-yathā kṛṣṇo raktaścākāśa iti vivekināmapi kadācitkṛṣṇatā raktatā ca ākāśasya saṃvyavahāramātrālambanārthatvaṃ pratipadyata iti, na paramārthataḥ kṛṣṇo rakto vā ākāśo bhavitumarhati /
ato na paṇḍitairbrahmasvarūpapratipattiviṣaye brahmaṇoṃ'śāṃśyekadeśaikadeśivikāravikāritvakalpanā kāryā, sarvakalpanāpanayanārthasāraparatvātsarvopaniṣadām /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] But such a figurative cognition is seen both in the non-discriminating and in the discriminating. [Reply:] No — because for the non-discriminating, it is a false cognition; and for the discriminating, it is merely for the purpose of conventional usage. Just as even for the discriminating, the blackness or redness of space [is spoken of] — the discriminating too understand that the blackness or redness of space is merely for the purpose of conventional usage — space cannot in reality be black or red. Therefore, the wise should not, in the matter of understanding the true nature of <s>Brahman</s>, engage in the postulation of part-whole, portion-possessor, modification-modifier relationships for <s>Brahman</s> — since all <s>Upaniṣads</s> have as their essential purport the removal of all such postulations.

children.text:
ato hitvā sarvakalpanāmākāśasyeva nirviśeṣatā pratipattavyā-"ākāśavatsarvagataśca nityaḥ" "na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyaḥ"ityādiśrutiśatebhyaḥ; nātmānaṃ brahmavilakṣaṇaṃ kalpayet-uṣṇātmaka ivāgnau śītaikadeśam, prakāśātmake vā savitari tamekadeśam-sarvakalpanāpanayanārthasāraparatvātsarvopaniṣadām /
tasmānnāmarūpopādhinimittā eva ātmanyasaṃsāradharmiṇi sarve vyavahārāḥ;"rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva" "sarvāṇi rūpāṇi vicitya dhīro nāmāni kṛtvābhivadanyadāste"ityevamādimantravarṇebhyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, abandoning all postulations, the quality-less nature [of the self] — like space — should be understood, from hundreds of <s>śruti</s> passages such as: 'Like space, all-pervading and eternal' and 'Not touched by the suffering of the world, being external.' One should not postulate the self as different from <s>Brahman</s> — as one would postulate a cold part in fire whose nature is heat, or a dark part in the sun whose nature is light — since all <s>Upaniṣads</s> have as their essential purport the removal of all postulations. Therefore, all transactions regarding the self — which is by nature free from <s>saṃsāra</s> — are caused by the limiting adjuncts of name and form alone, from mantra passages such as 'He became the counterpart of every form' (RV 6.47.18) and 'The wise one, having fashioned all forms and created all names, sits uttering [them]' (TaiĀ 3.12.7).

children.text:
na svata ātmanaḥ saṃsāritvam, alaktakādyupādhisaṃyogajanitaraktasphaṭikādibuddhivadbhrāntameva, na paramārthataḥ /
"dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva" "na vardhate karmaṇā no kanīyān" "na lipyate karmaṇā pāpakena" "samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhantam" "śuni caiva śvapāke ca"ityādiśrutismṛtinyāyebhyaḥ paramātmano 'saṃsāritaiva /
ata ekadeśo vikāraḥ śaktirvā vijñānātmā anyo veti vikalpayituṃ niravayavatvābhyupagame viśeṣato na śakyate /
aṃśādiśrutismṛtivādāścaikatvārthāḥ, na tu bhedapratipādakāḥ, vivakṣitārthaikavākyayogāt-ityavocāma /
children.translated_text: The <s>saṃsāric</s> nature of the self is not intrinsic — it is a delusion, like the cognition of redness in a crystal produced by the contact with the red adjunct of lac and the like — not in ultimate reality. From <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and reasoning such as: 'It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were' (BṛUp 4.3.7), 'It is not increased by action nor diminished' (BṛUp 4.4.23), 'It is not tainted by sinful action' (BṛUp 4.4.23), 'Dwelling equally in all beings' (BhG 13.27), and 'In a dog and in a dog-eater' (BhG 5.18) — the non-<s>saṃsāric</s> nature of the <s>Paramātman</s> alone [is established]. Therefore, given the acceptance that [<s>Brahman</s>] is partless, it is particularly impossible to hypothesize that the <s>vijñānātman</s> is a different [entity] — whether a part, a modification, or a power. And the <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> statements about parts and the like have oneness as their meaning, and are not meant to establish difference — because they form a syntactical unity with the intended meaning. This we have stated.

children.text: sarvopaniṣadāṃ paramātmaikatvajñāpanaparatve atha kimarthaṃ tatpratikūlor'tho vijñānātmabhedaḥ parikalpyata iti? karmakāṇḍaprāmāṇyavirodhaparihārāyetyekeca karmapratipādakāni hi vākyāni anekakriyākārakaphalabhoktṛkartrāśrayāṇi, vijñānātmabhedābhāve hyasaṃsāriṇa eva paramātmana ekatve kathamiṣṭaphalāsu kriyāsu pravartayeyuḥ? aniṣṭaphalābhyo vā kriyābhyo nivartayeyuḥ? kasya vā baddhasya mokṣāyopaniṣadārabhyeta? api ca paramātmaikatvāvādipakṣe kathaṃ paramātmaikatvopadeśaḥ? kathaṃ vā tadupadeśagrahaṇaphalam? baddhasya hi bandhanāśāyopadeśastadabhāva upaniṣacchāsraṃ nirviṣayameva /
children.translated_text: If all <s>Upaniṣads</s> have as their purport the making known of the oneness of the <s>Paramātman</s>, then for what purpose is the contrary meaning — the difference of the <s>vijñānātman</s> — postulated? [Answer:] Some say, for the purpose of avoiding contradiction with the authority of the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s> (ritual section). For the sentences that establish ritual action are based on multiple actions, instruments, fruits, enjoyers, agents, and their substrata; and in the absence of the difference of the <s>vijñānātman</s>, if the <s>Paramātman</s> alone, being a non-transmigrator, is one — how could [those sentences] impel [anyone] toward actions yielding desired fruits? Or turn [anyone] away from actions yielding undesired fruits? Or for whose bondage would the <s>Upaniṣad</s> be commenced for the purpose of liberation? Moreover, on the view that advocates the oneness of the <s>Paramātman</s>, how would the teaching of the oneness of the <s>Paramātman</s> [work]? Or how would the fruit of receiving that teaching [work]? For teaching is for the destruction of the bondage of one who is bound — in the absence of that [bondage], the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> scripture would be without subject matter.

children.text:
evaṃ tarhi upaniṣadvādipakṣasya karmakāṇḍavādipakṣeṇa codyaparihārayoḥ samānaḥ panthāḥ-yena bhedābhāve karmakāṇḍaṃ nirālambanamātmānaṃ na labhte prāmāṇyaṃ prati tathopaniṣadapi /
evaṃ tarhi yasya prāmāṇye svārthavidhāto nāsti, tasyaiva karmakāṇḍasyāstu prāmāṇyam;upaniṣadāṃ tu prāmāṇyakalpanāyāṃ svārthavighāto bhavediti mā bhūtprāmāṇyam /
na hi karmakāṇḍaṃ pramāṇaṃ sadapramāṇaṃ bhavitumarhati;na hi pradīpaḥ prakāśyaṃ prakāśayati, na prakāśayati ceti /
pratyakṣādipramāṇavipratiṣedhācca-na kevalamupaniṣado brahmaikatvaṃ pratipādayantyaḥ svārthavighātaṃ karmakāṇḍaprāmāṇyavighātaṃ ca kurvanti;pratyakṣādiniścitabhedapratipattyarthapramāṇaiśca virudhyante /
tasmādaprāmāṇyamevopaniṣadām;anyārthatā vāstu;na tveva brahmaikatvapratipattyarthatā /
children.translated_text: In that case, the method of raising and resolving objections is the same for the proponent of the <s>Upaniṣads</s> as for the proponent of the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s> — by whatever [reasoning] the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s>, in the absence of difference, finds no support for its authority and cannot establish the self — the same applies to the <s>Upaniṣads</s>. [Reply:] In that case, let the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s> alone — whose authority does not involve the destruction of its own meaning — have authority; but if authority is attributed to the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, there would be the destruction of their own meaning — so let them not have authority! [Reply:] No — for the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s>, being a valid means of knowledge, cannot [at the same time] be a non-valid means of knowledge. For a lamp does not both illumine and fail to illumine what is to be illuminated. And because of the contradiction with the means of valid knowledge such as perception and the like — not only do the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, by establishing the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, destroy their own meaning and the authority of the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s>; they also contradict the other means of valid knowledge — perception and the like — which ascertain the cognition of difference. Therefore, the <s>Upaniṣads</s> are without authority; or let them have a different meaning — but their meaning is certainly not the cognition of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text:
na;uktottaratvāt /
pramāṇasya hi pramāṇatvamapramāṇatvaṃ vā pramotpādanānutpādananimitm, anyathā cetstambhādīnāṃ prāmāṇyaprasaṅgācchabdādau prameye /
kiñcātaḥ? yadi tāvadupaniṣado brahmaikatvapratipattipramāṃ kurvanti, kathamapramāṇaṃ bhaveyuḥ? sa bhavānevaṃ vadanvaktavyaḥ-upaniṣatprāmāṇyapratiṣedhārthaṃ bhavato vākyamupaniṣatprāmāṇyapratiṣedhaṃ kiṃ na karotyevāgnirvā rūpaprakāśam? atha karoti /
yadi karoti bhavatu tadā pratiṣedhārthaṃ pramāṇaṃ bhavadvākyam, agniśca rūpaprakāśako bhavet;pratiṣedhavākyaprāmāṇye bhavatyevopaniṣadāṃ prāmāṇyam /
atra bhavanto bruvantu kaḥ parihāra iti?
children.translated_text: [Reply:] No — because [these objections] have already been answered. For the validity or invalidity of a means of knowledge depends on whether it produces or fails to produce valid cognition — otherwise there would be the absurd consequence that even posts and the like would have validity regarding knowable objects like sound and the rest. Moreover, what follows? If the <s>Upaniṣads</s> do produce the valid cognition of the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, how could they be invalid? You, speaking thus, should be asked: does your statement, aimed at negating the authority of the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, in fact negate the authority of the <s>Upaniṣads</s> — or not? Does fire not in fact illuminate forms? If it does [illuminate them], then your statement [negating the authority of the Upaniṣads] is indeed a valid means of knowledge for its [stated] purpose of negation, and fire too would be an illuminator of forms. But if your negating statement is a valid means of knowledge, then the authority of the <s>Upaniṣads</s> is itself [thereby] established. Now you [opponents] — tell us: what is the way out of this?

children.text:
nanvatra pratyatrā madāvākya upaniṣatprāmāṇyapratiṣedhārthapratipattiragnau ca rūpaprakāśanapratipattiḥ pramā /
kastarhi bhavataḥ pradveṣo brahmaikatvapratyaye pramāṃ pratyakṣaṃ kurvatīṣūpaniṣatsūpalabhyamānāsu pratiṣedhānupapatteḥ /
śokamohādinivṛttiśca pratyakṣaṃ phalaṃ brahmaikatvapratipattipāramparyajanitamityavocāma /
tasmāduktottaratvādupaniṣadaṃ pratyaprāmāṇyaśaṅkā tāvannāsti /
yaccoktaṃ svārthavighātakaratvādaprāmāṇyamiti, tadapi na, tadarthapratipatterbādhakābhāvāt /
na hi
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] [Objection:] But here, in the rebutting statement itself, the knowledge that the Upaniṣadic [sentences] lack authority is [itself] valid knowledge, and [likewise] the knowledge that fire reveals forms is valid knowledge. What then is your hostility toward the cognition of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness? Since the Upaniṣads are observed to produce directly experienced valid knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness, a denial [of their authority] is untenable. And we have said that the cessation of sorrow, delusion, and the like is the directly experienced fruit, produced by the successive unfolding of the cognition of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness. Therefore, since [the objection] has already been answered, there is no suspicion of the Upaniṣads' lack of authority. As for the statement that [the Upaniṣads] lack authority because they undermine their own meaning — that too is wrong, because there is no sublating cognition for the knowledge of their meaning. For there is no

children.text:
upaniṣadbhyaḥ-brahmaikamevādvitīyam, naiva ca-iti pratipattirasti;yathāgniruṣṇaḥ śītaścetyasmādvākyādviruddhārthadvayapratipattiḥ /
abhyupagamya caitadavocāma;na tu vākyaprāmāṇyasamaya eṣanyāyaḥ-yadutaikasya vākyasyānekārthatvam /
sati cānekārthatve, svārthaśca syāt, tadvighātakṛcca viruddho 'nyor'thaḥ /
na tvetat-vākyapramāṇakānāṃ viruddhamaviruddhaṃ ca, evaṃ vākyam, anekamarthaṃ pratipādayatītyeṣa samayaḥ;arthaikatvādvyekavākyatā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] cognition arising from the Upaniṣads of the form '<s>Brahman</s> is one alone, without a second' and simultaneously 'it is not so' — as in the case of the sentence 'fire is hot and cold,' from which two contradictory cognitions arise. And we have said this by way of concession; but in fact, this principle — that a single sentence has multiple meanings — is not [valid in] the convention of sentence-based knowledge. If there were multiple meanings, there would be its own meaning, and [also] a contradictory other meaning that undermines it. But this is not [the case]: for those whose knowledge is based on sentences, the convention is not that a sentence conveys contradictory and non-contradictory [meanings together]; rather, because of the unity of meaning, there is unity of the sentence.

children.text:
na ca kānicidupaniṣadvākyāni brahmaikatvapratiṣedhaṃ kurvanti /
yattu, laukikaṃ vākyam-agniruṣṇaḥ śītaśceti, na tatraikavākyatā, tadekadeśasya pramāṇāntaraviṣayānuvāditvāt /
agniḥ śīta ityetadekaṃ vākyam;agniruṣṇa iti tu pramāṇāntarānubhavasmārakam, na tu svayamarthāvabodhakam /
ato nāgniḥ śīta ityanenaikavākyatā, pramāṇāntarānubhavasmāraṇenaivopakṣīṇatvāt /
yattu viruddhārthapratipādakamidaṃ vākyamiti manyate, tacchītoṣṇapadābhyām agnipadasāmānādhikaraṇyaprayoganimittā bhrāntiḥ;na tvevaikasya vākyasyānekārthatvaṃ laukikasya vaidikasya vā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And no Upaniṣadic sentences deny the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>. As for the worldly sentence 'fire is hot and cold' — there is no unity of sentence there, because one part of it merely restates what is the object of another means of knowledge. 'Fire is cold' — this is one sentence. But 'fire is hot' is merely a reminder of the experience of another means of knowledge, and is not itself productive of new understanding. Therefore, there is no unity of sentence between it and 'fire is cold,' since [the latter] is already exhausted by merely reminding one of the experience of another means of knowledge. The belief that this sentence conveys contradictory meanings is a confusion caused by the co-referential usage of the words 'hot' and 'cold' with the word 'fire.' But in reality, no single sentence — whether worldly or Vedic — has multiple meanings.

children.text:
yaccoktaṃ karmakāṇḍaprāmāṇyavighātakṛdupaniṣadvākyamiti, tanna; anyārthatvāt /
brahmaikatvapratipādanaparā hyupaniṣado neṣṭārthaprāptau sādhanopadeśaṃ tasminvā puruṣaniyogaṃ vārayanti, anekārthatvānupapattereva /
na ca karmakāṇḍavākyānāṃ svārthe pramā notpadyate /
asādhāraṇe cetsvārthe pramāmutpādayati vākyam, kuto 'nyena virodhaḥ syāt? brahmaikatve nirviṣayatvātpramānotpadyata eveti cet? na, pratyakṣatvātpramāyāḥ /
"darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta" "brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ"ityevamādivākyebhyaḥ pratyakṣā pramā jāyamānā; 'sā naiva bhaviṣyati, yadyupaniṣado brahmaikatvaṃ bodhayiṣyanti' ityanumānam; na cānumānaṃ pratyakṣavirodhe prāmāṇyaṃ labhate; tasmādasadevaitadgīyate-pramaiva notpadyata iti /
api ca yathāprāptasyaiva avidyāpratyupasthāpitasya kriyākārakaphalasyāśrayaṇena iṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihāropāyasāmānye pravṛttasya tadviśeṣamajānataḥ tadācakṣāṇā śrutiḥ kriyākārakaphalabhedasya lokaprasiddhasya satyatāmasatyatāṃ vā nācaṣṭe na ca vārayati, iṣṭāniṣṭaphalaprāptiparihāropāyavidhiparatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] As for the claim that the Upaniṣadic sentences undermine the authority of the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s> (ritual section) — that is not so, because they have a different purpose. The Upaniṣads, being directed at establishing the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, do not obstruct the teaching of means for attaining desired goals, nor do they prohibit a person's engagement therein — since the impossibility of multiple meanings [in a single sentence] has been established. And it is not the case that the <s>karmakāṇḍa</s> sentences do not produce valid knowledge in their own domain. If a sentence produces valid knowledge in its own exclusive domain, how could there be conflict with another? [Objection:] Since in the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, valid knowledge does not arise because there is no object [to be known] — [we say:] no, because valid knowledge is directly experienced. From sentences such as 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>' and 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should not be killed' — directly experienced valid knowledge arises. [The objection is:] 'That valid knowledge would not arise if the Upaniṣads were to teach the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>' — this is an inference. But an inference does not obtain authority when it contradicts direct experience. Therefore, it is sung in vain that valid knowledge does not arise. Moreover, scripture, dealing with the already given — the action, agents, and results that are presented by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — when a person is already engaged in the general pursuit of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired but does not know the specifics, teaches him those specifics of the relationship between end and means — like a lamp [revealing] forms in darkness. But scripture does not forcefully restrain or compel people like servants; for people are seen to transgress even scripture because of the force of attachment and the like.

children.text:
yathā kāmyeṣu pravṛttā śrutiḥ kāmānāṃ mithyājñānaprabhavatve satyapi yathāprāptāneva kāmānupādāya tatsādhanānyeva vidhatte, na tu kāmānāṃ mithyājñānaprabhavatvādanartharūpatvaṃ ceti na vidadhāti /
tathā nityāgnihotrādiśāsramapi mithyājñānaprabhavaṃ kriyākārakabhedaṃ yathāprāptamevādāya iṣṭaviśeṣaprāptimaniṣṭaviśeṣaparihāraṃ vā kimapi prayojanaṃ paśyadagnihotrādīni karmāṇi vidhatte /
nāvidyāgocarāsadvastuviṣayamiti na pravartate yathā kāmyeṣu /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Just as scripture, though engaged in [teaching] optional rites (<s>kāmya karmas</s>), even while the desire [that motivates them] is the product of false knowledge — takes those desires as given and prescribes the means for [fulfilling] them, without teaching that desires are purposeless because they arise from false knowledge — similarly, scripture dealing with obligatory rites such as the daily <s>Agnihotra</s>, taking the differentiation of action and agents — which is the product of false knowledge — as given, and seeing some purpose in [prescribing] the attainment of a specific desired goal or the avoidance of a specific undesired result, prescribes actions such as <s>Agnihotra</s>. It does not refrain from operating [merely] because [the differentiation] is within the domain of <s>avidyā</s> and pertains to unreal objects — just as in the case of optional rites.

children.text: na ca puruṣā na pravarterannavidyāvantaḥ, dṛṣṭatvādyathā kāminaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And it is not the case that persons possessed of <s>avidyā</s> would not engage [in action] — because this is observed, just as those who have desires [do engage].

children.text:
vidyāvatāmeva karmādhikāra iti cet? na, brahmaikatvavidyāyāṃ karmādhikāravirodhasyoktatvāt /
etena brahmaikatve nirviṣayatvādupadeśena tadgrahaṇaphalābhāvadoṣaparihāra ukto veditavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] [Objection:] Only those who have knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) are qualified for action. [We say:] No — because the contradiction between the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness and qualification for action has already been stated. By this, the objection that 'in the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, because there is no object, the teaching [is futile] and the fruit of grasping that teaching is absent' should be understood as having been answered.

children.text:
puruṣecchārāgādivaicitryācca-anekā hi puruṣāṇamicchāḥ, rāgādayaśca doṣā vicitrāḥ;tataśca bāhyaviṣayarāgādyapahṛtacetaso na śāsraṃ nivartayituṃ śaktam;nāpi svabhāvato bāhyaviṣayaviraktacetaso viṣayeṣu pravartayituṃ śaktam;kintu śāsrādetāvadeva bhavati-idamiṣṭasādhanamidamaniṣṭasādhanamiti sādhyasādhanasambandhaviśeṣābhivyaktiḥ-pradīpādivattamasi rūpādijñānam /
na tu śāsraṃ bhṛtyāniva balānnivartayati niyojayati vā;dṛśyante hi puruṣā rāgādigauravācchāsramapyatikrāmantaḥ /
tasmāt puruṣamativaicitryamapekṣya sādhyasādhanasambandhaviśeṣānanekadhopadiśati /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And because of the variety of human desires, attachments, and the like — for the desires of persons are many, and defects such as attachment and the like are varied. Therefore, scripture is not capable of turning away one whose mind is drawn to external objects by attachment and the like; nor is it capable of directing toward sense-objects one whose mind is naturally detached from external objects. Rather, from scripture only this much results: the disclosure of the specific relationship between end and means — 'this is the means to the desired, this is the means to the undesired' — like the knowledge of forms and the like [produced by] a lamp in darkness. But scripture does not forcefully restrain or compel people like servants; for people are seen to transgress even scripture because of the force of attachment and the like. Therefore, taking into account the variety of human dispositions, [scripture] teaches the specifics of the relationships between end and means in manifold ways.

children.text:
tatra puruṣāḥ svayameva yathāruci sādhanaviśeṣeṣu pravartante, śāsraṃ tu savitṛpradīpādivadudāsta eva /
tathā kasyacitparo 'pi puruṣārtho 'puruṣārthavadavabhāsate; yasya yathāvabhāsaḥ, sa tathārūpaṃ puruṣārthaṃ paśyati; tadanurūpāṇi sādhanānyupāditsate /
tathā cārthavādo 'pi-"trayāḥ prājāpatyāḥ prajāpatau pitari brahmacaryamūṣuḥ"ityādiḥ /
tasmānna brahmaikatvaṃ jñāpayiṣyanto vedāntā vidhiśāsrasya bādhakāḥ /
na ca vidhiśāsrametāvatā nirviṣayaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therein, persons of their own accord, according to their preference, engage in specific means. But scripture, like the sun or a lamp, remains indifferent. Similarly, for some persons, even the highest human goal appears to be no goal at all. Each person sees the human goal in the form corresponding to how it appears to him, and seeks the means appropriate to that. And thus there is also an <s>arthavāda</s> (narrative passage): 'The three [groups of] <s>Prajāpati</s>'s offspring lived the life of <s>brahmacarya</s> with <s>Prajāpati</s>, their father' (BṛUp 5.2.1) and so forth. Therefore, the Vedānta texts, in making known the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, do not sublate the injunctive scripture. Nor would the injunctive scripture thereby become objectless.

children.text:
nāpyuktakārakādibhedaṃ vidhiśāsramupaniṣadāṃ brahmaikatvaṃ prati prāmāṇyaṃ nivartayati /
svaviṣayaśūrāṇi hi pramāṇāni, śrotrādivat /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Nor does the injunctive scripture, with its stated differentiation of agents and the like, nullify the authority of the Upaniṣads with respect to the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>. For the means of knowledge are valiant in their own domain — like the ear and the other [senses, each in its own sphere].

children.text: tatra paṇḍitaṃmanyāḥ kecitsvacittavaśātsarvaṃ pramāṇamitaretaraviruddhaṃ manyante, tachā pratyakṣādivirodhamapi codayanti brahmaikatve-śabdādayaḥ kila śrotrādiviṣayā bhinnāḥ pratyakṣata upalabhyante, brahmaikatvaṃ bruvatāṃ pratyakṣavirodhaḥ
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Among these, certain persons who fancy themselves learned, on the basis of their own minds, consider all means of knowledge to be mutually contradictory. They also raise the objection of contradiction with perception and the like regarding the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>: 'Sounds and the like, the objects of the ear and the other [senses], are perceived as distinct through direct perception. For those who assert the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, there would be contradiction with perception.'

children.text:
syāt; tathā śrotrādibhiḥ śabdādyupalabdhāraḥ kartāraśca dharmādharmayoḥ pratiśarīraṃ bhinnā anumīyante saṃsāriṇaḥ; tatra brahmaikatvaṃ bruvatāmanumānavirodhaśca /
tathā ca āgamavirodhaṃ vadanti-"grāmakāmo yajeta" "paśukāmo yajeta" "svargakāmo yajeta"ityevamādivākyebhyo grāmapaśusvargādikāmāstatsādhanādyanuṣṭhātāraśca bhinnā avagamyante /
atrocyate-te tu kutarkadūṣitāntaḥkaraṇā brāhmaṇādivarṇāpasadā anukampanīyā āgamārthavicchinnasampradāyabuddhaya iti /
katham? śrotrādidvāraiḥ śabdādibhiḥ pratyakṣata upalabhyamānairbrahmaṇa ekatvaṃ virudhyata iti vadanto vaktavyāḥ-kiṃ śabdādīnāṃ bhedenākāśaikatvaṃ virudhyata iti;atha na viruddhyate, na tarhi pratyakṣavirodhaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'Similarly, those who perceive sounds and the like through the ear and other [senses], and who are the agents of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, are inferred to be distinct transmigrating selves in each body. For those who assert the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, there would be contradiction with inference.' And they also assert contradiction with scripture: 'From sentences such as "one who desires a village should sacrifice," "one who desires cattle should sacrifice," "one who desires heaven should sacrifice" — distinct desires for village, cattle, heaven, and the like, and distinct practitioners who perform the corresponding means, are understood.' To this we say: those whose inner faculties are corrupted by sophistical reasoning, who are degraded from the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> and other <s>varṇas</s>, are to be pitied — for their understanding of the meaning of scripture is cut off from the tradition. How so? Those who say that the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> is contradicted by sounds and the like, perceived as distinct through the doorway of the ear and the other [senses], should be asked: 'Is the oneness of space contradicted by the distinctness of sounds and the like?' If it is not contradicted, then there is no contradiction with perception [regarding <s>Brahman</s>'s oneness either].

children.text: yaccoktaṃ pratiśarīraṃ śabdādyupalabdhāro dharmādharmayośca kartāro bhinnā anumīyante, tathā ca brahmaikatve 'numānavirodha iti;bhinnā kairanumīyanta iti praṣṭavyāḥ;atha yadi brūyuḥ-sarvairasmābhiranumānakuśalairiti-ke yūyamanumānakuśalā ityevaṃ pṛṣṭānāṃ kimuttaram /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] As for the statement that those who perceive sounds and the like in each body, and who are agents of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, are inferred to be distinct, and that therefore in the oneness of <s>Brahman</s> there would be a contradiction with inference — [such persons] should be asked: by whom are the distinct [selves] inferred? If they reply: 'By all of us who are skilled in inference' — [they should be asked:] 'Who are you, the ones skilled in inference?' — when thus asked, what would be their answer?

children.text:
śarīrendriyamana ātmasu ca pratyekamanumānakauśalapratyākhyāne, śarīrendriyamanaḥsādhanā ātmāno vayamanumānakuśalāḥ, anekakārakasādhyatvātkriyāṇāmiti cet? evaṃ tarhyanumānakauśalebhavatāmanekatvaprasaṅgaḥ; anekakārakasādhyā hi kriyeti bhavadbhirevābhyupagatam /
tatrānumānaṃ ca kriyā; sā śarīrendriyamana ātmasādhanaiḥ kārakairātmakartṛkā nirvartyata ityetatpratijñātam /
tatra vayamanumānakuśalā ityevaṃ vadadbhiḥ-śarīrendriyamanaḥsādhanā ātmānaḥ pratyekaṃ vayamaneka ityabhyupagataṃ syāt /
aho anumānakauśalaṃ darśitamapucchaśṛṅgaistārkikabalīvardaiḥ /
yo hyātmānameva na jānāti sa kathaṃ mūḍhastadgataṃ vā jānīyāt? tatra kimanuminoti? kena vā liṅgena? na hyātmanaḥ svato bhedapratipādakaṃ kiñcilliṅgamasti, yena liṅgenātmabhedaṃ sādhayet; yāni liṅgānyātmabhedasādhanāya nāmarūpavantyupanyasyanti, tāni nāmarūpagatānyupādhaya evātmano ghaṭakarakāpavarakabhūcchidrāṇīvākāśasya /
yadākāśasya bhedaliṅgaṃ paśyati, tadātmano 'pi bhedaliṅgaṃ labheta saḥ; na hyātmanaḥ parato 'pi viśeṣamabhyupagacchadbhistārkikaśatairapi bhedaliṅgamātmano darśayituṃ śakyate; svatastu dūrādapanītameva, aviṣayatvādātmanaḥ /
yadyatpara ātmadharmatvenābhyupagacchati, tasya tasya nāmarūpābhyāṃ cātmano 'nyatvābhyupagamāt,"ākāśo vai nāma nāmarūpayornirvahitā te yadantarā tadbrahma"iti śruteḥ"nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi"iti ca /
utpattipralayātmake hi nāmarūpe, tadvilakṣaṇaṃ ca brahma-ato 'numānasyaivāviṣayatvātkuto 'numānavirodhaḥ? etenāgamavirodhaḥ pratyuktaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] If, rejecting the individual claim to skill in inference on the part of body, senses, mind, and self [respectively], they say: 'We — the selves equipped with body, senses, and mind as instruments — are the ones skilled in inference, because actions are accomplished through multiple agents' — then, for you, the absurd consequence of multiplicity of inferring-agents [within a single person] would follow. For you yourselves accept that actions are accomplished through multiple agents. Now, inference too is an action. And it is claimed by you that it — being accomplished through the agents of body, senses, mind, and the self as agent — is performed with the self as agent. But in saying 'we are skilled in inference,' [if] the selves — each equipped with body, senses, and mind as instruments — are [each] accepted as 'we are many' — what a display of skill in inference by these logician-bullocks without tail or horns! For one who does not even know his own self — how could that confused person know something pertaining to [the self]? What does he infer? And by what mark (<s>liṅga</s>)? For there is no mark belonging to the self itself that would establish its distinctness. Those marks that [the logicians] adduce — marks possessing name and form — to establish the distinctness of the self, those are merely limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) belonging to name and form — like the pots, sheaths, curtains, and cavities [that appear to delimit] space. When one sees a mark of distinction in space [due to such adjuncts], then one might find a mark of distinction in the self; but even hundreds of logicians, who accept no intrinsic distinction in the self, cannot demonstrate a mark of distinction in the self. And intrinsically, [distinction] is removed from afar, because the self is not an object [of knowledge]. Whatever the opponent accepts as a property of the self — that is accepted as belonging to name and form, which are other than the self. [This follows] from the <s>śruti</s>: 'Space indeed is the separator of name and form; that which is between them is <s>Brahman</s>' (ChUp 8.14.1); and 'Let me separate out name and form' (ChUp 6.3.2). For name and form are subject to origination and dissolution, while <s>Brahman</s> is of a different character from them. Therefore, since inference itself has no [valid] object [regarding <s>Brahman</s>], how could there be contradiction with inference? By this, the [alleged] contradiction with scripture is also answered.

children.text:
yaduktaṃ brahmaikatve yasmā upadeśaḥ, yasya copadeśagrahaṇaphalam, tadabhāvādekatvopadeśānarthakyamiti, tadapi na, anekakārakasādhyatvātkriyāṇāṃ kaścodyo bhavati /
ekasminbrahmaṇi nirupādhike nopadeśaḥ, nopadeṣṭā, na copadeśagrahaṇaphalam; tasmādupaniṣadāṃ cānarthakyamityetadabhyupagatameva /
athānekakārakaviṣayānarthakyaṃ codyate-na, svato /
ñabhyupagamavirodhādātmavādinām /
tasmāttārkikacāṭabhaṭarājāpraveśyam abhayaṃ durgamidamalpabuddhyagamyaṃ śāsraguruprasādarahitaiśca,"kastaṃ madāmadaṃ devaṃ madanyo jñātumarhati" "devairatrāpi vicikitsitaṃ purā" "naiṣā tarkeṇa matirāpaneyā"-varaprasādalabhyatvaśrutismṛtivādebhyaśca;"tadejati tannaijati taddūre tadvantike"ityādiviruddhadharmasamavāyitvaprakāśakamantravarṇebhyaśca /
gītāsu ca-"matsthāni sarvabhūtāni"ityādi /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And in the <s>Gītā</s>: 'All beings abide in Me' (BhG 9.4) and the like.

children.text: tasmātparabrahmavyatirekeṇa saṃsārī nāma nānyadvastvantaramasti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, apart from the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, there is no other entity called a transmigrator.

children.text: tasmātsuṣṭhūcyate"brahma vā idamagra āsīt tadātmānamevāved ahaṃ brahmāsmi" "nānyadato 'sti draṣṭṛ nānyadato 'sti śrotṛ"ityādiśrutiśatebhyaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, it is well said — from hundreds of <s>śrutis</s> such as: '<s>Brahman</s> alone was this in the beginning; it knew itself alone — I am <s>Brahman</s>' (BṛUp 1.4.10); 'There is no other seer; there is no other hearer' (BṛUp 3.8.11) and the like.

children.text: tasmātparasyaiva brahmaṇaḥ"satyasya satyam"nāmopaniṣatparā //20//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, the supreme <s>Brahman</s> alone, called 'the Truth of truth,' is the ultimate purport of the Upaniṣads. (20)

[Commentary:] As for the claim that in the oneness of <s>Brahman</s>, there would be no one to teach, no one to receive the teaching, and no fruit of grasping the teaching, and therefore the teaching of oneness would be purposeless — that too is wrong. What objection is there, since actions are accomplished through multiple agents? In the one <s>Brahman</s> without limiting adjuncts, there is no teaching, no teacher, and no fruit of grasping the teaching. Therefore, the purposelessness of the Upaniṣads too is accepted. But if the objection of purposelessness is raised with respect to the domain of multiple agents — [we say:] no, because of its own [self-refuting nature]. Because of the contradiction with the self-admission of those who assert the self [as multiple]. Therefore, this fearless [teaching], this impregnable fortress, is not to be entered by the logicians' chariot-warriors and kings; it is inaccessible to those of small intellect and to those devoid of the grace of scripture and teacher — [as stated in:] 'Who other than I could know that God who is intoxicated and not-intoxicated?' (KaUp); 'Even the gods had doubts about this in ancient times' (KaUp 1.1.21); 'This understanding is not to be attained by reasoning' (KaUp 1.2.9) — from such <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> statements [declaring] that it is to be obtained by grace.
