children.text: tato hoṣastaścākrāyaṇa upararāma //2//
children.translated_text: Thereupon, <s>Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa</s> fell silent. // 2 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 3.4.2: <s>Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa</s> said — just as someone, having first promised one thing but then having changed his mind, says something different — [as if] having first promised 'I shall show you directly a [cow] that moves and runs,' and then subsequently indicating it through inferential marks such as moving and running — 'that is a cow, that is a horse' — in the same way, this <s>Brahman</s> has been indicated by you through inferential marks such as breathing and the rest.
In short — abandoning the pretext motivated by the thirst for a cow — 'that which is <s>Brahman</s> directly, without intermediary — which is the self, the innermost of all — explain that to me.'
The other replied: 'As I initially asserted — your self is of such a nature — I maintain that very assertion. It is exactly as stated by me.' [<s>Uṣasta</s> objects:] 'But you have said to make that self an object, like a pot' — [<s>Yājñavalkya</s> replies:] 'that cannot be done, because it is impossible.' 'Why then is it impossible?' He says: 'Because of the very nature of the thing (<s>vastu</s>).' 'What then is that nature of the thing?' 'The seer-hood of seeing' — i.e., being the seer of the act of seeing.
For the self is the seer of seeing. And seeing is of two kinds: mundane and ultimate. Therein, mundane seeing is the mental modification (<s>antaḥkaraṇavṛtti</s>) connected with the eye. It is produced — it arises and perishes. But the seeing that belongs to the self — like the heat and light of fire — being the essential nature of the seer, neither arises nor perishes.
When it is associated with the produced [mundane seeing], which serves as a limiting adjunct, it is figuratively spoken of as 'seeing' — and as if there were a difference, [one speaks of] 'the seer' and 'the seeing' [as distinct]. That mundane seeing, emerging through the door of the eye, tinged by form — even as it arises, being as if merged with the eternal seeing of the self — being its reflection, as if pervaded by it — it arises and also perishes. Therefore, figuratively, the seer, though always seeing, is said 'to see' and 'not to see.' But there is never any alteration of the seer's seeing. And thus [the text] will say in the sixth [chapter]: 'It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were' (BṛUp 4.3.7). And: 'For there is no cessation of the seer's seeing' (BṛUp 4.3.23).
This is the meaning [the text] states: 'Of the mundane seeing, which is an object of action, you cannot see the seer — the one who pervades it with his own eternal seeing.' That mundane seeing, which is an object — tinged by form, manifesting form — does not reach the inner self, its own pervader. Therefore, you cannot see that inner self, the seer of seeing.
Similarly, 'of the hearing, you cannot hear the hearer.' Similarly, 'of the thinking — of the mere mental modification — you cannot think its pervader.' Similarly, 'of the knowing — of the mere intellectual modification (<s>buddhivṛtti</s>) — you cannot know its pervader.'
This is the very nature of the thing — therefore it indeed cannot be shown like a cow and the like.
'You cannot see the seer of seeing' — some interpret these words differently: 'Of seeing, the seer — the agent of seeing — without making a division of seeing, the agent of mere seeing, you cannot see.' 'Of seeing' (<s>dṛṣṭeḥ</s>) — the sixth case is in the objective sense. That seeing, when being produced, becomes an object like a pot. 'The seer' — by the agent-suffix <s>tṛ</s>, it indicates the seer's agency of seeing. Thus, 'the seer of seeing' means 'the agent of seeing' — this is the intent of those commentators. Therein, they do not see the fault that the word 'seeing' in the genitive (<s>dṛṣṭeḥ</s>) is purposeless; or, among those who do see [the fault], [they dismiss it as] mere repetition, insubstantial, or a scribal error, and disregard it.
But how [can it be purposeless]? Since the agency of seeing is already established by the <s>tṛ</s>-suffix alone, '<s>dṛṣṭeḥ</s>' (of seeing) is redundant. Then, one should simply say: 'you cannot see the seer.' For the <s>tṛ</s>-suffix is understood as [denoting] the agent of the verbal root from which it is derived. [One says] 'he leads the goer' or 'the eater,' and that much alone is the expression employed. But 'the goer of going' or 'the breaker of breaking' should not be employed when there is no specific difference in meaning. Nor should it be discarded as <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) when a real meaning is available. Nor is it a scribal error — because all [recensions] are in agreement.
Therefore, it is the intellectual weakness of those commentators, not a scribal error. Just as we have explained — distinguishing mundane seeing from eternal seeing — the self qualified by eternal seeing is to be demonstrated; accordingly, the twofold use of the word 'seeing' — as a qualifier of agent and object respectively — is appropriate for determining the essential nature of the self.
And with the passage from elsewhere — 'For there is no cessation of the seer's seeing' — coherence as a single statement is achieved. Similarly, with another <s>śruti</s> — 'The eyes see' (ChUp), 'This hearing is heard' — coherence as a single statement is achieved. And by reasoning too — for only in this way is the eternality of the self established: in the absence of modification, and [yet if it were] subject to modification, [it would be] both eternal and non-eternal — which is self-contradictory.
'It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were' (BṛUp 4.3.7); 'For there is no cessation of the seer's seeing' (BṛUp 4.3.23); 'This is the eternal greatness of the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>' (BṛUp 4.4.23) — these words of <s>śruti</s> cannot be taken otherwise.
[Objection:] But the words 'seer,' 'hearer,' 'thinker,' 'knower' — these too do not fit if the self is without modification. [Reply:] No — because they are restatements of what is already established in common parlance. Those [words] are not for determining the essential nature of the self. But 'of seeing, the seer' and the like — since no other meaning is possible, their intent in the meaning as explained is understood.
Therefore, it is precisely because of non-comprehension that the qualifier '<s>dṛṣṭeḥ</s>' (of seeing) was abandoned [by those commentators]; since no other meaning is possible for 'of seeing, the seer' and the like, their intent in the meaning as explained is understood.

children.translated_text: Then <s>Kahola Kauṣītakeya</s> questioned him: '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>,' he said, 'that which is <s>Brahman</s> directly, without intermediary — which is the self, the innermost of all — explain that to me.' 'This is your self, the innermost of all.' 'Which one, O <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, is the innermost of all?' 'That which transcends hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death. Having known this very self, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of mendicants. For the desire for sons is the same as the desire for wealth; the desire for wealth is the same as the desire for worlds — for both of these are mere desires. Therefore, a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, having become disgusted with learning, should remain in childlike [simplicity]. Having become disgusted with both childlike [simplicity] and learning, then [he becomes] a <s>muni</s> (silent sage). Having become disgusted with both non-silence and silence, then [he becomes] a [true] <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>. That <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> — by whatever means he may be such — is indeed of this very nature. Everything other than this is afflicted.' Thereupon <s>Kahola Kauṣītakeya</s> fell silent. // BṛhUp 3.5.1 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 3.5.1:] Bondage, together with its impelling cause, has been stated. And the existence of the one who is bound, as well as his separateness [from <s>Brahman</s>], has been ascertained. Now, the means of liberation from that bondage — namely, self-knowledge (<s>ātmajñāna</s>) accompanied by renunciation (<s>saṃnyāsa</s>) — is to be stated. Hence <s>Kahola</s>'s question is commenced: 'Then <s>Kahola</s>' — by name, the offspring of <s>Kuṣītaka</s>, hence <s>Kauṣītakeya</s> — 'questioned [<s>Yājñavalkya</s>]: "<s>Yājñavalkya</s>," he said' — as before. 'Explain to me that <s>Brahman</s> which is directly present and not remote — which is the self, the innermost of all.' That by knowing which one is freed from bondage. <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said: 'This is your self.' [Question:] Was one and the same self asked about by <s>Uṣasta</s> and <s>Kahola</s>, or were two different selves — having similar characteristics — [asked about]? [Answer:] It is fitting [to say they are] different, because [otherwise] there would be the impossibility of non-repetition between the two questions. For if one and the same self were intended in the questions of <s>Uṣasta</s> and <s>Kahola</s>, then — since it would already be known through just one question — a second question on the same subject would be purposeless. Nor is the sentence [merely] an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage). Therefore, some explain that these are two different selves — called the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (individual knower) and the <s>Paramātman</s>. That is wrong — because of the commitment through 'your' (<s>ta</s>). For in the reply, it was committed: 'This is your (<s>ta</s>) self.' And two selves for a single aggregate of body and senses are not tenable. For a single aggregate of body and senses is ensouled by a single self. Nor is the self of <s>Uṣasta</s> one thing and the self of <s>Kahola</s> another, different by birth. Because for both, if [the self were] non-primary (<s>gauṇa</s>), selfhood and innermost-ness would be untenable. If one is the non-primary <s>Brahman</s>, the other must necessarily be primary — and likewise for selfhood and innermost-ness — because the meanings of the words are mutually contradictory. If one is the innermost <s>Brahman</s>, the primary self, the other must necessarily be non-innermost and non-self and non-primary. Therefore, the hearing [of the same self] twice is with the intention of a particular distinction. That which is the same in the second [question] as what was previously stated — that much is merely a restatement of the previous; and some particular distinction of that very [self], not [yet] stated, is to be stated. What then is that distinction? It is said: in the first question, [the topic is] that there exists a separate self for whom this bondage with its impelling cause has been stated. In the second, however, the distinction stated is that very self's transcendence of the <s>saṃsāric</s> properties such as hunger and the like — through the complete knowledge of which distinction, accompanied by renunciation, one is freed from the previously stated bondage. Therefore, in the question and answer — both ending with 'This is your self' — there is equality of meaning. [Objection:] But how can there be the co-existence of contradictory properties in one and the same self — transcendence of hunger and the like, and possession of hunger and the like? [Reply:] No — because this has been resolved. We have said repeatedly that <s>saṃsāric</s> nature is merely a delusion born from the contact with the different limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) characterized by the aggregate of body and senses — which are modifications of name and form. And [this is resolved] in the context of explaining contradictory <s>śruti</s> statements. Just as rope, mother-of-pearl, and sky are [perceived as] endowed with snake, silver, and dirt respectively — qualified by superimposed properties — [while] intrinsically, rope, mother-of-pearl, and sky are just themselves alone. And thus, there is no contradiction in the co-existence of contradictory properties in things. [Objection:] If [<s>Brahman</s>] has the limiting adjuncts of name and form, the <s>śrutis</s> 'One alone, without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1) and 'There is no plurality whatsoever here' (BṛUp 4.4.19) would be contradicted. [Reply:] No — because this has been resolved through the illustration of water-foam and the illustrations of clay and the like. When, from the standpoint of ultimate reality, in accordance with <s>śruti</s>, name and form — being examined as different from the essential reality of the <s>Paramātman</s> — are in truth not [real] entities, just like modifications such as clay [into pots] or water-foam and pot-like modifications — then, with reference to that [examination], the statements 'One alone without a second' and 'There is no plurality whatsoever here' and the like pertain to the domain of the vision of ultimate reality. But when, through natural <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the essential nature of <s>Brahman</s> — which, like the essential nature of rope, mother-of-pearl, and sky, exists in its own form, untouched in its nature by anything — is not discriminated from the limiting adjuncts of body and senses constituted by name and form, and the vision of the limiting adjuncts of name and form alone is the natural [condition] — then all this transactional usage of the existence of other entities [operates]. And this false transactional usage created by difference [exists] for those for whom there exists a real entity different from the reality of <s>Brahman</s>, and for those for whom there does not. But for those who speak of ultimate reality, when the entity is examined in accordance with <s>śruti</s> — [the question:] does a real entity truly exist, or does it not? — <s>Brahman</s> alone, one without a second, devoid of all transactional usage, is determined. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. For we do not admit the existence of another entity when established in the determination of ultimate reality — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'One alone without a second' (ChUp 6.2.1) and 'Without an interior, without an exterior' (BṛUp 2.5.19). Nor is it denied that, at the time of transactional usage involving name and form, for those who lack discrimination, the transactional usage of action, agent, fruit, and the like does not exist. Therefore, all transactional usage — both pertaining to the science [of <s>Brahman</s>] and worldly — is relative to knowledge and ignorance. Hence, there is no suspicion of any contradiction. The transactional usage created by the [distinction between] ultimate reality and conventional reality is unavoidable for all disputants.

Therein, with reference to the essential nature of the ultimate self, the question [is asked] again: 'Which one, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, is the innermost of all?' The answer follows: 'He who transcends hunger and thirst' — '<s>aśanāyā</s>' is the desire to eat; '<s>pipāsā</s>' is the desire to drink. 'He who transcends hunger and thirst' — the connection is with what will be said [next]. Just as space, even while being perceived by the undiscriminating as having dirt and stain, transcends that dirt and stain — because in ultimate reality its nature is untouched by them — similarly, <s>Brahman</s>, even while being perceived by the deluded as having hunger, thirst, and the like — 'I am hungry, I am thirsty' — transcends them, because in ultimate reality its nature is untouched by them. From the <s>śruti</s>: 'Not touched by the suffering of the world, being external' (KaUp 2.2.11). The meaning is: [untouched] by the suffering superimposed by the world of the ignorant. The compounding of hunger and thirst [into a single compound] is because both are properties of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) alone. '<s>Śoka</s>' (sorrow) and '<s>moha</s>' (delusion) — '<s>śoka</s>' here means desire (<s>kāma</s>). The unhappiness that arises when one, overwhelmed by craving, contemplates a desired object — that is the seed of desire, for desire is indeed kindled by it. '<s>Moha</s>' (delusion) is wrong cognition, non-discrimination, confusion — born from contrary understanding. And that is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the generative seed of all misfortune. Because of the difference in their effects, sorrow and delusion are not compounded [together]. These two have the mind as their locus. Similarly, old age (<s>jarā</s>) and death (<s>mṛtyu</s>) — which have the body as their locus — he transcends. '<s>Jarā</s>' (old age) is the transformation of the aggregate of body and senses, marked by wrinkles, grey hair, and the like. '<s>Mṛtyu</s>' (death) is the disintegration of that [aggregate], the conclusion of transformation. These two — old age and death — having the body as their locus, he transcends. Those [properties] — hunger and the like, having <s>prāṇa</s>, mind, and body as their loci, constantly operating in living beings, like day and night, like ocean waves — are called <s>saṃsāra</s> in living beings. He — the one characterized [in the <s>śruti</s>] as 'the seer of seeing' (BṛUp 3.4.2) and the like, who is directly present, not remote, non-figurative, the innermost self of all beings from <s>Brahmā</s> down to a blade of grass — is never touched by the <s>saṃsāric</s> properties of hunger, thirst, and the like, just as space [is never touched] by clouds, dust, and impurities.

Having known this very self — one's own essential reality — 'This I am, the supreme <s>Brahman</s>, eternally free from all <s>saṃsāra</s>, eternally satisfied' — the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> [renounce]. The mention of '<s>brāhmaṇas</s>' is because <s>brāhmaṇas</s> alone are qualified for renunciation (<s>vyutthāna</s>). 'Having risen up' (<s>vyutthāya</s>) — having made a turning away in the contrary direction. From what? This he says: from the desire for sons (<s>putraiṣaṇā</s>) — the desire for a son is <s>putraiṣaṇā</s>. 'By a son I shall conquer this world' — the desire directed toward a son as the means of conquering the world; the acquisition of a wife [is implied]. [That is,] not having acquired a wife — this is the meaning. And from the desire for wealth (<s>vittaiṣaṇā</s>) — the acquisition of wealth such as cattle and the like, the instruments of action; 'By this [wealth], having performed <s>karma</s>, I shall conquer the world of the fathers' — or, 'by knowledge conjoined [with <s>karma</s>], the world of the gods' — or, 'by the knowledge of <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s> alone, through celestial wealth, the world of the gods.' Some [say] there is no rising up (<s>vyutthāna</s>) from celestial wealth — because it is said that one rises up by its very power. That is wrong — because [celestial wealth] is included among the desires, as stated: 'This much alone is desire' (<s>etāvān vai kāmaḥ</s>). Knowledge that has the deities such as <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s> and others as its object — that is called '<s>citta</s>' (mind-oriented [knowledge]) — because it is the cause of the world of the gods. For the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> that has as its object the mass of consciousness (<s>prajñānaghana</s>) free from all limiting adjuncts is not the cause of attaining the world of the gods — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'Therefore, he became all' (BṛUp 1.4.10) and 'He becomes their self' (BṛUp 1.4.10). For it is by its power that one rises up. From the specific statement: 'Having known this very self' (BṛUp 3.5.1). Therefore, having risen up from all three — the desires whose objects are means to the attainment of non-self worlds. Desire is <s>kāma</s> — from the <s>śruti</s>: 'This much alone is <s>kāma</s>.' Not having developed craving for this threefold means of attaining the non-self worlds — this is the meaning. For every desire for means is itself a desire for fruit. Therefore, he explains: the <s>śruti</s> [treats] these as one desire. How? Because the desire for sons is itself the desire for wealth — since both equally serve as means to a visible fruit. The desire for wealth is itself the desire for worlds — for it is solely for the purpose of fruit. For everyone, impelled by the purpose of fruit alone, takes up every means. Therefore, [these three] are one desire alone — because the desire for worlds cannot be accomplished without means; thus, through the division into end and means, both are desires. Therefore, for the knower of <s>Brahman</s>, there is no action (<s>karma</s>) nor any means of action. Therefore, the <s>brāhmaṇas</s> who have gone beyond — [having abandoned] all action and all means of action — all [instruments] such as the sacred thread (<s>yajñopavīta</s>) and the like, which are the occasions for divine (<s>daiva</s>), ancestral (<s>pitṛ</s>), and human (<s>mānuṣa</s>) rites — for by these [instruments] divine, ancestral, and human rites are performed, from the <s>śruti</s>: '<s>Nivīta</s> is for human beings' (BṛUp 6.4.25) and the like. Therefore, the former <s>brāhmaṇas</s> — knowers of <s>Brahman</s> — having risen up from actions and from the means of action such as the sacred thread and the like, having adopted the state of the <s>paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka</s> (supreme wandering ascetic), live by begging (<s>bhikṣācarya</s>) — they practice going about for the purpose of alms; having abandoned all conventional marks (<s>smārta liṅga</s>), [begging is] merely the means of sustenance for those who have taken refuge in the order of renunciation alone, the mark of the wandering ascetic. [The renunciant is] devoid of distinguishing marks (<s>liṅga</s>). From <s>smṛtis</s> such as: 'Therefore, the knower of <s>dharma</s> is without marks, of unmanifest marks, of unmanifest conduct' and the like. From <s>śrutis</s> such as: 'Then the wandering ascetic, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, without possessions' and the like. And: 'Cutting off the tuft and hair, discarding the sacred thread.' [Objection:] But from the present-tense statement 'having risen up, they then live by begging' — this is an <s>arthavāda</s> (descriptive passage), not an injunctive form; no injunctive verbal ending such as <s>liṅ</s>, <s>loṭ</s>, or <s>tavya</s> is heard. Therefore, by a mere <s>arthavāda</s>, the abandonment of means such as the sacred thread prescribed by <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s> cannot be effected. One should perform [rites] wearing the sacred thread, or have [them] performed, or [at least] sacrifice.

iti vedaparityāge doṣaśravaṇāt /
"upāsane gurūṇāṃ vṛddhānāmatithīnāṃ home japyakarmaṇi bhojana ācamane svādhyāye ca yajñopavītī syādi"ti parivrājakadharmeṣu ca gurūpāsanasvādhyāyabhojanācamānādīnāṃ karmaṇāṃ śrutismṛtiṣukartavyatayā coditatvādgurvādyupāsanāṅgatvena yajñopavītasya vihitatvāttatparityāgo naivāvagantuṃ śakyate /
yadyapyeṣaṇābhyo vyutthānaṃ vidhīyata eva tathāpi putrādyeṣaṇābhyastisṛbhya eva vyutthānaṃ na tu sarvasmātkarmaṇaḥ karmasādhanācca vyutthānam /
sarvaparityāge cāśrutaṃ kṛtaṃ syācchutaṃ ca yajñopavītādi hāpitaṃ syāt /
tathā ca mahānaparādho vihitākaraṇapratiṣiddhācaraṇanimittaḥ kṛtaḥ syāt /
tasmādyajñopavītādiliṅgaparityāgo 'ndhaparamparaiva /
na /
"yajñopavītaṃ vedāṃśca sarva tadvarjayedyatiḥ"iti śruteḥ /
api cā'tmajñānaparatvātmarvasyā upaniṣadaḥ /
ātmā draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavya iti hi prastutaṃ sa cā'tmaiva sākṣādaparokṣātsarvāntaro 'śanāyādisaṃsāradharmavarjita ityevaṃ vijñeya iti tāvatprasiddham /
sarvā hīyamupaniṣadevaṃpareti vidhyantaraśeṣatva tāvannāstyato nārthavādaḥ /
ātmajñānasya kartavyatvāt /
ātmā cāśanāyādidharmavānna bhavatīti sādhanaphalavilakṣaṇo jñātavyaḥ /
ate 'vyatirekeṇā'tmano jñānamavidyā /
"anyo 'sāvanyo 'hamasmīti na sa veda" "mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati""ekadhaivānudraṣṭavyam""ekamevādvitīyam" "tattvamasi"ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /
kriyāphalaṃ sādhanaṃ cāśanāyādisaṃsāradharmātītādātmano 'nyadavidyāviṣayam /
"yatra hi dvaitamiva bhavati" "anyo 'sāvanyo 'hamasmīti na sa veda" "atha ye 'nyathāto viduḥ"ityādivākyaśatebhyaḥ /
na ca vidyāvidye ekasya puruṣasya yaha bhavato virodhāttamaḥ prakāśāviva /
tasmādātmavido 'vidyāviṣayo 'dhikāro na draṣṭavyaḥ kriyākārakaphalabhedarūpaḥ /
"mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti"ityādi ninditatvāt /
sarvakriyāsādhanaphalānāṃ cāvidyāviṣayāṇāṃ tadviparītātmavidyayā hātavyatveneṣṭatvāt /
yajñopavītādisādhanānāṃ ca tadviṣayatvāt /
tasmādasādhanaphalasvabhāvādātmano 'nyaviṣayā vilakṣaṇaiṣaṇā /
ubhe hyete sādhanaphale eṣaṇe eva bhavataḥ /
yajñopavītādestatsādhyakarmaṇāṃ ca sādhanatvāt /
ubhe hyete eṣaṇe eveti hetuvacanenāvadhāraṇāt /
yajñopavītādisādhanāttatsādhyebhyaśca karmabhyo 'vidyāviṣayatvādeṣaṇārūpatvācca jihāsitavyarūpatvācca vyutthānaṃ vidhitsitameva /
nanu upaniṣada ātmajñānaparatvād vyutthānaśrutiḥ tatstutyarthā, na vidhiḥ /
na;vidhitsitavijñānena samānakartṛkatvaśravaṇāt /
na hi akartavyena kartavyasya samānakartṛkatvena vede kadācidapi śravaṇaṃ sambhavati;kartavyānāmeva hi abhipavabahomabhakṣāṇāṃ yathā śravaṇam, abhiputya hutvā bhakṣayantīti, tadvadātmajñānaiṣaṇāvyutthānabhikṣācaryāṇāṃ kartavyānāmeva samānakartṛkatvaśravaṇaṃ bhavet /
avidyāviṣayatvādeṣaṇātvācca arthaprāpta ātmajñānavidhereva yajñopavītādiparityāgaḥ, na tu vidhātavya iti cet!sutarāmātmajñānavidhinaiva vihitasya samānakartṛkatvaśravaṇena dārḍhyepapattiḥ, tathā bhikṣācaryasya ca /
yat punaruktaṃ vartamānāpadeśādarthavādamātramiti - na, audumbarayūpādividhisamānatvādadoṣaḥ /
'vyutthāya bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti'ityanena pārivrājyaṃ vidhīyate, pārivrājyāśrame ca yajñopavītādisādhanāni vihitāni, liṅgaṃ ca śrutibhiḥ smṛtiśca /
atastad varjayitvā anyasmād vyutthānam eṣaṇātve 'pīti cet? na, vijñānasamānakartṛkāt pārivrājyādeṣaṇāvyutthānalakṣaṇāt pārivrājyāntaropapatteḥ;yaddhi tadeṣaṇābhyo vyutthānalakṣaṇaṃ pārivrājyaṃ tadātmajñānāṅgam, ātmajñānavirodhyeṣaṇāparityāgarūpatvāt, avidyāviṣayatvāccaiṣaṇāyāḥ, tadvyatirekeṇa cāstyāśramarūpaṃ pārivrājyaṃ brahmalokādiphalaprāptisādhanam, yadviṣayaṃ yajñopavītādisādhanavidhānaṃ siṅgavidhānaṃ ca /
na ca eṣaṇārūpasādhanāpādānasya āśramadharmamātreṇa pārivrājyāntare viṣaye sambhavati sati, sarvopaniṣadvihitasya ātmajñānasya bādhanaṃ yuktam, yajñopavītādyavidyāviṣayaiṣaṇārūpasādhanopāditsāyāṃ cāvaśyam asādhanaphalarūpasya aśanāyādisaṃsāradharmavarjitasya ahaṃ brahmāsmi, ithi vijñānaṃ bādhyate, na ca tadrādhanaṃ yuktam. sarvopaniṣadāṃ tadarthaparatvāt /
'bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti'ityeṣaṇāṃ grāhayantī śrutiḥ svayameva bādhata iti cet? athāpi syādeṣaṇābhyo vyutthānaṃ vidhāya punareṣaṇakadeśaṃ bhikṣācaryagrāhayantī tatsambaddhamanyadapi grāhayatīti cet? na, bhikṣācaryasyāprayojakatvād hutvottarakālabhakṣaṇāt /
śeṣapratipattikarmatvādaprayojakaṃ hi tat, asaṃskāramapi syāt, na tu bhikṣācaryam;niyamādṛṣṭasyāpi brahmavido 'niṣṭatvāt /
niyamādṛṣṭasyāniṣṭatve kiṃ bhikṣācaryeṇeti cet! na, anyasādhanād vyutthānasya vihitatvāt /
tathāpi kiṃ teneti cet? yadi syāt, bādhamabhyupagamyate hi tat /
yāni pārivrājye 'bhihitāni vacanāni'yajñopavītyevādhīyīta'ityādīni, tānyavidvatpārivrājyamātraviṣayāṇīti parihṛtāni;itarathā ātmajñānabādhaḥ syāditi hyuktam,"nirāśiṣamanārambhaṃ nirnamastāramastutim /
akṣīṇaṃ kṣīṇakarmāṇaṃ taṃ devā brāhmaṇe viduḥ"iti sarvakarmābhāvaṃ darśayati smṛtirviduṣaḥ,"vidvāṃliṅgo dharmajñaḥ"iti ca /
tasmāt paramahaṃsapārivrājyameva vyutthānalakṣaṇaṃ pratipadyetātmavit sarvakarmasādhanaparityāgarūpamiti /
yasmāt pūrve brāhmaṇā etamātmānam asādhanaphalasvabhāvaṃ viditvā sarvasmāt sādhanaphalasvarūpādeṣaṇālakṣaṇād vyutthāya bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti sma, dṛṣṭādṛṣṭārthaṃ karma tatsādhanaṃ ca hitvā, tasmād adyatve 'pi brāhmaṇo brahmavit pāṇḍityaṃ paṇḍitabhāvam, etadātmavijñānaṃ pāṇḍityam, nirvidya niḥśeṣaṃ viditvā ātmavijñānaṃ niravaśeṣaṃ kṛtvetyarthaḥ - ācāryata āgamataśca, eṣaṇābhyo vyutthāya-eṣaṇāvyutthānāvasānameva hi tat pāṇḍityam eṣaṇātiraskārodbhavatvādeṣaṇāvirudvatvāt;eṣaṇāmatiraskṛtya na hyātmajñānenaiva vihitameṣaṇāvyutthānam ātmajñānasamānakartṛkatvāpratyayopādānaliṅgaśrutyād daḍhīkṛtam /
tasmādepaṇābhyo vyutthāya jñānabanabhāvena bālyena tiṣṭhāset sthātumicchet /
sādhanaphalāśrayaṇaṃ hi balamitareṣāmanātmavidām, tad balaṃ hitvā vidvān asādhanaphalasvarūpātmavijñānameva balaṃ tadbhāvameva kevalamāśrayet, tadāśrayaṇe hi karaṇānyeṣaṇāvipaye enaṃ hratvā sthāpayituṃ nītsahante;jñānabalahīnaṃ hi mūḍhaṃd daṣṭādṛṣṭaviṣayāyām eṣaṇāyāmevainaṃ karaṇāni niyojayanti;balaṃ nāma ātmavidyayāśeṣaviṣayadṛṣṭitiraskaraṇam;atastadbhāvena bālyena tiṣṭhāset;tathā"ātmanā bindate vīryam"iti śrutyantarāt /
"nāyamātmā balahīnena labhyaḥ"iti ca /
bālyaṃ ca pāṇḍityaṃ ca nirvidya niḥśeṣaṃ kṛtvātha mananānmuniryogī bhavati;etāvadvi brāhmaṇena kartavyam, yaduta sarvānātmapratyayatiraskaraṇam;etat kṛtvā kṛtakṛtyo yogī bhavati /

amaunaṃ ca ātmajñānānātmapratyayatiraskārau pāṇḍityabālyasaṃjñakau niḥśeṣaṃ kṛtvā, maunaṃ nāma anātmapratyayatiraskaraṇasya parthavasānaṃ phalam, tacca nirvidyātha brāhmaṇaḥ kutakṛtyo bhavatibrahmaiva sarvamiti pratyaya upajāyate /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And <s>amauna</s> (non-silence) — having thoroughly accomplished the two — namely self-knowledge and the dispelling of cognitions of non-self, called <s>pāṇḍitya</s> (scholarship) and <s>bālya</s> (childlike simplicity) — <s>mauna</s> (silence) is the final result of the completion of the dispelling of non-self cognitions. Having accomplished that (<s>nirvidya</s>), then the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, one whose purpose is fulfilled — the cognition arises that '<s>Brahman</s> alone is everything.'

children.text: sa brāhmaṇaḥ kutakṛtyaḥ, ato brāhmaṇaḥ, nirūpacaritaṃ hi tadā tasya brāhmaṇyaṃ prāptam;kena syāt kena caraṇena bhavet? yena syād yena caraṇena bhavet, tenedṛśa evāyam-yena kenaciccaraṇena syāt tenedṛśa eva uktalakṣaṇa eva brāhmaṇo bhavati;yena kenaciccaraṇeneti stutyartham-yeyaṃ brāhmaṇyāvasthā seyaṃ stūyate, na tu caraṇe 'nādaraḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] That <s>brāhmaṇa</s> has fulfilled his purpose; therefore [he is called] a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — for then his <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-hood is attained in the literal sense, not figuratively. 'By what would he be? By what conduct would he become [such]?' — by whatever [conduct] he might be, by whatever conduct he might become [such], he is exactly of this [described] character. By whatever conduct he might be — he is of exactly this described character as a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>. 'By whatever conduct' — this is said for the purpose of praise; it is this state of <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-hood that is being praised, not a disregard for conduct.

children.text: ata etasmād brāhmaṇyāvasthānāda aśanāyādyatītātmasvarūpād nityatṛptād anyad avidyāvipayam eṣaṇālakṣaṇaṃ vastvantaram, ārta vināśi ārtiparigṛhītam, svapnamāyāmarīcyudakasamam asāram, ātmaivākaḥ kevalo nityamukta iti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, from this state of <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-hood — from the essential nature of the self which has transcended hunger and the like, which is eternally satisfied — everything else, belonging to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>, having the character of desire (<s>eṣaṇā</s>), constituting a different entity — is <s>ārta</s> (afflicted), perishable, seized by suffering, equal to a dream, an illusion, or a mirage-water, devoid of substance. The self alone is one, solitary, eternally liberated.

children.text: tato ha kaholaḥ kaupātakeyaḥ upararāma //1//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Thereupon, <s>Kahola Kauṣītakeya</s> held his peace. (1)

[Commentary:] Because there is the hearing of fault in abandoning the <s>Veda</s> — 'In service of teachers, elders, and guests; in oblation (<s>homa</s>); in recitation (<s>japya</s>); in eating; in sipping water (<s>ācamana</s>); and in self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) — one should wear the sacred thread (<s>yajñopavīta</s>)' — and since, even among the duties of a wandering ascetic (<s>parivrājaka</s>), acts such as service of the teacher, self-study, eating, sipping water, and the like are enjoined as obligatory by <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>, and since the sacred thread is enjoined as an accessory to service of the teacher and the like, its abandonment is simply impossible to countenance. Even though rising above the [three] desires (<s>eṣaṇās</s>) is indeed enjoined, still the rising above is only from the three desires — for sons, wealth, and worlds — not from all action and the instruments of action. And if everything were abandoned, what is unheard of would be done, and what is heard [as enjoined] — the sacred thread and the like — would be violated. And thus a great offense would be committed, caused by non-performance of what is enjoined and performance of what is prohibited. Therefore, the abandonment of markers (<s>liṅga</s>) such as the sacred thread is merely a case of the blind leading the blind. [Answer:] No — because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'The <s>yati</s> (renunciant) should discard the sacred thread, the <s>Vedas</s>, and everything.' Moreover, because the Upaniṣad is dedicated to the knowledge of the self (<s>ātmajñāna</s>). 'The self is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon' — this is the topic that has been introduced; and that self is directly, immediately, the innermost of all, free from the properties of <s>saṃsāra</s> such as hunger and the like — thus it is to be known; this much is well established. This entire Upaniṣad leads toward this [conclusion]; and since it is not subordinate to any other injunction, it is not mere <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage) — because the knowledge of the self is to be accomplished. And since the self is not characterized by hunger and the like, it is to be known as different in nature from means (<s>sādhana</s>) and results (<s>phala</s>). Therefore, knowledge of the self in terms of anything other than it is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — [as known] from <s>śrutis</s> such as: 'He who thinks "that is one, I am another" does not know'; 'He who sees manifoldness here goes from death to death'; 'It is to be seen as one alone'; 'One alone, without a second'; '<s>Tat tvam asi</s>' ('That thou art'), and the like. The results of action and the means [thereto] — being other than the self which transcends <s>saṃsāra</s>-properties such as hunger — belong to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>; [this is known] from hundreds of statements such as: 'Where there is, as it were, duality'; 'He who thinks "that is one, I am another" does not know'; 'But those who know otherwise,' and the like. And <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) and <s>avidyā</s> cannot co-exist in one and the same person — being mutually contradictory, like darkness and light. Therefore, the qualification (<s>adhikāra</s>) pertaining to the domain of <s>avidyā</s> — in the form of differentiation of action, agent, and result — is not to be attributed to the knower of the self; because [such differentiation] is condemned [by <s>śruti</s>]: 'He goes from death to death' and the like; and because all action, means, and results — belonging to the domain of <s>avidyā</s> — are desired to be abandoned through self-knowledge, which is the opposite of that [<s>avidyā</s>]. And since the instruments such as the sacred thread belong to the domain of that [<s>avidyā</s>], therefore the desire (<s>eṣaṇā</s>) pertaining to anything other than the self — whose nature is free from means and results — is of a different character. For both of these — means and results — are nothing but desires. Since the sacred thread and the like are means, and the actions accomplished through them are [also] means — and since [the text] emphatically states through the causal clause that 'both of these are nothing but desires' — therefore, rising above (<s>vyutthāna</s>) from the instruments such as the sacred thread and from the actions accomplished through them is indeed intended — since they belong to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>, since they have the nature of desire, and since they are of the nature of what is to be abandoned. [Objection:] Since the Upaniṣad is devoted to self-knowledge, the <s>śruti</s> about rising above [desires] is meant for praising [self-knowledge], not as an injunction. [Answer:] No — because [the text] states that [the rising above has] the same agent as the knowledge that is intended to be enjoined. For in the <s>Veda</s>, it is never possible that what is not to be done would be stated as having the same agent as what is to be done. Just as the acts of sprinkling, offering, and eating are [heard as having] the same agent — 'having sprinkled, having offered, [they] eat' — so too the knowledge of the self, the rising above desires, and the practice of mendicancy (<s>bhikṣācarya</s>) — these are heard as having the same agent, because all are to be done. [Objection:] Since desires belong to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>, the abandonment of the sacred thread and the like follows as a natural consequence of the injunction of self-knowledge alone, and need not be separately enjoined. [Answer:] All the more, then — since [the abandonment is] enjoined by the very injunction of self-knowledge — its strength is confirmed by the statement of same-agenthood; and likewise for the practice of mendicancy. As for the claim that [the passage] is merely <s>arthavāda</s> because it uses the present tense [describing what the ancients did] — this is not a fault, because it is analogous to the injunction of the <s>audumbara</s> (fig-wood) sacrificial post and the like. [The <s>śruti</s>] 'Having risen above, they practice mendicancy' — by this, the state of <s>parivrājya</s> (wandering asceticism) is enjoined. And in the <s>parivrājya āśrama</s>, instruments such as the sacred thread are enjoined, and the marker (<s>liṅga</s>) [is prescribed] by <s>śrutis</s> and <s>smṛtis</s>. [Objection:] Therefore, rising above is from something other [than the sacred thread], even though the desires [are to be abandoned]? [Answer:] No — because the <s>parivrājya</s> characterized by rising above desires — having the same agent as <s>vijñāna</s> (knowledge) — can be subsumed within another form of <s>parivrājya</s> [i.e. the <s>paramahaṃsa</s> form]. For that <s>parivrājya</s> which is characterized by rising above desires is an auxiliary to self-knowledge — since it has the nature of abandoning desires that are opposed to self-knowledge, and since desires belong to the domain of <s>avidyā</s>. And separately from that, there is [another] <s>parivrājya</s> having the form of an <s>āśrama</s> — which serves as the means to attain results such as <s>brahmaloka</s> — and it is with reference to this that the injunction of instruments like the sacred thread and the injunction of markers are given. And it is not reasonable that, when there exists another domain — that of mere <s>āśrama</s>-dharma — for the adoption of instruments in the form of desires, the self-knowledge enjoined by all the Upaniṣads should be sublated; for in the desire to adopt instruments [like the sacred thread] which belong to the domain of <s>avidyā</s> and have the form of desires, the knowledge 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' — which pertains to what is free from means and results, free from <s>saṃsāra</s>-properties like hunger — would necessarily be sublated; and the sublation of that is not reasonable, since all the Upaniṣads are devoted to that purpose. [Objection:] The <s>śruti</s> 'they practice mendicancy' — by making one grasp the desires [again] — itself sublates [the earlier teaching of abandonment]? [Or alternatively:] Having enjoined rising above desires, by making one grasp mendicancy — which is a part of desires — [the text] also makes one grasp other things connected to it? [Answer:] No — because mendicancy is not a motivating [factor for desires]; it is [merely] eating after having offered — it serves the function of utilizing the remainder (<s>śeṣa</s>). For it is that [eating of the remainder] which serves no motivating purpose; [the eating] could even be without ritual preparation — it need not be mendicancy specifically. For the knower of <s>Brahman</s> has no desire even for the unseen result (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) produced by [ritual] regulation. [Objection:] If the unseen result of regulation is undesirable, what use is mendicancy? [Answer:] No — because rising above other means [of livelihood] is enjoined. [Objection:] Even so, what is the use of that? [Answer:] If [you must ask] — very well, it is accepted. Those statements that are made regarding the <s>parivrājya</s> [āśrama] — such as 'wearing the sacred thread, he should study' and the like — these pertain exclusively to the <s>parivrājya</s> of the unenlightened; they have been resolved thus. Otherwise, there would be the sublation of self-knowledge — as has been stated. [As the <s>smṛti</s> says:] 'Without desires, without undertakings, without salutations, without hymns of praise; with inexhaustible [knowledge], having exhausted all <s>karma</s> — the gods know him as a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>' — this <s>smṛti</s> shows the complete absence of all action for the knower. And: 'The wise one is known by [absence of external] marks, being a knower of <s>dharma</s>.' Therefore, the knower of the self should adopt the <s>paramahaṃsa parivrājya</s> — characterized by rising above [desires] — which consists in the abandonment of all means of action. Since the ancient <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, having known this <s>Ātman</s> — whose nature is free from means and results — rose above everything of the nature of means, results, and desires, and practiced mendicancy; having abandoned action for both seen and unseen purposes, together with its instruments — therefore, even today, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, a knower of <s>Brahman</s>, [should seek] <s>pāṇḍitya</s> (scholarship) — the state of being learned, that is, this knowledge of the self. Having thoroughly accomplished this (<s>nirvidya</s>) — having completely known [it] — the knowledge of the self, having made it complete — from the teacher and from scripture — having risen above the desires — for the conclusion of that rising above desires is itself <s>pāṇḍitya</s>, since it arises from the dispelling of desires and is opposed to desires. For without dispelling desires, the rising above desires that is enjoined by the injunction of self-knowledge — together with the same-agent marker and the confirmatory <s>śruti</s> — is strengthened. Therefore, having risen above desires, through the strength of knowledge, he should abide in <s>bālya</s> (childlike simplicity) — he should desire to remain [thus]. For the strength of others — of those who do not know the self — consists in relying on means and results; having abandoned that strength, the knower should rely solely upon the strength of self-knowledge — that state alone, nothing else. For when [one has] the strength of that [self-knowledge], the sense-organs, in the domain of desires, are unable to carry him away and establish him [in worldly engagement]. For the sense-organs engage the confused, strength-less one in desires pertaining to the seen and unseen [worlds]. Strength is the dispelling, through self-knowledge, of all object-directed vision. Therefore, through that state — through <s>bālya</s> — one should abide. And likewise, from another <s>śruti</s>: 'By the self one obtains strength.' And: 'This self is not to be attained by the strength-less.' Having thoroughly accomplished both <s>bālya</s> and <s>pāṇḍitya</s> — having made [them] complete — then, from meditative [practice], [he becomes] a <s>muni</s> (sage), a <s>yogin</s>. This much alone is to be done by a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> — namely, the dispelling of all cognitions of what is not the self. Having done this, he becomes a <s>yogin</s>, one whose purpose is fulfilled.

yat sākṣādaparokṣād brahma sarvantara ātmetyuktam, tasya sarvāntarasya svarūpādhigamāya ā śākalyabrāhmaṇād grantha ārabhyate /
pṛthivyādīni hyākāśāntāni bhūtāni antarvahirbhāvena vyavasthitāni;teṣāṃ yad bāhyaṃ bādyam avigamyādhigamya nirākurvan draṣṭuḥ sākṣāt sarvāntaro 'gauṇa ātmā sarvasaṃsāradharmavinirmukto darśayitavya ityārambhaḥ----
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Since it was said that <s>Brahman</s> is directly, immediately the self, the innermost of all — for the purpose of comprehending the essential nature of that innermost [self], a section of text is commenced extending up to the <s>Śākalya Brāhmaṇa</s>. For the elements such as earth and the rest, up to space, are established in the form of exterior and interior. By comprehending and then negating the external [element] among them, [starting from] the outermost — the self of all, the direct, non-figurative innermost — free from all the properties of <s>saṃsāra</s> — is to be shown. This is the commencement [of this section].

atha hainaṃ gārgī vācaknavī papraccha -- yājñavalkyeti hovāca |
yad idaṃ sarvam apsv otaṃ ca protaṃ ca kasmin nu khalv āpa otāś ca protāś ceti |
vāyau gārgīti |

gandharvalokeṣu gārgīti |

adityalokeṣu gārgīti |

candralokeṣu gārgīti |

nakṣatralokeṣu gārgīti |
kasmin nu khalu nakṣatralokā otāś ca protāś ceti |

brahmalokeṣu gārgīti |

sa hovāca -- gārgi mātiprākṣīḥ |
mā te mūrdhā vyapaptat |
anatipraśnyāṃ vai devatām atipṛcchasi |
gārgi mātiprākṣīr iti |

children.translated_text: Then <s>Gārgī Vācaknavī</s> questioned him: '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>,' she said, 'since all this is woven, warp and woof, in water — in what are the waters woven, warp and woof?' 'In wind, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what is wind woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the atmosphere, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of the atmosphere woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the <s>Gandharvas</s>, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of the <s>Gandharvas</s> woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of <s>Āditya</s> (the sun), <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of <s>Āditya</s> woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the moon, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of the moon woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the stars, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of the stars woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the gods, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of the gods woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of <s>Indra</s>, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of <s>Indra</s> woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of <s>Prajāpati</s>, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of <s>Prajāpati</s> woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of <s>Brahman</s>, <s>Gārgī</s>.' 'In what are the worlds of <s>Brahman</s> woven, warp and woof?' He said: '<s>Gārgī</s>, do not question beyond. Let not your head fall off. You are questioning about a deity that is not to be questioned beyond. <s>Gārgī</s>, do not question beyond.' Thereupon, <s>Gārgī Vācaknavī</s> held her peace. (BṛUp 3.6.1)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_3,6.1 atha hainaṃ gārgī nāmataḥ, vācaknavīvacakrorduhitā, papraccha;yājñavalkyeti hovāca;yadidaṃ sarvaṃ pārthivaṃ dhātujātam apsūdake otaṃ ca protaṃ ca, otaṃ dīrghapaṭatantuvat protaṃ tiryaktantuvad viparītaṃ vā-adbhiḥ sarvato 'ntarbahirbhūtābhirvyāptamityarthaḥ, anyathā saktumuṣṭivad viśīryeta /
idaṃ tāvadanumānamupanyastam-yat kāryaṃ paricchinnaṃ sthūlam, kāraṇenāparicchinnena sūkṣmeṇa vyāptamitid daṣṭam-yathā pṛthivī adbhiḥ, tathāpūrvaṃ pūrvamuttareṇottareṇa vyāpinā bhavitavyam, ityeṣa ā sarvāntarādātmanaḥ praśnārthaḥ /
tatra bhūtāni pañca saṃhatānyevottaramuttaraṃ sūkṣamabhāvena vyāpakena kāraṇarūpeṇa ca vyavatiṣṭhante, na ca paramātmanor'vāk tadvayatirekeṇavastvantaramasti"satyasya satyam"iti śruteḥ /
satyaṃ ca bhūtapañcakam satyasya satyaṃ ca para ātmā /
kasminnu khalvāpa otāścaprotāśceti-tāsāmapi kāryatvāt sthūlatvāt paricchinnatvācca kacidvi otaprotabhāvena bhavitavyam;kva tāsāmetayotabhāva iti /
evamutarottaraprakṣaṇasaṅgoyojayitavyaḥ /
vāyau gārgīti /
nanvagnāviti vaktavyam!naipa doṣaḥ, agneḥ pārthivaṃ vā āpyaṃ vā dhātumanāśritya itarabhūtavat svātantryeṇa ātmalābho nāstīti tasminnotaprotabhāvo nopadiśyate /
kasminnu khalu vāyurotaśca protaścetyantarikṣalokeṣu gārgīti tānyeva bhūtāni saṃhatānyantarikṣalokāḥ, tānyapi gandharvalokeṣu, gandharvalokā ādityalokeṣu, ādityalokāścandralokeṣu, candralokā nakṣatralokeṣu, nakṣatralokā devalokeṣu, devalokā indralokeṣu, indralokā virāṭśarīrāraṃmakeṣu bhūteṣu prajāpatilokeṣu, prajāpatilokā brahmalokeṣu /
brahmalokā nāma aṇḍāraṃmakāṇi bhūtāni;sarvatra hi sūkṣmatāratamyakrameṇa prāpyubhogāśrayākārapariṇatāni bhūtāni saṃhatāni tānyeva pañceti bahuvacanamāñji /
children.translated_text: The worlds of <s>Brahman</s> are the elements that constitute the cosmic egg (<s>aṇḍa</s>). For everywhere, by the graduated sequence of increasing subtlety, the elements — having been transformed into the form of substrates for experience and enjoyment — in their aggregate, are referred to [with] the plural [number].

children.text: kasminnu khalu brahmalokā otāśca protāśceti-sa hovāca yājñavalkyo he gārgī mātiprākṣīḥ svaṃ praśnam, nyāyaprakāramatītya āgamena praṣṭabyāṃ devatāmanumānena mā prākṣīrityarthaḥ, pṛcchantyāśca mā te tava mūrdhā śiro vyapatad vispaṣṭaṃ patet;devatāyāḥ svapraśna āgamaviṣayaḥ;taṃ praśnaviṣayamatikrānto gārgyāḥ praśnaḥ;ānumānikatvāt sa yasyā devatāyāḥ praśnaḥ sātipraśnyā, nātipraśnyānatipraśnyā, svapraśraviṣayaiva, kevalāgamagamyetyarthaḥ, tāmanatipraśnyāṃ vai devatāmatipṛcchasi /
children.translated_text: 'In what are the worlds of <s>Brahman</s> woven, warp and woof?' He, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, said: 'O <s>Gārgī</s>, do not question beyond' — do not [pursue] your own question beyond the proper method; the deity that is to be inquired about through scripture, do not inquire about through inference — this is the meaning. And if you keep questioning, 'let not your head fall off' — your head will surely fall off. The deity's own question is a matter for scripture; <s>Gārgī</s>'s question has exceeded the scope of that question, because it proceeds by inference. That deity whose [nature is] the subject of inquiry — she is '<s>anatipraśnyā</s>' (not to be questioned beyond), i.e. [to be inquired about] only within the scope of her own question, accessible only through scripture alone — this is the meaning. That <s>anatipraśnyā</s> deity, you are questioning beyond.

children.text: ato gārgi mātiprākṣīḥ, martuṃ cennecchasi /
children.translated_text: Therefore, <s>Gārgī</s>, do not question beyond — if you do not wish to die.

children.text: tato ha gārgī vācaknavī upararāma //1//
children.translated_text: Thereupon, <s>Gārgī Vācaknavī</s> held her peace. // 1 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 3.6.1:] Then <s>Gārgī</s> by name, <s>Vācaknavī</s> — daughter of <s>Vacaknu</s> — questioned him. '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>,' she said. 'Since all this' — all earthly matter made of mineral substances — 'is woven, warp and woof, in water' — 'warp' (<s>ota</s>) means like the longitudinal threads of a cloth, and 'woof' (<s>prota</s>) means like the transverse threads, or conversely — meaning: pervaded by water internally and externally on all sides — this is the sense. Otherwise, it would disintegrate like a fistful of barley flour. This much, then, is the inference presented: whatever is an effect, limited, and gross is seen to be pervaded by a cause that is unlimited and subtle — just as the earth [is pervaded] by water. Similarly, each preceding [level] must be pervaded by each succeeding, more pervasive [level] — this is the purport of the questioning, all the way up to the innermost Self. Therein, the five elements, in their aggregate, stand one above the other in successively subtler form as pervading causes. And there is no other entity below the supreme Self apart from these — because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'the truth of the true.' The truth is the pentad of elements; the truth of the truth is the supreme Self. 'In what are the waters woven, warp and woof?' — since they too are effects, gross, and limited, there must be something in which they are woven as warp and woof; where is their warp-and-woof [nature]? — thus the successive questioning is to be connected. '<s>Gārgī</s>, in wind.' [Objection:] Should it not be said 'in fire'? There is no fault, because fire has no independent self-existence without depending on an earthy or watery material substrate, unlike the other elements; therefore its warp-and-woof status is not taught. 'In what is wind woven, warp and woof?' 'In the worlds of the atmosphere, <s>Gārgī</s>.' Those very elements in their aggregate are the worlds of the atmosphere; these too [are woven] in the worlds of the <s>Gandharvas</s>; the <s>Gandharva</s> worlds in the worlds of <s>Āditya</s>; the <s>Āditya</s> worlds in the worlds of the moon; the moon worlds in the worlds of the stars; the star worlds in the worlds of the gods; the god worlds in the worlds of <s>Indra</s>; the <s>Indra</s> worlds in the elements that constitute the <s>Virāj</s> body, the worlds of <s>Prajāpati</s>; the <s>Prajāpati</s> worlds in the worlds of <s>Brahman</s>.

children.text: iti tṛtīyādhyāye ṣaṣṭhaṃ gārgībrāhmaṇam //6//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixth <s>Gārgī Brāhmaṇa</s> in the third chapter. // 6 //

children.text: idānīṃ brahmalokānāmantaratamaṃ sūtraṃ va ktavyamiti tadartha ārambhaḥ, tacca āgamenaiva praṣṭavyamitītihāsena āgamopanyāsaḥ kriyate--
children.translated_text: Now, what is innermost to the worlds of <s>Brahman</s> — the thread (<s>sūtra</s>) — must be stated. For that purpose, the commencement [of this section is made]. And since that is to be inquired about through scripture alone, the presentation of scriptural authority is made through a narrative (<s>itihāsa</s>).
