abravīn me gardabhīvipīto bhāradvājaḥ |
śrotraṃ vai brahmeti |
yathā mātṛmān pitṛmān ācāryavān brūyāt tathā tad bhāradvājo 'bravīc chrotraṃ vai brahmeti |
aśṛṇvato hi kiṃ syād iti |
abravīt tu te tasyāyatanaṃ pratiṣṭhām |
na me 'bravīd iti |
ekapād vā etat samrāḍ iti |
sa vai no brūhi yājñavalkya |
śrotram evāyatanam ākāśaḥ pratiṣṭhānantam ity enad upāsīta |
kānantatā yājñavalkya |
diśa eva samrāḍ iti hovāca |
tasmād vai samrāḍ api yāṃ kāñca diśaṃ gacchati naivāsyā antaṃ gacchati |
anantā hi diśaḥ |
diśo vai samrāṭ śrotram |
śrotraṃ vai samrāṭ paramaṃ brahma |
nainaṃ śrotraṃ jahāti |
sarvāṇy enaṃ bhūtāny abhikṣaranti |
devo bhūtvā devān apyeti |
ya evaṃ vidvān etad upāste |
hastyṛṣabhaṃ sahasraṃ dadāmīti hovāca janako vaidehaḥ |
sa hovāca yājñavalkyaḥ -- pitā me 'manyata nānanuśiṣya hareteti || BrhUp_4,1.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'Whatever someone told you, let us hear that.' '<s>Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja</s> told me: "The ear indeed is <s>Brahman</s>." As one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would say, so did <s>Bhāradvāja</s> say: "The ear indeed is <s>Brahman</s>." For what would there be for one who cannot hear?' 'But did he tell you its abode and support?' 'He did not tell me.' 'Then it is only one-footed, O sovereign.' 'Do tell us, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' 'The ear itself is the abode; space is the support. One should meditate upon it as the infinite (<s>ananta</s>).' 'What is that infinitude, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>?' 'The directions themselves, O sovereign,' he said. 'Therefore, O sovereign, to whatever direction one goes, one never reaches its end; for the directions are infinite. The directions indeed, O sovereign, are the ear. The ear indeed, O sovereign, is the supreme <s>Brahman</s>. The ear does not forsake him; all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon this.' 'I give a thousand [cows] with a bull-elephant,' said <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s>. <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said: 'My father thought that one should not take [gifts] without having instructed.' (BṛUp 4.1.5)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,1.5 yadeva te gardabhīvipīta iti nāmato bhāradvājo gotrataḥ śrotraṃ vai brahmeti /
śrotre digdevatānanta ityenadupāsīta /
kānantatā śrotrasya /
diśa eva śrotrasyā'nantyaṃ yasmāttasmādvai samrāṭprācīmudīcāṃ vā yāṃ kāñcidapi diśaṃ gacchati naivāsyā antaṅgacchati kañcidapu /
ato 'nantā hi diśaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, the directions are infinite.

children.text: diśo vai samrāṭśrotram /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'The directions indeed, O sovereign, are the ear.'

children.text: tasmāddigānantyameva śrotrasyā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, the infinitude of the directions is itself

children.text: ṣa'nantyam //4,1.5//
children.translated_text: the infinitude of the ear. (4.1.5)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.1.5:] 'Whatever someone told you' — <s>Gardabhīvipīta</s> by name, <s>Bhāradvāja</s> by lineage — 'the ear indeed is <s>Brahman</s>.' The deity pertaining to the ear is the directions. 'One should meditate upon it as the infinite.' What is the infinitude of the ear? 'The directions themselves' — because the directions are the infinitude of the ear. Therefore, O sovereign, whether one goes to the east, the north, or any other direction whatsoever, one never reaches its end at all.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,1.6
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.1.6]

children.text:
yad eva te kaścid abravīt tac chṛṇavāmeti |
abravīn me satyakāmo jābālaḥ -- mano vai brahmeti |
yathā mātṛmān pitṛmān ācāryavān brūyāt tathā taj jābālo 'bravīn mano vai brahmeti |
amanaso hi kiṃ syād iti |
abravīt tu te tasyāyatanaṃ pratiṣṭhām |
na me 'bravīd iti |
ekapād vā etat samrāḍ iti |
sa vai no brūhi yājñāvalkya |
mana evāyatanam ākāśaḥ pratiṣṭhānanda ity enad upāsīta |
kānandatā yājñavalkya |
mana eva samrāḍ iti hovāca manasā vai samrāṭ striyam abhi hāryati tasyāṃ pratirūpaḥ putro jāyate |
sa ānandaḥ |
mano vai samrāṭ paramaṃ brahma |
nainaṃ mano jahāti |
sarvāṇy enaṃ bhūtāny abhikṣaranti |
devo bhūtvā devān apyeti |
ya evaṃ vidvān etad upāste |
hastyṛṣabhaṃ sahasraṃ dadāmīti hovāca janako vaidehaḥ |
sa hovāca yājñavalkyaḥ -- pitā me 'manyata nānanuśiṣya hareteti || BrhUp_4,1.6 ||
children.translated_text: 'Whatever someone told you, let us hear that.' '<s>Satyakāma Jābāla</s> told me: "The mind indeed is <s>Brahman</s>." As one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would say, so did <s>Jābāla</s> say: "The mind indeed is <s>Brahman</s>." For what would there be for one without a mind?' 'But did he tell you its abode and support?' 'He did not tell me.' 'Then it is only one-footed, O sovereign.' 'Do tell us, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' 'The mind itself is the abode; space is the support. One should meditate upon it as bliss (<s>ānanda</s>).' 'What is that bliss-character, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>?' 'The mind itself, O sovereign,' he said. 'For by the mind, O sovereign, a man is attracted to a woman; from her, a son resembling [the father] is born — that is bliss. The mind indeed, O sovereign, is the supreme <s>Brahman</s>. The mind does not forsake him; all beings flow toward him. Having become a god, he goes to the gods — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon this.' 'I give a thousand [cows] with a bull-elephant,' said <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s>. <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said: 'My father thought that one should not take [gifts] without having instructed.' (BṛUp 4.1.6)

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,1.6 satyakāma iti nāmato jabālāyā apatyaṃ jābālaḥ /
candramā manasi devatā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The moon is the deity pertaining to the mind.

children.text: ānanda ityupaniṣati /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The <s>upaniṣad</s> is: bliss (<s>ānanda</s>).

children.text: yasmānmana evā'nandastasmānmanasā vai samrāṭastriyamabhikāmayamāno 'bhihāryate prārthayata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Since the mind itself is bliss — therefore, 'by the mind, O sovereign, a man, being desirous of a woman, is attracted' — he desires her, this is the meaning.

children.text: tasmādyāṃ striyamabhikāmayamāno 'bhihāryate tasyāṃ pratirūpo 'nurūpaḥ putro jāyate sa ānandahetuḥ sa yena manasā nirvartyate tanmana ānandaḥ //4,1.6//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, the woman whom he desires, being attracted [to her] — from her, a son resembling [the father], conforming [to him], is born; that [son] is the cause of bliss. That by which the mind is fulfilled — that mind is bliss. (4.1.6)
[Commentary on BṛUp 4.1.6:] <s>Satyakāma</s> by name; offspring of <s>Jabālā</s>, hence <s>Jābāla</s>.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,1.7
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.1.7]

children.text:
yad eva te kaścid abravīt tac chṛṇavāmeti |
abravīn me vidagdhaḥ śākalyaḥ |
hṛdayaṃ vai brahmeti |
yathā mātṛmān pitṛmān ācāryavān brūyāt tathā tac chākalyo 'bravīd dhṛdayaṃ vai brahmeti |
ahṛdayasya hi kiṃ syād iti |
abravīt tu te tasyāyatanaṃ pratiṣṭhām |
na me 'bravīd iti |
ekapād vā etat samrāḍ iti |
sa vai no brūhi yājñavalkya |
hṛdayam evāyatanam ākāśaḥ pratiṣṭhā |
sthitir ity enad upāsīta |
kā sthititā yājñavalkya |
hṛdayam eva samrāḍ iti hovāca |
hṛdayaṃ vai samrāṭ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānām āyatanam |
hṛdayaṃ vai samrāṭ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ pratiṣṭhā |
hṛdaye hy eva samrāṭ sarvāṇi bhūtāni pratiṣṭhitāni bhavanti |
hṛdayaṃ vai samrāṭ paramaṃ brahma |
nainaṃ hṛdayaṃ jahāti |
sarvāṇy enaṃ bhūtāny abhikṣaranti |
devo bhūtvā devān apyeti |
ya evaṃ vidvān etad upāste |
hastyṛṣabhaṃ sahasraṃ dadāmīti hovāca janako vaidehaḥ |
sa hovāca yājñavalkyaḥ -- pitā me 'manyata nānanuśiṣya hareteti || BrhUp_4,1.7 ||
children.translated_text: 'Whatever someone told you, let us hear that.' '<s>Vidagdha Śākalya</s> told me: the heart is <s>Brahman</s>.' 'As one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would say — so did <s>Śākalya</s> say: the heart is <s>Brahman</s>. For what would one be without a heart?' 'But did he tell you its abode and support?' 'He did not tell me.' 'This [<s>Brahman</s> as taught] has but one foot, O emperor.' 'Then please tell us, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' 'The heart itself is the abode; space is the support. One should meditate upon it as stability (<s>sthiti</s>).' 'What is stability, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>?' 'The heart itself, O emperor,' he said. 'The heart, O emperor, is the abode of all beings. The heart, O emperor, is the support of all beings. For in the heart, O emperor, all beings are established. The heart, O emperor, is the supreme <s>Brahman</s>. The heart does not abandon one [who knows this]. All beings flow toward such a one. Having become a god, one goes to the gods — [this comes to] one who, knowing this, meditates thus.' 'I give you a thousand [cows] with a bull the size of an elephant,' said <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s>. <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said: 'My father was of the opinion that one should not accept [gifts] without having imparted instruction.' (BṛUp 4.1.7)

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,1.7 vidagdhaḥ śākalyo hṛdayaṃ vai brahmeti /
hṛdayaṃ vai samrāṭsarveṣāṃ bhūtānāmāyatanam /
children.translated_text: 'The heart, O emperor, is the abode of all beings.'

children.text: nāmarūpakarmātmakāni hi bhūtāni hṛdayāśrayāṇītyavocāma śākalyabāhmaṇe hṛdayapratiṣṭhānu ceti /
children.translated_text: For beings constituted of name, form, and action depend on the heart — as we have stated in the <s>Śākalya Brāhmaṇa</s> — and are established in the heart.

children.text: tasmādvadhṛtaye hyeva samrāṭsravāṇi bhūtāni pratiṣṭhitāni bhavanti /
children.translated_text: Therefore indeed, 'in the heart alone, O emperor, all beings are established.'

children.text: tasmāddhṛdayaṃ sthitirityupāsīta hṛdaye ca prajāpatirdevatā //4,1.7//
children.translated_text: Therefore, one should meditate upon the heart as stability; and the deity [presiding over] the heart is <s>Prajāpati</s>. // 4.1.7 //
[Commentary on BṛUp 4.1.7:] <s>Vidagdha Śākalya</s> [said]: 'The heart is <s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text: iti bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣye caturthādhyāyasya prathamaṃ brāhmaṇam //1//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> of the fourth chapter in the commentary on the <s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s>. // 1 //

children.text: atha caturthādhyāyasya dvitīyaṃ brāhmaṇam
children.translated_text: Now the second <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> of the fourth chapter.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,2.1
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.2.1]

children.text:
janako ha vaidehaḥ kūrcād upāvasarpann uvāca -- namas te 'stu yājñavalkya |
anu mā śādhīti |
sa hovāca yathā vai samrāṇ mahāntam adhvānam eṣyan rathaṃ vā nāvaṃ vā samādadītaivam evaitābhir upaniṣadbhiḥ samāhitātmāsi |
evaṃ vṛndāraka āḍhyaḥ sann adhītaveda uktopaniṣatka ito vimucyamānaḥ kva gamiṣyasīti |
nāhaṃ tad bhagavan veda yatra gamiṣyāmīti |
atha vai te 'haṃ tad vakṣyāmi yatra gamiṣyasīti |
bravītu bhagavān iti || BrhUp_4,2.1 ||
children.translated_text: <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s>, rising from his seat, approached [<s>Yājñavalkya</s>] and said: 'Salutations to you, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. Please instruct me.' He [<s>Yājñavalkya</s>] said: 'Just as, O emperor, one about to go on a great journey would prepare a chariot or a ship — even so, by these <s>Upaniṣadic</s> [teachings], your self has been well-equipped. Being thus distinguished (<s>vṛndāraka</s>), wealthy, having studied the <s>Vedas</s>, and having been taught the <s>Upaniṣads</s> — when you are released from this [body], where will you go?' 'I do not know, sir, where I will go.' 'Then I shall tell you where you will go.' 'Please tell me, sir.' (BṛUp 4.2.1)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,2.1 janako ha vaidehaḥ /
yasmātsaviśeṣaṇāni sarvāṇi brahmāṇi jānāti yājñavalkyastasmādācāryakatvaṃ hitvā janakaḥ kūrcādāsanaviśeṣādutthāyopa samīpamavasarpanyādayornipatannityarthaḥ /
uvācoktavānnamaste tubhyamastu he yājñavalkyānu mā śādhyanuśādhi māmityarthaḥ /
itiśabdo vākyaparisamāptyarthaḥ /
sa hovāca yājñavalkyo yathā vai loke he samrāḍmahāntaṃ dīrghamadhvānameṣyangamiṣyanrathaṃ vā sothalena gamiṣyannāvaṃ vā jalena gamiṣyansamādadīta /
evamevaitāni brahmāṇyetābhirupaniṣadbhiryuktānyupāsīnaḥ samāhitatmāsyatyantametābhirupaniṣadbhiḥ saṃyuktātmāsi na kevalamupaniṣatsamāhita evaṃ vṛndārakaḥ pūjyaścā'ḍhyaśceśvaro na daridra ityarthaḥ /
adhītavedo 'dhīto vedo yena sa tvamadhītaveda uktāścopaniṣada ācāryaistubhyaṃ sa tvamuktopaniṣatka evaṃ sarvavibhūtatisaṃpanno 'pi sanbhayayamadhyaścha eva paramātjñānena vinākṛtārtha evatāvadityarthaḥ /
yāvatparaṃ brahma na vetsi /
ito 'smāddehādimucyamāna etābhirtorathasthānīyābhiḥ samāhitaḥ kva kasmingamiṣyasi kiṃ vastu prāpsyasīti /
nāhaṃ tadvastu bhagavanpūjāvanveda jāne yatra gamiṣyāmīti /
children.translated_text: 'I do not know, sir — O venerable one — that reality, where I will go.'

children.text: atha yadyevaṃ na jānīṣe yatra gataḥ kṛtārthaḥ syā ahaṃ vai tubhyaṃ tadvakṣyāmi yatra gamiṣyasīti /
children.translated_text: 'Well then, if you do not know where, having gone, you would be fulfilled — I shall tell you where you will go.'

children.text: bravītu bhagavāniti, yadi prasanno māṃ prati /
children.translated_text: 'Please tell me, sir' — if you are graciously inclined toward me.

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.2.1:] <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s>. Since <s>Yājñavalkya</s> knows all the forms of <s>Brahman</s> with their qualifications — therefore, <s>Janaka</s>, abandoning [the stance of being] the master, rose from his special seat (<s>kūrca</s>) and approached, coming near, falling [at his feet] — this is the meaning. He said: 'Salutations to you, O <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. Instruct me' — 'teach me' is the meaning. The word 'thus' (<s>iti</s>) marks the completion of the sentence. He, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, said: 'Just as in the world, O emperor, one about to go on a great, long journey would prepare a chariot — if going by land — or a ship — if going by water. Even so, [you have prepared yourself with] these forms of <s>Brahman</s>; having meditated upon them equipped with these <s>Upaniṣads</s>, your self has become thoroughly equipped — completely united with these <s>Upaniṣads</s>. And not merely equipped with the <s>Upaniṣads</s> — you are also distinguished (<s>vṛndāraka</s>), worthy of honor, and wealthy, a lord, not poor — this is the meaning. One whose <s>Veda</s> has been studied — you have studied the <s>Veda</s>; and the <s>Upaniṣads</s> have been taught to you by teachers — you are one who has been taught the <s>Upaniṣads</s>. Even being endowed with all these excellences, even so — you are incomplete indeed without the knowledge of the supreme Self — this is the meaning. As long as you do not know the supreme <s>Brahman</s>. Being released from this body — equipped with these [teachings] serving as chariots, as it were — where will you go? What reality will you attain?'

children.text: START BrhUp 4,2.2
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.2.2]

children.text:
indho ha vai nāmaiṣa yo 'yaṃ dakṣiṇe 'kṣan puruṣaḥ |
taṃ vā etam indhaṃ santam indra ity ācakṣate parokṣeṇaiva |
parokṣapriyā iva hi devāḥ pratyakṣadviṣaḥ || BrhUp_4,2.2 ||
children.translated_text: The person in the right eye is indeed named <s>Indha</s> (the kindler). Though he is <s>Indha</s>, they call him <s>Indra</s> — indirectly (<s>parokṣeṇa</s>). For the gods are fond of the indirect, as it were, and averse to the direct. (BṛUp 4.2.2)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,2.2 indho ha vai nāma /
indha ityevaṃnāmā /
yaścakṣurvai brahmeti purokta ādityāntaragta puruṣaḥ sa eṣa yo 'yaṃ dakṣiṇe 'kṣannakṣaṇi viśeṣeṇa vyavasthitaḥ /
sa ca satyanāmā /
children.translated_text: And he has a true name.

children.text: taṃ vā etaṃ puruṣaṃ dīptiguṇatvātpratyakṣaṃ nāmāsyendha iti tamindhaṃ santamindra ityācakṣateparokṣeṇa /
children.translated_text: This person — because of his quality of luminosity, his direct name is <s>Indha</s>. Though he is <s>Indha</s>, they call him <s>Indra</s> — indirectly (<s>parokṣeṇa</s>).

children.text: yasmātparokṣapriyā iva hi devāḥ pratyakṣadviṣaḥ pratyakṣanāmagrahaṇaṃ dviṣanti /
children.translated_text: Because the gods are fond of the indirect, as it were, and are averse to the direct — they dislike the use of direct names.

children.text: eṣa tvaṃ vaiśvānaramātmānaṃ saṃpanno 'si //4,2.2//
children.translated_text: You have become accomplished in this <s>Vaiśvānara</s> Self. // 4.2.2 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.2.2:] 'He is indeed named <s>Indha</s>.' The person previously mentioned [in the passage] 'The eye is <s>Brahman</s>,' situated within the sun [cosmically] — he is this one who is specially established in the right eye.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,2.3
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.2.3]

children.text:
athaitad vāme 'kṣaṇi puruṣarūpam eṣāsya patnī virāṭ |
tayor eṣa saṃstāvo ya eṣo 'ntar hṛdaya ākāśaḥ |
athainayor etad annaṃ ya eṣo 'ntar hṛdaye lohitapiṇḍaḥ |
athainayor etat prāvaraṇaṃ yad etad antar hṛdaye jālakam iva |
athainayor eṣā sṛtiḥ saṃcaraṇī yaiṣā hṛdayād ūrdhvā nāḍy uccarati |
yathā keśaḥ sahasradhā bhinna evam asyaitā hitā nāma nāḍyo 'ntar hṛdaye pratiṣṭhitā bhavanti |
etābhir vā etad āsravad āsravati |
tasmād eṣa praviviktāhāratara iva bhavaty asmāc chārīrād ātmanaḥ || BrhUp_4,2.3 ||
children.translated_text: Now, the person-form in the left eye — she is his wife, <s>Virāj</s>. Their meeting-place is the space within the heart. Their food is the red lump within the heart. Their covering is the net-like [membrane] within the heart. Their path of travel is the <s>nāḍī</s> (channel) that goes upward from the heart. As a hair split a thousandfold — even so are these <s>nāḍīs</s> called <s>hitā</s>, established within the heart. Through these, that [subtle essence] flows and flows. Therefore, this [subtle self] has, as it were, a more refined diet than this bodily self. (BṛUp 4.2.3)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,2.3 athaitadvāme 'kṣaṇi puruṣarūpameṣāsya patnī yaṃ tvaṃ vaiśvānaramātmānaṃ saṃpanno 'si tasyāsyendrasya bhokturbhogyaiṣā patnī virāḍannaṃ bhogyatvādeva tadetadannaṃ cāttā caikaṃ mithunaṃ svapne /
ko 'sau /
ya eṣo 'ntarahṛdaya ākāśo 'ntarhṛdaye hṛdayasya māṃsapiṇḍasya madhye /
athainayoretadvakṣyamāṇamannaṃ bhojyaṃ sthitihetuḥ /
kiṃ tat /
ya eṣe 'ntarhṛdaye lohitapiṇḍo lohita eva piṇḍākārāpannā lohitapiṇḍaḥ /
annaṃ jagdhaṃ dvedhā pariṇamate yatsthūlaṃ tadadho gacchati /
yadanyattatpunarāgninā pacyamānaṃ dvedhā pariṇamate /
yo madhyamo rasaḥ sa lohitādakrameṇa pāñcabhautikaṃ piṇḍaṃ śarīramupacinoti /
yo 'ṇiṣṭho rasaḥ sa eṣa lohitapiṇḍa indrasya liṅgātmano hṛdaye mithunībhūtasya /
yaṃ taijasamācakṣate sa tayorindrendrāṇyorhṛdaye mithunībhūtayoḥ sūkṣmāsu nāḍīṣvanupraviṣṭaḥ sthitiheturbhavati /
tadetaducyate 'thainayoretadannamityādi /
kiñcānyat /
athainayoretatpravāraṇam /
bhuktavatoḥ svapatośca prāvaraṇaṃ bhavati loke tatsāmānyaṃ hi kalpayati śrutiḥ /
ki tadiha prāvaraṇam /
yadetadantarhṛdaye jālakamivānekanāḍīchidrabahulatvājjālakamiva /
athainayoreṣā sṛtirmārgaḥ saṃcanarato 'nayeti saṃcaraṇī svapnajjāgaritadeśāgamanamārgaḥ /
kā sā sṛtiḥ /
yaiṣā hṛdayādahṛdayadeśādūrdhvābhimukhī satyuccarati nāḍī /
tasyāḥ parimāṇamidamucyate /
yathā loke keśaḥ sahasradhā bhinno 'tyantasūkṣmo bhavatyevaṃ sūkṣmā asya dehasya saṃbandhinyo hitā nāma hitā ityevaṃ khyātā nāḍyāstāścāntarhṛdaye māsaṃpiṇḍe pritiṣṭhitā bhavanti hṛdayādviprarūḍhāstāḥ sarvatra kadambakesapavadetābhirnāḍobhiratyantasūkṣmābhiretadannamāsravadgacchadāsravati gacchati /
tadetaddevatāśarīramanenānnena dāmabhūtenopacīyamānaṃ tiṣṭhati /
tasmādyasmātsthūlenānnenopacitaḥ piṇḍa idaṃ tu devatāśarīraṃ liṅgaṃ sūkṣmeṇānnenopacitaṃ tiṣṭhati /
piṇḍopacayakaramapyannaṃ praviviktameva mūtrapurīṣādisthūlamapekṣya liṅgasthitikaraṃ tvannaṃ tato 'pisākṣmataram /
children.translated_text: even the food that builds up the physical lump is itself refined compared to gross [waste products like] urine and feces; but the food that sustains the subtle body is even finer than that.

children.text: ataḥ praviviktāhāraḥ piṇḍaḥ /
children.translated_text: Hence, the physical lump [has] a refined diet.

children.text: tasmātpraviviktāhārādapi praviviktāhāratara eṣa liṅgātmevaiva bhavatyasmāccharīrācchārīrameva śārīraṃ tasmācchārīrāt /
children.translated_text: Therefore, more refined in diet (<s>praviviktāhāratara</s>) even than the physical lump with its refined diet, this subtle-body self comes to be — from this bodily self, the body-born bodily one.

children.text: ātmano vaiśvānarāttaijasaḥ sūkṣmānnopacito bhavati //4,2.3//
children.translated_text: From the <s>Vaiśvānara</s> self, the <s>taijasa</s> (luminous self), nourished by subtle food, arises. // 4.2.3 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.2.3:] 'Now, the person-form in the left eye — she is his wife.' She is the wife of this <s>Vaiśvānara</s> Self with which you have become accomplished — of this <s>Indra</s>, the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment is this wife <s>Virāj</s>, the food. The food and the eater — [these constitute] one pair (<s>mithuna</s>) in dream. Who is that [paired entity]? The space within the heart — in the middle of the heart, the flesh-lump. Their food — now to be stated — is the sustenance, the cause of their maintenance. What is that? The red lump within the heart — blood itself having assumed the form of a lump. Food that is eaten is transformed in two ways: what is gross descends below. What is other [than that] is again cooked by fire and transforms in two ways. The middle essence gradually builds up the body, the fivefold-elemental lump, through blood. The finest essence — this red lump — is for <s>Indra</s>, the subtle-body self, who has become a pair in the heart. That which they call <s>taijasa</s> (luminous) — he, having entered the subtle <s>nāḍīs</s> of <s>Indra</s> and <s>Indrāṇī</s> who have become a pair in the heart, serves as the cause of their maintenance. This is stated: 'Their food' and so forth. Moreover — 'their covering' is mentioned. For those who have eaten and who sleep, there is a covering in the world; the <s>śruti</s> draws this analogy. What is the covering here? 'The net-like [membrane] within the heart' — called 'net-like' because of the abundance of openings of numerous <s>nāḍīs</s>. 'Their path of travel' — the path, the passage from the dream state to the waking state. What is that path? 'The <s>nāḍī</s> that goes upward from the heart-region.' Its dimension is stated: 'As a hair in the world, split a thousandfold, becomes extremely fine — even so fine are the <s>nāḍīs</s> belonging to this body, called <s>hitā</s>' — known by that name — 'established in the heart,' the flesh-lump, having grown out from the heart in all directions, like the filaments of a <s>kadamba</s> flower. Through these extremely subtle <s>nāḍīs</s>, this food, flowing, moves and flows. This deity-body is sustained, being nourished, by this food that acts as a bond. Therefore — because the physical lump is nourished by gross food, while this deity-body, the subtle body (<s>liṅga</s>), is sustained by subtle food —

children.text: START BrhUp 4,2.4
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.2.4]

children.text:
tasya prācī dik prāñcaḥ prāṇāḥ |
dakṣiṇā dig dakṣiṇe prāṇāḥ |
pratīcī dik pratyañcaḥ prāṇāḥ |
udīcī dig udañcaḥ prāṇāḥ |
ūrdhvā dig ūrdhvāḥ prāṇāḥ |
avācī dig avāñcaḥ prāṇāḥ |
sarvā diśaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ |
sa eṣa neti nety ātmā |
agṛhyo na hi gṛhyate |
aśīryo na hi śīryate |
asaṅgo na hi sajyate |
asito na vyathate |
na riṣyati |
abhayaṃ vai janaka prāpto 'sīti hovāca yājñavalkyaḥ |
sa hovāca janako vaideho 'bhayaṃ tvā gacchatād yājñavalkya yo no bhagavann abhayaṃ vedayase |
namas te 'stu |
ime videhā ayam aham asmīti || BrhUp_4,2.4 ||
children.translated_text: His eastern direction is the eastern <s>prāṇas</s>; his southern direction is the southern <s>prāṇas</s>; his western direction is the western <s>prāṇas</s>; his northern direction is the northern <s>prāṇas</s>; his upward direction is the upward <s>prāṇas</s>; his downward direction is the downward <s>prāṇas</s>; all his directions are all the <s>prāṇas</s>. This Self is [described as] 'not this, not this' (<s>neti neti</s>). It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped. It is indestructible, for it is not destroyed. It is unattached, for it does not attach. It is unfettered, it does not suffer, it is not injured. 'You have attained fearlessness, O <s>Janaka</s>,' said <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s> said: 'May fearlessness come to you, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, you who make us know fearlessness. Salutations to you. Here are the <s>Videhas</s>, and here am I [at your service].' (BṛUp 4.2.4)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,2.4 sa eṣa hṛdayabhūtastaijasaḥ sūkṣmabhūtena prāṇena vidhriyamāṇaḥ prāṇa eva bhavati /
tasyāsya viduṣaḥ krameṇa vaiśvānarāttaijasaṃ prāptasya hṛdayātmānamāpannasya hṛdayātmanaśca prāṇātmānamāpannasya prācī dikprāñcaḥ prāggatāḥ prāṇāḥ.tathā dakṣiṇā digdakṣiṇe prāṇāḥ /
sarvā diśaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ /
evaṃ vidvānkreṇa sarvātmakaṃ prāṇamātmatvenopagato bhavati /
taṃ sarvātmānaṃ pratyagātmanyupasaṃhṛtya draṣṭurhi draṣṭubhāvaṃ neti netītyātmānaṃ turīyaṃ pratipadyate /
yameṣa vidvānanena krameṇa pratipadyate sa eṣa neti netyātmetyādi na riṣyatītyantaṃ vyākhyātametat /
abhayaṃ vai janmamaraṇādinimittabhayaśūnyaṃ he janaka prāpto 'sīti haivaṃ kilovācoktavānyājñavalkyaḥ /
tadetaduktamatha vai te 'haṃ tadvakṣyāmi yatra gamiṣyasīti /
children.translated_text: This is what was [previously] stated: 'I shall tell you where you will go.'

children.text: sa hovāca janako vaideho 'bhayameva tvā tvāmapi gacchatādgacchatu yastvaṃ no 'smānhe yājñavalkya bhagavānpūjāvannabhayaṃ brahma vedayase jñāpayasi prāpitavānupādhikṛtājñānavyavadhānāpanayanenetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Janaka</s> of <s>Videha</s> said: 'May fearlessness come to you as well' — may it reach you too, O <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, sir, O venerable one, who make us know fearlessness — [that is,] who make us know the fearless <s>Brahman</s>, who have caused [us] to attain [it] — by removing the obstruction of the veil of ignorance caused by limiting adjuncts. This is the meaning.

children.text: kimanyadahaṃ vidyāniṣkriyārthaṃ prayacchāmi sākṣādātmānameva dattavate /
children.translated_text: What else could I give as a counter-gift to one who has given the very Self itself?

children.text: ato namaste 'stvime videhāstava yatheṣṭaṃ bhujyantāmayaṃ cāhamasmi dāsabhāve sthito yatheṣṭaṃ māṃ rājyaṃ ca pracatipadyasvetyarthaḥ //4,2.4//
children.translated_text: Therefore, salutations to you. Here are the <s>Videhas</s> — may they be enjoyed by you as you wish. And here am I — standing in the position of a servant. Take possession of me and the kingdom as you wish — this is the meaning. // 4.2.4 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.2.4:] This [<s>taijasa</s>], situated in the heart, being sustained by the subtle element of <s>prāṇa</s>, becomes <s>prāṇa</s> itself. For this knower (<s>viduṣa</s>), who has progressively attained — from the <s>Vaiśvānara</s>, the <s>taijasa</s>; having attained the heart-self; and from the heart-self, having attained the <s>prāṇa</s>-self — the eastern direction is the eastern <s>prāṇas</s>; similarly, the southern direction is the southern <s>prāṇas</s>; all directions are all the <s>prāṇas</s>. Thus, the knower, having progressively attained the <s>prāṇa</s> that is the self of all, accepts [it] as his own self. Having withdrawn that all-self into the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) — for the seer cannot [remain as] the seen — one attains the fourth (<s>turīya</s>) Self, [described as] 'not this, not this.' That which this knower attains by this progressive [method] — that Self [described as] 'not this, not this' — and so forth up to 'it is not injured' — this has been explained [previously]. 'Fearlessness' — devoid of the fear born of birth, death, and the like — 'O <s>Janaka</s>, you have attained' — thus indeed, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> said.

children.text: iti bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadi caturthādhyāyasya dvitīyaṃ brāhmaṇam //2//
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> of the fourth chapter in the <s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s>. // 2 //

children.text: atha caturthādhyāyasya tṛtīyaṃ brāhmaṇam //
children.translated_text: Now the third <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> of the fourth chapter. //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.1
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.1]

children.text:
janakaṃ ha vaidehaṃ yājñavalkyo jagāma |
sam enena vadiṣya iti |
atha ha yaj janakaś ca vaideho yājñavalkyaś cāgnihotre samūdāte |
tasmai ha yājñavalkyo varaṃ dadau |
sa ha kāmapraśnam eva vavre |
taṃ hāsmai dadau |
taṃ ha samrāḍ eva pūrvaḥ papraccha || BrhUp_4,3.1 ||
children.translated_text: <s>Yājñavalkya</s> went to <s>Janaka</s>, king of <s>Videha</s>. He thought: 'I shall not speak [about <s>Brahman</s>].' But previously, when <s>Janaka Vaideha</s> and <s>Yājñavalkya</s> had conversed about the <s>Agnihotra</s>, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> had granted him a boon. He had chosen the freedom to ask any question he wished. That [boon] he had granted him. And so the king himself questioned him first. // BṛhUp 4.3.1 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.1 janakaṃ ha vaidehaṃ yājñavalkyo jagāmetyasyābhisaṃbandhaḥ /
vijñānamaya ātmā sākṣādaparokṣādbrahma sarvāntaraḥ para eva /
"nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā nānyadato 'sti draṣṭi"tyādiśrutibhyaḥ /
sa eṣa iha praviṣṭo vadanādiliṅgo 'sti vyatirikta iti madhukāṇḍe 'jātaśatrusaṃvāde prāṇādikartṛtvabhoktṛtvapratyākhyānenādhigato 'pi satpunaḥ prāṇanādiliṅgamupanyasyauṣastapraśne prāṇanādiliṅgo yaḥ sāmānyenādhigataḥ prāṇena prāṇitītyādinā dṛṣṭerdraṣṭetyādināluptaśaktisvabhāvo 'dhigataḥ /
tasya ca paropādhinimittaḥ saṃsāro yathā rajjūṣaraśuktikāgaganādiṣu sarpedakarajamalinatvādi parādhyāropaṇanimittameva na svatastathā nirupādhiko nirupākhyo neti netīti vyapadeśyaḥ sākṣādaparokṣātsarvāntara ātmā brahmākṣaramantaryāmī praśastaupaniṣadaḥ puruṣo vijñānamānandaṃ brahmetyadhigatam /
tadeva punarindhasajñaḥ praviviktāhārastato 'ntarhṛdaye liṅgātmā praviviktāhāratarastataḥ pareṇa jagadātmā prāṇopādhistato 'pi pravilāpya jagadātmānamupādhibhūtaṃ rajjvādāviva sarpādikaṃ vidyayā sa eṣa neti netīti sākṣātsarvāntaraṃ brahmādhigatam /
evamabhayaṃ pariprāpito janako yājñavalkyenā'gamataḥ saṃkṣepataḥ /
atra ca jāgratsvapna suṣuptaturīyāṇyupanyanyaprasaṅgenendhaḥ praviviktāhārataraḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sa eṣa neti netīti /
idānīṃ jāgratsvapnādvāreṇāva mahatā tarkeṇa vistarato 'dhigamaḥ kartavyaḥ /
abhayaṃ prāpayitavyaṃ /
sadbhāvāścā'tmano vipratipattyāśaṅkānirākaraṇadvāreṇa /
vyatiriktatvaṃ śuddhatvaṃ svayañjyotiṣṭvamaluptaśaktisvarūpatvaṃ niratiśayānandasvābhāvyamadvaitatvaṃ cādhigantavyamitīdamārabhyate /
ākhyāyayikā tu vidyāsaṃpradānagrahaṇavidhiprakāśanārthā /
vidyāstutaye ca viśeṣataḥ /
varadānādisūcanāt /
janakaṃ ha vaidehaṃ yājñavalkyo jagāma /
sa ca gacchannevaṃ mene cintitavānna vadiṣye kiñcidapu rājñe /
gamanaprayojanaṃ tu yogakṣemārtham /
na vadiṣya ityevaṃsaṃkalpo 'pi yājñavalkyo yadyajjanakaḥ pṛṣṭavāṃstattatpratipede tatra ko hetuḥ saṃkalpitasyānyathākaraṇa ityatrā'khyāyikāmācaṣṭe /
pūrvatra kila janakayājñavalkyoḥ saṃvāda āsīdagnihotre nimitte /
tatra janakasyāgnihotraviṣayaṃ vijñānamupalabhya parituṣṭo yājñavalkyastasmai janakāya ha kila varandadau /
sa ca janako ha kāmapraśnameva varaṃ vavre vṛtavāṃstaṃ ca varaṃ hāsmai dadau yājñavalkyaḥ /
tena varapradānasāmarthyenāvyācikhyāsumapidāviti /
yājñavalkyaṃ tūṣṇaiṃ sthitamapi samrāḍeva janakaḥ pūrvaṃ papraccha /
children.translated_text: The king himself questioned first, even though <s>Yājñavalkya</s> was sitting in silence.

children.text: tatraivānuktirbrahmavidyāyāḥ karmaṇā viruddhatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therein, the non-initiative [of <s>Yājñavalkya</s> in teaching] is because <s>Brahmavidyā</s> (knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>) is contradictory to <s>karma</s> (ritual action).

children.text: vidyāyāśca svātantryāt /
children.translated_text: And because of the independence of <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge).

children.text: svatantrā hi brahmavidyā sahakārisādhanāntaranirapekṣā puruṣārthasādhaneti ca //4,3.1//
children.translated_text: For <s>Brahmavidyā</s> is independent — not dependent on any other auxiliary means — as a means to the supreme human goal. // 4.3.1 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.1: '<s>Yājñavalkya</s> went to <s>Janaka Vaideha</s>' — this is the connection.
The self constituted of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>) is the directly perceived, non-mediate <s>Brahman</s>, the innermost of all, the supreme indeed — [as known] from <s>śrutis</s> such as: 'There is no other seer than he; there is no other hearer' (BṛUp 3.7.23) and the like.
This [self], having entered here [into the body], marked by speech and the like — its distinction [from the body] was ascertained in the Honey Chapter (<s>Madhukāṇḍa</s>) and the <s>Ajātaśatru</s> dialogue through the negation of agentship and enjoyership belonging to the <s>prāṇas</s> and the like. And though it was [thus] ascertained, again, in the <s>Uṣasta</s> questions, presenting the marks of breathing and the like, it was ascertained in general terms through 'that which breathes by <s>prāṇa</s>' and so forth, and [then more specifically] through 'of seeing, the seer' and so forth — as having the nature of undiminished power.
And its <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) is caused by extraneous limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) — just as in the case of a rope, shell, or sky, the superimposition of snake, silver, or dirt is caused by something else and is not intrinsic. Thus, the unconditioned, undesignable [self], to be described as '<s>neti neti</s>' (not this, not this) — directly perceived, non-mediate, innermost of all — the self, <s>Brahman</s>, the Imperishable, the Inner Controller, the praiseworthy <s>Upaniṣadic</s> person, <s>Brahman</s> as consciousness and bliss — [all this] was ascertained.
That very [self], then, under the name '<s>indha</s>' (the kindler), is the one who feeds on subtly differentiated food; interior to that, in the heart, is the subtle body (<s>liṅgātman</s>), the one who feeds on even more subtly differentiated food; beyond that, through the limiting adjunct of <s>prāṇa</s>, is the cosmic self; and then, having dissolved even that cosmic self — which serves as a limiting adjunct — through knowledge, just as one [dissolves] a snake and the like [superimposed] on a rope — [one reaches] 'this is that [self described as] <s>neti neti</s>' — the directly perceived, innermost <s>Brahman</s> was ascertained.
Thus, in brief, <s>Janaka</s> was brought to fearlessness by <s>Yājñavalkya</s> through scripture. And here, the states of waking, dream, deep sleep, and the fourth (<s>turīya</s>) were presented incidentally — [through] the kindler, the one feeding on subtly differentiated food, 'all the <s>prāṇas</s>,' 'all the <s>prāṇas</s>,' [and] 'this is that [self described as] <s>neti neti</s>.'
Now, the ascertainment must be made in detail, through the gateway of waking and dream, with extensive reasoning. Fearlessness must be bestowed. The real existence of the self must be [established] through the removal of doubts [arising from] conflicting views. Its distinctness [from the body], purity, self-luminosity, nature of undiminished power, intrinsic unsurpassed bliss, and non-duality must be ascertained — for this purpose, this [section] is commenced.
The narrative, however, is for the purpose of illuminating the procedure for the transmission and reception of knowledge, and specifically for the praise of knowledge — as indicated by the granting of boons and the like.
<s>Yājñavalkya</s> went to <s>Janaka Vaideha</s>. And while going, he thought thus: 'I shall not speak anything at all to the king.' The purpose of going was for the sake of material support (<s>yogakṣema</s>). Yet, even though <s>Yājñavalkya</s> had resolved not to speak, whatever <s>Janaka</s> asked, he answered — what is the reason for acting contrary to his resolution? To explain this, [the text] narrates the story. Previously, it is said, there had been a conversation between <s>Janaka</s> and <s>Yājñavalkya</s> occasioned by the <s>Agnihotra</s>. There, having perceived <s>Janaka</s>'s knowledge regarding the <s>Agnihotra</s>, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, being pleased, granted him, <s>Janaka</s>, a boon. And <s>Janaka</s> chose as his boon the freedom to ask any question he wished. And <s>Yājñavalkya</s> granted him that boon. By the force of that boon-granting, he was compelled to speak even though he had not wished to.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.2

yājñavalkya kiṃjyotir ayaṃ puruṣa iti |
ādityajyotiḥ samrāḍ iti hovāca |
ādityenaivāyaṃ jyotiṣāste palyayate karma kurute vipalyetīti |
evam evaitad yājñavalkya || BrhUp_4,3.2 ||
children.translated_text: '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>, what serves as the light for this person?' 'The sun serves as his light, O King — for by the light of the sun one sits, goes about, does one's work, and returns.' 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // BṛhUp 4.3.2 //
[Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.2]

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.2 he yājñavalkyetyevaṃ saṃbodhyābhimukhīkaraṇāya kiñjyotirayaṃ puruṣa iti kimasya puruṣasya jyotiryena jyotiṣā vyavaharati so 'yaṃ kiñjyotirayaṃ prākṛtaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātarūpaḥ śiraḥpāṇyādimānpuruṣaḥ pṛcchyate /
kimayaṃ svāvayavāsaṃghātabāhyena jyotirantareṇa vyavaharatyāhosvitsvāvayavasaṃghātamadhyapātinā jyotiṣā jyotiṣkāryamayaṃ puruṣo nirvartayatītyetadabhipretya pṛcchati /
kiñcāto yadi vyatiriktena yadi vāvyatiriktena-jyotiṣā jyotiṣkāryaṃ nirvartayati /
śṛṇu tatra kāraṇam yadi vyatiriktenaivajyotiṣā jyotiṣkāryanirvartakatvamasya svabhāvo nirdhārito bhavati tato 'dṛṣṭajyotiṣkāryaviṣaye 'pyanumāsyāmahe vyatiriktajyotirnimittamevedaṃ kāryamiti /
athāvyatiriktenaiva svātmanā jyotiṣā vyavaharati tato 'pratyakṣe 'pi jyotiṣi jyotiṣkāryadarśane 'byatiriktameva jyotiranumeyam /
athāniyama eva vyatiriktamavyatiriktaṃ vā jyotiḥ puruṣasya vyavahārahetustato 'nadhyavasāya eva jyotirviṣaya ityevaṃ manvānaḥ pṛcchati janako yājñavalkyaṃ kiñjyotirayaṃ puruṣa iti /
nanvevamanumānakauśale janakasya kiṃ praśnena svayameva kasmānna pratipadyata iti /
satyametat /
tathāpi liṅgaliṅgisaṃbandhaviśeṣāṇāmatyantasaukṣmyādduravabodhyatāṃ manyate bahūnāmapu paṇḍitānāṃ kimutaikasya /
ata eva hi dharmasūkṣmanirṇaye pariṣadvyāpāra iṣyate /
puruṣaviśeṣaścāpekṣyate /
daśāvarā pariṣattrayo vaiko veti /
tasmādyadyapyanumānakauśalaṃ rājñastathāpi tu yukto yājñavalkyaḥ praṣṭum /
vijñānakauśalatāratamyopapatteḥ puruṣāṇām /
athavā śrutiḥ svayamevā'khyāyikāvyājenānumānamārgamupanyasyāsmānbodhayati puruṣamatimanusartī /
yājñavalkyo 'pi janakābhiprāyabhijñatayā vyatiriktamātmajyotirbodhayiṣyañjanakaṃ vyatiriktapratipādakameva liṅgaṃ pratipede yathā prasiddhamādityajyotiḥ samrāḍiti hovāca /
children.translated_text: <s>Yājñavalkya</s> too, knowing <s>Janaka</s>'s intent — wishing to make known the distinct light that is the self — accepted the very mark that establishes the distinct [light], [saying] as is well known: 'The sun serves as his light, O King.'

children.text: katham /
children.translated_text: How so?

children.text: ādityenaiva svāvayavasaghātavyatiriktena cakṣuṣo 'nugrāhakeṇa jyotiṣāyaṃ prākṛtaḥ puruṣa āsta upaviśati palyayate prayeti kṣetramaraṇyaṃ vā tatra gatvā karma bāhyanekajyotiḥpradarśanaṃ ca liṅgasyāvyabhicāritvadarśanārtham /
children.translated_text: By the sun alone — distinct from his own bodily aggregate, serving as the supporter of the eye — by that light, this ordinary person sits, moves about, goes to a field or forest, and there performs work. And the showing of multiple external lights [serves] to demonstrate the non-deviation of the mark [i.e., that action always requires a light].

children.text: evamevaitadyājñavalkya //4,3.2//
children.translated_text: 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // 4.3.2 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.2: 'O <s>Yājñavalkya</s>' — thus addressing him to gain his attention — 'what serves as the light for this person?' — what is the light of this person, by which light he functions? This ordinary person, in the form of the aggregate of effects and instruments, possessing head, hands, and the like — this is the person being asked about.
Does this person function by a light external to his own bodily aggregate, or does he accomplish the work requiring light by a light that falls within his own bodily aggregate? — this is the intent of the question.
Moreover — whether by a light that is distinct [from the body] or by one that is not distinct — [the question is:] does he accomplish the work of light? Listen to the reason: if it is established that his nature is to accomplish the work of light only by a distinct light, then even in cases where the work of light is accomplished but no distinct light is seen, we shall infer that 'this work [of light] must be caused by a distinct light.' But if he functions by a light that is not distinct, by his own self, then even when no light is perceptible, from seeing the work of light, a non-distinct light alone is to be inferred. Or if there is no fixed rule — whether the person's cause of functioning is a distinct or non-distinct light — then there would be no definite conclusion regarding light. Thinking thus, <s>Janaka</s> asks <s>Yājñavalkya</s>: 'What serves as the light for this person?'
[Objection:] If <s>Janaka</s> possesses such skill in inference, why does he not determine this himself? Why this question?
[Reply:] True. Nevertheless, because of the extreme subtlety of the specific connections between the marks and the things marked, he considers it difficult for many learned persons to understand — how much more so for one person. For this very reason, the functioning of a council is desired in the determination of subtle <s>dharma</s>. And specific persons are required: 'a council of at least ten, or three, or one.' Therefore, even though the king possesses skill in inference, it is appropriate for him to question <s>Yājñavalkya</s> — because there are degrees of excellence in the knowledge of persons. Alternatively, the <s>śruti</s> itself, under the guise of a narrative, presents the path of inference, following the [natural] understanding of persons, in order to instruct us.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.3
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.3]

children.text:
astamita āditye yājñavalkya kiṃjyotir evāyaṃ puruṣa iti |
candramā evāsya jyotir bhavatīti |
candramasaivāyaṃ jyotiṣāste palyayate karma kurute vipalyetīti |
evam evaitad yājñavalkya || BrhUp_4,3.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'When the sun has set, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, what serves as the light for this person?' 'The moon serves as his light — for by the light of the moon one sits, goes about, does one's work, and returns.' 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // BṛhUp 4.3.3 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,3.3 tathāstamita āditye yājñavalkya kiñjyotirevāyaṃ puruṣa iti candramā evāsya jyotiḥ //4,3.3//
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.3: Similarly, when the sun has set — '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>, what serves as the light for this person?' — the moon alone serves as his light. // 4.3.3 //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.4
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.4]

children.text:
astamita āditye yājñavalkya candramasy astamite kiṃjyotir evāyaṃ puruṣa iti |
agnir evāsya jyotir bhavatīti |
agninaiva jyotiṣāste palyayate karma kurute vipalyetīti |
evam evaitad yājñavalkya || BrhUp_4,3.4 ||
children.translated_text: 'When the sun has set, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, and the moon has set, what serves as the light for this person?' 'Fire serves as his light — for by the light of fire one sits, goes about, does one's work, and returns.' 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // BṛhUp 4.3.4 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,3.4 astamiti āditye candramasyastamite 'gnirjyotiḥ //4,3.4//
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.4: When the sun has set and the moon has set — fire is the light. // 4.3.4 //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.5
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.5]

children.text:
astamita āditye yājñavalkya candramasy astamite śānte 'gnau kiṃjyotir evāyaṃ puruṣa iti |
vāg evāsya jyotir bhavatīti |
vācaivāyaṃ jyotiṣāste palyayate karma kurute vipalyeti |
tasmād vai samrāḍ api yatra svaḥ pāṇir na vinirjñāyate 'tha yatra vāg uccaraty upaiva tatra nyetīti |
evam evaitad yājñavalkya || BrhUp_4,3.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'When the sun has set, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what serves as the light for this person?' 'Speech serves as his light — for by the light of speech one sits, goes about, does one's work, and returns. Therefore, O King, even where one's own hand is not discerned, when speech is uttered, one goes toward it.' 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // BṛhUp 4.3.5 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.5 śānte 'gnau vāgjyotiḥ vāgiti śabdaḥ parigṛhyate /
śabdena viṣayeṇa śrotramindriyaṃ dīpyate /
śrotrendriye saṃpradīpte manasi viveka upajāyate /
tena manasā bāhyāṃ ceṣṭāṃ pratipadyate /
"manasā hyova paśyati manasā śṛṇotī"ti brāhmaṇam /
kathaṃ purvāgjyotiriti vācojyotiṣṭvamaprasiddhamityata āha-tasmādvai samrāḍyasmādvācā jyotiṣānugṛhīto 'yaṭaṃ puruṣo vyavaharati tasmātprasiddhametadvāco jyotiṣṭvam /
kathamapi yatra yasminkāle prāvṛṣi prāyeṇa medhāndhakāre sarvajyotiḥpratyastamaye svo 'pi prāṇirhasto na vispaṣṭaṃ nirjñāyate /
atha tasminkāle sarvaceṣṭānirodhe prāpte bāhyajyotiṣo 'bhāvādyatra vāguccarati śvā vā bhaṣati gardabho vā rautyupaiva tatra nyeti tena śabdena jyotiṣā śrotramanasornairantayaṃ bhavati tena jyotiṣkāryatvaṃ vākpratipadyeta tena vācā jyotiṣopanyetyevopagacchatyeva tatra sannihito bhavatītyarthaḥ /
tatra ca karma kurute vipalyeti /
tatra vāgyotiṣo grahaṇaṃ gandhādīnānupalakṣaṇārtham /
children.translated_text: Therein, the mention of speech as light is for the purpose of implying odors and the like as well.

children.text: gandhādibhirapi hi ghrāṇādiṣvanugṛhīteṣu pravṛttinivṛtyādayo bhavanti /
children.translated_text: For by odors and the like too, when the organs of smell and the rest are supported, activities of engagement and withdrawal occur.

children.text: tena tairapyanugraho bhavati kāryakaraṇasaṃghātasya /
children.translated_text: Therefore, by those [senses] too, there is support for the aggregate of effects and instruments.

children.text: evamevaitadyājñavalkya //4,3.5//
children.translated_text: 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.' // 4.3.5 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.5: When the fire has gone out — speech is the light. By 'speech' (<s>vāc</s>), sound is indicated. By sound, the sense-object, the sense-organ of hearing is illuminated. When the organ of hearing is kindled, discrimination arises in the mind. By that mind, one engages in external activity. [As the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> states:] 'For by the mind one sees, by the mind one hears.' But how is speech the light? — since the light-nature of speech is not well known — to this he says: 'Therefore, O King, since this person functions supported by the light of speech — therefore the light-nature of speech is well known. How so? When — at the time when, generally during the rainy season, in the darkness of clouds, when all lights have set — even one's own hand, one's own limb, is not clearly discerned. But at that time, when all activity has ceased because of the absence of external light — when speech is uttered, or a dog barks, or a donkey brays — one goes toward it; by that sound, as light, the continuity of hearing and mind is established; thereby, [the sound] attains the status of accomplishing the work of light; by that speech as light, one goes toward [it], approaches, comes near — this is the meaning. And there one does one's work and returns.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.6
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.6]

children.text:
astamita āditye yājñavalkya candramasy astamite śānte 'gnau śāntāyāṃ vāci kiṃjyotir evāyaṃ puruṣa iti |
ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavatīti |
ātmanaivāyaṃ jyotiṣāste palyayate karma kurute vipalyetīti || BrhUp_4,3.6 ||
children.translated_text: 'When the sun has set, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, and speech has become silent — what serves as the light for this person?' 'The self alone serves as his light — for by the light of the self alone one sits, goes about, does one's work, and returns.' // BṛhUp 4.3.6 //

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.6 śāntāyā punarvāci gandhādiṣvapi ca śānteṣu /

etaduktaṃ bhavati /

tataścetatsiddhaṃ bhavati yaḥ svapne paśyati dṛṣṭapūrvaṃ vastu sa eva pūrvaṃ vidyamāne cakṣuṣyadrākṣīnna deha iti /

ādityādibhistatsamānajātīyairevopakriyamāṇatvāditi /

upakāryopakārakabhāvasyāniyamadarśanāt /

anenaiva jyotirantarasyātmatvamapi pratyuktam /

children.translated_text: [Commentary:] As for the further statement that <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> necessarily have the intrinsic nature of bestowing fruits —

children.text: tadabhyubagame bhavataḥ siddhāntahānāt /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] accepting that would lead to the abandonment of your own established position.

children.text: etenānavasthādoṣaḥ pratyuktaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] By this, the fault of infinite regress is also answered.

children.text: tasmādasti vyatiriktaṃ cāntaḥsthaṃ jyotirātmeti //4,3.6//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, there exists a separate, inner light — the self. (4.3.6)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.6:] When speech has ceased, and when the external [objects] — odors and the like — have also ceased, when the external helpers [i.e. light-sources] have all withdrawn, a complete cessation of all activity is reached for this person. What is being said is this: In the waking state, when the external organs — eye and the like — are assisted by the lights of the sun and the like, acting outwardly, then the transactions of this person — as the seer — are most clear. Therefore, we hold that even when all external light has set — in the states of dream, deep sleep, and even in that condition during waking [when external light is absent] — the accomplishment of the function of light is through a light that is distinct from the aggregate of his own bodily parts. And the accomplishment of the function of light is seen in dreams — such as meeting and separating from relatives, traveling to other places, and so forth. And upon waking from deep sleep: 'I slept happily; I knew nothing.' Therefore, there exists some distinct light. What then is that light when speech has ceased? It is said: 'The self alone is his light.' By 'self' is meant that which is distinct from the aggregate of effects and instruments [i.e., body and senses], which illuminates the effects and instruments — like the external light of the sun and the like — which is not itself illuminated by anything else. This light is inner — by the process of elimination. That it is distinct from the effects and instruments — this much is established. And that which is distinct from the effects and instruments and which assists the aggregate of effects and instruments as a light — that is not perceived by the external instruments like the eye; not like the light of the sun and the like, when those have withdrawn. But the effect of the light is seen [in dream and memory]; therefore, it is understood that this [person] exists, eats, acts, and moves about by the light of the self alone. Hence it is indeed understood that there is an inner light. Moreover, that [inner light] is of a character different from the light of the sun and the like, and is non-material — the very reason being that it is not grasped by the eye and the like, unlike the sun and the like. [Objection by the materialist:] No — [we infer that the inner light must be] of the same class only. The light of the sun and the like — being material — is observed to assist the material aggregate of effects and instruments. What has been observed [as the pattern] should be the basis for inference. Even if the light that assists the aggregate of effects and instruments is a separate entity, it should be inferred to be of the same class as the aggregate of effects and instruments — because it assists the aggregate of effects and instruments, just like the light of the sun and the like. As for the alleged difference in character from being inner and imperceptible — that is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) with respect to the lights of the eye and the like. For the lights of the eye and the like are imperceptible and inner, yet they are material. Therefore, the distinct inner light of the self is merely your wishful thinking. And since [this alleged light] exists and ceases to exist along with the aggregate of effects and instruments, it is inferred to be a property of the aggregate. Moreover, the inference based on general observation (<s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s>) is unreliable because it is subject to deviation. For you establish a light distinct from the effects and instruments — like the sun and the like — by the force of general observation. But perception cannot be overridden by inference. This very aggregate of effects and instruments is the one that is directly perceived as seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing. Even if there were another light assisting it — like the sun and the like — it would not thereby be the self; it would be [merely] another light, like the sun and the like. But the one who directly performs the act of seeing — that alone would be the self, and that is the aggregate of effects and instruments, not another. For inference has no validity when it contradicts perception. [Objection:] But if this aggregate is the agent of seeing and the like, how is it that this very same [aggregate], while intact, sometimes performs the act of seeing and sometimes does not? [Reply:] This is no fault — because it is observed. What is observed cannot be called impossible. For when a firefly is observed to be sometimes luminous and sometimes not, no other cause need be inferred. And if inference were [required], then by some common feature, everything would be inferrable everywhere — and that is undesired. And there does exist intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) of things — for the heat of fire is not due to some other cause, nor is the coldness of water. [Objection:] [This depends on] the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> of living beings! [Reply:] Then <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> themselves would require another cause as their intrinsic nature — and so on [ad infinitum]. [Objection:] Let it be so! [Reply:] No — that would lead to an infinite regress. And that is undesirable. [Śaṅkara's refutation:] No [to the materialist position] — because what has been seen previously is [re-]seen in dream and memory. What was said by the advocate of intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāvavādin</s>) — that the act of seeing belongs to the body alone, not to something separate — that is wrong. For if the act of seeing belonged to the body alone, then in dreams, only what has been previously seen would not be seen [by a separate seer]. A blind person sees in dreams only what he has previously seen; he does not see the unfamiliar forms of places like <s>Śākadvīpa</s>. From this, it is established that the one who sees in dreams the previously seen object is the very same one who, when the eye existed [before blindness], saw — not the body. For if the body were the seer, then when the eye — by which it saw — has been removed, it should not see in dreams the very same previously seen [objects]. And there is a well-known recognition in the world: 'The peak of <s>Himavat</s> that I saw before — I saw it today in a dream' — even among the blind whose eyes have been removed. Therefore, even when the eye has not been removed, the one who is the seer in dreams is the same [eternal] seer — not the body; this is understood. Similarly, in memory: when the identity of the seer and the rememberer is [established], the very one who was the seer is the rememberer. And when this is so, even one whose eyes are closed sees the previously seen form as if seeing it [again]. Therefore, that which is seen when the eyes are closed is not the seer; [rather,] the one who, when the eyes are closed, sees the remembered form — that very one was the seer even when the eyes were open; this is understood. And when the body dies — even though it is intact — there is no seeing of forms and the like. If the body itself were the seer, seeing and the like would occur even in a dead [body]. Therefore, it is understood that the one in whose absence from the body seeing does not occur, and in whose presence [it does] occur — that agent of seeing and the like is not the body. [Objection:] The eye and other [organs] alone are the agents of seeing! [Reply:] No — because the recognition 'What I saw, I now touch' would be impossible if there were different agents [for each]. [Objection:] Then the mind [is the agent]! [Reply:] No — because the mind too is an object [of awareness], like forms and the like; hence agency of seeing and the like does not apply to it. Therefore, it is established that there is an inner, separate [entity] like the sun and the like. As for the claim that the inner light must be inferred to be of the same class as the aggregate of effects and instruments — because the aggregate is assisted by the lights of the sun and the like which are of the same class — that is wrong. For no fixed rule is observed [governing] the relationship between what is assisted and what assists. How so? Earthen fuel — straw, cow-dung, and the like, which are of the same class as earth — is observed to assist fire in blazing. But it should not therefore be inferred that fire is assisted in blazing only by things of the same class everywhere. For water — which is of a different class — is observed to assist the blazing of lightning-fire and stomach-fire. Therefore, there is no rule that what assists and what is assisted must be of the same class. Sometimes humans are assisted by humans of the same class; sometimes by plants, animals, and the like, of a different class. Therefore, the argument 'because the aggregate of effects and instruments is assisted by the lights of the sun and the like, which are of the same class' is inconclusive. As for your further statement that the inner light's imperceptibility by the eye and the like — like the sun and the like — does not establish its inner nature or its difference in character, because this [reason] is inconclusive with respect to the eye and the like — that is wrong. For the reason is qualified: 'being different from the instruments such as the eye' — and thus the qualification is justified. As for the claim that the light is a property of the aggregate of effects and instruments — that is wrong, because of the contradiction with inference. The inference has been stated: 'The light is a separate entity from the aggregate of effects and instruments, like the light of the sun and the like.' This inference contradicts the proposition that the light is a property of the aggregate. The alleged co-presence and co-absence [of the light with the aggregate] is unestablished — because the light is not observed [to cease] when the body dies [for the body may die but the light persists in dreams of others about the dead]. The invalidity of inference based on general observation would lead to the absurd consequence of the collapse of all transactions such as eating, drinking, and the like — and that is undesirable. For in the case of eating and drinking, having observed that hunger and thirst cease [upon eating and drinking], the adoption of eating and drinking based on that general [observation] — which is seen in the world — would not be possible. For those who have observed [the effect of] eating and drinking are seen to infer, by general observation, that further eating and drinking will again remove hunger and thirst, and to engage accordingly. What was said — that 'this body alone is the agent of seeing and the like' — that has been refuted at the outset: in dream and memory, the seer is an entity distinct from the body. By this very [argument], the selfhood of the inner light is also answered. As for [the claim about] the occasional luminosity and non-luminosity of the firefly — that is [explained as follows]: its luminosity and non-luminosity have a definite cause — namely, the contraction and expansion of the wing-parts and the like.

children.translated_text: 'Which is the self?' 'This <s>Puruṣa</s> who consists of consciousness (<s>vijñānamaya</s>), who is among the <s>prāṇas</s> (vital breaths), who is the inner light in the heart. He, remaining the same, wanders through both worlds, as if thinking, as if moving. Having become sleep, he transcends this world — the forms of death.' (BṛUp 4.3.7)

children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Through this chain of succession, the self illuminates the entire aggregate of effects and instruments with the light of its own nature as consciousness.

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.7:] Even though the separateness [of the self from the body] and the like has been established, [<s>Janaka</s>] asks out of lack of discrimination — 'Which one?' — because of the confusion caused by the observation of the capacity of similar entities to assist [each other, leading to the thought:] 'Perhaps it is simply one of the senses that is separate.' The confusion is understandable because the subtlety of the reasoning is difficult to comprehend. Alternatively, even when the [self's] separateness from the body has been established, since all the senses appear to possess consciousness, and since the self, when discriminated [from them], is not apprehended — therefore, 'I ask: which is the self?' — meaning: 'which among the body, senses, vital breaths, and mind is that self of which you have spoken?' — 'by which light it sits' — as was said. Or alternatively: 'that self which you intend — the <s>vijñānamaya</s> (constituted of consciousness) — all these vital breaths (<s>prāṇas</s>) appear to be constituted of consciousness; among these <s>prāṇas</s>, which one is [the self]?' — just as, when <s>brāhmaṇas</s> are assembled, [one might ask:] 'All of these are brilliant — which one among them is the knower of the six limbs [of the <s>Veda</s>]?'
In the first interpretation, 'which is the self?' — this alone constitutes the question-sentence; [in the second interpretation, the question extends to:] 'which is the <s>vijñānamaya</s>, the light within the heart, the <s>puruṣa</s>?' The phrase 'this <s>vijñānamaya</s>' — the specific meaning determined for this word [governs the sentence]; and the word 'which is the self?' serves to complete the question-sentence. Without requiring a remote connection, this is fitting — and thus the question-sentence extends only to 'which is the self?'; and everything beginning with 'this <s>vijñānamaya</s>' constitutes the answer — this is determined.
'This' (<s>yo 'yam</s>) — the designation is due to the perceptibility of the self. '<s>Vijñānamaya</s>' (constituted of consciousness) — predominantly of the nature of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>); because the distinction between the intellect's cognition (<s>buddhivijñāna</s>) and [the self] as its limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) is not discerned, [the self] is called <s>vijñānamaya</s>. For [the self] is always apprehended as associated with the cognition of the intellect, like <s>Rāhu</s> [who is visible only when] associated with the sun and moon. For the intellect is the instrument of [apprehending] all objects — like a lamp placed in front [of objects] in darkness. For it has been said: 'By the mind alone one sees; by the mind alone one hears' (BṛUp 1.5.3). The entire class of sense-objects is apprehended as qualified by the light of the intellect's cognition alone — just as [objects] in darkness [are apprehended as qualified] by the light of a lamp placed in front [of them]. But the other senses are mere doorways for the intellect. Therefore, [the self] is specially designated by that [intellect] alone as '<s>vijñānamaya</s>.' For those who explain [<s>vijñānamaya</s>] as 'a modification of the cognition of the <s>Paramātman</s>' — since the word <s>vijñānamaya</s> is seen to have a different meaning in [the phrase] '<s>manomaya</s>' (constituted of mind) and so forth — the non-scriptural meaning is concluded. And a word whose meaning is doubtful can be determined from the observation of its settled usage elsewhere, or from the remainder of the sentence, or by the force of settled reasoning. And [this is confirmed] from the reading '<s>sadhīḥ</s>' ('endowed with intellect') in the subsequent [passage]. From the statement 'within the heart' (<s>hṛdy antar</s>), the meaning 'predominantly consisting of consciousness' alone is fitting.
'Among the <s>prāṇas</s>' — the seventh [locative] case is for the purpose of showing separateness, like [the expression] 'a stone among trees' — denoting proximity. For with respect to the <s>prāṇas</s>, there is doubt as to whether the self is separate or non-separate. 'Among the <s>prāṇas</s>' means 'separate from the <s>prāṇas</s>' — this is the meaning. For that which is 'among' [certain things] is indeed separate from them — just as a stone among trees.
[Objection:] But if it is in the heart, the intellect, being among the <s>prāṇas</s>, would be of the same class as the <s>prāṇas</s>. [Reply:] Therefore, [the text] says 'within the heart' (<s>hṛdy antar</s>). By the word 'heart' (<s>hṛd</s>), the lotus-shaped flesh-lump is [denoted]; the intellect is [stationed] in the heart — [so] 'in the heart' means 'in the intellect.' 'Within' (<s>antar</s>) is for the purpose of showing separateness from the modifications of the intellect. 'Light' (<s>jyotiḥ</s>) — because of its nature as illumination, the self is called [light]. For by that illuminating self — by that light — it sits, it moves, it performs action. For this lump of effects and instruments is entirely dependent [on the self's light], just as a pot placed in sunlight, or just as a gem such as an emerald cast into a liquid like milk for the purpose of examination makes that milk and the like take on its own reflected color — similarly, the light of the self makes even the intellect — though situated within the heart and subtle — and the entire aggregate of effects and instruments starting with the heart, unified [with itself], take on its own reflected light.
By a chain of succession, through the gradation from subtle to gross, [the self] is the innermost of all. To begin with, the intellect — because of its transparency and immediate proximity — becomes the reflector of the light of the self's consciousness. Therefore, even for the discriminating, the sense of 'I' (<s>ātmābhimāna</s>) with respect to the intellect arises first. Then, because of its immediate proximity, in the mind too — the appearance of consciousness, through contact with the intellect. Then in the senses — through contact with the mind. Then next, in the body — through contact with the senses.
