tatra nāmarūpopādhisādṛśyaṃ bhrāntinimittaṃ yattadeva heturna svata ityetaducyate /
yasmātsa samānaḥ sannubhau lokāvanukrameṇa sañcarati tadetatpratyakṣamityetaddarśayati-yato dhyāyatīva dhyānavyāpāraṃ karotīva cintayatīva dhyānavyāpavatīṃ buddhiṃ sa tatsthena citsvabhāvajyotarūpeṇāvabhāsayaṃstatsadṛśastatsamānaḥ sandhyātīvālokavadeva /
ato bhavati cintayatīti bhrāntirlokasya /
na tu paramārthato dhyāyati /
tathā lelāyatīvātyarthaṃ calatīva /
teṣveva karameṣu buddhyādiṣu vāyuṣu ca calatsu tadavabhāsakatvāttatsadṛśaṃ taditi lelāyatīva /
na tu paramārthataścalanadharmakaṃ tadātmajyotiḥ /
kathaṃ punaretadavagamyate tatsamānatvabhrāntirevobhayalokasaṃcaraṇādirhetutvaṃ svata ityasyārthasya pradarśanāya hetarupadiśyate- sa ātmā hi yasmātsvapno bhūtvā /
sa yayā dhiyā samānaḥ sā dhīryadyadbhavati tattadasāvapu bhavatīva tasmādyadāsau svapno bhavati svāpavṛttiṃ pratipadyate dhīstadā so 'pi svapnavṛttiṃ pratipadyate /
dā dhīrjajāgariṣati tadāsāvapyata āha-svapno bhūtvā svapnavṛttimavabhāsayandhiyaḥ svāpavṛtyākāro bhūtvema lokaṃ jāgaritavyavahāralakṣaṇaṃ kāryakaraṇasaṅghātātmakaṃ laukikaśāstrīyavyavahārāspadamatikrāmatyatītya krāmati viviktena svenā'tmajyotiṣā svapnātmikā dhīvṛttamavabhāyannavatiṣṭhate yasmāttasmātsvayañjyotaḥsvabhāva evāsau viśuddhaḥ sa kartṛkriyākārakaphalaśūnyaḥ /
paramārthato dhīsādṛśyameva tūbhayalokasaṃcārādisaṃvyavahārabhrāntihetuḥ /
mṛtyorūpā ṇi mṛtyuḥ karmāvidyādirna tasyānyadrūpaṃ svataḥ kāryakaraṇānyevāsya rūpāṇi /
atastānu mṛtyo rūpāṇyatikrāmati kriyāphalāśrayāṇi /
nanu nāstyeva dhiyā samānamanyaddhiyo 'vabhāsakamātmajyotiḥ pratyakṣeṇa vānumānena palambhāt /
yathānyā tatkāla eva dvitīyā dhīḥ /
yattvāvabhāsyāvabhāsakayoranyatve 'pi vivekānupalambhātsādṛśyamiti (tiḥ) ghaṭādyālokayoḥ /
tatra bhavatvanyatvenā'lokasyopambhādghaṭādeḥ saṃśliṣṭayoḥ sādṛśyaṃ bhinnayoreva na ca tatheha ghaṭāderiva dhiyoṣa'vabhāsakaṃ jyotirintaraṃ pratyakṣeṇa vānumānena vopalabhāmahe /
dhīreva hi citsvarūpāvabhāsakatvenasvākārā viṣayākārā ca /
tasmānnānumānato nāpi pratyakṣato dhiyo 'vabhāsakaṃ jyotiḥ śakyate pratipādayituṃ vyatiriktam /
yadapi dṛṣṭāntarūpamabhihitamavabhāsyāvaśāsakayorbhinnayoreva ghaṭādyālokayoḥ saṃyuktāyoḥ sādṛśyamiti /
tatrābhyupagamamātramasmābhiruktaṃ na tatra ghaṭādyavabhāsyāvabhāsakau bhinnau /
paramārthastu ghaṭādirevāvabhāsātmakaḥ sālokaḥ /
anyo 'nyo hi ghaṭādirutpadyate /
vijñānamātrameva sālokaghaṭādiviṣayākāramavabhāsate /
yadevaṃ tadā na bāhyo dṛṣṭānto 'sti vijñānalakṣaṇamātratvātsarvasya /
eṃ tasyava vijñānas grāhyāgrāhakākāratāmalaṃ pakarikalpya tasyaiva punarviśuddhaṃ parikalpayanti /
tadgrāhakavinirmuktaṃ vijñānaṃ svacchībhūtaṃ kṣaṇikaṃ vyavatiṣṭhata iti kecit /
tasyāpu śāntiṃ kecidicchanti /
tadapi vijñānaṃ saṃvṛtaṃ grāhyagrāhakāṃśavinirumuktaṃ śūnyameva ghaṭādibāhyavastuvadityapare mādhyamikā ācakṣate /
sarvā etāḥ kalpanā buddhavijñānāvabhāsakasya vyatiriktasyā'tmajyotiṣo 'pahnavādasya śreyomārgasya pratipakṣabhūtā vaidikasya /
tatra yeṣāṃ bāhyor'tho 'sti tānpratyucyate tāvat /
na svātmāvabhāsakatvaṃ ghaṭādeḥ /
tamasyavasthito ghaṭādistāvanna kadācidapu svātmanāvabhāsyate /
pradīpādyālokasaṃyogena tu niyamenaivāvabhāsyamāno dṛṣṭaḥ sāloko ghaṭa iti /
saṃśliṣṭayorapu ghaṭālokayoranyatvameva punaḥ punaḥ saṃśleṣe viśleṣe ca viśeṣadarśanādrajjughaṭayoriva /
anyatve ca vyatiriktāvabhāsakatvaṃ na svātmanaiva svamātmānamavabhāsayati /
nanu pradīpaḥ svātmānamevāvabhāsayantadṛṣṭa iti /
na hi ghaṭādivatpradīpadarśanāya pkāśāntaramupādadate laukikāḥ /
tasmātpradīpaḥ svātmānaṃ prakāśayati /
na /
avabhāsyatvāviśeṣāt /
yadyapi pradīpo 'nyasyāvabhāsakaḥ svayamavabhāsātkatvāttathāpu vyatiriktacaitanyāvabhāsyatvaṃ na vyabhicarati ghaṭādivadeva /
yadā caivaṃ tadā vyatiriktāvabhāsyatvaṃ tāvadavaśyaṃbhāvi /
nanu yathā ghaṭaścaitanyāvabhāsyatve 'pi sannātmānaṃ ghaṭaṃ cāvabhāsayati /
na /
svataḥ parato vā viśeṣābhāvāt /
yathā caitanyāvabhāsyatvaṃ ghaṭasya tathā pradīpasyāpi caitanyāvabhāsyatvamaviśiṣṭam /
yattūcyate pradīpa ātmānaṃ ghaṭaṃ cāvabhāsayatīti tadasat /
kasmāt /
yadā'tmānaṃ nāvabhāsayati tadā kīdṛśaḥ syāt /
na hi tadā pradīpasya svato vā parato vā viśeṣaḥ kaścidupalabhyate /
sa hyavabhāsyo bhavati yasyāvabhāsakasaṃnidhāvasaṃnidhau ca viśeṣa ātmānaṃ pradīpaḥ prakāśayatīti mṛṣaivācyot /
caitanyagrāhyatvaṃ tu ghaṭādibhiraviśiṣṭaṃ pradīpasya /
tasmādvijñanasyā'tmagrāhakatve na pradīpo dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
caitanyagrāhyatvaṃ ca vijñānasya bāhyaviṣayairaviśiṣṭam /
caitanyagrāhyatve ca vijñānasya kiṃ grāhyavijñānagrāhyataiva kiṃvā grāhakavijñānagrāhyateti tatrasaṃdihyamāne vastuni yo 'nyatra dṛṣṭo nyāyaḥ sa kalpayituṃ yukto na tu dṛṣṭaviparītaḥ /
tathā ca sati yathā vyitiriktenaiva grāhakeṇa bāhyānāṃ pradīpānāṃ grāhyatvaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ tathā vijñānasyāpi caitanyagrāhyatvātpkāśakatve satyāpi pradīpavadvyatiriktacaitanyagrāhyatvaṃ yuktaṃ kalpayituṃ na tvananyagrāhyatvam /
yaśvānyo vijñānasya grahītā sa ātmā jyotirantaraṃ vijñānāt /
tadānavastheti cet /
naḥ grāhyatvamātra hi tadgrāhakasya vastvantaratve liṅgamuktaṃ nyāyataḥ /
na tvekāntato grāhakatve tadgrāhakāntarāstitve vā kadācidapi liṅgaṃ saṃbhavati /
tasmānna tadanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ /
vijñānasya vyaktiriktagrāhyatve karaṇāntarāpekṣāyāmanavastheti cet /
na /
niyamābhāvāt /
na hi sarvatrāyaṃ niyamo bhavati /
yatra vastvantareṇa gṛhyate vastvantaraṃ tatragrāhyagrāhakavyatiriktaṃ karaṇāntaraṃ syāditi naikāntena niyantuṃ śakyate /
vaicitryadarśanāt /
katham /
ghaṭastāvatsvātmavyatiriktenā'tmanā gṛhyate tatpa pradīpādirāloko grāhyagrāhakavyatiriktaṃ karaṇam /
na hi pradīpādyāloko ghaṭāṃśaścakṣuraṃśo vā /
ghaṭavaccakṣurgrāhyatve 'pi pradīpasya cakṣuḥ pradīpavyatirekeṇa na bāhyamālokasthānīyaṃ kiñcitkaraṇāntaramapekṣate /
tasmānnaiva niyantuṃ śakyate yatra yatra vyatiriktagrāhakagrāhyatvaṃ tatra tatra karaṇāntaraṃ syādeveti /
tasmādvijñānasya vyaktiriktagrāhakagrāhyatve na karaṇadvārānavasthā nāpi grāhakatvadvārā kadācidapyupapādayituṃ śakyate /
tasmātsiddhaṃ vijñānavyatiriktamātmajyotirantaramiti /
nanu nāstyeva bāhyor'tho ghaṭādiḥ pradīpo vā vijñānavyatiriktaḥ /
yaddhi yadvyatirekeṇa nopalamyate tattāvanmātraṃ vastu dṛṣṭam /
yathāsvapnavijñānagrāhyaṃ ghaṭapaṭādivastu svapnavijñānavyatirekeṇānupalambhātsvapnaghaṭapradīpādeḥ svapnavijñānamātratāvagamyate, tathā jāgarite 'pi ghaṭapradīpāderjāgarite 'pi ghaṭapradīpāderjāgradvijñānamātrameva tu sarvam /
tatra yaduktaṃ vijñānasya vyatiriktāvabhāsyatvādvijñānavyatiriktamasti jyotirantaraṃ gaṭāderiveti tanmithyā /
sarvasya vijñānamātratve dṛṣṭāntābhāvāt /
na /
yāvattāvadabhyupagamāt /
na tu bāhyor'tho bhavataikāntenaiva nābhyupagamyate /
nanu mayā nābhyupagamyata eva /
na /
vijñānaṃ ghaṭaḥ pradīpa iti ca śabdārthapṛthaktvādyāvattāvajadapi bāhyamarthāntaramavaśyamabhyupagantavyam /
vijñānādarthāntaraṃ vastu na cedabhyupagamyate vijñānaṃ ghaṭaḥ paṭa ityevamādīnāṃ bhabdānāmekārthatve paryāyaśabdatvaṃ prāpnoti /
tathā sādhanānāṃ phalasya caikatve sādhyasādhanabhedopadśaśāstrānarthaprasaṅgaḥ /
tatkarturajñānaprasaṅgo vā /
kiñcānyat /
vijñānavyatirekeṇa vādiprativādavādadoṣabhyupagamāt /
na hyātmavijñānamātrameva vādiprativādivādastaddoṣo vābhyugamyate nirākartavyatvātprativādyādīnām /
na hyātmīyaṃ vijñāna nirākartavyamabhyupagamyate svayaṃ vā'tmā kasyacit /
tathā ca sati sarvasaṃvyavahāralopaprasaṅgaḥ /
na ca pravādyādayaḥ svātmanaiva gṛhyanta ityabhyupagamaḥ /
vyatiriktagrāhyā hi te 'bhyupagamyante /
tasmāttadvatsarvameva vyatiriktagrāhyaṃ vastu jāgradviṣayatvājjāgradvastupratipādyādivaditi salābhau dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
saṃtatyantaravadvijñānāntaravacceti /
tasmādvijñānavādināpi na śakyaṃ vijñānavyatiriktaṃ jyotirantaraṃ nirākartum /
svapne vijñānavyatirekābhāvādayuktamiti cet /
na /
abhāvādapi bhāvasya vastvantaratvopapatteḥ /
bhavataiva viṣayo ghaṭādiryadyabhāvo yadi vā bhāvaḥ syādubhayathāpi ghaṭādivijñānasya bhāvabhūtatvamabhyupagatameva /
na tu tannivartayituṃ śakyate tannivartakanyāyābhāvāta /
etena sarvasya śūnyatāpratyuktā /
pratyagātmāgrāhyatā cā'tmano 'hamiti mīmāṃsakapakṣaḥ pratyuktaḥ /
yattūktaṃ sāloko 'nyaścānyaśca ghaṭo jāyata iti tadasat /
kṣaṇāntare 'pi sa evāyaṃ ghaṭa iti pratyabhijñānāt /
sādṛśyātpratyayabhijñānaṃ kṛttotthitakeśanakhādiṣveveti cet /
na /
tatrāpi kṣaṇikatvasyāsiddhatvāt /
jātyekatvācca /
kṛtteṣu punarutthiteṣu /
ca keśanakhādiṣu keśanakhatvājāterekeśanakhatvapratyayastannimitto 'bhrānta e /
na hi dṛśyamānalūnotthitakeśanakhādiṣu vyaktinimittaḥ sa eveti pratyayo bhavati /
kasyaciddīrkhakālavyavahitadṛṣṭeṣu sa eveti pratyayaḥ /
tasmānna samo dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
pratyakṣeṇa hi pratyabhijñāyamāne vastuni tadeveti na cānyatvamanumātuṃ yuktaṃ pratyakṣavirodhe liṅgasyā'bhāsatvopapatteḥ /
sādṛśyapratyayānupapatteśca /
jñānasya kṣaṇikatvāt /
ekasya hi vastudarśino vastvantaradarśane sādṛśyapratyayaḥ syāt /
na tu vastudarśyeko vastvantaradarśanāya kṣaṇāntaramavatiṣṭhate /
vijñānasya kṣaṇikatvātsakṛdvastudarśanenaiva kṣayopapatteḥ /
tenedaṃ sadṛśamiti hi sādṛśyapratyayo bhavati /
teneti dṛṣṭasmaraṇam imiti vartamānapratyayaḥ /
teneti dṛṣṭaṃ smṛtvā yāvadidimiti vartamānakṣaṇakālamavatiṣṭheta tataḥ kṣaṇikavādahāniḥ /
atha tenetyavopakṣīṇaḥ smārtaḥ pratyaya idamiti cānya eva vārtamānikaḥ pratyayaḥ kṣīyate tataḥ sādṛśyapratyatānupapattistenedaṃ sadṛśamiti /
anekadarśina ekasyābhāvāt /
vyapadeśānupapattiśca draṣṭavyadarśanenaivopakṣayādvijñānasyedaṃ paśyāmyado 'drākṣamitivyapadeśānupapaccardṛṣṭavato vyapadeśakṣaṇānavasthānāt /
athāvatiṣṭeta kṣaṇikavādahāniḥ /
athādṛṣṭavato vyapadeṣaḥ sādṛśyapratyayaśca tadānūṃ jātyandhasyeva rūpaviśeṣavyapadeśastatsādṛśyapratyayaśca sarvamandhaparampareti prasajyeta sarvajñaśāstrapraṇayanādi /
na caitadiṣyate /
akṛtābhyāgamakṛtavipraṇāśadoṣau tu prasiddhatarau kṣaṇavāde /
dṛṣṭavyapadeśahetuḥ pūrvettarasahita eka eva hi śṛṅgalāvatpratyayo jāyata iti cet /
tenedaṃ sadṛśamiti ca /
na /
varmānātītayorbhinnakālatvāt /
tatra vartamānapratyaya ekaḥ śṛṅgalāvayavasthānīyo 'tītaścāparastau pratyayau bhinnakālau tadubhayapratyayaviṣayaspṛkcecchṛṅkhalāpratyayastataḥ kṣaṇadvayāvyāpitvādekasya vijñānasya punaḥ kṣaṇavādahāniḥ /
mamatavatādiviśeṣānupapatteśca sarvasaṃvyavahāraloprasaṅgaḥ /
sarvasya ca svasaṃvedyavijñānamātratve vijñānasya ca svacchāvabodhābhāsamātrasvābhāvyābhyupagamāttaddarśinaścānyasyābhāve 'nityaduḥkha- śūnyānātmatvādyanekakalpanānupattiḥ /
na ca dāḍimāderiva viruddhānekāṃśavatvaṃ vijñānasya /
svacchāvabhāsasvābhāvyāddvijñānasya /
anityaduḥkhādīnāṃ vijñānāṃśatve ca satyanubhīyamānatvādvyatiriktaviṣayatvaprasaṅgaḥ /
athānityaduḥkhādyātmaikatvameva vijñānasya tadā tadviyogādviśuddhikalpanānupapattiḥ /
saṃyogimalavigāddhi viśuddharbhavati /
yathā'darśaprabhṛtīnām /
na tusvābhāvikena raktatvādīnāṃ dravyāntarayogena viyojanaṃ dṛśyate tatrāpi saṃyogapūrvatvamanumīyate /
bījabhāvanayā puṣpaphalādīnāṃ guṇāntarotpattidarśanāt /
ato vijñānasya viśuddhikalpanānupapattiḥ /
ato vijñānasya viśuddhikalnānupattiḥ /
viṣayaviṣayyābhāsatvaṃ ca yanmalaṃ parikalpyate vijñānasya tadapyanyasaṃsargābhāvādānupapannam /
na hyavidyamānena vidyamānasya saṃsargaḥ syāt /
asati cānyasaṃsargeyo dharmo yasya dṛṣṭaḥ sa tatsvabhātvānna tena viyogamarhati /
yathāgnerauṣṇyaṃ saviturvā prabhā /
tasmādanityasaṃsargeṇa malinatvaṃ tadviśuddhiśca vijñānasyetīyaṃ kalpanāndhaparamparaiva pramāṇaśūnyetyavagamyate /
yadapi tasya vijñānasya nirvāṇaṃ puruṣārthaṃ kalpayanti tatrāpi phalāśrayānupapattiḥ /
kaṇṭakaviddhasya hi kaṇṭakavedhajanitaduḥkhanivṛttiḥ phalaṃ na tu kaṇṭakaviddhamaraṇe tadduḥkhanivṛttaphalasyā'śraya upapadyate /
tadvatsarvanirvāṇe 'sati ca phalāśraye puruṣārthakalpanā vyarthaiva /
children.translated_text: Similarly, when everything is extinguished and there is no substrate for the fruit, the postulation of a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) is entirely futile.

children.text: yasya hi puruṣaśabdavācyasya satvasyātmano vijñānasya cārthaḥ parikalpyate tasya punaḥ puruṣasya nirvāṇe kasyārthaḥ puruṣārtha iti syāt /
children.translated_text: For the being (<s>satva</s>) denoted by the word '<s>puruṣa</s>' — the self, the consciousness — for whose sake a purpose is postulated — when that <s>puruṣa</s> is extinguished, whose purpose would the 'human goal' be?

children.text: yasya punarastyanekārthadaśīṃ vijñānavyatirikta ātmā tasya dṛṣṭasmaraṇadukhasaṃyogaviyogādi sarvamevopapannamanyasaṃyoganimittaṃ kāluṣyaṃ tadviyoganimittā ca viśuddhiriti /
children.translated_text: But for one who holds that there exists a self distinct from consciousness, which passes through manifold states — for such a one, everything is tenable: the turbidity caused by contact with other [things] — seeing, remembering, suffering, union, separation, and the like — and the purification caused by separation from those [contacts].

children.text: śūnyavādipakṣastu sarvapramāṇavipratiṣiddha iti tannirākaraṇāya nā'daraḥ kriyate //4,3.7//
children.translated_text: The position of the <s>Śūnyavādins</s> (proponents of the void), however, is contradicted by all means of valid knowledge. Therefore, no effort is made to refute it. // 4.3.7 //

And also "the light that belongs to the sun" and so forth; and in the <s>Kāṭhaka</s>, "the eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious ones" and "Him alone shining, everything shines after; by His light all this shines"; and "by which the sun blazes, raised up by its light" — this is a <s>mantra</s> passage. Therefore this one is the inner light of the heart. <s>Puruṣa</s> — because like <s>ākāśa</s> (space) he is all-pervading, he is full (<s>pūrṇa</s>), hence <s>Puruṣa</s>. And his self-luminosity (<s>svayañjyotiṣṭva</s>) is unsurpassed, because he illuminates everything and is himself not illuminated by anything else. This <s>Puruṣa</s> is by his very nature self-luminous — he whom you ask about, 'which is the <s>Ātman</s>?' When the external lights, which assist all the sense-organs, have set, the <s>Puruṣa</s>, the <s>Ātman</s>, is the inner light of the heart through the gateway of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), assisting the sense-organs — thus it has been stated. Even when the external lights such as the sun and others, which assist the outer sense-organs, are present, still, because those lights of the sun and so forth exist for the sake of others, and because the aggregate of body and organs (<s>kāryakaraṇasaṃghāta</s>) being insentient cannot serve its own purpose, without the assistance of the <s>Ātman</s> which is a light serving its own purpose, this aggregate of body and organs is not fit for any activity. For all transactions at all times occur only through the assistance of the light of the <s>Ātman</s>. This follows from another <s>śruti</s>: "That which is this heart and mind, namely consciousness." For all activity of all living beings involves self-identification (<s>abhimāna</s>). And we have explained the cause of self-identification through the illustration of the emerald gem (<s>marakatamaṇi</s>). Although this is so, still, in the waking state, because the light of the <s>Ātman</s> is beyond the reach of all sense-organs, and because of the confusion caused by the concurrence of the activities of all external and internal instruments such as the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and others, that light called <s>Ātman</s> cannot be extracted and shown separately, like the pith from a <s>muñja</s> reed. Therefore, wishing to demonstrate it in the dream state, he proceeds: 'Being the same, he wanders through both worlds.' The <s>Puruṣa</s> who is by his very nature the self-luminous <s>Ātman</s> — he, being the same, that is, being similar. Similar to what? To the heart, because it is the subject under discussion and is proximate. And what is denoted by the word 'heart' (<s>hṛd</s>) is the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), which is both the subject under discussion and proximate. Therefore the similarity is with that alone. What then is this similarity? It is the non-apprehension of distinction, as between a horse and a buffalo — the <s>buddhi</s> is the illuminated, and that light of the <s>Ātman</s> is the illuminator, like a lamp. The non-apprehension of the distinction between the illuminated and the illuminator is well known. For light, being pure, becomes similar to the illuminated object. Just as when illuminating something red, it becomes similar to the red, taking on a red form; just as when illuminating green, blue, or red, the light becomes similar to those — so too, illuminating the <s>buddhi</s>, it illuminates the entire field through the gateway of the <s>buddhi</s>, as was stated through the illustration of the emerald gem. Therefore, being similar to everything through the similarity with the <s>buddhi</s> — and hence it will be said 'consisting of everything' (<s>sarvamaya</s>). Therefore, that one cannot be separated from something and shown in its own luminous form, like the pith from a <s>muñja</s> reed. Hence, superimposing all activities upon it, and the luminous quality belonging to name and form upon it, and name and form upon the light of the <s>Ātman</s>, the whole world is deluded — 'this is the <s>Ātman</s>', 'this is not the <s>Ātman</s>', 'this is <s>dharma</s>', 'this is not <s>dharma</s>', 'doer', 'non-doer', 'pure', 'impure', 'bound', 'liberated', 'stationary', 'gone', 'come', 'exists', 'does not exist' — through such false alternatives. Therefore, being the same, he wanders through both worlds — the world of waking experience already attained and the world yet to be attained, this world and the other world — through hundreds of sequences of taking up and abandoning aggregates of body, sense-organs, and so forth. The similarity with the <s>buddhi</s> alone is the cause of wandering through both worlds, not anything inherent in the self. In that regard, the similarity with the limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>) of name and form, which is the cause of delusion — that alone is the cause, not anything inherent — this is what is being stated. Because he, being the same, wanders through both worlds in sequence, this is directly perceived — this he demonstrates: 'He seems to meditate' — he appears to perform the act of meditation, 'he seems to think' — illuminating the <s>buddhi</s> which is engaged in the activity of meditation with the light of his own consciousness-nature situated in it, being similar to it, being the same, he seems to meditate, just like a lamp. Hence arises the world's delusion that 'he thinks.' But in ultimate reality, he does not meditate. Similarly, 'he seems to move about greatly' — he seems to move exceedingly. When those very organs such as the <s>buddhi</s> and the vital airs (<s>vāyu</s>) move, because he illuminates them, he appears similar to them — hence 'he seems to move about.' But in ultimate reality, that light of the <s>Ātman</s> does not have the nature of movement. But how is this understood — that the delusion of similarity with it is the cause of wandering through both worlds and so forth, not anything inherent? To demonstrate this meaning, the reason is given: 'For this <s>Ātman</s>, having become dream.' Whatever state the <s>buddhi</s> to which he is similar assumes, he too appears to assume that state. Therefore, when it becomes dream — when the <s>buddhi</s> enters the dream state — he too enters the dream state. When the <s>buddhi</s> will awaken, then he too — hence it says: 'Having become dream' — having assumed the form of the dream state of the <s>buddhi</s> by illuminating it, he transcends this world characterized by waking transactions, consisting of the aggregate of body and organs, which is the locus of worldly and scriptural activities — he crosses beyond it. He does not remain illuminating the <s>buddhi</s> activity whose nature is dream, with his own distinct light of the <s>Ātman</s>. Because of this, he is by nature self-luminous, pure — devoid of agent, action, instrument, and result. But in ultimate reality, the similarity with the <s>buddhi</s> alone is the cause of the delusion of all transactions such as wandering through both worlds. The forms of death — death is <s>karma</s> (action), <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and so forth — he has no other form of his own; the body and organs alone are his forms. Therefore he transcends those forms of death, which are the substrata of action and its results. [Objection:] But there is simply no light of the <s>Ātman</s> distinct from the <s>buddhi</s> that illuminates it — neither by perception nor by inference is it apprehended. Just as at that very moment there is another, second cognition. As for the argument that even though the illuminated and the illuminator are different, there is similarity due to non-apprehension of distinction — as between a pot and light: there, let there be similarity between a pot and light which are conjoined yet apprehended as different — similarity exists only between things that are distinct. But here, we do not apprehend by perception or inference any light distinct from the <s>buddhi</s> that illuminates it, as we apprehend light distinct from a pot. For the <s>buddhi</s> itself, being of the nature of consciousness and self-illuminating, has both its own form and the form of objects. Therefore, neither by inference nor by perception can an illuminator distinct from the <s>buddhi</s> be established. As for the illustration that was cited — that between a pot and light, which are distinct and conjoined, there is similarity: we made that concession merely for the sake of argument. In reality, the pot and its illuminator are not distinct. In ultimate truth, the pot itself, together with the light, is of the nature of appearance (<s>avabhāsa</s>). For one pot after another arises. It is mere consciousness (<s>vijñānamātra</s>) alone that appears in the form of objects such as pots-with-light. [Reply:] If this is so, then there is no external illustration, since everything is merely of the nature of consciousness. [Buddhist response:] Thus, having imagined the consciousness itself as having the forms of grasped and grasper (<s>grāhyagrāhaka</s>), which is a defilement, they then imagine a purified state of that very consciousness. Some (<s>Vijñānavādins</s>) hold that consciousness, freed from the grasper, remains clear and momentary. Others desire even the cessation of that. Still others, the <s>Mādhyamikas</s>, declare that even that consciousness is conventional (<s>saṃvṛta</s>), and freed from the aspects of grasped and grasper, is simply void (<s>śūnya</s>), just like external objects such as pots. All these fabrications are opposed to the Vedic path to the highest good, which affirms the light of the <s>Ātman</s> as distinct from the <s>buddhi</s> and its cognitions as the illuminator. Among these, those who accept external objects are addressed first. The pot and such objects are not self-illuminating. A pot situated in darkness is never illuminated by itself. Rather, it is invariably seen as illuminated only through contact with a light such as a lamp — thus 'a pot with light.' Even between a pot and light that are conjoined, their distinctness is established, because a specific difference is observed each time they are conjoined and separated, just as with a rope and a pot. And given their distinctness, the illumination is by something other — the pot does not illuminate itself by itself. [Objection:] But a lamp is seen to illuminate itself. For ordinary people do not employ another light to see a lamp, as they do for a pot and such objects. Therefore, the lamp illuminates itself. [Reply:] No. Because there is no distinction in being an object of illumination. Although the lamp illuminates other things and is itself not illuminated by another, still it does not escape being illuminated by a distinct consciousness, just like a pot. And if this is so, then being illuminated by something distinct is inevitable. [Objection:] But just as a pot, even while being illuminated by consciousness, does not illuminate itself or the pot — [Reply:] No. Because there is no distinction either inherently or from another source. The pot's being illuminated by consciousness and the lamp's being illuminated by consciousness are identical. The claim that 'the lamp illuminates itself and the pot' is false. Why? Because if it did not illuminate itself, what would it be like? For no distinction whatsoever is apprehended in the lamp, either inherently or from another source. For that is said to be illuminated in whose case a difference is observed between the presence and absence of an illuminator. The claim that a lamp illuminates itself is therefore simply false. The lamp's being grasped by consciousness is no different from that of pots and other objects. Therefore, the lamp is not a valid illustration for consciousness being self-apprehending. And consciousness's being grasped by consciousness is no different from its being grasped along with external objects. When it is doubtful whether consciousness is grasped by the object-consciousness or by the subject-consciousness, the principle observed elsewhere should be applied — not one contrary to what is observed. This being so, just as it is observed that external objects like lamps are grasped by a distinct grasper, so too, since consciousness is grasped by consciousness, even though it has the capacity to illuminate, it is reasonable to posit, like a lamp, that it is grasped by a distinct consciousness — not that it is ungrasped by anything else. And that other which is the grasper of consciousness — that is the <s>Ātman</s>, a light distinct from consciousness. [Objection:] This leads to infinite regress. [Reply:] No. For being an object of apprehension has been stated, based on reason, as the mark of the existence of another entity that apprehends it. But being a grasper does not invariably serve as a mark that another grasper of it exists. Therefore, there is no occasion for infinite regress. [Objection:] If consciousness is grasped by something distinct, an infinite regress arises from requiring another instrument of knowledge. [Reply:] No. Because there is no such universal rule. For this rule does not hold everywhere: 'wherever one entity is grasped by another entity, there must be an instrument distinct from both grasped and grasper' — this cannot be established as a universal rule. Because variety is observed. How so? A pot is grasped by an entity distinct from itself — there, the light of a lamp and so forth is the instrument distinct from both grasped and grasper. But the light of a lamp is neither a part of the pot nor a part of the eye. Even though the lamp, like a pot, is an object grasped by the eye, the eye does not require any other external instrument corresponding to light, distinct from the lamp. Therefore, it simply cannot be established as a rule that wherever there is grasping by a distinct grasper, there must be a distinct instrument. Therefore, when consciousness is grasped by a distinct grasper, neither an infinite regress through instruments nor an infinite regress through graspers can ever be established. Therefore, it is established that there is a light of the <s>Ātman</s> distinct from consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). [Objection:] But there simply is no external object such as a pot or lamp distinct from consciousness. For whatever is not apprehended apart from something else is observed to be merely that thing. Just as objects such as pots and cloths grasped in dream consciousness, since they are not apprehended apart from dream consciousness, are understood to be nothing but dream consciousness — so too in the waking state, pots, lamps, and such are nothing but waking consciousness. Therefore, the claim that because consciousness is illuminated by something distinct, there exists another light distinct from consciousness, just as with a pot — that is false. For if everything is mere consciousness, there is no illustration. [Reply:] No. Because as far as it goes, it is conceded. The external object is not absolutely denied with certainty. [Objection:] But I certainly do not concede it. [Reply:] No. Because the words 'consciousness,' 'pot,' 'lamp' have distinct meanings, at least to some extent, an external entity that is something other must necessarily be conceded. If no entity other than consciousness is conceded, then the words 'consciousness,' 'pot,' 'cloth,' and so forth, having a single referent, would become synonyms. Furthermore, if the means of accomplishment (<s>sādhana</s>) and the result (<s>phala</s>) are identical, then the teachings that distinguish between what is to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment would become purposeless — or the teacher of such teachings would be charged with ignorance. Moreover, since the disputant, the opponent, the argument, and its defects are conceded to be distinct from consciousness — for the disputant does not accept that his own consciousness alone constitutes the opponent's argument and its defects, since the opponent and others are to be refuted. Nor does anyone accept that one's own consciousness is to be refuted, or that one refutes oneself. If this were so, the consequence would be the collapse of all transactions. And it is not the case that the opponent and others are grasped by one's own self alone — for they are conceded to be grasped as distinct. Therefore, like those, every entity is grasped as distinct, because it is an object of waking experience, just like the objects established in waking — thus the illustration stands. Just as something belonging to another continuum of consciousness, just as another cognition. Therefore, even the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (consciousness-only proponent) cannot deny a light distinct from consciousness. [Objection:] Since in dream there is no distinction from consciousness, this is unjustified. [Reply:] No. Because even from the absence of an entity, the existence of another entity is established. For you yourself accept that the object — pots and such — whether it is non-existent or existent, in either case the consciousness of pots and such is accepted as a real entity. And that cannot be negated, because there is no valid reasoning to negate it. By this, the doctrine that everything is void (<s>śūnyatā</s>) is also refuted. And the <s>Mīmāṃsaka</s> position that the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) is ungrasped and that the <s>Ātman</s> is known as 'I' is also refuted. As for the claim that 'one pot with light arises, and then another' — that is false. Because even in the next moment, there is recognition: 'this is the same pot.' [Objection:] The recognition is due to similarity, as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and have grown back. [Reply:] No. Because even there, momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>) is unestablished. And because of the unity of the universal (<s>jāti</s>). In the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back, the cognition of their being hair and nails arises from the universal 'hair-ness' and 'nail-ness,' and that cognition caused by it is not erroneous. For in the case of hair and nails visibly cut and regrown, no cognition of 'this is the same individual' arises. Only someone who has seen them after a long interval might have the cognition 'this is the same.' Therefore, the illustration is not parallel. For when a thing is recognized by direct perception as 'this is the same,' it is not proper to infer its difference — because when perception is contradicted, the inferential mark is exposed as fallacious. And the cognition of similarity is itself impossible, because of the momentariness of cognition. For the cognition of similarity would arise when a single perceiver of one object perceives another object. But the perceiver of one object does not persist to the next moment to perceive another object, because of the momentariness of consciousness — since it is possible for it to perish with a single perception of an object. For the cognition of similarity takes the form: 'this is similar to that.' 'That' involves the memory of what was previously seen; 'this' involves the present cognition. Having remembered what was seen as 'that,' if one were to persist until the present moment of 'this' — then the doctrine of momentariness would be abandoned. But if the memory-cognition of 'that' has already perished, and the present cognition of 'this' is yet another that also perishes, then the cognition of similarity — 'this is similar to that' — becomes impossible, since there is no single perceiver of multiple things. And the ability to make statements becomes impossible too, since consciousness perishes with the very act of seeing what is to be seen — the statements 'I see this' and 'I saw that' become impossible, because the one who saw does not persist until the moment of making the statement. If he were to persist, the doctrine of momentariness would be abandoned. And if statements and cognitions of similarity belong to one who has not seen, then, like a person born blind making statements about particular colors and having cognitions of similarity regarding them, everything would be a case of the blind leading the blind — including the composition of scriptures by the omniscient one. And this is not acceptable. Moreover, the well-known defects of gaining what was not earned (<s>akṛtābhyāgama</s>) and losing what was earned (<s>kṛtavipraṇāśa</s>) are all the more obvious in the doctrine of momentariness. [Objection:] The cognition that is the cause of statements about what was seen arises as a single unit combined with the prior and subsequent, like links in a chain. And likewise 'this is similar to that.' [Reply:] No. Because the present and the past belong to different times. The present cognition is one link in the chain, and the past cognition is another — these two cognitions belong to different times. If the chain-cognition were to touch both cognition-objects, then since a single consciousness would span two moments, the doctrine of momentariness would again be abandoned. And because particularities such as 'mine' and so forth cannot be accounted for, the consequence would be the collapse of all transactions. And if everything is merely self-aware consciousness (<s>svasaṃvedyavijñānamātra</s>), and if the nature of consciousness is accepted as being merely the appearance of transparent self-awareness, then in the absence of another who sees it, the various fabrications about impermanence, suffering, voidness, non-self, and so forth become impossible. Nor does consciousness have multiple contradictory aspects like a pomegranate. Because of the nature of consciousness as transparent self-appearance. And if impermanence, suffering, and so forth are real aspects of consciousness and are experienced, the consequence would be that they are objects of a distinct subject. But if impermanence, suffering, and so forth are identical with consciousness, then the fabrication of purification through separation from them becomes impossible. For purification occurs through separation from a defilement that was conjoined. As in the case of a mirror and such things. But it is not seen that things whose redness and such properties are inherent can be separated from them through contact with another substance — even there, a prior conjunction is inferred. Because one observes the arising of different qualities such as flowers and fruits through the cultivation of seeds. Therefore, the fabrication of purification of consciousness is impossible. Moreover, the defilement attributed to consciousness — namely its appearing in the form of subject and object — that too is impossible, because there is no contact with anything else. For what does not exist cannot have contact with what exists. And in the absence of contact with another, whatever quality is observed in something is its own nature, and it does not deserve to be separated from it — just as heat belongs to fire, or radiance to the sun. Therefore, the notion that consciousness is defiled through a non-eternal contact and then purified from it — this fabrication is understood to be a chain of blind leading the blind, devoid of any valid means of knowledge. As for the <s>nirvāṇa</s> (cessation) of that consciousness which they fabricate as the highest goal of a person — there too, the impossibility of a substratum for the result arises. For one who is pierced by a thorn, the cessation of the suffering born from the thorn-prick is the result; but when the one pierced by the thorn has died, there is no substratum for the one whose suffering from the thorn-prick has ceased to experience that result.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.8
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.8]

children.text:
sa vā ayaṃ puruṣo jāyamānaḥ śarīram abhisampadyamānaḥ pāpmabhiḥ saṃsṛjyate |
sa utkrāman mriyamāṇaḥ pāpmano vijahāti || BrhUp_4,3.8 ||
children.translated_text: This person, when being born, when coming into contact with a body, is conjoined with evils (<s>pāpmans</s>). When departing, when dying, he leaves those evils behind. (BṛUp 4.3.8)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.8 yathaivehaikasmindehe svapno bhūtvā mṛtyo rūpāṇi kāryakaraṇānyatikramya svapne sva ātmajyetiṣyāsta evaṃ sa vai prakṛtaḥ puruṣo 'jāyamānaḥ /
kathaṃ jāyamāna ityucyate-śarīraṃ dehendriyasaṃghātamabhisaṃpadyamānaḥ śarīra ātmabhāvamāpadyamāna ityarthaḥ /
pāpmabhiḥ pāpmasamavāyibhirdharmādharmāśrayaiḥ kāryakaraṇairityarthaḥ, saṃsṛjyate saṃyujyate /
sa evotkrāmañcharīrāntaramūrdhaṃva krāmangacchanmriyamāṇa ityetasya vyākhyānamutkrāmanniti /
children.translated_text: He himself, departing — proceeding upward to another body — dying — the explanation of this is: 'departing.'

children.text: tāneva saṃśliṣyānpāpmarūpakāryakaraṇopādānaparityāgābhyāmanavaracaṃ saṃcarati dhiyā samānaḥ san, tathā so 'yaṃ puruṣa ubhāvihalokaparokau janmamaraṇābhyāṃ kāryakaraṇopādānaparityāgāvanavarataṃ pratipadyamāna ā saṃsāramokṣātsaṃcarati /
children.translated_text: Clinging to those very [evils], through the taking up and discarding of effects and instruments in the form of evils, he transmigrates ceaselessly, being united with the intellect (<s>dhī</s>). Thus, this person, through birth and death, ceaselessly taking up and discarding effects and instruments, traverses both worlds — this world and the other — until liberation from <s>saṃsāra</s>.

children.text: tasmātsiddhamasyā'tmayajyotiṣo 'nyatvaṃ kāryakaraṇarūpebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ saṃyogaviyogābhyām /
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is established that this self-luminous [Self] is different from the evils in the form of effects and instruments — through [its] conjunction and disjunction [with them].

children.text: na hi taddharmatve sati taireva saṃyogo viyogo vā yuktaḥ //4,3.8//
children.translated_text: For if [the evils] were its own properties, conjunction and disjunction with those very [evils] would not be tenable. // 4.3.8 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.8:] Just as in this very [life], in one body, having entered the dream [state], having transcended the forms of death — the effects and instruments — one shines by one's own self-light in dream — even so, this person under discussion, [though seemingly] being born — how is it said that he is 'being born'? — meaning: attaining a body, coming to identify with the aggregate of body and sense-organs — this is the meaning. By evils (<s>pāpmans</s>) — meaning: by the effects and instruments that are inherently conjoined with evil, that serve as the substrates of merit and demerit — he is conjoined, connected.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.9
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.9]

children.text:
tasya vā etasya puruṣasya dve eva sthāne bhavataḥ |
idaṃ ca paralokasthānaṃ ca |
sandhyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ svapnasthānam |
tasminsandhye sthāne tiṣṭhan ubhe sthāne paśyatīdaṃ ca paralokasthānaṃ ca |
atha yathākramo 'yaṃ paralokasthāne bhavati |
tam ākramam ākramyobhayān pāpmana ānandāṃś ca paśyati |
sa yatra prasvapity asya lokasya sarvāvato mātrām apādāya svayaṃ vihatya svayaṃ nirmāya svena bhāsā svena jyotiṣā prasvapiti |
atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotir bhavati || BrhUp_4,3.9 ||
children.translated_text: Of this person, there are indeed two states: this [world] and the state of the other world. The dream state is a third, intermediate (<s>sandhya</s>) [state]. Standing in that intermediate state, he sees both states — this [world] and the state of the other world. Now, whatever approach (<s>ākrama</s>) he has toward the state of the other world — having taken that approach, he sees both: evils and joys. When he sleeps deeply, having taken a portion from this all-encompassing world, himself dismantling [the waking body], himself constructing [the dream body], he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light. Therein, this person becomes self-luminous (<s>svayaṃjyotis</s>). (BṛUp 4.3.9)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.9 nanu na syo 'syobhau lokau yau janmamaraṇābhyāmanukrameṇa saṃcarati svapnajāgarite iva /
svapnajāgarite tu pratyakṣamavagamyete na tvihalokaparalokau kenacitpramaṇena /
tasmādete eva svapnajāgagarite ihalokaparalokāviti /
ucyate-tasyaitasya puruṣasya vai dve e sthāne bhavato na tṛtacīyaṃ caturthaṃ vā /
ke te /
idaṃ ca .tpratipannaṃ vartamānaṃ janma śarīrenjadriyaviṣayavedanāviśiṣṭaṃ sthānaṃ pratyakṣato 'nubhūyamānam /
paraloka eva sthānaṃ paralokasthānam /
tacca śarīrādiviviyogottarakālānubhāvyam /
nanu svapno 'pi paralokasthā ca sati dve evetyavadhāraṇamayuktam /
na /
kathaṃ tarhi /
saṃdhyaṃ tat /
ihalokaparalokayoryaḥ saṃdhistasminbhavaṃ saṃdhyaṃ yattṛtīyaṃ tatsvapnasthānam /

yatastasminsaṃdhye svapnasthāne tiṣṭanbhavanvartamāna ete ubhe sthāne paśyati /
ke te ubhe /
idañca paralokasthānaṃ ca /

kimāśrayaḥ kena vidhineti /

tamākramaṃ paralokasthānāyonmukhībhūtaṃ prāptāṅkurībhāvamiva bījaṃ tamākramyāvaṣṭabhyā'śrityobhayānpaśyati bahuvacanaṃ dharmādharmaphalonekatvādubhayaprakārānityarthaḥ /
kāṃstānpāpmanaḥ pāpaphalāni /
na tu punaḥ sākṣādeva pāpmanāṃ darśanaṃ saṃbhavati tasmātpāpaphalāni duḥkhānītyarthaḥ /
ānandāṃśca dharmaphalāni sukhānītyetat /
tānubhayānpāpmana ānandāṃśca paśyati janmāntaradṛṣṭavāsanāmayāt /
yāni ca pratipattavyajanmaviṣayāṇi kṣudradharmādharmaphalāni dharmādharmaprayukto devatānugrahādvāpaśyati /
tatkathamavagamyate paralokasthānasaṃbandhipāpmānāndadarśanaṃ svapna iti /
ucyate-yasmādiha janmanyananubhāvyamapi paśyati bahu /
na ca svapno nāmāpūrvaṃ darśanam /
pūrvadṛṣṭasmṛtirhi svapnaḥ prāyeṇa /
tena svapnjāgaritasthānavyatirekeṇa sta ubhau lokau /
yadādityādibāhyajyotiṣāmabhāve 'yaṃ kāryakāraṇasaṃgātaḥ puruṣo yena vyatiriktenā'tmanā jyotiṣā vyavaharatītyuktam tadeva nāsti /
yadā'dityādijyotiṣāmabhāvagamanaṃ yatredaṃ viviktaṃ svayañjyotirupalabhyota /
yena sarvadaivāyaṅkāryakaraṇasaṃghātaḥ saṃsṛṣṭa evopalabhyeta /
tasmādasatsamo 'sanneva vā svena viviktasvabhāvena jyotīrūpeṇā'tmeti /
atha kvacidviviktaḥ svena jyotīrūpeṇopalabhyeta bāhyādhyātmikabhūtabhautikasaṃsargaśūnyastato yathoktaṃ sarvaṃ bhaviṣyatītyedarthamāha-sa yaḥ prakṛta ātmā yatra yasminkāle prasvapiti prakarṣeṇa svāpamanubhavati tadā kimupādānaḥ kena vidhinā svapiti saṃdhyaṃ sthānaṃ pratipadyata ityacyate /
asya dṛṣṭasya lokasyajāgaritalakṣaṇasya sarvāvataḥ sarvamavatīti sarvāvānayaṃ lokaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghāto viṣayavedanāsaṃyuktaḥ /
sarvāvatvamasya vyākhyātamannatrayaprakaraṇe 'tho ayaṃ vā ātmetyādinā /
sarvā vā bhūtabhautikamātrā asya saṃsargakāṇabhūtā vidyanta iti sarvavānsarvāneva sarvāvāṃstasya sarvāvato mātrāmekadeśamavayavamapādāyāpacchidyā'dāya gṛhītvā dṛṣṭajanmavāsanāvāsitaḥ sannityarthaḥ /
svayamātmanaiva vihatya dehaṃ pātayitvā niḥsaṃbodhamāpādya /
jāgarite hyodityādīnāṃ cakṣurādiṣvanugraho dehavyavavahārārthaḥ /
dehavyavahāraścā'tmano dharmādharmaphalopabhogaprayuktastaddharmādharmaphalopabhogoparamaṇamasmindeha ātmakarmoparamakṛtamityātmāsya vihantetyucyate /
svayaṃ nirmāya nirmāṇaṃ kṛtvā vāsanāmayaṃ svapnadehaṃ māyāmayamiva /
nirmāṇamapi tatkarmāpekṣatvātsvayaṅkartṛkamucyate /
svenā'tmīyena bhāsā mātropādānalakṣaṇena bhāsā dīptyā prakāśena sarvavāsanātmakenāntaḥkaraṇavṛkkiprakāśenetyarthaḥ /
sā hi tatra viṣayabhūtā sarvavāsanāmayī prakāśate /
sā tatra svayaṃ bhā ucyate /
tena svena bhāsā viṣayabhūtena svena ca jyotiṣā tadviṣayiṇā viviktarūpeṇāluptadṛksvabhāvena tadbhāvarūpaṃ vāsanātmakaṃ viṣayīkurvanprasvapiti /
yadevaṃ vartanaṃ tatprasvapitītyucyate /
atraitasyāmavasthāyāmetasminkāle 'yaṃ puruṣa ātmā svayameva vivaktajyotirbhavati /
bāhyādhyātmikabhūtabhautikasaṃsargarahitaṃ jyotirbhavati /
nanvasya lokasyamātropādānaṃ kṛtaṃ kathaṃ tasminsatyatrāyaṃ puraṣaḥ svayañjyotirbhavatītyucyate /
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
viṣayabhūtameva hi tat /
tenaiva cātrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃ jyotirdarśayituṃ śakyaḥ /
children.translated_text: And precisely because of that [object existing], this person can be shown here to be self-luminous.

children.text: na tvanyathāsati viṣaye kasmiṃścitsuṣuptakāla iva /
children.translated_text: But not otherwise — when no object exists at all, as in the time of deep sleep.

children.text: yadā punaḥ sā bhā vāsanātmikā viṣayabhūtopalabhyamānā bhavati tadāsiḥ kośādiva niṣkṛṣṭaḥ sarvasaṃsargarahitaṃ cakṣurādikāryakaraṇavyāvṛttasvarūpamaluptadṛgātmajyotiḥ svena rūpeṇāvabhāsayadgṛhyate /
children.translated_text: But when that radiance, constituted by residual impressions, exists as an apprehendable object — then, like a sword drawn from its sheath, [the Self] — devoid of all contact, having a nature distinct from the effects and instruments such as the eye and the rest, whose seeing-nature is unimpaired — illuminating [everything] by its own form, is grasped [as self-luminous].

children.text: tenātrāyaṃ puruśaḥ svayañjyotirbhavatīti siddham //4,3.9//
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is established that this person here is self-luminous. // 4.3.9 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.9:] [Objection:] But there should not be two worlds for this [person] through which he transmigrates sequentially by birth and death — like the dream and waking [states]. Dream and waking are directly apprehended; but the two worlds — this world and the other — are not [apprehended] by any means of valid knowledge. Therefore, dream and waking themselves are the two worlds — this world and the other world. [Response:] It is said: of this person, there are indeed two states — not a third or fourth. What are they? This [world] — the present, ongoing birth, characterized by the aggregate of body, senses, objects, and sensations, directly experienced — is one state. The state of the other world — the other world itself as a state — is to be experienced after separation from the body and the rest. [Objection:] But with the dream [state] as well as the other-world state existing, the restriction 'two only' is not proper. [Response:] No. How then? That [dream state] is intermediate (<s>saṃdhya</s>) — existing at the junction (<s>saṃdhi</s>) of this world and the other world; the third [state], which is the dream state, belongs to that junction. Hence the restriction to two states [holds]. For the junction between two villages does not merit being counted as a third [entity] in relation to those very two villages. But how is the existence of the other-world state ascertained — in reference to which the dream state would be intermediate? Because, standing in that intermediate dream state — being present — he sees both states. Which two? This [world] and the state of the other world. Therefore, beyond the dream and waking states, these two worlds exist — through which [the person], being united with the intellect, transmigrates in the continuous series of birth and death. But how, while situated in dream, does he see the two worlds? On what basis? By what method? It is answered: listen to how he sees. '<s>Yathākrama</s>' — <s>ākrama</s> is that by which one approaches, meaning a support, a foundation. Whatever kind of support he has — that is his '<s>yathākrama</s>.' This person, when the occasion for attaining the state of the other world arises, has [his particular] approach — meaning he is equipped with a particular means for attaining the other world, characterized by knowledge, <s>karma</s>, and the foregoing impressions. Having taken up that approach — [like] a seed that has begun to sprout, oriented toward the state of the other world — relying on it, he sees both kinds [of experiences] — the plural is because of the multiplicity of the fruits of merit and demerit — meaning both types. What are those 'evils'? The fruits of sin — but it is not that one sees sins directly; therefore, the meaning is: sufferings, the fruits of sin. And 'joys' — pleasures, the fruits of merit. He sees both — evils and joys — because of [his mind being] constituted by the residual impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) of [things] seen in previous lives. And the minor fruits of merit and demerit pertaining to the birth yet to be attained — impelled by merit and demerit, or by divine grace — he sees [in dream]. How is it known that the seeing of evils and joys pertaining to the other-world state constitutes dream? Because in this birth, he sees many things that have not been experienced [in this life]. And dream is not an entirely novel perception; for dream is mostly the recollection of what was previously seen. Therefore, distinct from the dream and waking states, these two worlds exist. [The text continues:] when, in the absence of external lights such as the sun and the rest, this person — the aggregate of effects and instruments — functions by a self-light distinct [from external lights] — that was stated [previously]. But that [self-light] simply does not [appear on its own]; [rather,] when external lights like the sun and the rest are absent — there, this distinct, self-luminous [Self] is apprehended. By which [Self] the aggregate of effects and instruments is always apprehended as conjoined — therefore, like the non-existent [in deep sleep], or as if non-existent, [the Self] is of its own nature — distinct, luminous in form — this is the Self. Now, if somewhere it were apprehended as distinct, in its own luminous nature, devoid of all contact with external, internal, elemental, and derivative [entities] — then everything stated [above] would be fulfilled. For this purpose [the text] says: this Self under discussion — when, at whatever time, he sleeps deeply — experiences deep sleep — then, with what material, by what method, does he sleep, does he attain the intermediate state? This is answered. 'Of this world' — this world characterized by waking, which is 'all-encompassing' — because it encompasses everything; this world is the aggregate of effects and instruments conjoined with the experience of objects. Its all-encompassing nature was explained in the section on the three [types of] food, beginning with 'Now, this Self.' All elemental and derivative portions — being the causes of contact — exist in him; therefore he is 'all-encompassing.' 'Having taken a portion' — a part, a fragment — of this all-encompassing [world], cutting off, taking, grasping — meaning: being imbued with the residual impressions of [things] seen in [this] birth. 'Himself dismantling' — having caused the body to fall, rendering it unconscious. For in waking, the facilitation of [lights like] the sun and the rest in the eye and the other organs is for the purpose of the body's functioning. And the body's functioning is impelled by the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit belonging to the self; the cessation of that experience of merit and demerit fruits in this body is caused by the cessation of the self's <s>karma</s> — therefore, the self 'dismantles' it, it is said. 'Himself constructing' — creating a dream-body made of residual impressions, as if made of <s>māyā</s> (illusion). Even the construction is said to be self-done, because it depends on <s>karma</s>. 'By his own radiance' — the radiance, the light, the illumination that is his own — characterized by the material of impressions — meaning: the illumination of the internal organ's function, constituted by all residual impressions. For there, it shines as the object, constituted by all residual impressions. There, it is called his own radiance (<s>svayambhā</s>). By that own radiance — which serves as the object — and by his own light — which is the subject, of distinct nature, whose seeing-nature is unimpaired — objectifying [the content] whose nature consists of impressions, he sleeps deeply. When such activity [occurs], that is called 'sleeping deeply.' Therein, in this state, at this time, this person, the Self, himself becomes self-luminous. He becomes a light devoid of all contact with external, internal, elemental, and derivative [entities]. [Objection:] But the material of this world's impressions was taken up — how, when that exists, is this person said to be self-luminous here? This is not a fault. For that [impression-material] is merely the object.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.10
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.10]

children.text:
na tatra rathā na rathayogā na panthāno bhavanti |
atha rathān rathayogān pathaḥ sṛjate |
na tatrānandā mudaḥ pramudo bhavanti |
athānandān mudaḥ pramudaḥ sṛjate |
na tatra veśāntāḥ puṣkariṇyaḥ sravantyo bhavanti |
atha veśāntān puṣkariṇīḥ sravantīḥ sṛjate |
sa hi kartā || BrhUp_4,3.10 ||
children.translated_text: There are no chariots there, no chariot-horses, no roads. But he creates chariots, chariot-horses, and roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights. But he creates joys, pleasures, and delights. There are no pools there, no lotus-ponds, no streams. But he creates pools, lotus-ponds, and streams. For he is the creator. (BṛUp 4.3.10)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.10 nanvatra kathaṃ puruṣaḥ svayañjyotiryena jāgarata iva grāhyagrāhakādilakṣaṇaḥ sarve vyavahāro dṛśyate /
cakṣurādyanugrāhakāścā'dityādyā lokāstathaiva dṛśyante yathā jāgarite /
tatra kathaṃ viśeṣāvadhāraṇaṃ kriyate 'trāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃ jyotirbhavatīti /
ucyate-vailakṣaṇyātsvapnadarśanasya /
jāgaritaṃ hīndriyabuddhamana ālokādivyāpārasaṃkīrṇamātmajyotiḥ /
iha tu svapn indriyābhāvāttadanugrāhakādityādyālokābhāvācca viviktaṃ kevalaṃ bhavati /
tasmādvilakṣaṇam /
nanu tathaiva viṣayā upalabhyante svapne 'pi yathā jāgarite tatra kathamindrāyābhāvādvailakṣamyamucyate iti /
śṛṇu- na tatra liṣayāḥ svapne rathādilakṣaṇāḥ /
tathā na rathayogā ratheṣu yujyanta iti rathayogā aśvādayastatra na vidyante /
na ca panthāno rathamārgā bhavanti /
atha rathānrathayogānpathaśca sṛjate svayam /
kathaṃ punaḥ sṛjate rathādisādhanānāṃ vṛkṣādīnāṃmabhāve /
ucyete-nanūktamasya lokasya sarvāvato mātrāmapādāya svayaṃ vihatya svayaṃ nirmāyetyantaḥkaraṇavṛttirasya lokasya vyavatiṣṭhate taducyate svayaṃ nirmāyeti /
tadevā'ha-rathādīnsṛjata iti /
natu tatra karaṇaṃ vā karaṇānugrāgakāṇivā'dityādijyotīṃṣi tadavabhāsyā vā rathādayo viṣayā vidyante /
tadvāsanāmātraṃ tu kevalaṃ tadupalabdhikarmanimittacoditodbhūtāntaḥkaraṇavṛtyāśrayaṃ dṛśyate /
tadyasya jyotiṣo dṛśyate 'luptadṛśastadātmajyotiratra kevalamasiriva kośādvivivaktam /
tathā na tatrā'nandāḥ sukhaviśeṣā mudo harṣā putrādilābhanimittāḥ pramudasta eva prakorṣopetāḥ /
atha cā'nandādīnsṛjate /
tathā na tatra veśāntāḥ palvalāḥpuṣkariṇyastaḍāgāḥ sravantyo nadyo bhavanti /
atha veśāntādīnsṛjate vāsanāmātrarūpān /
yasmātsa hi kartā /
tdavāsanāśracittavṛtyudbhavanimittakarmahetutvenetyavocāma /
tasya kartṛtvaṃ na tu sākṣādeva tatra kriyā saṃbhavati sādhanābhāvāt /
na hi kārakamantareṇa kriyā saṃbhavati /
na ca tatra hastapādādīni kriyākārakāṇi saṃbhavanti /
yatka tu tāni vidyante jāgarite tatrā'tmajyotiravabhāsitaiḥkāryakaraṇai rathādivāsanāśrayāntaḥkaraṇavṛtyudbhavanimittaṃ karma nivartyate tenocyate sa hi karteti /
taduktamātmanaivāyaṃ jyotiṣā'ste palyayate karma kuruta iti /
tatrāpi na paramārthataḥ svataḥ kartṛtvaṃ caitanyajyotiṣo 'vabhāsakatvavyatirekeṇa /
children.translated_text: Even there, however, the consciousness-light does not have agentship in the ultimate sense, apart from [its role as] illuminator.

children.text: yaccaitanyātmajyotiṣāntaḥkaraṇadvāreṇāvabhāsayati kāryakaraṇāni sadavabhāsitāni karmasu vyāpriyante kāryakaraṇāni tatra kartṛtvamupacaryata ātmanaḥ /
children.translated_text: Because the consciousness-self-light, through the doorway of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), illuminates the effects and instruments — and those effects and instruments, being constantly illuminated, engage in actions — agentship is figuratively attributed to the self.

children.text: yaduktaṃ dhyāyatīva lelāyatīveti tadevānūdyate /
children.translated_text: What was stated — 'it meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were' (BṛUp 4.3.7) — that very [teaching] is being restated.

children.text: sa hi kartetīha hetvartham //4,3.10//
children.translated_text: 'For he is the agent' — here, this is for the purpose of [stating] the reason. // 4.3.10 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.10: [Objection:] But how is the person self-luminous here [in dream], where all transactions characterized by the grasped and the grasper and the like are seen as in the waking state? And the lights like the sun and the rest, which support the eye and the other [sense-organs], are seen there just as in waking. How then is the specific determination made that 'here this person is self-luminous'?
[Reply:] Because of the dissimilarity of dream-experience [from waking]. For waking is the self-light mixed with the operations of sense-organs, intellect, mind, illumination, and the like. But here in dream, because of the absence of the sense-organs, and because of the absence of the supporting lights of the sun and the rest — [the self-light] becomes isolated, pure. Therefore it is dissimilar.
[Objection:] But objects are experienced in dream just as in waking — how then is dissimilarity stated on the ground of the absence of sense-organs?
[Reply:] Listen — there are no real objects in dream, characterized as chariots and the like. Likewise, no horses and the like that are harnessed to chariots exist there. Nor do roads for chariots exist. Yet he creates chariots, horse-teams, and roads by himself.
But how does he create, in the absence of materials like trees and the like for making chariots? [Reply:] Was it not stated: 'having taken the measure of this entire world, having himself destroyed [it], he himself creates' — the mental modification (<s>antaḥkaraṇavṛtti</s>) of this [waking] world persists — that is what is meant by 'he himself creates.' This is what [the text] says — 'he creates chariots and the like.'
But there are no sense-organs there, nor lights of the sun and the like that support the sense-organs, nor objects like chariots and the like illuminated by them. Rather, only the latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) alone — resting on the mental modifications that have arisen, impelled by the <s>karma</s> that is the cause of those cognitions — are seen.
That by whose light these are seen — [the self] whose power of seeing is undiminished — that self-light here [in dream] is isolated alone, like a sword drawn from its sheath.
Similarly, there are no real joys (<s>ānandas</s>), specific pleasures, gladness (<s>muda</s>), or delights (<s>harṣa</s>) caused by obtaining a son and the like; nor excessive joys (<s>pramuda</s>). Yet he creates joys and the like.
Similarly, there are no real pools, ponds, lotus-lakes, tanks, or flowing rivers there. Yet he creates pools and the like — in the form of mere latent impressions.
Because he is the agent. His agentship — being the cause of the <s>karma</s> that gives rise to the mental modifications resting on latent impressions — this we have stated. His agentship, however — actual action is not possible there because of the absence of instruments. For without agents [of action], action is not possible. And hands, feet, and the like — the agents of action — are not available there. Rather, in waking, where they do exist, by means of effects and instruments illuminated by the self-light, the <s>karma</s> that is the cause of the arising of mental modifications resting on the latent impressions of chariots and the like is accomplished — therefore it is said 'he is the agent.' This is what was stated: 'By the light of the self alone, one sits, moves about, does one's work' and so forth.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.11
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.11]

children.text:
tad ete ślokā bhavanti --
svapnena śārīram abhiprahatyāsuptaḥ suptān abhicākaśīti |
śukram ādāya punar aiti sthānaṃ hiraṇmayaḥpuruṣa ekahaṃsaḥ || BrhUp_4,3.11 ||
children.translated_text:
On this there are these verses:
'Having struck down the bodily [self] by dream, the sleepless one watches over the sleeping ones. Having taken up the shining [sense-faculties], he returns again to his station — the golden person, the lone swan.' // BṛhUp 4.3.11 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,3.11 tadeva etasminnukter'tha ete ślokā mantrā bhavanti /
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.11: On this very subject that has been stated, there are these verses, these <s>mantras</s>.

children.text: svapnena svapnabhāvena śārīraṃ śarīramabhihatya niśceṣṭamāpādyāsuptaḥ svayamaluptadṛgādiśaktisvābhāvyātsuptānvasanākārodbhūtānantaḥkaraṇavṛtyāśrayā- nbāhyādhyātmikānsarvānela bhāvānsvena rūpeṇa pratyastamitānsuptānabhicākaśītyalupyā'tmadṛṣṭyā paśyatyavabhāsatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'By dream' — by the state of dream — 'having struck down the bodily [self]' — the body — having rendered it motionless — 'the sleepless one' — himself, because of his natural undiminished power of seeing and the rest — 'watches over the sleeping ones' — the mental modifications that have arisen in the form of latent impressions, both external and internal — all those entities that have subsided into their own forms, that are 'sleeping' — he watches over them, sees them, illuminates them — by his undiminished self-seeing. This is the meaning.

children.text: śukraṃ śuddhaṃ jyotiṣmadindriyamātra rūpamādāya gṛhītvā punoḥ karmaṇe jāgaritasthānamaiti āgacchati hiraṇmayo hiraṇmaya iva caitanyajyotiḥsvabhāvaḥ puruṣa ekahaṃsa eka iva hantītyekahaṃsaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The shining one' (<s>śukra</s>) — the pure, luminous, consisting merely of the sense-faculties — 'having taken up,' having gathered — he returns again to his station of waking, for the purpose of action. 'The golden one' (<s>hiraṇmaya</s>) — like gold, being of the nature of the light of consciousness — 'the person,' 'the lone swan' (<s>ekahaṃsa</s>) — 'one who goes alone,' hence <s>ekahaṃsa</s>.

children.text: eko jāgratsvapnehalokaparalokādīn gacchatītyekahaṃsaḥ //4,3.11//
children.translated_text: One who goes alone through this world and the next, waking and dream — hence <s>ekahaṃsa</s> (the lone swan). // 4.3.11 //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.12
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.12]

children.text:
prāṇena rakṣann avaraṃ kulāyaṃ bahiṣkulāyād amṛtaś caritvā |
sa īyate 'mṛto yatrakāmaṃ hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣa ekahaṃsaḥ || BrhUp_4,3.12 ||
children.translated_text: 'Guarding the lower nest by <s>prāṇa</s>, the immortal one moves about outside the nest. That immortal one goes wherever he wishes — the golden person, the lone swan.' // BṛhUp 4.3.12 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,3.12 tathā prāṇena pañcavṛttinā rakṣanparipālayannanyathā mṛtabhrāntiḥ syādavaraṃ nikṛṣṭamanekāśucisaṃghātatvādatyantabībhatsaṃ kulāyaṃ nīḍaṃ śarīraṃ svayaṃ tu bahistasmātkulāyāccaritvā /
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.12: Similarly, 'guarding by <s>prāṇa</s>' — by the five-fold vital breath — 'protecting' the 'lower' — inferior, being an aggregate of manifold impurities, extremely repulsive — 'nest' (<s>kulāya</s>), the body. But he himself moves about outside that nest.

children.text: yadyapi śarīrastha eva svapnaṃ paśyati tathāpi tatsaṃbandhābhāvāttatstha ivākāśo bahiścaritvetyucya /
children.translated_text: Although he sees dreams while situated in the body itself, nevertheless — because of the absence of connection with it [in dream] — he is said to move about outside, as space [moves about outside] while being [within something].

children.text: amṛtaḥ svayamamaraṇadharmeyate gacchati yatra kāmaṃ yatra yatra kāmī viṣayeṣūdbhūtavṛttirbhavati taṃ taṃ kāmaṃ vāsanārūpeṇodbhūte gacchati //4,3.12//
children.translated_text: 'The immortal one' — himself being of a nature not subject to death — 'goes' wherever he wishes — wherever desire arises, wherever the latent impressions of objects have arisen as mental modifications — to each such desire he goes in the form of latent impressions. // 4.3.12 //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.13
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.13]

children.text:
svapnānta uccāvacam īyamāno rūpāṇi devaḥ kurute bahūni |
uteva strībhiḥ saha modamāno jakṣad utevāpi bhayāni paśyan || BrhUp_4,3.13 ||
children.translated_text: 'In the realm of dream, moving high and low, the luminous one (<s>deva</s>) creates many forms — now, as it were, enjoying with women; now laughing, as it were; now, as it were, seeing frightful things.' // BṛhUp 4.3.13 //

children.text: BrhUpBh_4,3.13 kiñca svapnānte svapnasthāna uccāvacamuccaṃ devādibhāvamavacaṃ tiryagādibhāvaṃ nikṛṣṭaṃ taduccāvacamīyamāno gamyamānaḥ prāpnuvanrūpāṇi devo dyotanāvānkurute nirvartayati vāsanārūpāṇi bahūnyasaṃkhyeyāni utāpi strībhiḥ saha modamāna iva jakṣadiva hasanniva vayasyaiḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.13: Moreover, 'in the realm of dream' — in the state of dream — 'moving high and low' — 'high' meaning the state of gods and the like, 'low' meaning the inferior state of animals and the like — moving through, attaining those high and low [states] — 'the luminous one' (<s>deva</s>), because of possessing the quality of luminosity — 'creates' — produces — 'many forms,' innumerable, in the nature of latent impressions. 'Now, as it were, enjoying with women'; 'now laughing, as it were,' as if playing with friends.

children.text: utevāpi bhayāni bibhetyebhya iti bhayāni saṃhavyghrādīni paśyanniva //4,3.13//
children.translated_text: 'Now, as it were, seeing frightful things' — things from which one fears — 'frightful things' such as lions, tigers, and the like — as if seeing [them]. // 4.3.13 //

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.14
children.translated_text: [Start of <s>BṛhUp</s> 4.3.14]

children.text:
ārāmam asya paśyanti na taṃ paśyati kaś caneti |
taṃ nāyataṃ bodhayed ity āhuḥ |
durbhiṣajyaṃ hāsmai bhavati yam eṣa na pratipadyate |

yāni hy eva jāgrat paśyati tāni supta iti |
atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotir bhavati |
so 'haṃ bhagavate sahasraṃ dadāmi |
ata ūrdhvaṃ vimokṣāya brūhīti || BrhUp_4,3.14 ||
children.translated_text: 'They see his pleasure-ground, but no one sees him.' They say: 'One should not suddenly wake him.' For the cure is difficult for one to whom he does not return. Others indeed say: 'This is just his waking state' — for what he sees while awake, he sees when asleep. Here, in this [state], this person is self-luminous. 'I give your honor a thousand [cows]. Teach me further, for the sake of liberation.' // BṛhUp 4.3.14 //

BrhUpBh_4,3.14 ārāmamāramaṇamākrīḍāmanena nirmitāṃ vāsanārūpāmasyā'tmanaḥ paśyanti sarve janāḥ /

children.translated_text: what is useful for that, being subservient to that, is just one part of it.

children.text: itastvāṃ niyokṣyāmi samastakāmapraśnanirṇayaśravaṇena vimokṣāyāta ūrdhvaṃ brūhīti /
children.translated_text: Henceforth, I shall engage you — by hearing the resolution of my complete question — for the sake of liberation — teach me further.'

children.text: yena saṃsārādvipramucyeyam, tvatprasādāt /
children.translated_text: 'By which I may be freed from <s>saṃsāra</s>, through your grace.'

children.text: vimokṣapadārthaikadeśanirṇayahetoḥ sahasradānam //4,3.14//
children.translated_text: The gift of a thousand is for the purpose of resolving one part of the topic of liberation. // 4.3.14 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.14: 'His pleasure-ground' (<s>ārāma</s>) — his sport, his play — the play-world created from latent impressions by this self — all people see. Village, city, women, food, and the like — the play-world created from latent impressions. But 'him — no one sees.' Alas, how distressing! — though it has become utterly isolated, though it has come within the range of vision — oh, the misfortune of the world, that it does not see the self even though it is capable of being seen! Thus the <s>śruti</s> displays compassion toward the world. The import is: the utterly isolated, self-luminous self exists in dream.
'One should not suddenly wake him' — they say. There is also a well-known [belief] in the world regarding the distinctness of the self-light in dream. What is that? That self who is asleep — one should not suddenly, forcefully, wake him — thus physicians and the like say in the world. Surely they see [the truth]: 'Having departed from the body, the sense-organs, and the rest — he exists alone, outside.' Since they say: 'One should not suddenly wake him.' And they see a defect therein: 'For one being suddenly awakened may not find [his way back to] those sense-organ doors.' This is what [the text] says: 'The cure is difficult for him' — for the body — 'to whom' — to which sense-organ location, from which location the self had departed, taking up the shining [sense-faculties] — 'he does not return' — this self does not return to that sense-organ location. Sometimes he enters the sense-faculties in a reversed manner. From that, upon the affliction of blindness, deafness, and the like — 'the cure is difficult' — the body becomes difficult to treat, requiring painful medical care — this is the meaning.
Therefore, even from common experience, the self-luminosity [of the self] in dream is understood.
The dream having occurred and passed — [represents] the forms of death. Therefore, in dream, the self is self-luminous.
Others indeed say: 'This is just his waking state' — [meaning] the dream is not a distinct state separate from this world and the next — rather, this world alone, the waking state [is the reality of dream]. If so, what of it? Listen to what results: if this dream is just the waking state, then this self has not been separated from the effects and instruments — it remains mixed with them. Therefore, the self would not be self-luminous — and thus, for the purpose of refuting [the thesis of] self-luminosity, others say: 'This is just his waking state.' And they state their reason: 'For the elephants and the other classes of objects that he sees while awake in the waking state — those very same [things] he sees when asleep too.' But that [argument] is invalid — because the sense-organs have ceased [functioning in dream]. For when the sense-organs have ceased, one sees dreams. Therefore, there is no possibility of any other light there. This has been stated: 'There are no chariots there, no horse-teams' and so forth.
Therefore, here this person is indeed self-luminous. That the self is self-luminous has been demonstrated by the example of dream. And that [the self] transcends the forms of death — and [that it] moves progressively through this world, the next world, and the rest, being distinct from this world and the next — and similarly, distinct from the nests of waking and dream — and that it wanders freely by desire — all this was taught by <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. Therefore, <s>Janaka</s> says: 'I, thus instructed by you, give your honor, the venerable one, a thousand [cows]. And liberation is the question I intended [to ask about] —

children.translated_text: 'This one, in this state of deep serenity (<s>saṃprasāda</s>), having enjoyed himself, having moved about, and having seen merit and demerit, returns again along the same path, the way he came, back to dream. Whatever he sees there — he is not followed by it; for this person is unattached.' 'Just so, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. I give your honor a thousand [cows]. Teach me further, for the sake of liberation indeed.' // BṛhUp 4.3.15 //

children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'Even so it is, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>.'

children.text: so 'haṃ bhagavate sahasraṃ dadāmyata ūrdhvaṃ vimokṣāyaiva brūhi /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'I give a thousand to the venerable one. Beyond this, please speak only for liberation.'

children.text: mokṣapadārthakadeśasya karmapravivekasya samyagdarśutatvāt /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Because a partial [exposition] of the distinction between the self and <s>karma</s> — the content of liberation — has been properly shown.

children.text: ata ūrdhvaṃvimokṣāyaiva brūhīti //4,3.15//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] 'Beyond this, please speak only for liberation.' (4.3.15)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.15:] What has been stated as the topic — 'this person exists by the light of the self alone' — that has been demonstrated directly by showing that 'this person is self-luminous' in dream. But what was said — 'having become sleep, he transcends this world — the forms of death' — therein this suspicion arises: he transcends only the forms of death, not death itself. For it is directly perceived in dreams that, even though [the dreamer] is withdrawn from the effects and instruments [of the body], there is the experience of joy, fear, and the like. Therefore, surely this [self] does not transcend death at all. For joy, fear, and the like are seen as effects of <s>karma</s>, which is death. And if this [self] is bound by death by its very nature, then liberation would be impossible. For no one is liberated from what is their own nature. But if death is not its nature, then liberation from it would be possible. 'Show how death is not a natural property of the self; and beyond that, tell me about liberation' — thus pressed by <s>Janaka</s>, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>, with the desire to show this, proceeded: That very self-luminous person who is the topic — this one who was shown in dreams — in this <s>saṃprasāda</s> (deep sleep), he becomes completely serene (<s>samyak prasīdati</s>); hence it is called <s>saṃprasāda</s>. In the waking state, having abandoned the turbidity (<s>kāluṣya</s>) born of the impact of hundreds of activities of the body and senses, freed from them, he becomes slightly serene in dream. But here, in deep sleep, he becomes completely serene — therefore deep sleep is called <s>saṃprasāda</s>. [As the text] will say of the self in deep sleep: 'Then he has crossed over all sorrows' (BṛUp 4.3.22); 'a single seer, in water' (BṛUp 4.3.32). This very self, having progressively become serene in this <s>saṃprasāda</s> — in deep sleep — [first] having been established [there]. How did he become serene? Wishing to enter deep sleep from the dream [state], while still in the dream state itself — having delighted, having experienced pleasure, having seen meetings with friends and relatives, having sported — having experienced variously the fruit of his conduct, the fatigue — this is the meaning. Having 'seen only' — not 'having done' — this is the meaning — both merit and the fruit of merit, and sin and the fruit of sin. But we have said that there is no direct seeing of merit and sin [themselves]. Therefore, he is not bound by merit and sin. For one who acts [producing] merit and sin is bound by them. But by mere seeing, one would not be bound by them. Therefore, having become sleep, he indeed transcends death — not merely the forms of death. Hence there is no suspicion that death is the nature of the self. For if death were [its] nature, it would act [as death] even in dream. But it does not act [thus]. And if it were [its] nature, there would be action, and there would be no liberation. But [death] is not [its] nature, because of its absence in dream. Therefore, liberation from death — from merit and sin — is possible for this [self]. [Objection:] But in the waking state, it is surely [the self's] very nature! [Reply:] No — for that is caused by the limiting adjuncts of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and the like. And that has been demonstrated by 'he thinks, as it were; he moves, as it were.' Therefore, by the conclusive transcendence of death's forms in dream alone, there is no suspicion of [death being] the self's nature, nor [fear of] non-liberation. Therein, 'having sported' means 'having experienced the fruit of conduct, the fatigue' — this is the meaning. Then, after the experience of <s>saṃprasāda</s>, again, <s>pratinyāya</s> — 'in accordance with the course' — according to the established path, as he came. The established course (<s>nyāya</s>) is the path (<s>ayana</s>). Coming (<s>āyana</s>) is going forth; the return journey in the same order as the going is <s>pratinyāya</s>. He returns as he came — this is the meaning. To his own place (<s>pratiyoni</s>) — to his own station. For having passed from the dream station into deep sleep, he returns to his own station again. He runs back to the dream state, to the dream station itself. [Objection:] If he does not act [producing] merit and sin in dream, how is it determined that the fruits of merit and sin are [merely seen]? For just as he acts in the waking state, so too in dream, since the seeing is equivalent. To this, [the text] says: This self, whatever he sees there in the dream — the fruits of merit and sin — he comes along with (<s>anvāgata</s>) but is not bound (<s>ananubaddha</s>) by that. For if what was seen in dream were actually done, he would be bound by it; even upon waking from the dream, he would remain affected by it. But in the world, there is no well-known [consequence of] being affected by an action done in dream. For no one considers himself a sinner on account of a sin committed in dream. Nor does the world censure or shun one upon hearing of a dream-seen sin. Therefore, he indeed comes along unbound by that. And the narrators of dreams indicate this with the word 'as it were' (<s>iva</s>): 'Today elephants were being driven together — as it were, I saw [it].' Therefore, there is no agency for him [in dreams]. But how is his non-agency [established]? Contact with material effects and instruments — of a material [self] — that is seen as the cause of action. No one who is immaterial is ever seen to have action. And the self is immaterial — therefore [it is] unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>). And because this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached, therefore he is not bound by what was seen in dreams. For this very reason, agency in action does not apply to him in any way. For agency would arise from contact with effects and instruments; but that contact, that attachment, does not belong to him — since 'this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached.' Therefore, he is immortal.
