children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.16]

children.text:
sa vā eṣa etasmin svapne ratvā caritvā dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca punaḥ pratinyāyaṃ pratiyony ādravati buddhāntāyaiva |
sa yat tatra kiñcit paśyaty ananvāgatas tena bhavati |
asaṅgo hy ayaṃ puruṣa iti |
evam evaitat yājñavalkya |
so 'haṃ bhagavate sahasraṃ dadāmi |
ata ūrdhvaṃ vimokṣāyaiva brūhīti || BrhUp_4,3.16 ||
children.translated_text: This very self, having delighted in this dream, having sported, having seen only merit and sin, runs back again by the same path, by the same origin, to the waking state (<s>buddhānta</s>). Whatever he sees there, he is not bound by it — for this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached. 'Even so it is, <s>Yājñavalkya</s>. I give a thousand to the venerable one. Beyond this, please speak only for liberation.' (BṛUp 4.3.16)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.16 tatrāsaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣa ityasaṅgatākartṛtve heturuktaḥ /
uktaṃ ca pūrvaṃ karmavaśātsa īyate yatra kāmamiti /
kāmaśca saṅga'to 'siddho heturukto 'saṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣa iti /
na tvetadasti /
kathaṃ tarhi /
asaṅga evetyetaducyate- sa vā eṣa etasminsvapne va vā eṣa puruṣaḥ /
saṃpradātpratyāgataḥ svapne ratvā caritvā yathākāmaṃ dṛṣṭaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ceti sarvaṃ pūrvavat /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Having returned from deep sleep, in the dream — having delighted, having sported, according to his wish, having seen only merit and sin — everything is as before.

children.text: buddhāntāyaiva jāgaritasthānāya /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] '<s>Buddhānta</s>' means 'to the waking state.'

children.text: tasmādasaṅga evāyaṃ puruṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, this <s>puruṣa</s> is indeed unattached.

children.text: yadi svapne saṅgavānsyātkāmī tatastatsaṅgajairdeṣairbuddhāntāya pratyāgato lipyeta //4,3.16//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] For if he were attached in dream, being desirous, then returning to the waking state, he would be stained by the defects born of that attachment. (4.3.16)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.16:] Therein, 'for this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached' — non-attachment has been stated as the reason for non-agency. And it was previously said that 'he is impelled by <s>karma</s>' and 'by desire.' But desire too presupposes attachment — therefore the stated reason 'for this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached' would be unestablished. This is not so. Then how? That he is indeed unattached — this is what is stated: 'This very self, in this dream' — this very <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.17
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.17]

children.text: sa vā eṣa etasmin buddhānte ratvā caritvā dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca punaḥ pratinyāyaṃ pratiyony ādravati svapnāntāyaiva || BrhUp_4,3.17 ||
children.translated_text: This very self, having delighted in this waking state (<s>buddhānta</s>), having sported, having seen only merit and sin, runs back again by the same path, by the same origin, to the dream state (<s>svapnānta</s>). (BṛUp 4.3.17)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.17 yathāsau svapne 'saṅgatvātsvapnasaṅgajairdeṣairjāgarite pratyāgato na lipyata evaṃ jāgaritasaṅgajairapu doṣānra lipyata eva buddhāntena tadetaducyate- sa vā eṣa etasminbuddhānte jāgarite ratvā caritvetyādi pūrvavat /
sa yattatra buddhānte kiñcitpaśyatyanatvāgatastena bhavatyasaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣa iti /
nanu dṛṣṭvaiveti kathamavadhāryate karoti ca tatra puṇyapāpe tatphalaṃ ca paśyati /
kārakāvabhāsakatve kartṛtvopapatteḥ /
ātmanaivāyaṃ jyotiṣā'sta ityādinā'tmajyotiṣāvabhāsitaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṅghāto vyavaharati tenāsya kartṛtvamupacaryate na svataḥkartṛtvam /
tathā coktaṃ dhyāyatīva lelāyatīveti /
buddhyādyupādhikṛtameva na svataḥ /
iha tu paramārthāpekṣayopādhinirapekṣa ucyate dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpañca na kṛtveti tena na pūrvāparavyāghātāśaṅkā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] But here, from the standpoint of ultimate reality (<s>paramārtha</s>), without reference to limiting adjuncts, it is said: 'having seen only merit and sin — not having done.' Therefore, there should be no suspicion of contradiction between the earlier and later [statements].

children.text: yasmānnirupādhikaḥ paramārthato na karoti na lipyate kriyāphalena /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] For, being without limiting adjuncts, from the standpoint of ultimate reality, he does not act and is not stained by the fruits of action.

children.text: tathā ca bhagavatoktam-"anāditvānnirguṇatvātparamātmāyamavyayaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And thus the Lord [<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>] has said: 'Because of beginninglessness and being without qualities, this supreme self is imperishable;

children.text: śarīrastho 'pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate" //
children.translated_text: though dwelling in the body, O son of <s>Kuntī</s>, it neither acts nor is stained.' (BhG 13.31)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.17:] Just as in dream, because of non-attachment, the defects born of dream-attachment do not stain [the self] upon returning to waking — even so, the defects born of waking-attachment also do not stain [the self]. This is what is stated: 'This very self, in this waking state — having delighted, having sported' — and so forth, as before. Whatever he sees there in the waking state, he is not bound by it — for this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached. [Objection:] But given [the phrase] 'having seen only,' how is it determined [whether] he also acts, producing merit and sin there, and [merely] sees their fruits? [Reply:] Because the aggregate of effects and instruments is illuminated by the self-light, agency is attributed [to the self]. 'This person exists by the light of the self alone' — by the self-light the aggregate of effects and instruments is illuminated and transacts; thereby agency is figuratively attributed to [the self], but there is no inherent agency. And thus it was said: 'he thinks, as it were; he moves, as it were.' It is caused by the limiting adjuncts of <s>buddhi</s> and the like alone — not inherent.

children.text: iti //

tathā sahasradānaṃ tu kāmapravivekasya darśitatvāt /
tathā sa vā eṣa etasminsvapne sa vā eṣa etasminbuddhānta ityetābhyāṃ kaṇḍikābhyāmasaṅgataiva pratipāditā /
yasmādbuddhānte kṛtena svapnānte gataḥ saṃprasanno 'saṃbaddho bhavati stainyādikāryādarśanāttasmāttriṣvapi sthāneṣu svato 'saṅga evāyam /
ato 'mṛtaḥ /
sthānatrayadharmavilakṣaṇaḥ pratiyonyādravati svapnāntāyaiva saṃprasādāyetyarthaḥ /
darśanavṛtteḥ svapnasyasvapnaśabdenābhidhānadarśanādantaśabdena ca viśeṣaṇopapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Because of the seeing that the word '<s>svapna</s>' (dream) denotes the function of seeing [in general], and because the qualification by the word '<s>anta</s>' (state/end) is appropriate [only when distinguishing from deep sleep].

children.text: etasmā antāya dhāvatīti ca suṣuptaṃ darśayiṣyati /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And [the text] will demonstrate deep sleep with [the words] 'he runs to the end of this.'

children.text: yadi punarevamucyate"svapnānte ratvā caritvaitāvubhāvantāvanusaṃcarati svapnāntaṃ ca buddhāntaṃ ce"ti darśanātsvapnāntāyaivetyatrāpu darśavṛttireva svapna ucyata iti tathāpi na kiñcidduṣyatyasaṅgatā hi siṣādhayiṣitā sidhyatyeva /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] If however one reads it thus: 'Having delighted and sported in the dream state, he wanders through both these states — the dream state and the waking state' — as is seen [in the <s>śruti</s>] — then even in 'to the dream state,' the word '<s>svapna</s>' denotes the function of seeing. And even so, nothing is contradicted — for the non-attachment that is intended to be established is indeed established.

children.text: yasmājjāgarite dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca ratvā caritvā ca svapnāntamāgato na jāgaritadoṣāṇānugato bhavati //4,3.17//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Because, having delighted and sported in waking, and having seen only merit and sin, upon coming to the dream state, he is not followed by the defects of waking. (4.3.17)

[Commentary:] The gift of a thousand [cows] is [made here] because the distinction between desire [and the self] has been demonstrated. Similarly, 'this very self, in this dream' and 'this very self, in this waking state' — by these two sections, the non-attachment alone of the self has been demonstrated. Because, having acted in waking, upon going to dream [and then] to deep sleep, the self becomes serene and unconnected — since there is no seeing of effects such as theft and the like — therefore, in all three states, the self is intrinsically unattached. Therefore, it is immortal — different in character from the properties of the three states. 'He runs back to the dream state' — means to the dream state, to <s>saṃprasāda</s> (deep sleep) — this is the meaning.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.18
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.18]

children.text:
tad yathā mahāmatsya ubhe kūle anusaṃcarati pūrvaṃ cāparaṃ ca |
evam evāyaṃ puruṣa etāv ubhāv antāv anusaṃcarati svapnāntaṃ ca buddhāntaṃ ca || BrhUp_4,3.18 ||
children.translated_text: Just as a great fish moves along both banks — the hither and the farther — even so does this <s>Puruṣa</s> move along both these states — the dream state and the waking state. (BṛUp 4.3.18)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.18 evamayaṃ puruṣa ātmā svayañjyotiḥ kāryakaraṇavilakṣaṇastatprayojakābhyā kāmakarmabhyāṃ vilakṣa ṇo yasmādasaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣo 'saṅtvādityayamarthaḥ"sa vā eṣa etasminsaṃprasāda"ityādyābhistasṛbhiḥ kaṇḍakābhiḥ pratipāditaḥ /
tatrāsaṅgataivā'tmanaḥ kuto yasmājjāgaritātsvapnaṃ svapnācca saṃprasādaṃ saṃprasādācca punaḥ svapn krameṇa buddhāntaṃ jāgaritaṃ buddhantācca punaḥ svapnāntamityevamanukmasaṃcāreṇa sthātrayasya vyatirekaḥ sādhitaḥ /
pūrvamapyupanyasto 'yamarthaḥ svapne bhūtvemaṃ lokamatikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇīti taṃ vistareṇa pratipādya kevalaṃ dṛṣṭāntamātramavaśiṣṭaṃ tadvakṣyāmītyārabhyate- tattatraitasminyathāpradarśiter'the dṛṣṭānte 'mupādīyate-yathā loke mahāmatsyo mahāṃścāsau matsyaśca nādeyena srotasāhārya ityarthaḥ /
srotaśca viṣṭambhayati svacchandacāryubhe kūle nadyāḥ pūrvaṃ cāparaṃ cānukrameṇa saṃcarati /
saṃcarannapikūladvayaṃ tanmadhyavartonadakasrotovegena na paravaśī kriyate /
evamevāyaṃ puruṣa atāvubhā antā anusaṃcarati /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Even so, this <s>Puruṣa</s> moves along both these states.

children.text: kau tau /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Which are these two?

children.text: svapnāntaṃ ca buddhāntaṃ ca /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The dream state and the waking state.

children.text: dṛṣṭāntapradarśanaphalaṃ tu mṛtyurūpaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātaḥ saha tatprayojakābhyāṃ kāmakarmabhyāmanātmadharmoyaṃ cā'tmaitasmādvilakṣaṇa iti vistarato vyākhyātam //4,3.18 //
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] The result of presenting the illustrations is that the aggregate of effects and instruments — which is in the form of death — together with its impelling causes, desire and action, is a non-self property, and this self is distinct from it — this has been explained in detail. (4.3.18)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.18:] Thus, this <s>Puruṣa</s>, the self, self-luminous, different in character from the effects and instruments, different from desire and <s>karma</s> which impel them — because 'this <s>puruṣa</s> is unattached,' because of non-attachment — this meaning has been demonstrated by the three sections beginning with 'this very self, in this <s>saṃprasāda</s>.' Therein, the non-attachment of the self [is established] from the fact that it moves successively from waking to dream, from dream to deep sleep, from deep sleep again to dream, and then to waking, and from waking again to dream — by this sequential movement, the self's distinction from the three states has been established. This meaning was introduced earlier: 'Having become sleep, he transcends this world — the forms of death.' Having demonstrated that in detail, only the illustration remains — 'I shall now state that,' [the text] commences. There — in this matter as demonstrated — an illustration is adduced: Just as in the world, a great fish — great and being a fish — is [seemingly] carried by the stream of a river, yet it holds back the current and, moving of its own accord, moves along both banks of the river — the hither and the farther — in sequence. Even while moving, it is not rendered helpless by the force of the water current flowing between the two banks.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.19
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.19]

children.text:
tad yathāsminn ākāśe śyeno vā suparṇo vā viparipatya śrāntaḥ saṃhatya pakṣau saṃlayāyaiva dhriyate |
evam evāyaṃ puruṣa etasmā antāya dhavati |
yatra supto na kaṃ cana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kaṃ cana svapnaṃ paśyati || BrhUp_4,3.19 ||
children.translated_text: Just as in this space, a hawk or an eagle, having flown about and become exhausted, folds its wings and glides down to its nest — even so, this <s>puruṣa</s> hastens toward that state where, having fallen asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever. (BṛUp 4.3.19)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.19 atra ca sthānatrayānusaṃtāreṇa svayañjyotiṣa ātmanaḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃghātavyatiriktasya kāmakarmabhyāṃ vivaktatoktā svato nāyaṃ saṃsāradharmavānupādhinimittameva tvasya saṃsāritvamavidyādhyāropitamityeṣa samudāyārtha uktaḥ /
tatra ca jāgratsvapnasuṣuptasthānānāṃ trayāṇāṃ viprakīrṇarūpa ukto na puñjīkṛtyaikatra darśitaḥ /
yasmājjāgarite sasaṅgaḥ samṛtyuḥ sakāryakaraṇasaṃghāta upalakṣyate 'vidyayā /
svapne tu kāmasaṃyukto mṛtyurūpavinirmukta upalabhyate /
suṣupte punarbuddhāntamāgato buddhāntācca suṣupte saṃprasanno 'saṅgo bhavatītyasaṃgatāpi dṛśyate /
ekavākyatayā tūpasaṃhrayamāṇaṃ phalaṃ nityamuktabuddhaśuddhasvabhāvatāsya naikatra puñjīkṛtya pradarśiteti tatpradarśanāya kaṇḍikā'rabhyate /
suṣupte hyevaṃrūpatāsya vakṣyamāṇā"tadvā asyaitadaticchandā apahatapāpmābhayaṃ rūpāmi"ti /
yasmādevaṃrūpaṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ suṣuptaṃ pravivikṣati /
tatkathamityāha-dṛṣṭāntenāsyārthasya prakaṭībhāvo bhavatīti tatra dṛṣṭānta upādīyate /
tadyathāsminnākāśe bhautike śyeno vā suparṇo vā /
supraṇaśabdena kṣipraḥ śyena ucyate /
yathā'kāśe 'sminvihṛtya viparipatya śrānto nānāparipatanalakṣaṇena karmaṇā parikhinnaḥ saṃhṛtya pakṣau saṃgamayya pakṣau samyaglīyate 'sminniti saṃlayo nīḍo nīḍāyaiva dhriyate svātmanaiva dhrāyate svayameva /
yathāyaṃ dṛṣṭānta evamevāyaṃ puruṣa etasyā etasmai antāya dhāvati /
antaśabdavācyasya viśeṣaṇaṃ yatra yasminnante supto na kañcana na kañcidapi kāmaṃ kāmayate /
tathā ca na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyati /
na kañcana kāmiti svapnbuddhāntayoraviśeṣeṇa sarvaḥ kāmaḥ pratiṣidhyate /
kañcanetyavaśeṣitābhidhānāt /
tathā na kañcana svapnamiti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Likewise, 'he sees no dream whatsoever.'

children.text: jāgarite 'pi yaddarśanaṃ tadapi svapnaṃ manyate śrutirata āha-na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyatīti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Even the perception [that occurs] in the waking state — that too the <s>śruti</s> considers a dream; therefore it says: 'he sees no dream whatsoever.'

children.text: tathā ca śrutyantaram"tasya traya āvasathāstrayaḥ svapnāḥ"iti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And thus another <s>śruti</s> [says]: 'His are three abodes, three dreams' (ChUp 8.10.1).

children.text: yathā dṛṣṭānte pakṣiṇaḥ paripatanajaśramāpanupattaye svanīḍaupasarpaṇamevaṃ jāgratsvapnayoḥ kāryakaraṇasaṃyogajakriyāphalaiḥ saṃyujyamānasya pakṣiṇaḥ paripatanaja iva śramo bhavaci tacchmāpanuttaye svātmano nīḍāmāyatanaṃ sarvasaṃsāradharmavilakṣaṇaṃ sarvakriyākārakaphalāyāsaśūnyaṃ svamātmānaṃ praviśati //4,3.19//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Just as, in the illustration, the bird's approaching its own nest is for the cessation of the fatigue born of flying about — so too, [the self,] in the waking and dream states, being conjoined with the fruits of activity born from the conjunction with the aggregate of effects and instruments — a fatigue like the bird's flying-fatigue arises; for the cessation of that fatigue, [the self] enters its own nest, its own abode — its own self, which is distinct from all <s>saṃsāric</s> properties, devoid of all action, agents, fruits, and effort. (4.3.19)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.19:] Here, through the traversal of the three states, it has been stated that the self — which is self-luminous and separate from the aggregate of effects and instruments — is distinct from desire and action. Of its own nature, this [self] does not possess <s>saṃsāric</s> properties; rather, its <s>saṃsāric</s> nature is superimposed through <s>avidyā</s> and caused by limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhis</s>) alone — this is the collective meaning that has been stated. Therein, the three states of waking, dream, and deep sleep have been described in scattered form — not gathered together and shown in one place. For in the waking state, [the self] is apprehended through <s>avidyā</s> as associated [with objects], as subject to death, and as possessing the aggregate of effects and instruments. In dream, however, it is apprehended as conjoined with desire but released from the form of death. In deep sleep, again, having reached the limit of the intellect, and from the limit of the intellect [entering] deep sleep, [the self] becomes serene (<s>saṃprasanna</s>) and unattached — thus its non-attachment too is seen. But the fruit — namely, its nature as eternally liberated, awakened, and pure — when consolidated into a single [statement], has not been demonstrated in one place. Therefore, a section is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating that. For in deep sleep, this nature of its will be stated [thus:] 'That indeed is its form — beyond desire, free from evil, free from fear' (BṛUp 4.3.21). Since [the text] wishes to enter into [the description of] deep sleep, which is of such a distinct nature — how [does it do so]? It says: [the meaning of] this [passage] is made manifest through an illustration — therefore an illustration is employed. 'Just as in this space' — the physical [space] — 'a hawk or an eagle' — by the word '<s>suparṇa</s>' (eagle), a swift hawk is meant. Just as in this space, having roamed about, having flown around, [the bird] becomes exhausted — wearied by the activity characterized by flying about in various ways — having folded its wings, having drawn together its wings, [it glides] toward its nest (<s>saṃlaya</s>) — '<s>saṃlaya</s>' means nest — it is sustained by its own self alone, it supports itself. As is this illustration, even so this <s>puruṣa</s> hastens toward that state (<s>anta</s>). The qualification of what is denoted by the word '<s>anta</s>' (state/end) [is:] 'where' — in which state, having fallen asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever. Likewise, he sees no dream whatsoever. 'No desire whatsoever' — without distinction between the dream and waking states, every desire is negated — because of the expression 'whatsoever' leaving nothing remaining.

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.20
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.20]

children.text:
tā vā asyaitā hitā nāma nāḍyo yathā keśaḥ sahasradhā bhinnas tāvatāṇimnā tiṣṭhanti |
śuklasya nīlasya piṅgalasya haritasya lohitasya pūrṇāḥ |
atha yatrainaṃ ghnantīva jinantīva hastīva vicchāyayati gartam iva patati |
yad eva jāgrad bhayaṃ paśyati tad atrāvidyayā manyate |
atha yatra deva iva rājevāham evedaṃ sarvo 'smīti manyate |
so 'sya paramo lokaḥ || BrhUp_4,3.20 ||
children.translated_text: These <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels) of his, called <s>hitā</s>, are as fine as a hair split a thousandfold. They are filled with white, blue, tawny, green, and red [fluids]. Now, when [in dreams] they seem to kill him, or seem to overpower him, or an elephant seems to chase him, or he seems to fall into a pit — whatever fear he sees in the waking state, that he imagines here [in dreams] through ignorance. And when [he dreams that] he is like a god, or like a king, [or thinks] 'I am this all' — that is his supreme world. (BṛUp 4.3.20)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.20 yadyasyāyaṃ svabhāvaḥ sarvasaṃsāradharmaśūnyatā paropādhinimittaṃ cāsya saṃsāradharmitvam /
yannimittaṃ cāsya paropādhikṛtaṃ saṃsāradharmitvaṃ sā cāvidyā /
tasyā avidyāyā kiṃ svābhāvikatvamāhosvitkāmakarmādivadāgantukatvam /
yadi cā'gantukatvaṃ tato vimokṣa upapadyate /
tasyāścā'gantukatve kopapattiḥ kathaṃ vā nā'tmadharmo 'vidyeti, sarvānarthabījabhūtāyā avidyāyāḥ satatvāvadhāraṇārthaṃ parā kaṇḍikā'rabhyate- tā vā asya śiraḥpāṇyādilakṣaṇasya puruṣasyaitā hitā nāma nāḍyo yathā keśaḥ sahasradhā bhinnastāvatā tāvatparimāṇenāṇimnāṇutvena tiṣṭhanti /
tāśṭa śuklasya rasasya nīlasya piṅgalasya haritasya lohitasya pūrṇā etaiḥ śuklatvādibhī rasaviśeṣaiḥ pūrṇā ityarthaḥ /
ethe ca rasānāṃ varṇaviśeṣā vātapittaśleṣmaṇāmitaretarasaṃyogavaiṣamyaviśeṣādvicitrā bahavaśca bhavanti /
tāsvevavidhāsu nāḍīṣu sūkṣmāsu bālāgrasahasrabhedaparimāṇāsu śuklādirasapūrṇāsu saraladehavyāpinīṣu saptadaśakaṃ liṅgaṃ vartate /
tadāśritāḥ sarvā vāsanā uccāvacasaṃsāradharmānubhavajanitāḥ /
talliṅgaṃ vāsanāśrayaṃ sūkṣmatvātsvacchaṃ sphaṭikamaṇikalpaṃ nāḍīgatarasopādhisaṃsargavaśāddharmādharmapreritodbhūtavṛttiviśeṣaṃ strīrathahastyādyākāraviśeṣairvāsanābhiḥ pratyavabhāsate /
athaivaṃ sati yatra yasminkāle kecana śatravo 'nye vā taskarā māmāgatya ghnantīti mṛṣaiva vāsanānimittaḥ pratyayo 'vidyākhyo jāyate tadetaducyata enaṃ svapnadṛśaṅghnantīveti /
tathā hastīvainaṃ vicchāyayati vicchādayati vidrāvayati dhāvayatīvetyarthaḥ /
gartamiva patati gartaṃ jīrṇakūpādikamiva patantamātmānamupalakṣayati /
tādṛśī hyasya mṛṣā vāsanodbhavatyatyantanikṛṣṭādharmodbhāsitāntaḥkaraṇavṛtyāśrayā duḥkhasvarūpavṛtyāśrayā duḥkhasvarūpatvāt /
kiṃbahunā yadeva jāgradbhayaṃ hastyādilakṣaṇaṃ tadeva bhayarūpamatrāsminsvapne vinaiva hastyādirūpaṃ bhayamavidyāvāsanayā mṛṣaivodbhūtayā manyate /
atha punaryatrāvidyāpakṛṣyamāṇā vidyā cotkṛṣyamāṇā kiṃviṣayā kiṃlakṣaṇā cetyucyate-atha punaryatra yasminkāle deva iva svayaṃ bhavati /
devatāviṣayā vidyā yadodbhūtā jāgaritakāle tadodbhūtayā vāsanayā devamivā'tmānaṃ manyate /
svapne 'pi taducyate deva iva rājeva rājyastho 'bhiṣiktaḥ svapne 'pi rājāhamiti manyate rājavāsanāvāsitaḥ /
evamatyantaprakṣīyamāṇāvidyodbhūtā ca vidyā sarvātmaviṣayā yadā yadā svapne 'pi tadbhāvito 'hamevedaṃ sarvo 'smīti manyate /
sa yaḥ sarvātmabhāvaḥ so 'syā'tmanaḥ paramo lokaḥ parama ātmabhāvaḥ svābhāvakaḥ /
yattu sarvātmabhāvādarvāgbālāgramātramapyanyatvena dṛśyate nāhamasmīti /
tadavasthāvidyī tayāvidyayā ye pratyupasthāpitā anātmabhāvā lokāste 'paramāḥ sthāvarāntāstānsaṃvyavahāraviṣayāṃllokānapekṣmāyaṃ sarvātmabhāvaḥ samasto 'nantaro 'bāhyaḥ so 'sya paramo lokaḥ /
tasmādapakṛṣyamāṇāyāmavidyāyāṃ vidyāyāṃ ca kāṣṭāṃ gatāyāṃ sarvātmabhāvo mokṣaḥ /
yathā svayañjyotiṣṭvaṃ svapne pratyakṣata evopalabhyate 'tha yatrainaṃ ghnantīva jinantīveti /
te ete vidyāvidyākārye sarvātmabhāvaḥ paricchinnātmabhāvaśca /
vidyayā śuddhayā sarvātmā bhavati /
avidyayā cāsarvo bhavati /
anyataḥ kutaścatpravibhakto bhavati /
yataḥ pravabhakto bhavati tena virudhyate /
viruddhatvāddhanyate jīyate vicchādyate ca /
asarvaviṣayatve ca bhinnatvādetadbhavati /
samastastu sankuto bhidyate yena virudhyetavirodābhāve kena hanyate jīyate vicchādyate ca /
ata idamavidyāyāḥ sattvamuktaṃ bhavati /
sarvātmānaṃ santamasarvātmatvena grāhayati /
ātmano 'nyaddhastvaramavidyamānaṃ pratyupasthāpayati /
ātmānamasarvamāpādayati /
tatastadviṣayaḥ kāmo bhavati /
yato bhidyate kāmataḥ kriyāmupādatte /
tataḥ phalam /
tadetaduktam /
vakṣyamāṇaṃ ca yatra hi dvaitamiva bhavati taditara itaraṃ paśyatītyādi /
idamavidyāyāḥ satatvaṃ sahakāryeṇa pradarśitam /
vidyāyāśca kāryaṃ sarvamātmabhāvaḥ pradarśito 'vidyāyā viparyeṇa /
sā cāvidyā nā'tmanaḥ svābhāviko dharmo yasmādvidyāyāmutkṛṣyamāṇāyāṃ svayamapacīyamānā satī kāṣṭhāṃ gatāyāṃ vidyāyāṃpariniṣṭhite sarvātmabhāve sarvātmanā nivartate rajjvāmiva sarpajñānaṃ rajjuniścaye /
taccoktaṃ yatra tvasya sarvamātmaivābhūttatkena kaṃ paśyedityādi /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And thus it was said: 'But when everything has become the self alone, then by what would one see whom?' (BṛUp 2.4.14) and so forth.

children.text: tasmānnā'tmadharmo 'vidyā /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, <s>avidyā</s> is not a property of the self.

children.text: na hi svābhāvikasyocchittiḥ kadācidapyupadyate saviturivoṣṇyaprakāśayoḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] For the destruction of an intrinsic property never occurs — like the heat and luminosity of the sun.

children.text: tasmāttasyā mokṣaupapadyate //4,3.20//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, liberation from it [<s>avidyā</s>] is established. (4.3.20)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.20:] If this is its true nature — freedom from all <s>saṃsāric</s> properties — and its <s>saṃsāric</s> nature is caused by external limiting adjuncts, and the cause of its <s>saṃsāric</s> nature created by external adjuncts is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — then is that <s>avidyā</s> intrinsic [to the self], or is it adventitious like desire and action? If it is adventitious, then liberation is tenable. And if it is adventitious, what is the proof? And how is <s>avidyā</s> not a property of the self? — for the purpose of ascertaining the real existence of <s>avidyā</s>, which is the seed of all misfortune, the next section is commenced.
'These <s>nāḍīs</s>' — of this <s>puruṣa</s> characterized by head, hands, and the like — 'called <s>hitā</s>, are as fine as a hair split a thousandfold — they stand with that measure of subtlety.' These are filled with the essence (<s>rasa</s>) of white, blue, tawny, green, and red — meaning: filled with these specific essences characterized by colors such as white and the like. And these color-variations of the essences are produced by the varying combinations and imbalances of <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm) — they are diverse and numerous.
In such <s>nāḍīs</s> — subtle, with the dimension of a hair-tip split a thousandfold, filled with essences of white and other colors, pervading the body in straight [lines] — the subtle body (<s>liṅga</s>) consisting of seventeen [elements] resides. Dependent on that [subtle body] are all <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) generated by the experience of high and low <s>saṃsāric</s> properties. That subtle body — the receptacle of <s>vāsanās</s> — being subtle and transparent, like a crystal gem, through contact with the limiting adjuncts of the essences within the <s>nāḍīs</s>, manifests specific mental modifications propelled by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, and is reflected through <s>vāsanās</s> in the specific forms of women, chariots, elephants, and the like.
This being so, when at some time enemies or thieves [appear to] come and kill him — this is merely a false cognition caused by <s>vāsanās</s>, called <s>avidyā</s>. This is what is stated: 'they seem to kill him.' Similarly, 'an elephant seems to chase him' — to cover, to make flee, to make run away — this is the meaning. 'He seems to fall into a pit' — a dilapidated well and the like — he perceives himself as falling. For such a false <s>vāsanā</s> arises in him — one whose substratum is a mental modification (<s>antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti</s>) illuminated by utterly debased <s>adharma</s>, because its nature is suffering.
In brief: whatever fear characterized by elephants and the like he sees in waking — that very fear, here in this dream, [appears] without the actual form of elephants and the like; fear, generated by the <s>avidyā-vāsanā</s> (latent impression of ignorance) that has falsely arisen, he imagines.
But then, when <s>avidyā</s> is being diminished and <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) is being elevated — what is the object and what is the characteristic [of <s>vidyā</s>]? This is said: when at some time he becomes like a god — when the <s>vidyā</s> pertaining to the deities arises in the waking state, then by the <s>vāsanā</s> arisen [from that], he imagines himself as a god, even in dream. Likewise, 'like a king' — an anointed sovereign — even in dream he thinks 'I am a king,' being pervaded by the <s>vāsanā</s> of kingship.
Similarly, when the <s>vidyā</s> that has arisen from <s>avidyā</s> being utterly diminished, the <s>vidyā</s> whose object is the self of all — whenever [this <s>vidyā</s> arises], even in dream, one who is imbued with it thinks: 'I am this all.' That state of being the self of all (<s>sarvātmabhāva</s>) — that is his supreme world (<s>paramo loka</s>), the supreme state of the self, the natural [state]. But whatever is perceived as other, even to the extent of a hair-tip, short of the state of being the self of all — 'I am not this' — that [perception] is conditioned by <s>avidyā</s>. The non-self states presented by that <s>avidyā</s> — the worlds that are non-supreme, ending with stationary beings, belonging to the domain of conventional usage — compared to those worlds, this state of being the self of all — complete, without interior, without exterior — is his supreme world.
Therefore, when <s>avidyā</s> is being diminished and <s>vidyā</s> has reached its culmination, the state of being the self of all is <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). Just as self-luminosity is directly perceived in dream — [as stated in] 'where they seem to kill him, seem to overpower him' — these are the products of <s>vidyā</s> and <s>avidyā</s>: the state of being the self of all, and the state of being a delimited self. Through pure <s>vidyā</s>, one becomes the self of all. Through <s>avidyā</s>, one becomes non-all — one becomes separated from something. That from which one becomes separated — by that one is opposed. Being opposed, one is killed, overpowered, and chased away. And this occurs when the object is non-all — because of separateness. But when one is complete — from whom would one be separated? By whom would one be opposed? In the absence of opposition, by whom would one be killed, overpowered, or chased away?
Therefore, this [demonstrates] the real existence of <s>avidyā</s>: it causes one who is the self of all to be apprehended as not the self of all; it presents as real another entity that is other than the self, [which entity is] non-existent; it makes the self non-all. From that, desire directed toward that [other entity] arises. From desire, one takes up action. From that, fruit [arises]. This has been stated [and] will be stated: 'Where there is duality, as it were, there one sees the other' (BṛUp 4.5.15) and so forth.
The real existence of <s>avidyā</s>, together with its effect, has been demonstrated. And the effect of <s>vidyā</s> — the state of being the self of all — has been demonstrated as the opposite of <s>avidyā</s>. And that <s>avidyā</s> is not an intrinsic property of the self — because, when <s>vidyā</s> is being elevated, [<s>avidyā</s>], being of itself diminished, [and] when <s>vidyā</s> has reached its culmination, when the state of being the self of all is fully established — [<s>avidyā</s>] ceases entirely, like the cognition of a snake on a rope when the determination of the rope [is established].

children.text:
tad vā asyaitad aticchando 'pahatapāpmābhayaṃ rūpam |
tad yathā priyayā striyā saṃpariṣvakto na bāhyaṃ kiṃ cana veda nāntaram |
evam evāyaṃ puruṣaḥ prājñenātmanā saṃpariṣvakto na bāhyaṃ kiṃ cana veda nāntaram |
tad vā asyaitad āptakāmam ātmakāmam akāmaṃ rūpam śokāntaram || BrhUp_4,3.21 ||
children.translated_text: That indeed is its form — beyond desire, free from evil, free from fear. Just as a man embraced by a beloved woman knows nothing external, nothing internal — even so, this <s>puruṣa</s>, embraced by the all-knowing self (<s>prājña ātman</s>), knows nothing external, nothing internal. That indeed is its form — in which all desires are fulfilled, in which the self alone is the desire, in which there is no desire — a form beyond sorrow. (BṛUp 4.3.21)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.21 idānīṃ yo 'sau sarvātmabhāvo mokṣo vidyāphalaṃ kriyākārakaphalaśūnyaṃ sa pratyakṣato nirdiśyate yatrāvidyākāmakarmāṇi na santi /
tadetadprastutaṃ yatra supto na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyātīti /
tadetadvā asya rūpaṃ yaḥ sarvātmabhāvaḥ 'so 'sya paramo lokaḥ'ityuktaḥ-tadaticchandā aticchandamityarthaḥ, rūpaparatvāt /
chandaḥ kāmaḥ, atigataścando yasmād rūpāt tadaticchandaṃ rūpam; anyo 'sau sāntaśchandaḥśabdo gāyatryādichandovācī; ayaṃ tu kāmavacanaḥ, ataḥ svarānta eva; tathāpyaticchandā iti pāṭhaḥ svādhyāyadharmo draṣṭavyaḥ /
asti ca loke kāmavacanaprayuttkaśchandaśabdaḥ 'svacchandaḥ' 'paracchandaḥ' ityādau; ataḥ 'aticchandam' ityevamupaneyam, kāmavarjitametad rūpamityasminnarthe /
tathāpahatapāpma-pāpmaṣabdena dharmādharmāvucyete,"pāpmabhiḥ saṃsṛjyate" "pāpmano vijahāti"ityuttkatvāt; apahatapāpma dharmādharmavarjitamityetat /
kiñca, abhayam-bhayaṃ hi nāmāvidyākāryam, 'avidyayā bhayaṃ manyate' iti hyuttkam /
tatkāryadvāreṇa kāraṇapratiṣedho 'yam; abhayaṃ rūpamityāvidyāvarjitamityetat /
tadetad vidyāphalaṃ sarvatmabhāvaḥ, tadetaditacchandāpahatapāpmābhayaṃ rūpam--sarvasaṃsāradharmavarjitam, ate 'bhayaṃ rūpametat /
idaṃ ca pūrvamevopanyasyamatītānantarabrahmaṇasamāptau "abhayaṃ vai janaka prāpto 'si"ityāgamataḥ /
iha tu tarkataḥ prapañcitaṃ darśitāgamārthapratyayadārḍhyāya /
ayamātmā svayaṃ caitanyajyotiḥ-svabhāvaḥ sarvaṃ svena caitanyajyotiṣāvabhāsayati /
sa yattatra kiñcit paśyati, ramate,carati,jānāti cetyuttkam /
sthitaṃ caitannyāyato nityaṃ svarūpaṃ caitanyajyotiṣṭvamātmanaḥ /
sa yadyātmātrāvinaṣṭaḥ svenaiva rūpeṇa vartate, kasmādayam-ahamasmītyātmānaṃ vā, bahirvā-imāni bhūtānīti, jāgratsvapnayoriva na jānāti? -ityatrocyate; śṛṇvātrājñānahetum-ekatvamevājñānahetuḥ; tat katham? ityucyate /
dṛṣṭāntena hi pratyakṣībhavati vivakṣitor'tha ityāha-tattatra yathā loke priyayeṣṭāyā striyā sampariṣvattakaḥ samyak pariṣvattkaḥ kāmayantyā kāmukaḥ san na bāhyamātmanaḥ kiñcana kiñcidapi veda-matto 'nyad vastviti, na cāntaram-ayamahamāsmi sukhī duḥkhī veti; apariṣvattkastu tathā pravibhattko jānāti sarvabheva brāhyam ābhyantaraṃ ca; pariṣvaṅgottarakālantvekatvāpatterna jānāti /
evameva, yathā dṛṣṭānto 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ kṣetrajño bhūtamātrāsaṃsargataḥ saindhavakhilyavat pravibhattkaḥ, jalādau candrādipratibimbavat kāryakaraṇa iha praviṣṭaḥ, so 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ, prajñena paramārthena svābhāvikena svenātmanā pareṇa jyotiṣā, sampariṣvattkaḥ samyakpariṣvakta ekībhūto nirantaraḥ sarvātmā, na bāhyaṃ kiñcana vastvantaram, nāpyāntaramātmani-ayamahamasmi sukhī duḥkhī veti veda /
tatra caitanyajyotiḥ svabhāvatve kasmādiha na jānātīti yadaprākṣīḥ, tatrāyaṃ heturmayottka ekatvam, yathā strīpuṃsayoḥ sampariṣvattkayoḥ /
tatrārthānnānātvaṃ viśeṣavijñānaheturityuttkaṃ bhavati; nānātve ca kāraṇ-ātmano vastavantarasya pratyupasthāpikāvidyetyuktam /
tatra cāvidyāyā yadā pravivikto bhavati tadā sarveṇaikatvamevāsya bhavati /
tataśca jñānajñeyādikārakavibhāge 'sati kuto viśeṣavijñānaprādurbhāvaḥ kāmo vā sambhavati svābhāvike svarūpstha ātmajyotiṣi /
yasmādevaṃ sarvaikatvamevāsya rūpamatastadvā asyā'tmanaḥ svayañjyotiḥ svabhavasyaitadrūpamāptakāmaṃ yasmātmastametattasmādāptāḥ kāmā asminrūpe tadidamāptakāmam /
sya hyanyatvena pravibhaktaḥ kāmastadanāptakāmaṃ bhavati /
yathā jāgaritāvasthāyāṃ devadattādirūpaṃ na tvidaṃ tathā kutaścitpravibhajyate 'tastadāptakāmaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: just as in the waking state, the form of <s>Devadatta</s> and the like — but this [form in deep sleep] is not differentiated from anything in any way — therefore it is <s>āptakāma</s> (one whose desires are fulfilled).

children.text: kimanyasmādvastvantarānna pravibhajyata āhosvidātmaiva tadvastvantaramata āha nānyadastyātmanaḥ /
children.translated_text: Is it that [this form] is not differentiated from some other object, or is the self itself that other object? — [the text] says: there is nothing other than the self.

children.text: katham /
children.translated_text: How so?

children.text: yata ātmakāmamātmaiva kāmā yasmin rūpe 'nyatra pravibhaktā ivānyatvena kāmyamānā yathā yathā jāgratsvapnayostasyā'tmaivānyatvapratyupasthāpakahetoravidyāyā abhāvādātmakāmamata evākāmametadrūpaṃ kāmyaviṣayābhāvācchokāntaraṃ śākacchidraṃ śokaśūnyamityetacchokamadhyamiti vā sarvathāpyaśokametadrūpaṃ śokavarjitamityarthaḥ //4,3.21//
children.translated_text: Because it is <s>ātmakāma</s> — the self alone is the object of desire in this form; [desires] that elsewhere [in waking and dream] appeared differentiated, as if other, being desired as other — as in waking and dream — [now,] because of the absence of <s>avidyā</s>, which is the cause of the presentation of otherness, [this form] is <s>ātmakāma</s>; and precisely for that reason it is <s>akāma</s> (desireless) — this form [is desireless] because of the absence of any object of desire. [It is also] <s>śokāntaram</s> — meaning: pierced through by the absence of grief, void of grief — this means 'in the midst of grief' — or in any case, this form is free from grief (<s>aśoka</s>), devoid of grief — this is the meaning. // 4.3.21 //

<s>BṛhUpBh</s> 4.3.21: Now, that universal selfhood (<s>sarvātmabhāva</s>) which is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), the fruit of knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), devoid of action, agent, and result — that is being directly pointed out, where <s>avidyā</s>, desire, and <s>karma</s> do not exist.
This is the topic under discussion: 'Where, asleep, he desires no desire, sees no dream.'
That indeed is his form — which is the state of universal selfhood — [of which it was] said: 'That is his supreme world' — that is <s>aticchandam</s> (beyond desire) — this is the meaning, because the word refers to [his] form.
<s>Chandas</s> means desire; the form from which desire has been transcended (<s>atigata</s>), that is <s>aticchandam</s>. There is another <s>chandas</s>-word with a final sibilant, denoting meters like <s>Gāyatrī</s> and the rest; but this one denotes desire, and therefore ends in a vowel. Even so, the reading '<s>aticchandā</s>' should be understood as a convention of the recitational tradition (<s>svādhyāyadharma</s>).
And in common usage, the word <s>chandas</s> is used in the sense of desire — as in '<s>svacchandaḥ</s>' (by one's own will) and '<s>paracchandaḥ</s>' (by another's will) and the like. Therefore it should be construed as '<s>aticchandam</s>' — meaning: this form is devoid of desire.
Likewise, <s>apahatapāpman</s> (one from whom evil has been removed) — by the word <s>pāpman</s>, both <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> are denoted, since it was said 'he is conjoined with <s>pāpmans</s>' and 'he leaves the <s>pāpmans</s> behind.' <s>Apahatapāpman</s> means: devoid of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — this is the meaning.
Moreover, <s>abhayam</s> (fearless) — for fear is indeed the product of <s>avidyā</s>, as it was stated: 'through <s>avidyā</s> one apprehends fear.'
This is the negation of the cause through [negation of] its effect; the form that is fearless means: devoid of <s>avidyā</s> — this is the meaning.
This is the fruit of knowledge — universal selfhood; this is that form which is beyond desire, free from evil, fearless — devoid of all attributes of <s>saṃsāra</s>, and therefore the form is fearless.
And this was previously introduced, at the conclusion of the preceding [section on] <s>Brahman</s>: 'You have attained fearlessness, O <s>Janaka</s>' — this from scripture.
But here it is elaborated through reasoning, for the purpose of strengthening conviction in the meaning shown by scripture.
This self is by nature the light of consciousness (<s>caitanyajyoti</s>) — it illuminates everything by its own consciousness-light.
That whatever it sees there, rejoices, moves about, and cognizes — this was stated.
And it is established by reasoning that the nature of consciousness-light is the eternal essential nature of the self.
But if the self exists here [in deep sleep] with its own form alone, undiminished, why does it not know itself — 'I am' — or [know] externally — 'these are the beings' — as in waking and dream? To this it is replied: listen here to the cause of non-cognition — oneness alone is the cause of non-cognition. How so? It is answered:
By means of an illustration the intended meaning becomes directly perceivable — therefore [the text] says: just as in the world, one who is fully embraced (<s>sampariṣvaktaka</s>) by a beloved, desired woman — being desirous, amorous — does not know anything external to himself — no other object whatsoever — nor anything internal — 'I am this, I am happy, I am suffering'; but when not embraced, being separate, he knows everything — both external and internal. After the embrace, however, because of the attainment of oneness, he does not know.
Just so — as in this illustration — this person, the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (knower of the field), being separate from the aggregate of elements, like a lump of salt, and having entered this [world] like the reflection of the moon and the like in water, [entering] into the effects and instruments — this person, being fully embraced, completely united, made one, without interval, with the supreme, essential, natural, cognizing self — the supreme light — [having become] the universal self — does not know anything external — no other object whatsoever — nor anything internal about [its own] self — 'I am this, I am happy, I am suffering.'
As to your question — 'given that its nature is the light of consciousness, why does it not know here [in deep sleep]?' — the reason stated by me is: oneness, just as in the case of the man and woman fully embraced.
Therein, the implication is that otherness, i.e., plurality, is the cause of specific cognition; and the cause of plurality — <s>avidyā</s>, which brings about the presentation of something other than the self — has been stated.
And when [the self] is separated from that <s>avidyā</s>, then there is only oneness with everything for it.
And when the division into factors such as knower, known, and the like does not exist, whence would specific cognition or desire arise in the natural, inherent self-light of the <s>ātman</s>?
Since its form is thus oneness with everything — therefore this form of the self, which is by nature self-luminous, is <s>āptakāma</s> (one whose desires are fulfilled), because desires have been attained in this form — this is <s>āptakāma</s>.
For when desire is differentiated as something other [than oneself], then there is unfulfilled desire (<s>anāptakāma</s>);

BrhUpBh_4,3.22 prakṛtaḥ svayañjyotirātmāvidyākāmakarmavinirmukta ityuktam /
asaṅgatvādātmana āgantukatvācca teṣām /
tatraivamāśaṅkā jāyate caitanyasvabhāvatve satyapyekībhāvānna jānāti strīpuṃsayoriva saṃpariṣvaktayorityuktam /
tatra prāsaṅgikametaduktaṃ kāmakramādivatsvayañjyotiṣṭvamapyasyā'tmano na svabhāvaḥ /
yasmātsaṃprasāde nopalabhyata ityāśaṅkāyāṃ prāptāyāṃ tannirākaraṇāya strīpuṃsayordṛṣṭāntopādānena vidyamānasyaiva svayañjyotiṣṭvasya suṣupte 'grahaṇamekībhāvāddhetorna tu kāmakarmādivadāgantukam /
ityetatprāsaṅgikamabhidhāya yatprakṛtaṃ tadevānupravartayati /
atra caitatprakṛtamavidyākāmakarmavinirmuktameva tadrūpaṃ yatsuṣupta ātmano gṛhyate pratyakṣata iti /
tadetadyathābhūtamevābhihitaṃ sarvasaṃbandhātītametadrūpamiti yasmādatraitasminsuṣuptasthāne 'tichchandāpahatapāpmābhayametadrūpaṃ tasmādatra pitā janakaḥ /
tasya ca janayitṛtvādyatpitṛtvaṃ putraṃ prati tatkarmanimittaṃ tena ca karmaṇāyamasaṃbaddho 'sminkāle tasmātpitāputrasaṃbandhanimittāt karmaṇo vinirmuktatvātpitāpyapitā bhavati /
tathā putro 'pi pituraputrobhavatīti sāmarthyādgamyate /
ubhayorhi saṃbandhanimittaṃ karma tamayatikrānto vartate /
apahatapāpmeti hyuktam /
tathāmātāmātālokāḥ karmaṇā jetavyā jitāśca tatkarmasaṃbandhābhāvāllokā alokāḥ /
tathā devāḥ karmāṅgabhūtāstatkarmasaṃbandhātyayāddevā adevāḥ /
tathā vedāḥ sādhyasādhanasaṃbandhābhidhāyakā mantralakṣaṇāścābhidhākatvena karmāṅgabhūtā adhītā adhyetavyāśca karmanimittameva saṃbadhyante puruṣeṇa tatkarmātikramaṇādetasminkāle vedā apyavedāḥ saṃpadyante /
na kevalaṃ śubhakarmasaṃbandhātītaḥ kiṃ tarhyaśubhairapyatyantaghoraiḥ karmabhirasaṃbaddha evāyaṃ vartata ityatamarthāmāha-atra steno brāhmaṇasuvarṇahartā bhrūṇaghnā saha pāṭhādavagamyate /
sa tena ghoroṇa karmaṇaitasminkāle vinirmukto bhavati /
yenāyaṃ karmaṇā mahāpātakī stena ucyate /
tathā bhrūṇahābhrūṇahā tathā cāṇḍālo na kevalaṃ pratyutpannenaiva karmaṇā vinirmuktaḥ /
kiṃ tarhi sahajenāpyatyantanikṛṣṭajātiprāpakeṇāpi vinirmukta evāyam /
cāṇḍālo nāma śūdreṇa brāhmaṇyāmutpannaścaṇḍāla eva cāṇḍālaḥ /
sa jātinimittena karmaṇāsaṃbaddhatvādacāṇḍālo bhavati /
paulkasaḥ pulkasa eva paulkasaḥ śūdreṇaiva kṣatriyāyāmutpannaḥ /
so 'pyapulkaso bhavati /
tathā'śramalakṣaṇaiśca karmabhirasaṃbagaddho bhavatītyucyate /
śramaṇaḥ parivrāḍyatkarmanimitto bhavati sa tena vinirmuktatvādaśramaṇaḥ /
tathā pāpaso vānaprastho 'tāpasaḥ sarveṣāṃ varṇāśramādīnāmupalakṣaṇārthamubhayorgrahaṇam /
kiṃ bahunānvāgataṃ nānvāgatamananvāgatamasaṃbandhamityetatpuṇyena śāstravihitena karmaṇā tathā pāpena vihitākaraṇapratiṣiddhakriyālakṣaṇena /
rūpaparatvānnapuṃsakaliṅgam /
abhayaṃ rūpiti hyanuvartate /
kiṃ punarasaṃbaddhatve kāraṇamiti taddheturucyate-tīrṇo 'tikrānto hi yasmādevaṃrūpastadā tasminkāle sarvāñchokāñśokāḥ kāmāḥ /
iṣṭaviṣayaprārthanā hi tadviṣayaviyoge śokatvamāpadyate /
iṣṭaṃ hi viṣayaṃmaprāptaṃ viyuktaṃ coddiśya cintayānastadguṇānsaṃtapyate puruṣo 'taḥ śoko ratiḥ kāma iti paryāyāḥ /
yasmātsaravakāmātīto hyatrāyaṃ bhavati /
na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate 'ticchandā iti hyuktaṃ tatprakriyāpatato 'yaṃ śokaśahdaḥ kāmavacana eva bhavitumarhati /
kāmaśca karmahetuḥ /
vakṣyati hi-"sa yathākāmo bhavati tatkrayurbhavati yatkraturbhavati tatkarma kurute"iti /
ataḥ sarvakāmātitīrṇatvādyuktamānanvāgataṃ puṇyenetyādi /
hṛdayasya hṛdayamiti puṇḍarīkākāro māṃsapiṇḍastatsthamantaḥkaraṇaṃ buddharhṛdayamityucyate /
tātsthānmañcakrośanavat /
hṛdayasya buddherye śokāḥ buddhisaṃśrayā hi te /
'kāmaḥ saṃkalpo vicikitsetyādi sarvaṃ mana eva'tyuktatvāt /
vakṣyati ca -"kāmā ye 'sya hṛdi śritāḥ"iti /
ātmasaṃśrayabhrāntyapanodāya hīdaṃ vacanaṃ-hṛdi śritā hṛdayasya śokā iti ca /
hṛdayakaraṇasaṃbandhātītaścāyamasminkāle 'tikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇīti hyuktam /
hṛdayakaraṇasahandhātītatvāttatsaṃśrayakāmasaṃbandhātīto bhavatīti yuktataraṃ vacanam /
ye tu vādino hṛdi śritāḥ kāmā vāsanāśca hṛdayasaṃbandhinamātmanamupasṛpyopaśliṣyanti hṛdayaviyoge 'pi cā'tmanyavatiṣṭhante puṭatailasya iva puṣpādigandha ityācakṣate /
teṣāṃ kāmaḥ saṃkalpo hṛdaye haryova rūpāṇi hṛdayasya śokā ityādīnāṃ vacanānāmānarthakyameva /
hṛdayakaraṇotpādyatvāditi cet /
na /
hṛdi śritā iti viśeṣaṇāt /
na hi hṛdayasya karaṇamātratve hṛdi śritā iti vacanaṃ samañjasaṃ hṛdaye hyeva rūpāṇi pratiṣṭhitānīti ca /
ātmaviśaddeśca vivakṣitatvāddhṛcchrayaṇavacanaṃ yathārthameva yuktam /
dhyāyatīva lelāyatīveti ca śrureranyārthāsaṃbhavāt /
kāmā ye 'sya hṛdi śritā iti viśeṣaṇādātmāśrayā api santīti cet /
na /
anāśritāpekṣatvāt nātrā'śrayāntaramapekṣya ye hṛdīti viśeṣaṇaṃ kiṃ tarhi ye hṛdyanāśritāḥ kāmāstānapekṣya viśeṣaṇam /
ye tvaprarūñā bhaviṣyā bhūtāśca pratipakṣato nivṛttāste naiva hṛdi śritāḥ saṃbhāvyante ca te /
ato yuktaṃ tānapekṣya viśeṣaṇam /
ye prarūḍhā vartamānā viṣaye te sarve pramucyanta iti /
tathāpi viśeṣaṇānarthakyamiti cet /
na /
teṣu yatanmādhikyāddheyārthatvāt /
itarathāśrutamaniṣṭaṃ cakalpitaṃ syādātmāśrayatvaṃ kāmānām /
na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayata iti prāptapratiṣedhādātmāśrayatvaṃ kāmānāṃ śrutameveti cet /
na /
sadhīḥ svapno bhūtveti paranimittatvātkāmāśrayatvaprāpterasaṅgavacanācca /
na hi kāmāśrayatve 'saṅgavacanamupapadyate /
saṅgaśca kāma ityavocāma /
ātmakāma iti śruterātmaviṣayo 'sya kāmo bhavatīti cet /
na vyatiriktakāmābhāvārthatvāttasyāḥ /
vaiśeṣikāditantranyāyopapannamātmanaḥ kāmādyāśrayatvamiti cet /
na hṛdi śritā ityādiviśeṣaśrutivirodhānapekṣyāstā veśeṣikāditantropapattayaḥ /
śrutivirodhe nyāyabhāsatvopagamāt /
svayañjyotiṣṭvabādhanācca /
kāmādīnāṃ ca svapne kevaladṛśimātraviṣayatvātsvayañjyotiṣṭvaṃ siddhaṃ sthitaṃ ca bādhyeta /
ātmasamavāyitve dṛśyatvānupapatteścakṣurgataviśeṣavat /
draṣṭurhi dṛśyamarthāntarabhūtamiti draṣṭuḥ svayañjyotiṣṭvaṃ siddham /
tadbādhitaṃ syādyadi kāmādyāśrayatvaṃ parikalpyet /
sarvaśāstrārtha vipratiṣedhācca /
parasyaikadeśakalpanāyāṃ kāmādyāśrayatve ca sarvaśāstrārthajātaṃ kupyeta /
children.translated_text: If [one imagines] a part of the supreme [Brahman], and if [one posits] the Self as the locus of desire and the rest, the entire body of scriptural teaching would be overturned.

children.text: etacca vistareṇa caturthe 'vocāma /
children.translated_text: This we have discussed at length in the fourth [chapter of the <s>Brahmasūtrabhāṣya</s>].

children.text: mahatā hi prayatnena kāmādyāśrayatvakalapnājha pratiṣeddhavyā ātmānaḥ pareṇaikatvaśāstrārthasiddhayeḥ tatkalpanāyāṃ punaḥ kriyamāṇāyāṃ śāstrārthaṃ eva bādhitaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: For the imagined attribution of desire and the rest to the Self must be refuted with great effort by the supreme [teaching of] oneness — for the attainment of the scriptural purpose. If that attribution were to be made again, the very purport of scripture would be undermined.

children.text: yatheccādhīnāmātmadharmatvaṃ kalpayanto vaiśeṣikā naiyāyikāścopaniṣacchāstrārthabādhanānnā'daraṇīyā //4,3.22//
children.translated_text: Just as the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> and <s>Naiyāyikas</s>, who imagine that properties such as desire (<s>icchā</s>) belong to the Self, are not to be heeded because they contradict the purport of <s>Upaniṣadic</s> scripture. // 4.3.22 //

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.22:] The self-luminous Self under discussion has been stated to be free from <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>kāma</s> (desire), and <s>karma</s> (action) — because of the Self's unattachedness and because those [avidyā, kāma, karma] are adventitious. Therein, the following doubt arises: although the nature of consciousness is [established], 'because of becoming one, he does not know' — as was stated with the simile of the man and woman in embrace. There, this was stated incidentally — like self-luminosity — that [the objector claims] the self-luminosity of this Self too is not its intrinsic nature, [analogous to] the sequence of desires and the like, because it is not apprehended in deep sleep. When this doubt has arisen, in order to refute it, [Śaṅkara says:] by adducing the illustration of the man and woman, [one shows that] the self-luminosity that does exist is simply not grasped in deep sleep because of [the Self's] having become one — not that it is adventitious like desire, <s>karma</s>, and the rest. Having thus stated this incidental point, he continues with the subject under discussion. And here, the subject under discussion is this: the very form that is free from <s>avidyā</s>, desire, and <s>karma</s> — that form is what is grasped directly as the Self in deep sleep. This has been stated just as it truly is: 'This form transcends all relations.' Because here, in this state of deep sleep — 'transcending desires, having destroyed evil, free from fear' — this is that form. Therefore, here [in deep sleep], the father who begets — his fatherhood with respect to the son is caused by <s>karma</s>, and with that <s>karma</s> this [Self] is unconnected at this time. Therefore, being freed from the <s>karma</s> that is the cause of the father-son relationship, the father becomes a non-father. Likewise, the son too becomes a non-son in relation to the father — this is understood by implication. For the <s>karma</s> that is the cause of the relationship between both has been transcended by [the Self] at this time. For it was said: 'having destroyed evil.' Similarly, the mother becomes a non-mother. The worlds, [which are] to be won and [already] won by <s>karma</s> — because of the absence of connection with that <s>karma</s>, the worlds become non-worlds. Similarly, the gods, who form parts of ritual action — because of the transcendence of connection with that <s>karma</s>, the gods become non-gods. Similarly, the <s>Vedas</s> — which declare the relation of end and means, and which as <s>mantras</s> form parts of ritual action by virtue of being expressive [of ritual meanings], [which are] studied and to be studied — are connected with the person only through <s>karma</s>. Because of the transcendence of that <s>karma</s> at this time, even the <s>Vedas</s> become non-<s>Vedas</s>. Not only is [the Self] beyond connection with auspicious <s>karma</s> — but even with inauspicious, extremely terrible actions this [Self] is utterly unconnected — to convey this meaning [the text] says: 'a thief.' From the reading together with '<s>brāhmaṇa</s>-gold-stealer' and 'embryo-slayer,' it is understood [that these are illustrations]. He is freed from that terrible <s>karma</s> at this time — the <s>karma</s> on account of which this great sinner is called a thief. Similarly, the embryo-slayer becomes a non-embryo-slayer. Similarly, the <s>caṇḍāla</s> — not only is [the Self] freed from <s>karma</s> that is actually being performed, but even from <s>karma</s> that is innate, that leads to extremely low birth, this [Self] is indeed freed. A <s>caṇḍāla</s> is one born of a <s>Śūdra</s> [father] and a <s>Brāhmaṇī</s> [mother] — that is what <s>caṇḍāla</s> means. Because of being unconnected with the <s>karma</s> caused by birth, he becomes a non-<s>caṇḍāla</s>. The <s>paulkasa</s> — a <s>pulkasa</s> indeed is a <s>paulkasa</s>, one born of a <s>Śūdra</s> [father] and a <s>Kṣatriyā</s> [mother]. He too becomes a non-<s>pulkasa</s>. Similarly, it is stated that [the Self] is unconnected with actions characterized by stages of life (<s>āśrama</s>). The <s>śramaṇa</s>, the <s>parivrāj</s> (wandering renunciant) — the <s>karma</s> on account of which that [identity] exists — because of being freed from that, [he becomes] a non-<s>śramaṇa</s>. Similarly, the ascetic (<s>tāpasa</s>), the forest-dweller (<s>vānaprastha</s>), becomes a non-ascetic. The mention of both [types — social and religious] is for the purpose of illustrating all classes, stages of life, and the like. In short: 'not followed' — not followed, meaning unconnected — by merit, [consisting of] action prescribed by scripture, or by sin, characterized by non-performance of what is prescribed and performance of what is prohibited. The neuter gender is because of referring to the form — for 'the form that is free from fear' is what continues [from the prior passage]. What, then, is the reason for [the Self's] non-connection? The reason for that is stated: 'for he has crossed over' — for he has transcended. Because [the Self] is of such a nature at that time, it has crossed over all sorrows — [meaning] desires. For the craving for a desired object, when there is separation from that object, takes the form of sorrow. For a person, longing for a desired object that has not been obtained or from which he is separated, broods over its qualities and suffers — therefore sorrow, attachment, and desire are synonyms. Because here [in deep sleep] this [Self] has transcended all desires. It does not desire any desire — for it was said: 'transcending desires.' Following from that context, this word 'sorrow' must mean desire itself. And desire is the cause of <s>karma</s>. For [the text] will say: 'As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the <s>karma</s> he performs' (BṛUp 4.4.5). Therefore, because [the Self] has crossed beyond all desires, it is proper [to say] 'not followed by merit' and the rest. '<s>Hṛdayasya hṛdayam</s>' (the heart of the heart) — the lotus-shaped lump of flesh, and the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) residing in it, the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), is called '<s>hṛdaya</s>' (heart) — [named] by locative relation, like 'the platform's cry.' The sorrows that belong to the heart — to the intellect — for they reside in the intellect. 'Desire, resolve, doubt — all this is mind alone' — thus it was stated. And [the text] will say: 'the desires that are lodged in the heart' (BṛUp 4.4.7). The statement 'lodged in the heart' and 'sorrows of the heart' is for the purpose of removing the misconception that they belong to the Self. And at this time, this [Self] has transcended the connection with the heart-instrument — for it was said: 'he crosses over the forms of death.' Because of having transcended connection with the heart-instrument, [the Self] transcends connection with the desires that reside in it — this is the more fitting statement. But those disputants who say that desires and <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) lodged in the heart approach and cling to the Self which is connected to the heart, and even upon separation from the heart persist in the Self like the scent of flowers in sesame oil — for them, the statements 'desire, resolve [are in the heart],' 'forms [are established] in the heart,' 'sorrows of the heart' and the like become entirely purposeless. [Objection:] Because they are produced by the heart as instrument? [Reply:] No — because of the qualifier 'lodged in the heart.' For if the heart were merely an instrument, the statement 'lodged in the heart' would not be coherent — [nor would] 'forms are indeed established in the heart.' And because [the text] intends to declare [something] about the Self specifically, the statement about residing in the heart is justified as literal. Also from the <s>śruti</s> 'it meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were' (BṛUp 4.3.7) — since no other meaning is possible. [Objection:] But from the qualifier 'desires that are lodged in his heart,' [one infers that] there also exist [desires] that belong to the Self? [Reply:] No — because that [qualifier] has reference to [desires that are] not lodged [in the heart]. The qualifier 'those that are in the heart' is not made with reference to some other locus of residence; rather, with reference to desires that are not lodged in the heart, the qualifier [is given]. Those desires that are unmanifest — future and past — and those that have been eliminated through their antidote — they are certainly not lodged in the heart, yet they can be conceived of. Therefore, the qualifier is appropriate with reference to them. Those that have sprouted and are presently [directed] toward objects — all those are released — thus [the text says]. [Objection:] Even so, the qualifier is purposeless? [Reply:] No — because its purpose is to indicate what is to be avoided, given the preponderance of effort [needed] regarding those [present desires]. Otherwise, what is unheard and undesired would have to be imagined — namely, that desires belong to the Self. [Objection:] 'He does not desire any desire' — from the negation of what has been obtained, the belonging of desires to the Self is indeed heard [in śruti]? [Reply:] No — because [the statement] 'having become [one with] the intellect, having become dream' indicates that [desires] have an extraneous cause. And from the statement of non-attachment [of the Self]. For if desires belonged to the Self, the statement of non-attachment would be untenable. And we have stated that attachment is desire. [Objection:] From the <s>śruti</s> '<s>ātmakāma</s>' (self-desiring), the Self has desire as its object? [Reply:] No — because the meaning of that [śruti] is the absence of any desire other [than the Self]. [Objection:] The Self's being the locus of desire and the rest is established by the reasoning of <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> and other systems? [Reply:] No — those reasonings of <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> and other systems are not to be regarded, because they contradict the specific <s>śruti</s> statements such as 'lodged in the heart.' For when there is contradiction with <s>śruti</s>, reasoning is accepted as merely pseudo-reasoning. And because [such a position] would undermine <s>svayaṃjyotiṣṭva</s> (self-luminosity). For in dream, desires and the rest are merely the objects of pure seeing alone — and self-luminosity is [thereby] established and confirmed. That would be undermined [if desires belonged to the Self]. For if [they were] inherent in the Self, seeing [them] would be untenable — like the specific features residing in the eye [cannot be seen by the eye itself]. For what is seen by the seer is something other [than the seer] — thus the seer's self-luminosity is established. That would be undermined if the Self were imagined to be the locus of desire and the rest. And because it would contradict the entire purport of all scriptures.

yad vai tan na paśyati paśyan vai tan na paśyati |

children.translated_text: Though not seeing, he is [yet] a seer; for there is no cessation of the seeing of the seer, because [the seer] is imperishable. But there is no second thing other than him, separate [from him], that he might see. // BṛUp 4.3.23 //

children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Because of their absence, there is no seeing of particulars.

children.text: karaṇādikṛtaṃ hi tannā'tmakṛtam /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] For that [seeing of particulars] is caused by the instruments — not by the self.

children.text: ātmakṛtamiva pratyavabhāsate /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] But it appears as if caused by the self.

children.text: tasmāttakṛteyaṃ bhrāntirātmano dṛṣṭiḥ parilupyataca iti //4,3.23//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Therefore, this delusion — that the self's seeing is destroyed — is itself caused [by the instruments]. (4.3.23)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.23:] 'Because of the oneness of the [embraced] couple, he does not see' — thus it was stated. And 'he is self-luminous' — this was also stated. Now, self-luminosity means the nature of having consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) as one's essential nature. If, like the heat of fire, the self's essential nature is consciousness, then how, even in oneness, could it abandon its own nature and not know? On the other hand, if it does not abandon [its nature], how does it not see here, in deep sleep? This seems contradictory — that consciousness is the self's nature and yet it does not know! [Reply:] There is no contradiction — both [statements] are indeed justified. How? That which, in deep sleep, it does not see — seeing indeed, it does not see there; it is seeing, and yet does not see. What you understand as 'it does not see in deep sleep' — do not take it in that way. Why? Because it is indeed seeing there. [Objection:] But we know that it does not see in deep sleep, because neither the eye nor the mind — the instruments of seeing — are active. For the conventional usage 'he sees' or 'he hears' occurs when the [activities of] seeing, hearing, and the like are active. And we do not observe the instruments as active [in deep sleep]. Therefore, this [self] simply does not see. [Reply:] This is not so. What then? It is indeed seeing. How? Because there is no destruction (<s>viparilopa</s>) of the seeing of the seer — of the one who performs the act of seeing. That destruction does not exist. For it [seeing] is like the heat of fire [to the self]. [Objection:] But this is contradictory — it is said that the seeing of the seer is not destroyed, and yet it cannot be said [that it sees]! [Objection:] And from the statement 'it is not destroyed,' [seeing] would be indestructible! [Reply:] No — because the statement serves merely to make known [what is the case]. For a destruction that follows from logical reasoning — of something that is produced — cannot be prevented even by a hundred statements. Because a statement [merely] makes known what is already the case. [Reply:] This is no fault — because seeing is justified in the manner of the illuminating [nature] of the sun and the like. Just as the sun and the like, being of an eternally luminous nature, illuminate by their inherent, eternal light — for they are not said to 'illuminate' as if they, being non-luminous, [first] produce luminosity — but rather [they illuminate] by their very nature, by their eternal light. Similarly, this self too is called 'seer' by its eternal, undiminished seeing. [Objection:] Then 'seer-hood' would be figurative! [Reply:] Not so — because the primary sense is justified. For if seeing of the self had been observed in some other manner [as well], then this seer-hood would be figurative. But since no other mode of seeing exists for the self, this very seer-hood is justified as primary, not otherwise — just as the illuminating nature of the sun and the like, [operating] by their inherent, non-active, eternal light, is primary, because no other mode of illumination is possible. Therefore, the seeing of the seer is not destroyed — there is not even a trace of contradiction. [Objection:] But the word [<s>draṣṭṛ</s>] ending in the <s>tṛc</s> suffix is observed to be used only with reference to the agent of a non-eternal action — as in 'cutter,' 'breaker,' 'goer' — and so too with 'seer'! [Reply:] No — because 'illuminator' [<s>prakāśayitṛ</s>] is observed [in the same form]. [Objection:] Let that be [the case] for illuminators, but not for the self, because it is impossible otherwise! [Reply:] No — because of the <s>śruti</s> that seeing is not destroyed. [Objection:] From the experience 'I see' and 'I do not see,' [it is clear that seeing is sometimes present and sometimes absent]! [Reply:] No — because [the expressions 'I see' and 'I do not see'] depend on the specific activity of the instruments [i.e. sense-organs]. And because, for those whose eyes have been removed, the non-destruction of the self's seeing is observed in dream. Therefore, the seeing of the self has indeed an undiminished nature. By that undiminished seeing — which has the nature of self-luminosity — it is indeed seeing even in deep sleep. Then why does it not see? It is said: 'But there is nothing second' — what is that? — '[nothing] second, as an object.' What remains? Nothing separate from the seer, divided as an 'other,' that it could see, that it could apprehend. For that which was the cause of particular seeing — the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), the eye, and form — that had been falsely presented as 'other' through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). But at this time [of deep sleep], it has become unified — because of the embrace with the supreme self. For the delimited seer, in order to see particular [objects], requires the instrument standing as an 'other.' But this [self] is embraced by its own self, by the supreme, all-knowing (<s>prājña</s>) self — by its own totality — like a man [embraced] by his beloved. Therefore, the instruments and objects do not stand as separate.

children.translated_text: When it does not smell — it is verily smelling, but it does not smell. For there is no destruction of the smelling of the smeller, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing, other than it and separate from it, that it could smell. (BṛUp 4.3.24)

children.text: etena dṛgādiśaktibhedānāṃ pṛthakcakṣurūpādibhedena pariṇāmabhedakalpanā paramātmani prayuktā //4,3.24-30 //
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] By this, the imagination of distinct transformations — corresponding to the distinct faculties of seeing and the like, and distinct [objects such as] form and the like of the eye and the rest — applied to the supreme self, is refuted. (4.3.24–30)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.24–30:] The rest is the same. 'When it does not smell'; 'when it does not taste'; 'when it does not speak'; 'when it does not hear'; 'when it does not think'; 'when it does not touch'; 'when it does not know' — thinking and knowing, even though they can operate with the cooperation of seeing and the like, also have activities pertaining to past, future, and present objects independently of the eye and the like — hence they are mentioned separately. Now, are the different faculties of seeing and the like distinct properties of the self — like the heat, luminosity, and burning [of fire] — or are they [merely] the appearance of different properties of a single [property], caused by the diversity of external limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>)? Regarding this, some explain: The self-substance has both oneness and manifoldness intrinsically — just as a cow-substance [has] both oneness and manifoldness, which are to be inferred. Since non-deviation is observed everywhere, the self too, like that, has manifoldness among seeing and the like [as distinct faculties], and oneness with the self. [Reply:] This is not [the correct view] — because [the passage] has a different purpose. This passage — 'when it does not...' and so forth — does not have as its purpose the demonstration of distinct properties like seeing and the like. What then [is its purpose]? When the suspicion has arisen — 'If the self-light is consciousness, how does it not know in deep sleep? Surely then it is not consciousness-light' — for the removal of that suspicion, this passage was commenced. That which, in waking and dream, is the consciousness-light — the self's inherent nature — observed through the many doorways of the limiting adjuncts of the eye and the like, [and which] has come to be conventionally designated by names such as 'seeing' and the like — in deep sleep, when the activities of the differentiated limiting adjuncts have ceased, though its nature is unmanifested, unperceived — yet as if differentiated by the difference of limiting adjuncts, [its existence] is stated by way of restating what is already the case. The intended meaning is not the imagination of distinct properties such as seeing and the like — because of unfamiliarity with the intended meaning. And because of the contradiction with the <s>śruti</s> that [the self] is a mass of pure consciousness (<s>prajñānaghana</s>), of one taste, like a lump of salt. And from <s>śrutis</s> such as: '<s>vijñānam ānandam</s>' ('consciousness is bliss'); '<s>satyaṃ jñānam</s>' ('truth is knowledge'); '<s>prajñānaṃ brahma</s>' ('consciousness is <s>Brahman</s>'), and the like. And from the usage of words — for the worldly usage is: 'He knows form by the eye; he knows sound by the ear; he knows the taste of food by the tongue' — and everywhere it shows that what is denoted by the words 'seeing' and the like is nothing but what is denoted by the word '<s>vijñāna</s>' (knowing). And word-usage is a means of valid knowledge. And because of the appropriateness of the illustration: just as in the world, a crystal, having an inherently clear nature, merely on account of association with diverse limiting adjuncts such as green, blue, red, and the like, takes on [the appearance of] those forms — so too, the self-light, whose nature is a mass of consciousness (<s>prajñānaghana</s>), on account of association with diverse limiting adjuncts such as the eye and the like, has the appearance of diverse faculties of seeing and the like. Because of the mass-of-consciousness nature and the inherent clarity — like the inherent clarity of a crystal — [the self has] self-luminosity. Just as the light of the sun, being associated with diverse illuminated objects — green, blue, yellow, red, and the like — while remaining indivisible, becomes of their form — so too, illuminating the entire world and the eye and the like, [the self-light] takes on their form. And thus it was said: 'This person exists by the light of the self alone' and so forth. And multiplicity of nature cannot be imagined in something that has no parts — because of the absence of an example. As for the claim that space possesses diverse properties such as all-pervasiveness and the like, and that atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) have multiple qualities such as smell, taste, and the like — when examined, this too is caused by external limiting adjuncts alone. For space — its so-called all-pervasiveness is not an intrinsic property. For the conventional usage 'all-pervading' is made only with reference to its existing in its own form in all limiting adjuncts — but space does not itself go anywhere or come from anywhere. For 'going' means the production of contact with a different location by something situated in one location — and such action is simply impossible in something that is without distinctions. Similarly, there are no distinct properties in space. And likewise for atoms and the like — an atom is the smallest particle of earth, which is a mass of smell, and has the nature of smell alone; it is impossible to imagine it as having smell additionally [on top of other qualities].

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.31
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.31]

children.text: yatra vā anyad iva syāt tatrānyo 'nyat paśyed anyo 'nyaj jighred anyo 'nyad rasayed anyo 'nyad vaded anyo 'nyac chṛṇuyād anyo 'nyan manvītānyo 'nyat spṛśed anyo 'nyad vijānīyāt || BrhUp_4,3.31 ||
children.translated_text: Where there were, as it were, another — there one would see the other; one would smell the other; one would taste the other; one would speak to the other; one would hear the other; one would think of the other; one would touch the other; one would know the other. (BṛUp 4.3.31)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.31 jāgratsvapnayoriva yadvijānīyāttaddvitīyaṃ pravibhaktamanyatvena nāstītyuktamataḥ suṣupte na vijānāti viśeṣamṣa nanu yadyasyāyameva svabhāvaḥ kiṃnimittamasya viśeṣavijñānaṃ svabhāvaparityāgena /
atha viśeṣavijñānamevāsya svabhāvaḥ kasmādeṣa viśeṣaṃ na vijānātīti /
ucyate śṛṇu /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] It is replied — listen!

children.text: yatra yasmiḍhjāgarite svapne vā anyadivā'tmano vastvantaramivāvidyayā pratyupasthāpitaṃ bhavati tatra tasmādavidyāpratyupasthāpitādanyo 'nyamivā'tmānaṃ manyamāno 'satyātmanaḥ pravibhakte vastvantare 'sati cātmani tataḥ pravibhakte 'nyo 'nyatpaśyedupalabheta /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Where, in whichever state — waking or dream — something other, as it were, than the self, some second object as it were, is presented through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), there, considering oneself as if other than that object falsely presented by <s>avidyā</s>, when there is a second object differentiated from the self and when there is [as it were] a differentiated self, then one, as if other, would see, would perceive the other.

children.text: tacca darśitaṃ svapne pratyakṣato ghnantīva jinantīveti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] And this has been shown directly in dream — 'as if they kill, as if they conquer,' and so on.

children.text: tathānyo 'nyajjighredrasayedvadecchṛṇuyānmanvāti spṛśedvijānīyāditi //4,3.31//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Likewise, one as if other would smell another thing, would taste, would speak, would hear, would think, would touch, would know. (4.3.31)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.31:] It has been stated that what one would perceive as in waking and dream — that second thing, differentiated as other — does not exist; therefore in deep sleep one does not perceive any distinction. Now, if this is indeed its own nature, what is the cause of its perceiving distinctions, abandoning its own nature? Or, if the perception of distinctions is indeed its own nature, why does it not perceive distinctions [in deep sleep]?

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.32
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.32]

children.text:
salila eko draṣṭādvaito bhavati |
eṣa brahmalokaḥ samrāṭ |
iti hainam anuśaśāsa yājñavalkyaḥ |
eṣāsya paramā gatiḥ |
eṣāsya paramā saṃpat |
eṣo 'sya paramo lokaḥ |
eṣo 'sya parama ānandaḥ |
etasyaivānandasyānyāni bhūtāni mātrām upajīvanti || BrhUp_4,3.32 ||
children.translated_text: Like water, he becomes a single seer, without a second. This is the <s>Brahmaloka</s> (world of <s>Brahman</s>), O Emperor — thus did <s>Yājñavalkya</s> instruct him. This is his highest goal; this is his highest treasure; this is his highest world; this is his supreme bliss. On a fraction of this very bliss, other beings live. (BṛUp 4.3.32)

children.text:
BrhUpBh_4,3.32 yatra punaḥ sāvidyā suṣupte vastvantarapratyupasthāpikā śāntā tenānyatvenāvidyāpravibhaktasya vastuno 'bhāvātkena kaṃ paśyejjighredvijānīyādvā /
ataḥ svenaiva hi prājñena''tmanā svayañjyotiḥsvabhāvena saṃpariṣvaktaḥsamastaḥ saṃprasanna āptakāma ātmakāmaḥ salilavastvacchībhūtaḥ salila iva eko dvitīyasyābhāvāt /
avidyāyā hi dvitīyasyābhāvāt /
etadamṛtamabhayameṣa bhmaloko brahmaiva loko brahmalokaḥ para evāyamasminkāle vyāvṛttakāryakaraṇopādhibhedaḥ svātmajyotiṣi śāntasarvasaṃbandho vartate /
he samrāḍiti haivaṃ hainaṃ janakamanuśaśāsānuṣṭavānyājñavalkya iti śrutivacanametat /
kathaṃ vānuśaśāsa /
eṣāsya vijñānamayasya paramā gatiḥ /
yāstvanyā dehagrahalakṣaṇā brahmādistambaparyantā avidyākalpitāstā gatayo 'to 'paramā avidyāviṣayatvāt /
iyaṃ tu devatvādigatīnāṃ karmavidyāsādhyānāṃ paramottamā yaḥ samastātmabhāvo yatra nānyatpaśyati nānyacchṛṇoti nānyadvijānātītyeṣaiva ca paramā saṃpatsarvāsāṃ saṃpadāṃ vibhūtīnāmiyaṃ paramā svābhāvikatvādasyāḥ kṛtakā hyanyāḥ saṃpadaḥ /
tathaiṣo 'sya paramo lokaḥ /
ye 'nye karmaphalāśrayā lokāste 'smādaparamāḥ /
ayaṃ tu na kenacana karmaṇā mīyate svābhāvikatvādeṣo.sya paramo lokaḥ /
tathaiṣo 'syaparama ānandaḥ /
yānyanyāni viṣayendriyasaṃbandhajanitānyānandajātāni tānyapekṣyaiṣo 'sya parama ānando nityatvāt /
"yo vai bhūmā tatsukham" iti śrutyantarāt /
yatrānyatpaśyanyadvijānāti tānyapekṣyaiṣo 'sya parama ānandonityatvāt /
"yo vai bhūmā tatsukham"iti śrutyantarāt /
yatrānyatpaśyadvijānāti tadalpaṃ martyamamukhyaṃ kṣukhamidaṃ tu tadviparītam /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] Where one sees another, knows another — that is small, mortal, not primary. But this [state of deep sleep as pure consciousness] is the opposite of that.

children.text: eta eṣo 'sya parama ānandaḥ /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] This is his supreme bliss.

children.text: etasyaivai''nandasya mātrāṃ kalāmavidyāpratyupasthāpitāṃ viṣayendriyasaṃbandhakālavibhāvyāmanyāni bhūtānyupajīvanti /
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] A fraction, a portion, of this very bliss — presented through <s>avidyā</s>, made manifest through the connection of sense organs and objects in time — is what other beings live upon.

children.text: kāni tāni tata evā'nandādavidyathāpravibhajyamānasvarūpāṇyanyatvena tāni brahmaṇaḥ parikalpyamānānyanyāni santyupajīvanti bhūtāni viṣayendriyasaṃparkadvāreṇa vibhāvyamānām //4,3.32//
children.translated_text: [Commentary:] What are those [beings]? From that very bliss, those whose own nature is being differentiated through <s>avidyā</s>, imagined as other than <s>Brahman</s> — those other beings live upon [that fraction], made manifest through the contact of sense organs and objects. (4.3.32)

[Commentary on BṛUp 4.3.32:] But where, in deep sleep, that <s>avidyā</s> which presents other objects is stilled, then because of the absence of any object differentiated as other through <s>avidyā</s> — with what would one see whom, or smell, or know? Therefore, embraced entirely by the self which is pure consciousness (<s>prājña</s>), whose nature is self-luminosity, he becomes serene, one who has attained his desire, whose desire is the self alone — like a transparent mass of water, like water, he becomes one, a single seer, without a second, because of the absence of a second. For there is no second thing due to the absence of <s>avidyā</s>. This is the immortal, the fearless — this is <s>Brahmaloka</s>, the world that is <s>Brahman</s> itself. This very self, at this time, with the distinctions of effects and instruments as limiting adjuncts removed, with all relations stilled in the light of its own self —

children.text: START BrhUp 4,3.33
children.translated_text: [Start of BṛUp 4.3.33]

children.text:
sa yo manūṣyāṇāṃ rāddhaḥ samṛddho bhavaty anyeṣām adhipatiḥ sarvair mānuṣyakair bhogaiḥ sampannatamaḥ sa manuṣyāṇāṃ parama ānandaḥ |
atha ye śataṃ manuṣyāṇām ānandāḥ sa ekaḥ pitṝṇāṃ jitalokānām ānandaḥ |
atha ye śataṃ pitṝṇāṃ jitalokānām ānandāḥ sa eko gandharvaloka ānandaḥ |
atha ye śataṃ gandharvaloka ānandāḥ sa ekaḥ karmadevānām ānando ye karmaṇā devatvam abhisampadyante |
atha ye śataṃ karmadevānām ānandāḥ sa eka ājānadevānām ānandaḥ |
yaś ca śrotriyo 'vṛjino 'kāmahataḥ |
atha ye śatam ājānadevānām ānandāḥ sa ekaḥ prajāpatiloka ānandaḥ |
yaś ca śrotriyo 'vṛjino 'kāmahataḥ |
atha ye śataṃ prajāpatiloka ānandāḥ sa eko brahmaloka ānandaḥ |
yaś ca śrotriyo 'vṛjino 'kāmahataḥ |
athaiṣa eva parama ānandaḥ |
eṣa brahmalokaḥ samrāṭ |
iti hovāca yājñavalkyaḥ |
